title: feat(server): converge snapshot status via watch and read-time sync

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
# Summary
- Restructures the Kubernetes snapshot status flow to the template-catalog pattern (mirroring `FastSandboxTemplateService`): **submit intent → converge asynchronously**. The blocking terminal wait and its polling loop are fully removed.
- `KubernetesSnapshotRuntime.create_snapshot` now persists the `SandboxSnapshot` CR and returns a non-terminal status immediately. Existing-CR paths (create conflict, PG-HA observe) do a single non-blocking inspect so already-terminal CRs converge inline.
- New `start_status_watch` reactor: one LIST/WATCH informer per namespace with snapshot work; CR events invoke the service callback with the snapshot id (from the `opensandbox.io/snapshot-id` label). Namespaces are registered lazily at create time; the default namespace at startup.
- `PersistedSnapshotService.start_background_sync` wires the callback: watch events CAS-complete CREATING rows through the existing `_complete_snapshot`/`update_if_state` machinery.
- **Read-time sync**: `get_snapshot`/`list_snapshots` re-check CREATING rows against runtimes that expose a change stream. Inline runtimes (Docker) keep completing their own rows and are never observed here, so Docker behavior is unchanged.
- Convergence never depends on the watch alone: read-time sync, the PostgreSQL recovery loop, and CR deletion (missing CR maps to FAILED, which makes the row deletable) all remain correctness paths.
- Kept from the first iteration: `WorkloadInformer.add_event_handler` — informers started lazily by handler-less read paths previously dropped late-attached watch handlers silently.

# Behavior notes
- A snapshot whose CR stays non-terminal indefinitely now keeps the row in Creating (no server-side timeout). Escape hatch is unchanged today: deleting the CR converges the row to Failed. `snapshot_create_timeout_seconds` is now unused by the runtime (kept for config compatibility; deprecation is a follow-up).
- Public API unchanged: create still returns 202 + Creating; delete still rejects Creating rows with 409.

# Testing
- [ ] Not run (explain why)
- [x] Unit tests
- [ ] Integration tests
- [ ] e2e / manual verification

- `uv run pytest`: 1889 passed, 31 skipped (full server suite; PG-HA integration tests skip without a DSN, Path-B flow verified against the existing HA tests by construction)
- New tests: watch reactor callback/namespaces/label filtering, submit-without-wait create, existing-terminal-CR convergence, background-sync convergence + terminal-row guard, read-time sync on get/list, no-change-stream runtime skip, close() stopping informers
- `uv run ruff check` clean; pyright 1511 errors vs 1512 baseline (no new errors)

- [ ] Added/updated docs (if needed)
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Security impact considered

## Summary

Implement `pause_sandbox` / `resume_sandbox` on `FastSandboxService` (previously explicit 501s), wiring the fsb runtime backend to the fast-sandbox FastPath v2 `PauseSandbox` / `ResumeSandbox` RPCs.

## Behavior

- Public contract is unchanged: `POST /sandboxes/{id}/pause` and `/resume` keep returning **202 Accepted**; completion is asynchronous and observed by polling `GET /sandboxes/{id}` through `Pausing → Paused` and `Resuming → Running` (per sandbox-lifecycle spec).
- Identity fencing follows the existing delete path: the CR provides namespace + UID, sent as `expected_uid` so a recreated same-name sandbox is rejected.
- New typed `FastPathFailedPrecondition` error maps to **409 Conflict** (e.g. pause on a terminal runtime, resume of a durably paused sandbox with no checkpoint); `NotFound` stays 404.
- `status_mapping` now maps `Pausing`/`Paused`/`Resuming` **before** the failure checks — a paused sandbox intentionally reports an unavailable data plane, which previously would have read as `Failed`.

## Generated stubs

The checked-in FastPath v2 stubs were regenerated from the fast-sandbox `api/proto/v2/fastpath.proto` (adds the Pause/Resume RPCs, expected_\*-fence fields) with the repo-pinned grpcio-tools; the pyright suppression headers removed by regeneration were restored.

title: [Feature] Support execution identity for file APIs to enforce per-session filesystem permissions
body:
> Reposted from #1842 under my correct GitHub account. The earlier issue was submitted through an unintended connected account. Please use this issue for discussion; could a maintainer close #1842 as a duplicate?

## Why do you need it?

Consider a single agent serving multiple concurrent conversation sessions in one sandbox. Each session has a separate workspace and an unprivileged Linux user:

```text
/workspace/session-a/   # owned by session A's user
/workspace/session-b/   # owned by session B's user
```

With appropriately configured ownership and group permissions, the intended policy is:

- A session can read and write its own workspace.
- It can read other sessions' workspaces, but cannot modify, delete, or rename their files.
- Command execution and file API operations should follow the same Linux filesystem permissions.
- Sessions should be able to run concurrently.

Here, "session" means an application-level conversation; it does not assume use of the isolated-session API. The scope is sessions of a single agent sharing a sandbox, rather than sharing across different agents or providing full tenant isolation.

The command API accepts UID/GID, but the ordinary file APIs do not appear to provide an equivalent execution identity. File `owner/group` metadata describes ownership, which is different from the identity whose permissions are checked when an operation runs.

From source inspection at `07f0a68dd230`:

- [Command requests forward UID/GID to the runtime](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/07f0a68dd230d5498645df2fbd0d5174b3edb5c1/components/execd/pkg/web/controller/command.go#L189-L201).
- [Downloads open files directly in the Execd process](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/07f0a68dd230d5498645df2fbd0d5174b3edb5c1/components/execd/pkg/web/controller/filesystem_download.go#L71).
- [Uploads open/create/truncate files directly](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/07f0a68dd230d5498645df2fbd0d5174b3edb5c1/components/execd/pkg/web/controller/filesystem_upload.go#L177), then [apply ownership/mode metadata](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/07f0a68dd230d5498645df2fbd0d5174b3edb5c1/components/execd/pkg/web/controller/filesystem_upload.go#L220).

Consequently, when Execd runs with elevated permissions, configuring session users for commands alone does not make file API operations obey those users' permissions. These observations are based on source review, not an end-to-end reproduction report.

## How could it be?

Support an explicit execution identity for filesystem operations, either per request or through a session-bound filesystem client. UID/GID are possible inputs; the exact API and supplementary-group behavior should follow the project's identity model.

Desired semantics:

- Actual filesystem access, including parent-directory traversal and creation, is checked under the selected identity.
- The behavior covers reads, writes/uploads, search/stat, directory creation, deletion, rename, and permission changes.
- Execution identity remains separate from target-file `owner/group/mode`; metadata changes must not bypass the selected identity's permissions.
- Concurrent operations with different identities cannot affect each other's execution identity.
- If an explicitly requested identity cannot be honored, the operation fails clearly instead of silently using Execd's default identity. SDK/server compatibility should make unsupported behavior detectable.
- Existing callers that omit the option retain their current behavior.

For example, with B's directory and files configured as readable but not writable by A, both a command and a file API request running as A should be able to read B's file, and both should be denied an overwrite or deletion.

A trusted application backend would select the session identity and retain sandbox administration credentials. This request does not propose giving session workloads unrestricted access to choose root or another session's identity.

The implementation is open for discussion. A dedicated filesystem worker running with reduced credentials could be one option; exposing shell commands through the file API is not a requirement.

## Other related information

Alternatives considered:

- **One sandbox per session:** provides a separate boundary but prevents the intended sandbox reuse.
- **Perform file operations through commands under the session UID/GID:** possible as an application workaround, but requires custom handling for structured errors, binary transfers, and streaming.
- **Isolated sessions:** may be a better fit if their filesystem proxy can provide the desired permission semantics. Guidance on using or extending that path would be helpful.

Related: #1064 concerns ownership of automatically created parent directories. This request concerns the identity performing the operation, rather than the ownership assigned afterward.

Questions for maintainers:

1. Is consistent execution identity across command and file APIs a supported direction?
2. Should this live in the ordinary filesystem API, the isolated-session API, or another existing abstraction?
3. Is there related work already planned, and would a new OSEP or an extension to an existing OSEP be the preferred next step?

This issue is intended to establish the use case and agree on direction before implementation.

title: feat(egress): build decision snapshots for OSEP-0023

labels.name: size/L

body:
# Summary

Continue OSEP-0023 after #1775, #1777, #1791, #1800, #1812, and #1834 by defining the canonical Go decision payload constructed before the coordinator allocates a revision identity.

- Serialize a versioned payload containing `vaultRevision`, `effectivePolicyEpoch`, fixed `credential-bound` mode, derived state, TLS host selectors, complete rendered bindings, and redactions.
- Keep `controlPlaneGeneration`, `subjectGeneration`, coordinator-allocated `decisionEpoch`, and the digest of these exact payload bytes in the outer revision envelope, avoiding a circular self-digest or preallocation contract.
- Derive TLS selectors only from HTTPS-eligible rendered bindings; callers cannot provide or mutate a separate selector list.
- Sort bindings/selectors deterministically while preserving the rendered substitution and redaction ordering used by request processing.
- Emit authoritative empty arrays rather than `null`, derive `active` versus `active-empty`, and reject invalid revisions, non-canonical selectors/match fields, duplicate binding identities, reserved headers, missing credential redactions, and non-canonical redaction order with one sanitized error.
- Preserve legacy 252/253-byte wildcard suffixes in the full binding data but omit them from TLS selectors because their wildcard language has no valid DNS member.

The builder accepts the existing rendered `ActiveSnapshot` but is not called by the live Vault mutation path. The matching Python payload parser, process token/socket handoff, coordinator construction, recovery, connection fences, and TLS decisions remain subsequent work. Existing ETag lookup and interception behavior are unchanged. The OSEP now records the envelope/payload serialization boundary.

Related: #1713. This is a canonical payload prerequisite, not live revision installation or the public interception mode.

# Testing

- [x] Unit tests

- Independent review found that empty substitution values are intentionally omitted from Store redactions; that path was reproduced with a custom source and fixed before commit. All non-empty encoded variants and the placeholder remain required.

title: SDK: Add commands.setEnv syntactic sugar for runtime environment variable injection
body:
### Problem
Updating environment variables at runtime currently requires a raw shell command manipulating the internal $EXECD_ENVS file:
await sandbox.commands.run("""printf '%s=%s\n' 'MY_TOKEN' 'value' >> "$EXECD_ENVS" """)
Issues:
1. Shell escaping risk — values with single quotes, backslashes, or special chars break the printf format string
2. Implementation detail leak — users must know $EXECD_ENVS (internal execd concept)
3. Inconsistent across languages — the shell snippet differs subtly between Python/Java/TS
4. No validation — keys/values are raw strings in a shell command

### Proposal
Add a setEnv method under the commands namespace:

```Python
await sandbox.commands.set_env("MY_TOKEN", "value")
```

```Java
sandbox.commands().setEnv("MY_TOKEN", "value");
```

```TypeScript
await sandbox.commands.setEnv("MY_TOKEN", "value");
```

Internally the SDK would:
• Resolve $EXECD_ENVS path
• Properly escape key/value (handle quotes, backslashes, newlines, = in values)
• Append KEY=VALUE\n to the file via commands.run

title: fix(js): reject negative command log cursors

labels.name: size/XS
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 0-9   lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

- reject negative background-command log cursors in the JavaScript SDK before transport
- add a regression test that proves invalid cursors never reach the generated client

## Root cause

The execd OpenAPI contract defines `cursor` with `minimum: 0`, and `SeekBackgroundCommandOutput` rejects negative offsets. The handwritten JavaScript command adapter still serialized negative values, unlike its isolated-session adapter, turning a deterministic client argument error into an avoidable server request and HTTP error.

This is the JavaScript follow-up to the merged Go fix in #1835 and follows the per-language incremental scope requested by #1768. No generated code or public signature changes are involved.

## Validation

```text
cd sdks/sandbox/javascript
pnpm run lint
pnpm run typecheck
pnpm run test
# 161 tests passed, 0 failed
```

The regression client throws if `GET` is called, so the test proves validation occurs before transport.

## Risk

Low. Undefined, zero, and positive cursors are unchanged. Only negative values—which the server already rejects—now fail locally with the same message used by the JavaScript isolated-session adapter.

Refs #1768
Follow-up to #1835

title: fix(go): reject negative command log cursors

labels.name: size/S
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 10-29 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

- reject negative background-command log cursors in the Go SDK before transport
- correct the Go API comment: `nil` or `0`, not `-1`, requests the full log
- add a regression test that proves invalid cursors cause no network request

## Root cause

`specs/execd-api.yaml` defines the command-log cursor as an `int64` with `minimum: 0`, and execd rejects negative offsets in `SeekBackgroundCommandOutput`. The Go SDK nevertheless documented `cursor=-1` as a full-log request and forwarded it to the server. This also drifted from the Go isolated-session log path, which already returns `InvalidArgumentError` locally for a negative cursor.

The validation lives in the handwritten `ExecdClient` adapter; no generated code or public signature changes are involved.

## Validation

```text
cd sdks/sandbox/go
go test ./...
ok  github.com/alibaba/OpenSandbox/sdks/sandbox/go  13.772s
```

The focused regression uses `http://unused.invalid`, so it fails if the client attempts transport instead of returning `InvalidArgumentError` locally.

## Risk

Low. Valid `nil`, zero, and positive cursors are unchanged. The only behavior change is replacing a guaranteed server-side 400 for negative cursors with the SDK's existing typed argument error.

Refs #1768

title: feat(egress): add revision receiver endpoint for OSEP-0023

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
# Summary

Continue OSEP-0023 after #1775, #1777, #1791, #1800, and #1812 with the Python half of the local revision IPC. This PR implements the receiver endpoint against the reviewed Go transport contract without enabling it in the live addon.

- Serve prepare, commit, abort, and metadata-only active readback over HTTP/1.1 on a Unix socket.
- Authenticate the per-process bearer token before reading request bodies, then strictly decode the camelCase identity and canonical base64 payload envelope from #1812.
- Reject duplicate/unknown fields, invalid revision types/digests, non-canonical base64, transfer encoding, oversized bodies/payloads, foreign generations, and invalid transitions.
- Return only fixed JSON errors and metadata acknowledgements; payloads, validator failures, tokens, and transition details are never echoed or logged.
- Require an owned non-writable parent directory, refuse existing paths, set the socket to 0600, bound request read time, and remove only the socket inode created by this server.
- Stop accepting work before closing the receiver; receiver generation/state fencing handles late in-flight validation.

The live `system.py` does not import this module. title: bug(docker): sandbox commit/snapshot can silently omit recently-created files, independent of concurrency
body:
## What happened

Forking a child from a live Docker-backed sandbox can come back missing files that exist on the
parent's live filesystem at fork time — in our repro, a globally `npm install -g`'d CLI binary.
The snapshot/commit and the resulting fork both report success; nothing surfaces the missing
files anywhere.

## Repro (no OpenSandbox code involved — bare `docker commit`)

```
docker exec <container> npm install -g <pkg>
docker exec <container> which <pkg-bin>        # present, works

docker commit <container> test-image
docker run --rm test-image which <pkg-bin>     # ABSENT
```

This reproduces on a **single, solo commit** — no concurrent commit anywhere near it, no retries,
nothing racing. We confirmed via `Alineo.spawn()`/`fork()`, which calls
`POST /v1/sandboxes/{id}/snapshots` and restores from it, and independently via a bare `docker
commit` of the same container outside any OpenSandbox code path — same result both times.

Ruled out:
- **Hardlinks** — every file under the missing package's tree has a link count of 1.
- **A separate mount/volume** — `docker inspect --format '{{json .Mounts}}'` is `[]`,
  `.Config.Volumes` is `null`, and the missing directory's device number matches every other
  directory under the same parent path (including a sibling package directory that *does*
  survive the commit).
- **Concurrency** — reproduces on a solo commit with nothing else in flight. (We originally
  suspected two simultaneous `fork()` calls against one sandbox as the trigger — see "Related" —
  but the same corruption occurs with only ever one commit in flight, so that wasn't it.)

## Environment

Docker runtime, `overlayfs` storage driver, kernel `6.19.14-108.fc42.x86_64` (Fedora 42),
`execd_image` `v1.0.19`/`v1.0.22`, `runsc` (gVisor) as the sandbox's own container runtime.

## Impact

Any workflow that installs something into a sandbox and then forks it (e.g. `alineo`'s RLM
fan-out, where a parent installs a CLI/dependency once and forks multiple children from it) can
silently produce children missing that install, with no error at any layer — the fork, the
snapshot, and the restore all report success.

## Related

Also worth closing regardless of the above: the Docker runtime's `createSnapshot()` has no
concurrency guard — two simultaneous `POST .../snapshots` against the *same* sandbox are both
accepted, unlike the Kubernetes runtime, which explicitly rejects a second in-flight snapshot per
sandbox with `409`. Not the cause of the corruption described above (confirmed reproducible on a
solo commit), but a separate, real gap in its own right — worth the same protection either way.

labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 30-99 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
# Summary

Fixes #1749

Follow-up to #1751, closing the remaining gap flagged in the [root-cause analysis comment](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/issues/1749) on #1749: `Sandbox.create()` still resolved the execd and egress endpoints with one-shot requests right after the create call, outside the `ready_timeout` budget. A transient `404 / KUBERNETES::POD_IP_NOT_AVAILABLE` while the Kubernetes pod IP was still being published therefore failed the whole `create()` immediately, even though the caller had passed a generous readiness timeout — exactly the race #1751 fixed for `connect()`/`resume()`.

This PR applies the same `ReadinessBudget` pattern to the Python SDK's `create()` (async and sync):

- Create one `ReadinessBudget` before endpoint resolution, so endpoint publication and health checks share the single `ready_timeout` deadline.
- Retry endpoint lookups only on `404 / KUBERNETES::POD_IP_NOT_AVAILABLE`, using the existing polling interval; everything else (missing sandbox, 401/403, other errors) still fails fast.
- Hand only the remaining budget to the health probe, so endpoint wait plus health wait cannot exceed `ready_timeout`.
- Keep awaiting endpoint publication when `skip_health_check` is set (same as connect/resume after #1751).
- Async `create()` keeps its existing parallel (gathered) endpoint resolution — now each branch goes through the budget; sync `create()` stays sequential.
- Failure semantics of `create()` are unchanged: on timeout or permanent endpoint error the created zombie sandbox is still terminated and the transport closed.

Docs: `docs/sdks/python.md` `ready_timeout` wording updated to "Total budget for endpoint publication and health checks".

title: fix(controller): stop attributing failures of deleting pods (PauseResume e2e on K8s >= 1.27)

labels.name: size/M
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 30-99 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
Fixes #1824

## Root cause

On Kubernetes >= 1.27 (kubernetes/kubernetes#115331, KEP-3329), when a pod's grace period expires during deletion, kubelet writes `phase: Failed` on the still-Terminating pod (SIGKILL, exit 137).

During pause -> resume, the controller deletes the old frozen pod (whose process cannot handle SIGTERM while frozen, so it always hits the full 30s grace) and then recreates a same-name replacement. The controller's failure attribution has no deletionTimestamp filter, so the dying OLD pod's exit-137 status is misattributed as a resume failure: the BatchSandbox goes terminal `Failed` and the replacement pod is never created. On v1.22.4 kubelet does not publish that terminal status on deleting pods, which is why CI passes there and consistently fails on v1.28.6 / v1.34.2.

## Fix

Skip failure attribution for pods that carry a `deletionTimestamp` (both failure detectors, including waiting states). Semantics:

- pods being deleted no longer contribute NEW failure conditions;
- failures already recorded on the sandbox remain terminal (no undo);
- failures of replacement pods are still reported normally.

## Tests

- **Table-driven unit tests**: terminal/waiting failure detection across Pending/Resuming/Succeed phases, active vs deleting pods.
- **Controller-level envtest regression** (deterministic, drives the real `Reconcile`): both observation orders — (1) deletion mark precedes first observation (the issue's sequence) → no `ResumeFailed`, replacement pod created with a different UID once the old object is gone → `Succeed`; (2) real failure observed before deletion → `Failed` written and preserved. **Differential property verified**: removing the guard turns case 1 red with the exact issue signature (`expected "Resuming", actual "Failed"`); restoring it is green.
- **e2e pause/resume now runs two scenarios**: resume after the old pod is fully gone, and resume immediately while the old pod is still Terminating. The latter asserts — after the resume patch returns — that the old pod still has its old UID and a non-empty `deletionTimestamp` (proving the race window was genuinely hit), then expects `Succeed`. Also fixes a stale `batchsandbox-name=` label selector (real label: `batch-sandbox.sandbox.opensandbox.io/name`) and asserts the replacement pod's UID differs.

## Verification

Locally on kind (arm64, all 7 PauseResume-labelled specs each):

| K8s | role | result |
|---|---|---|
| v1.28.6 | failing CI version in #1824 | 7 Passed / 0 Failed |
| v1.30.4 | same kubelet behavior family (>= 1.27) | 7 Passed / 0 Failed |
| v1.22.4 | passing CI version (pre-1.27) | 7 Passed / 0 Failed |

The immediate-resume scenario hit the race window (old UID + deletionTimestamp confirmed post-patch) on all three. v1.34.2 is covered by the CI matrix.

## Drive-by fix (required for CI)

`fieldindex.RegisterFieldIndexes` used a package-level `sync.Once`, so with a second envtest-backed manager in the same test binary the ginkgo suite's cache silently got no informer indexes and 23/36 specs timed out under the unfiltered `make test` run. Registration is now deduplicated per cache instance (separate commit; no behavior change for single-manager production processes).

## Follow-ups (out of scope for this PR)

- With this fix, resume is correct but not instant: the frozen old pod still waits out its full termination grace (~30s — SIGTERM cannot be handled while frozen) before the same-name replacement can be created. Shortening the grace for pods deleted at pause completion was considered as a follow-up; it needs its own impact review (preStop/lifecycle hooks, node failures, multi-container pods) and is intentionally not bundled here.
- What the `Paused` phase should promise (e.g., how quickly resume must return) is a contract question — happy to open a separate discussion if useful.

title: fix(egress): drain webhooks during bounded Docker deletion

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
# Summary

Docker deletion currently force-removes the egress sidecar, dropping queued webhook notifications. It also cleans up dependent resources after application deletion fails, while a retry after the application is already gone can leave its sidecar behind.

This change makes cleanup follow application removal and gives egress a bounded opportunity to finish accepted deliveries:

- On SIGTERM, stop accepting webhook events and drain queued/in-flight deliveries for up to **5 seconds** before tearing down DNS and network rules. Cancel outstanding requests and retry backoff when the drain expires.
- After application removal succeeds, stop the sidecar with a **9-second Docker grace**, then remove it and attempt managed runtime-volume cleanup. Keep the image supervisor's existing **20-second grace** unchanged; Docker enforces its own shorter limit.
- Preserve dependent resources and metadata when application deletion fails. Retry failed TTL removal after **30 seconds** without changing the sandbox expiration, re-reading ownership on retry to avoid releasing mount references twice after a concurrent DELETE.
- Attempt orphan sidecar cleanup when the application is already absent, while preserving DELETE's **404** response.

Deletion remains synchronous. These durations are upper bounds, not fixed waits; Docker API calls and other cleanup can extend the full HTTP request. Webhook delivery and sidecar cleanup remain best effort, so neither delivery completion nor complete resource removal is guaranteed after a cleanup failure.

# Testing

- [x] Unit tests
- [x] Integration tests
  - Covers queued delivery, application kill/remove failures, TTL retry, missing applications, slow/failing receivers, frozen worker/supervisor, stop transport failure, and concurrent repeated deletion. Tests inspect actual containers and volumes after cleanup.
- [x] e2e / manual verification
  - Real Docker experiments compared 500ms, 3s, and 5s drain budgets: for 20 events at 200ms per response, they completed 2, 15, and 20 deliveries respectively. This supports 5s as a modest-backlog allowance, not a delivery guarantee.

Real Kubernetes integration was not run. The worker's drain behavior also applies there

# Breaking Changes

- [x] None
- [ ] Yes (describe impact and migration path)

Public API, SDK and configuration shapes are unchanged. Docker DELETE can now wait for the sidecar stop grace; notifications remain best effort. Deploy the updated egress image to enable draining. The server's 9-second stop limit also applies when using an older image.

title: fix(sdk): reject negative readiness polling interval in Python and JavaScript

labels.name: size/M
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 30-99 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
# Summary

I noticed that the Kotlin SDK now rejects a non-positive ready polling interval (f4944838) because a no-op sleep turns the health check into a spin, and went looking at the Python SDK. `ReadinessBudget` hands `health_check_polling_interval` straight to the sleep call, with no check.

With a negative interval the two Python flavours fail differently:

- async: `asyncio.sleep()` returns immediately for a negative delay, so `create` / `connect` / `resume` / `check_ready` poll `/ping` in a tight loop until the deadline. Against a mock transport answering 503, a one-second `Sandbox.connect` sent 5 pings with the default 200 ms interval and about 3,500 with `timedelta(milliseconds=-1)`.
- sync: `time.sleep()` raises `ValueError`, which comes out as `SandboxInternalException: Failed to resume sandbox: sleep length must be non-negative`. For `SandboxSync.create` that happens after the sandbox has been provisioned, so it gets killed again because of a client-side argument.

This change raises `InvalidArgumentException` for a negative interval in `ReadinessBudget`, and checks it before any request in `create` (only when the health check is not skipped, since the interval is unused otherwise) and in `resume` (which calls the resume API before building the budget). `connect` and `check_ready` are covered by the budget itself, before any request.

After review I applied the same check to the JavaScript SDK, which passed `healthCheckPollingInterval` straight to `setTimeout`. Node clamps a negative delay to about 1 ms, so a one-second `Sandbox.connect` against a health check returning false made 67 attempts with `-1`. `create` (when the health check is not skipped), `connect`, `resume` and `waitUntilReady` now throw `InvalidArgumentException` before any request. The JS pool options already rejected negative values.

I deliberately left a zero interval allowed: the existing tests call `check_ready(..., polling_interval=timedelta(seconds=0))`, so I only reject values that never worked in sync mode.

# Testing
- [ ] Not run (explain why)
- [x] Unit tests
- [ ] Integration tests
- [ ] e2e / manual verification

New `tests/test_readiness_polling_interval.py` (16 cases, async and sync, create/connect/resume, asserting no HTTP request is sent). All 14 rejection cases fail on main and pass with the change; the full Python SDK suite passes (625 tests), and `ruff check` and `pyright` on the touched files are clean.

New `tests/sandbox.polling-interval.test.mjs` (create/connect/resume rejections plus a skipped health check case). The three rejection cases fail on main (health check timeout after 67 attempts) and pass with the change. I couldn't run `pnpm install` on my machine, so I ran the JS tests from the TypeScript sources with Node's type stripping and a stub for `openapi-fetch`: the new file plus the create, connect/resume, endpoint-readiness and pool suites give 71 passing tests. ESLint was not run locally.

# Breaking Changes
- [x] None
- [ ] Yes (describe impact and migration path)

A negative interval already crashed the sync SDK; in async it only produced a busy loop. Zero and positive intervals behave as before.

- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)

title: [Flaky CI] Controller E2E PauseResume consistently fails on Kubernetes v1.28.6 and v1.34.2
body:
## Problem

The `Controller E2E PauseResume` job in `.github/workflows/kubernetes-test.yml` has a very high failure rate on newer Kubernetes versions.

The job runs:

```bash
make test-e2e-pause-resume KIND_K8S_VERSION=v${{ matrix.version }}
```

against the matrix `["1.22.4", "1.28.6", "1.34.2"]`.

- **v1.22.4** consistently passes.
- **v1.28.6** and **v1.34.2** consistently fail at the same point in `kubernetes/test/e2e/pause_resume_test.go` (around line 285), while waiting for the resumed `BatchSandbox` to return to `phase: Succeed`.

## Observed Failure Pattern

From the controller logs of failing runs:

1. The internal `SandboxSnapshot` (`<sandbox-name>-pause`) reaches `phase: Succeed`.
2. The image-committer Job completes successfully.
3. The `BatchSandbox` template container image is rewritten to an immutable digest reference, e.g.:
   - v1.28.6: `docker-registry.default.svc.cluster.local:5000/test-pause-resume-sandbox-container@sha256:cb1ba94cb67f9b9372e095986c61323aca4cd7fad8ee1b989dc86611598003cb`
   - v1.34.2: `docker-registry.default.svc.cluster.local:5000/test-pause-resume-sandbox-container@sha256:da720fced9bf6db7b936062a96d99660e92a502a4e11290b04fed43881117be4`
4. The resumed pod is created, but the `BatchSandbox` eventually transitions to `phase: Failed` with conditions `ResumeFailed` / `PodFailed`.
5. The reported reason is `ContainerFailed` with message `1/1 observed pods failed; primary reason=ContainerFailed; sample pod=test-pause-resume-0`.

## Code Involved

- `kubernetes/test/e2e/pause_resume_test.go` – the e2e test and its `dumpPauseResumeDiagnostics` helper.
- `kubernetes/internal/controller/batchsandbox_pause_resume.go` – pause/resume state machine (`dispatchPauseResume`, `continueResume`, `completePause`).
- `kubernetes/internal/controller/batchsandbox_status.go` – terminal pod failure detection (`getTerminalPodFailureReasonAndMessage`, `terminatedContainerFailure`).

## Diagnostic Gap

The current `dumpPauseResumeDiagnostics` function does **not** capture:

- The failed resumed pod’s YAML (`kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml`).
- The resumed container logs (`kubectl logs <pod> -c sandbox-container`).
- The image-committer Job pod logs (`kubectl logs <commit-pod> -c commit`).

Because the failed pod is deleted during cleanup, the exact container exit reason / message is lost. This makes it impossible to tell whether the failure is in:

- image production (commit),
- image consumption (resume), or
- a Kubernetes / containerd version-specific behavior difference.

## Proposed Next Step

Enhance the e2e diagnostics to dump the failed resumed pod and commit-job pod details before deletion, then re-run the failing versions to obtain the container exit reason.

I’m opening this issue to track the root-cause investigation and a real fix rather than reducing the CI matrix.

## Reproduction

```bash
cd kubernetes
make test-e2e-pause-resume KIND_K8S_VERSION=v1.28.6
# or
make test-e2e-pause-resume KIND_K8S_VERSION=v1.34.2
```

title: fix(ingress): migrate WebSocket proxy off archived gorilla/websocket

labels.name: size/XL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 500-999 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

Replaces the archived `github.com/gorilla/websocket` with the actively maintained `github.com/coder/websocket` v1.8.15, hardens `isWebSocketRequest` to accept `Connection` header token lists (the strict equality check was silently routing some legitimate WebSocket requests to the plain HTTP proxy path), and documents the L7 frontend configuration required for WebSocket traffic to work end-to-end.

The rewrite preserves the required gorilla-era proxy semantics that become non-defaults with `coder/websocket`, while replacing the previous unbounded message allocation with a configurable 64 MiB default limit. Each behavior is covered by a focused regression test.

Refs: #1105, [coder/websocket#4](https://github.com/coder/websocket/issues/4)

## What changes

### Library migration

- `github.com/gorilla/websocket` (archived Q4 2022) → `github.com/coder/websocket v1.8.15`.
- `components/ingress/pkg/proxy/websocket.go` rewritten against the new API. The request lifecycle is unchanged: dial the backend, upgrade the client, relay frames in both directions until either side closes.

### Bug fix independent of #1105: `Connection` header token matching

Some L7 proxies (Envoy, older HAProxy) merge the client's `Connection: Upgrade` with their own `keep-alive` hop, producing `Connection: keep-alive, Upgrade` — an RFC 7230 §6.1 legal shape. The previous strict equality check (`r.Header.Get("Connection") != "Upgrade"`) missed these and routed the request through the plain HTTP proxy, producing WebSocket `close 1006` symptoms independent of #1105's HTTP/2 topology issue. `isWebSocketRequest` now performs case-insensitive token matching via `connectionHasToken`.

### Explicit migration behavior

The migration wires the following behavior explicitly and covers it with regression tests:

- **45s backend handshake timeout** via `context.WithTimeout`.
- **Bounded 64 MiB message size** in both directions, so terminals and Jupyter kernels can exceed the `coder/websocket` 32 KiB default without retaining the previous unbounded allocation risk.
- **Client subprotocol offer** forwarded to the backend `Dial` and the backend's selection echoed back to the client on `Accept`.
- **Set-Cookie headers** from the backend handshake response forwarded to the client so sticky-session logins are not silently broken.
- **Application close codes** (1008, 4001+, ...) propagated verbatim instead of being masked as 1000.
- **Backend handshake 4xx/5xx** responses relayed to the caller so operators can distinguish auth failures from ingress outages.
- **Backend redirects (3xx)** never followed at the ingress layer. `coder/websocket.Dial` delegates to `net/http`'s default `Client`, which follows redirects transparently; gorilla's `Dialer` never did. Following at the ingress would route WebSocket handshake traffic to a target the sandbox route did not resolve and could leak `Authorization` headers to an unrelated endpoint. See `clientWithoutRedirects`.
- **Connectivity observer** keeps its `"websocket"` protocol label so existing dashboards and alerts do not break.

### RFC 8441 HTTP/2 Extended CONNECT is intentionally not accepted

`coder/websocket v1.8.15` rejects any non-`GET` `Accept` (`accept.go:184-201`). HTTP/2 support is tracked upstream in [coder/websocket#4](https://github.com/coder/websocket/issues/4).

`isWebSocketRequest` filters non-`GET` methods before the WebSocket path, and `TestIsWebSocketRequestRejectsH2ExtendedConnect` locks that contract in so a future refactor cannot silently invert it.

The documentation calls this out explicitly and distinguishes the verified HTTP/1.1 fallback from L7-specific HTTP/2 strategies that still require deployment-level validation.

### Documentation

`docs/components/ingress.md` grows an **L7 Frontend Configuration for WebSocket** section that documents the actual protocol boundary:

- The ingress-facing WebSocket handshake must be RFC 6455 over HTTP/1.1.
- Forcing `tls-alpn: http/1.1` in HAProxy is the verified, portable fallback.
- Per-WebSocket HTTP/1.1 fallback and RFC 8441-to-RFC 6455 translation are L7- and version-specific; the documentation no longer claims a verified nginx-ingress or HAProxy translation configuration.
- Forwarding HTTP/2 Extended CONNECT to the ingress is not supported.

The section includes a bounded `curl --http1.1` diagnostic, explains that it validates the complete forced-H1 route rather than isolating a particular hop, and warns that ALPN `h2` alone does not prove WebSocket translation works.

## Non-goals

- **HTTP/2 Extended CONNECT at the ingress**. Requires either upstream support in `coder/websocket` (see coder/websocket#4) or replacing the WebSocket library. Filed as a follow-up rather than blocking the archived-library replacement.
- **Helm chart / Dockerfile / main.go changes**. Deliberately zero, so this PR has no deployment-side coupling and can be rolled back purely with a code revert.

## Test plan

Automated (all green, including `-race`):

- [x] `go build ./...`
- [x] `go vet ./...`
- [x] `gofmt -l ./...` clean
- [x] `go test ./... -race -count=1` — package coverage 86.4%
- [x] Regression tests added:
  - `Test_WebSocketProxy_Subprotocol`
  - `Test_WebSocketProxy_SetCookieForwarded`
  - `Test_WebSocketProxy_CloseCodePreserved`
  - `Test_WebSocketProxy_ClientCloseCodePreserved`
  - `Test_WebSocketProxy_AbruptClientDisconnectUnblocksBackend`
  - `Test_WebSocketProxy_LargeMessage` (128 KiB frame)
  - `Test_WebSocketProxy_MessageSizeLimit`
  - `Test_WebSocketProxy_BackendMessageSizeLimit`
  - `Test_WebSocketProxy_BackendHandshakeRedirectNotFollowed`
  - `Test_WebSocketProxy_BackendHandshake4xxPassthrough`
  - `TestIsWebSocketRequestRejectsH2ExtendedConnect`
  - `TestObservedWebSocketHTTPClientRecordsTCPConnect`
  - `TestIsWebSocketRequest` extended with token-list and case-sensitivity cases

Manual (Docker end-to-end):

- [x] `curl` HTTP/1.1 WebSocket upgrade → ingress proxy → real `codercom/code-server:latest` backend → `HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols`
- [x] `curl` through HAProxy 3.2 (`alpn http/1.1` fallback) → ingress → code-server → tunnel established, HAProxy log shows a full 3s tunnel duration
- [x] Full-chain Go WebSocket client: `DIAL OK` + `WRITE OK` + connection kept open through the deadline
- [x] Echo backend, 5 write/read cycles over 5 seconds — no idle timeout
- [x] Echo backend, 128 KiB binary frame — byte-for-byte preserved end-to-end
- [x] Echo backend, forced `StatusMessageTooBig` (1009) close from the backend — code and reason propagate cleanly through the ingress to the client

Not verified in this PR (deferred to deployment / staging):

- [ ] Real browser (Chrome/Firefox) + `opensandbox/vscode:latest` in a real Kubernetes cluster fronted by `haproxytech/kubernetes-ingress` 1.47.4
- [ ] Helm `upgrade` rolling replacement of the ingress-gateway Deployment with a long-lived WebSocket session in flight
- [ ] Jupyter kernel channels and noVNC websockify end-to-end

## Rollback

The change is code-only in `components/ingress/pkg/proxy/` plus one docs file. Revert this commit and rebuild the ingress image; no deployment migration is needed.

# Summary

`osb file download` currently opens the local destination with `wb` before requesting the remote file. A 404 therefore truncates an existing local file, and a dropped connection or Ctrl+C replaces its contents with a partial download.

title: fix(server): heal renew-intent drop after restart via cluster-wide sandbox lookup

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
# Summary
- Closes #1818

In multi-tenant mode (`[tenants] provider = "http"`), `HTTPTenantProvider` keeps tenant information only in memory and cannot enumerate tenants. After a server restart that information is empty, so background renew workers can no longer resolve a sandbox id to its tenant namespace. The lookup falls back to the configured `kubernetes.namespace`, `get_sandbox` raises 404, and `AccessRenewController` swallows the `HTTPException`: the renew intent is consumed from the queue with no log line, and in-use sandboxes are deleted at their original expiry. Full timeline and root-cause walkthrough in #1818.

The fix is three commits: the original bounded fallback, plus two follow-ups from review feedback.

1. `fix(server): heal renew-intent drop after restart via cluster-wide sandbox lookup`
   Cluster-wide label-selector LIST to locate the sandbox's namespace, a 600 s circuit breaker on 403 (one WARNING per window naming the missing RBAC instead of one live LIST per intent), and structured WARNING logs (`renew_skip_reason`) instead of silent swallowing.
2. `fix(server): harden cluster-wide namespace lookup in renew pipeline`
   - Single-tenant deployments (no tenant provider) never resolve beyond the configured namespace; previously a foreign id could reach another server's sandbox, and single-tenant proxy routes are authentication-exempt.
   - The per-attempt memo is reset at the start of every attempt, so a long-lived consumer cannot carry the previous attempt's resolution across attempts (deletion/recreation, namespace migration).
   - A cluster-wide lookup matching more than one namespace is rejected with a WARNING; 0 or >1 matches are both "unresolved", no arbitrary pick.
3. `feat(server): resolve renew intents via ingress-observed namespace`
   The renew-intent payload already carries the sandbox's namespace on routes where ingress knows it (today that is fast-sandbox signed routing). The consumer parses the field and the lookup tries it before the tenant scan, trusting it only after verifying a workload exists there. Messages without the field (agent-sandbox routes, older ingress) fall through to the existing chain.

# Design notes

Why a cluster-wide LIST instead of persisted state: the sandbox CR already lives in the tenant namespace with identity labels, so the API server already knows which namespace a sandbox is in. The alternatives add state and invalidation problems. Persisting sandbox→namespace mappings goes stale on deletion and couples the write path. Enumerating tenants is not possible: `HTTPTenantProvider.supports_enumeration` is `False` by design, and the tenant endpoint answers per-key lookups only. The LIST is stateless and self-healing.

Resolution order per attempt, first match wins: the configured `kubernetes.namespace` (as before), then the ingress-observed namespace from the intent payload when present (verified by a workload GET before it is trusted, skipped when it equals the configured namespace), then the tenant provider's cached information, then the cluster-wide LIST. Single-tenant deployments stop at the configured namespace; the LIST only runs in multi-tenant mode with an unknown namespace.

Which deployments get which path: the payload namespace is non-empty only where ingress itself knows the namespace at routing time (today that is fast-sandbox signed routing). Agent-sandbox routes (URI/header modes) encode only sandbox id and port, so their intents carry no namespace, with both the current and older ingress. For those deployments the recovery path after a restart is the cluster-wide LIST; the payload fast path is a no-op for them.

One cluster LIST per attempt, not a cache. `get_sandbox` may probe several candidate resource names, so the resolution result is memoized per attempt and checked against the sandbox id. The memo is reset at the start of every attempt in `_try_renew_sync`, so it cannot outlive the attempt it was computed for: sandbox→namespace mappings go stale on deletion, and the next attempt re-resolves from scratch.

# Testing
- [ ] Not run (explain why)
- [x] Unit tests
- [ ] Integration tests
- [x] e2e / manual verification

Unit: `server/tests/k8s/test_renew_intent_restart.py` (12 tests) plus payload parsing cases in `server/tests/test_renew_intent.py`: post-restart empty-provider window, 403 backoff window (fake clock), transient API errors, single-LIST-per-attempt memoization, two-attempt re-resolution after the sandbox moves, duplicate-match rejection, and the payload-namespace fast path (hit, stale-fallthrough, absent field).

e2e (live cluster; agent-sandbox provider, multi-tenant http tenant provider, Redis renew intents, a real ingress publishing intents):
- pre-fix `main`: intent consumed, no log line, `.spec.shutdownTime` unchanged. The silent drop from #1818 reproduced.
- with this PR, after a server restart: `renew_succeeded`, `.spec.shutdownTime` advanced to exactly intent time + extension, CR value matching the log byte-for-byte.
- restricted RBAC (no cluster list): exactly one denied LIST and one backoff WARNING; subsequent intents suppressed by the breaker with expiry unchanged (verified by request counts on a stub API server and on the cluster).
- single-tenant server, foreign-namespace id: the hardened code skips without issuing any LIST; the pre-hardening commit renewed it. That is the cross-tenant exposure from review, reproduced and then closed.
- intents with a namespace field (fast-sandbox payload shape, hand-published): resolved via the payload with zero cluster LISTs.

# Breaking Changes

- [ ] Yes (describe impact and migration path)

# Checklist

- [x] Added/updated docs (if needed)
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Security impact considered
- [x] Backward compatibility considered

title: Multi-tenant: renew intents are silently dropped after a server restart; in-use sandboxes are deleted at expiry
body:
## Summary

With the agent-sandbox provider in multi-tenant mode (control plane and data plane deployed separately), a server restart silently disables access renewal: every renew intent published after the restart is consumed from the Redis queue but processed as a no-op, so in-use sandboxes are deleted when their original `shutdownTime` arrives. There is no log line at any point in the drop path.

## Environment

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Version | current `main` (reproduced at `09e3584c`) |
| Runtime | Kubernetes, `workload_provider = agent-sandbox` |
| Mode | multi-tenant (`[tenants] provider = "http"`) |
| Renewal | `[renew_intent]` enabled, Redis source |
| Sandboxes | tenant namespaces, separate from the server's configured `kubernetes.namespace` |

## Observed timeline (controlled reproduction, identifiers redacted)

| Time | Event | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 11:37:58 | Sandbox created via API (tenant key), Running | CR `.spec.shutdownTime = 11:47:57` (= create + 600 s) |
| 11:38:12 | Server process restarted | graceful shutdown log |
| 11:39:18 | Renew intent published to queue | Redis `LPUSH`, queue length 1 |
| 11:39:19 | Intent consumed | queue length 0 — **and no log line is emitted** |
| 11:39:19 | CR `.spec.shutdownTime` | unchanged (`11:47:57`) |
| 11:47:57 | Sandbox deleted at the original expiry while the session is still active | shutdown policy `Delete` |

## Root cause

1. `HTTPTenantProvider` keeps its tenant information purely in memory (`server/opensandbox_server/tenants/http_provider.py`) and only learns tenants from per-key lookups made by control-plane API calls. A restart empties it, and `supports_enumeration` is `False`.
2. Background renew workers have no tenant `ContextVar`, so `KubernetesSandboxService._resolve_namespace_for_lookup` (`kubernetes_service.py`) falls into `_find_sandbox_namespace`: the server's configured namespace misses, no tenant information is available, and the method returns `None`.
3. The caller then falls back to the configured namespace, where the sandbox does not exist → `get_sandbox` raises 404.
4. `AccessRenewController._try_renew_sync` swallows it: `except HTTPException: return False` (`integrations/renew_intent/controller.py`) — **no logging**. The intent has already been consumed from the queue.

Redis is working correctly throughout — delivery, consumption, and staleness gating all behave; only the sandbox-id → namespace resolution fails.

## Impact

- Any multi-tenant deployment where tenant sandboxes live outside the server's configured namespace.
- The tenant information is repopulated on the tenant's next control-plane API call, so the failure window is *restart → next API call by that tenant*. A quiet session (long-running agent command, no API traffic) stays broken until expiry.
- A mass restart (rollout, OOM, node drain) drops renewal for **all** in-use sandboxes at once, silently.
- Not affected: single-tenant/direct-API-key mode (sandboxes in the configured namespace), and the in-process proxy path (has tenant context).

## Reproduction

1. Configure as in *Environment* above (any tenant namespace ≠ `kubernetes.namespace`).
2. Create a sandbox with `timeout: 600` and a renew extension (e.g. 600 s) using a tenant API key; confirm `Running` and read `.spec.shutdownTime` from the tenant namespace.
3. Restart the server process.
4. Push a renew intent — either from a real gateway session, or deterministically by `LPUSH`ing `{"sandbox_id": "...", "observed_at": "<now>", ...}` to the configured queue key.
5. Observe: the queue drains, no renew/failure log appears, `.spec.shutdownTime` does not advance, and the sandbox is deleted at the original expiry.

## Expected behavior

Renew intents should survive a server restart: resolve the sandbox id to its actual namespace via a fallback (e.g. a cluster-wide label-selector lookup), or at minimum fail loudly with a structured WARNING instead of a silent drop.

body:
# Summary

Closes #1815

Adds an opt-in, env-driven chained upstream proxy to the egress sidecar's transparent mitmproxy path, so deployments can route sandbox egress through a managed forward proxy (corporate egress gateway, DLP boundary, audit point).

- `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_UPSTREAM_PROXY=http(s)://host[:port]` loads the bundled `mitmscripts/upstream_proxy.py` after `system.py` and before user addons. The addon sets `server_conn.via` per flow, so mitmproxy's upstream-proxy layer dials the proxy and issues `CONNECT <request.host>:<port>` — the SNI/Host-derived FQDN for intercepted TLS, keeping CONNECT authority, SNI and Host consistent.
- `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_UPSTREAM_PROXY_AUTH` injects a complete `Proxy-Authorization` value on the upstream CONNECT only (never logged).
- `https://` proxies get TLS with SNI + hostname verification via the existing `ssl_verify_upstream_trusted_confdir`/`_trusted_ca` options.

Fail-closed semantics: flows that cannot be chained (TLS pass-through, UDP) are refused in `server_connect`; malformed URLs, userinfo credentials, `_AUTH` without `_PROXY`, non-`lazy` `connection_strategy`, and non-empty `ignore_hosts`/`tcp_hosts`/`udp_hosts` fail at startup. Default off: zero behavior change when unset; `system.py`, `networkPolicy` and Credential Vault semantics unchanged.

Component-level only: server-side typed `upstreamProxy` config and admin-controlled egress-only mounts are follow-ups; the new env vars are not request-settable (not in `ALLOWED_EGRESS_ENV_VARS`).

title: feat(egress): chain transparent mitmproxy egress through an upstream CONNECT proxy
body:
## Motivation

Sandboxed workloads in organizations typically must send outbound traffic through a managed forward proxy (corporate egress gateway, DLP boundary, or an audit point) rather than dialing the internet directly. Today the egress sidecar's transparent mitmproxy always dials the original destination itself, so there is no built-in way to chain it to an upstream `CONNECT` proxy.

`OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_MITMPROXY_SCRIPT` can technically load a custom addon that sets `server_conn.via`, but scripting the security boundary ad hoc means every deployment re-implements (and re-audits) the same mechanism — including the fail-closed details that are easy to get wrong (pass-through flows silently bypassing the proxy, credentials in URLs, incompatible `ignore_hosts` combinations).

## Proposal

Ship a bundled, opt-in upstream-proxy addon in the egress image:

- `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_UPSTREAM_PROXY=http(s)://host[:port]` — when set, every mitmproxy-handled connection is chained via `CONNECT <request.host>:<port>`. For intercepted TLS the authority is the SNI/Host-derived FQDN, keeping the CONNECT authority consistent with SNI and Host rather than the intercepted IP.
- `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_UPSTREAM_PROXY_AUTH` — optional complete `Proxy-Authorization` header value injected only on the upstream CONNECT (never logged).
- `https://` endpoints get TLS to the proxy with SNI + hostname verification through the existing `ssl_verify_upstream_trusted_confdir` / `_trusted_ca` options (default `/etc/ssl/certs`, overridable via `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_MITMPROXY_UPSTREAM_TRUST_DIR`).

Fail-closed semantics:

- Flows that cannot be chained (TLS pass-through from no-SNI or `ignore_hosts`/`tcp_hosts`/`udp_hosts`, UDP/QUIC dials) are refused — no silent direct egress.
- Malformed URLs, userinfo credentials, `..._AUTH` without `..._PROXY`, non-`lazy` `connection_strategy`, and non-empty pass-through lists fail at startup, not at runtime.
- Default off: no behavior change when the env is unset; `system.py`, `networkPolicy` and Credential Vault semantics are unchanged.

This is intentionally component-level only: the server-side typed `upstreamProxy` config (with admin-controlled CA/identity file mounts for the egress container) is a follow-up change, so request-level env remains unable to set or override these variables.

I have an implementation ready and will link a PR.

Add a Docker E2E matrix for foreground command stream completion through the Python SDK: direct and server-proxied connections, each with and without a `dns+nft` egress sidecar. The 12 cases cover empty commands, approximately 4 MiB of stdout/stderr, nonzero exits, and a delayed SDK consumer. They assert exact per-stream output/order, Unicode tails without final newlines, accumulated logs, exit status, and exactly one terminal event after the output.

Each case logs total call time and terminal-callback-to-return time for reproducible latency comparisons. Correctness is asserted in CI; latency is reported without a machine-speed threshold. Existing Python E2E discovery includes this file automatically. The README documents prerequisites and the Docker Desktop network topology.

This complements the runtime completion fix in #1281 and the user reports in #1277 / #1661. It adds coverage and measurements without copying the runtime fix into another PR.

# Testing

- [x] Real Docker E2E: **12/12 pass on main `4ba17adf`**, **12/12 pass with the #1281 production change applied to that same main**.
- [x] `uv run --frozen ruff check tests/test_command_stream_e2e.py`
- [x] `uv run --frozen ruff format --check tests/test_command_stream_e2e.py`

- [ ] Full cross-language E2E suite and Kubernetes runtime validation: not run; this change targets the Docker command transport matrix.

## Local A/B observations

The SDK's empty `true` command returned in:

| Path | Main `4ba17adf` | Main + #1281 completion change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Direct | 1011.9 ms | 4.9 ms |
| Server proxy | 1016.4 ms | 12.9 ms |
| Direct + egress | 1008.1 ms | 10.2 ms |
| Server proxy + egress | 1013.4 ms | 11.0 ms |

Across all 12 cases, the interval from the SDK terminal-event callback to `commands.run` returning was **913.7–1005.3 ms** on baseline versus **0.3–0.8 ms** on the candidate. Every output assertion passed in both variants. Passing these correctness tests alone does not prove the latency fix; the separately reported measurements provide that evidence for this local run.

Environment: Docker Desktop on macOS ARM64, Docker engine 29.4.1 Linux/ARM64, Python client 3.10.21, Go build toolchain 1.26.4, `python:3.12-slim` sandboxes, egress v1.1.4. Server and Python SDK source use `4ba17adf` with locked dependencies. Both execd binaries use that same source/toolchain/runtime image; the candidate removes the trailing sleep and unused import via a Go overlay, matching the production change reviewed in #1281 at `e6dbf6b7`. Run the same `uv run --frozen pytest tests/test_command_stream_e2e.py` against baseline and candidate execd images using the documented E2E connection settings. title: fix(execd): skip credential switch for same-identity uid/gid requests

labels.name: size/M
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 30-99 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

Fixes #1802.

Requests like `{"uid":0,"gid":0}` to `/command` failed with `fork/exec /usr/bin/bash: operation not permitted` in sandboxes with dropped capabilities, while the same request without uid/gid worked.

Root cause (one level below the issue's bwrap theory — the plain `/command` path never goes through bwrap): `buildCredential` built a non-nil `syscall.Credential` even when every requested id matched the identity execd already runs as. A non-nil Credential makes the child call `setgroups` before exec — even when all ids match — and `setgroups` requires `CAP_SETGID` regardless of the requested values. With capabilities dropped, that syscall fails and surfaces as the bare `fork/exec ...: operation not permitted` the issue describes.

- Same-identity uid/gid requests now return `nil` and stay on the plain exec path, which is semantically identical (this is also what the no-uid request already did). For uid-only requests the fast path applies only when the user entry's primary GID and supplemental groups match the daemon's own (`sameProcessGroups`), preserving the lookup-based switch otherwise.
- Genuine identity switches that fail due to missing capabilities now produce an actionable error naming the missing grant (`CAP_SETUID`/`CAP_SETGID`, pointing at the server's `docker.drop_capabilities` configuration), instead of a bare EPERM.

## Testing

- [x] `go test ./pkg/runtime/ -run 'TestBuildCredential|TestCredentialStartHint|TestSameProcessGroups'` — 6 new tests, all pass
- [x] `go vet ./pkg/runtime/`, `gofmt` clean, `GOOS=linux go build ./pkg/...`
- [x] Full `go test ./pkg/...` on macOS/arm64 passes except pre-existing PTY tests that require `/dev/ptmx` (also fail on a clean tree in this environment)
- [ ] Full Linux CI + a live sandbox with `drop_capabilities=["ALL"]` repro — not run here

## Breaking Changes

None — same-identity requests previously failed in capability-dropped sandboxes and now execute; all other paths unchanged.

title: fix(egress): cut DNS read amplification in domain revalidation

labels.name: size/M
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 30-99 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
Fixes #1805

## Problem

The domain revalidation loop introduced by #1804 queries A+AAAA for **every** tracked domain every 30 seconds, regardless of remaining lease time. At fleet scale this is synthetic control-plane DNS traffic that grows linearly with sandbox count (~33k QPS at 100k sandboxes × 5 domains), plus three amplification factors: no lease awareness, no failure backoff, no jitter.

## Changes (all in `components/egress/pkg/nftables/dynamic.go`, no semantic changes)

1. **TTL-aware scheduling** — a domain is queued for revalidation only when the earliest lease across its observed addresses expires within `domainRefreshLead` (2 × 30s). The expiry data is reused from the existing `tracker.dynamicIPs` lease mirror; no new state. Query volume becomes proportional to the number of leases about to expire instead of the number of tracked domains: a TTL=300s domain drops from one lookup per 30s to one per ~5min, and domains under active TCP renewal (360s leases) are not queried at all.
2. **Failure backoff** — a failed lookup doubles the per-domain retry delay from one interval up to 10 minutes; a successful revalidation clears it. Chronically failing domains (e.g. persistent SERVFAIL) no longer retry every tick.
3. **Per-tick jitter** — the fixed 30s ticker becomes a uniform [15s, 45s) timer (mean 30s), so batch-started sidecars do not pulse upstream resolvers in phase.
4. Failure logging now includes the next-retry countdown; success/skip paths stay silent.

## Testing

- Updated the four existing domain-refresh tests to use an injected clock and advance to lease-expiry due points.
- Added `TestDomainRefresh_SkipsFreshLeasesAndBacksOffFailures` covering: fresh lease ⇒ no query, near-expiry ⇒ query, backoff window ⇒ skip, backoff expiry + success ⇒ reset.
- `go test ./...` and `go test -race` pass for `pkg/nftables` and the full egress suite; `gofmt` clean.

## Docs

`docs/components/egress.md` revalidation paragraphs updated to describe TTL-aware due scheduling, backoff, and jitter.

title: DNS read amplification from the dns+nft domain revalidation loop: scale bottleneck risk
body:
## Background

#1804 introduces a domain revalidation loop for the sidecar `dns+nft` (default-deny) mode: every 30 seconds it re-queries A/AAAA for every tracked domain against upstream resolvers, renewing leases only for client-observed IPs still confirmed by DNS (fixing the #1738 OSSFS cached-IP reconnect issue).

The mechanism is reasonable for a single sandbox, but at fleet scale it creates **DNS read amplification** that we believe will become a scaling bottleneck.

## Quantification (at ~100,000 sandboxes)

Current query volume (`refreshDomains`):

- Every sandbox sends 2 queries (A + AAAA) per tracked domain every 30s, bounded at 128 domains ≈ **8.5 QPS/sandbox**
- A typical case (~5 tracked domains) ≈ 0.33 QPS/sandbox — but this is constant resident traffic, independent of whether the client is active
- Fleet aggregate: `S sandboxes × N domains × 2 / 30s`. **At 100k sandboxes with 5 tracked domains each, that is ~33,000 QPS**; even with just 1 domain per sandbox it is ~6,700 QPS. This is synthetic control-plane traffic, not user-driven, and it grows linearly with sandbox count
- At this scale it is the same order of magnitude as the cluster's entire normal DNS traffic — effectively doubling resolver capacity requirements. A single CoreDNS instance typically handles only a few tens of k QPS, so this forces sharding/replication purely to serve useless reads
- In k8s the upstream is CoreDNS; TTL-window hits are served from cache, but the packet rate and CoreDNS CPU still scale linearly with sandbox count, and conntrack entries / node-local resolver socket buffers take the same pressure

## Three amplification factors in the current design

1. **No awareness of remaining lease time**: `refreshDomains` unconditionally queries *all* tracked domains — even one whose nft dynamic entry still has 300s of lease left. `applyDomainRefresh` only skips the nft write; the DNS query has already been sent.
2. **No failure backoff**: a domain whose upstream keeps returning retryable failures (e.g. SERVFAIL) is retried every 30s forever, with no decay.
3. **No jitter**: every sidecar uses the same 30s ticker; pods started in batches have near-identical phases, producing synchronized pulses (thundering herd) against the resolver.

## Additional problem: invisible to operators

Background queries go through `forwardContext`, while `RecordDNSForward` / `RecordDNSQueryFailed` are only called in `serveDNS`. Revalidation volume and failure rate are completely invisible in metrics — only log.Warnf lines — so there is no early warning before this becomes an incident at scale.

## Possible mitigations (for discussion)

At 100k sandboxes, jitter/backoff alone only shaves peaks — **query volume must become proportional to the number of leases about to expire** before this is deployable:

- **TTL-aware scheduling (key)**: only query domains whose dynamic lease expires within the next refresh window. Leases already derive from DNS TTL (60–360s), so on-demand refresh cuts resident query volume by an order of magnitude or more
- **Longer interval / per-domain TTL-proportional refresh**: e.g. schedule at `min(TTL/2, 5min)` instead of a fixed 30s full sweep
- **Per-domain / per-instance jitter** to break synchronization
- **Failure backoff** (e.g. exponential up to 5–10 minutes)
- **Revalidation volume/failure metrics** (e.g. `egress.dns.revalidation.*`) plus tracked-domain and eviction counts — required before large-scale rollout
- Going further: only revalidate addresses with recent client activity / active users (leveraging the connection tracker); or dedupe by domain and refresh once at the node-local resolver layer instead of per sidecar

## References

- Introduced by: #1804
- Original motivation: #1738

title: [Bug] execd /command with explicit uid fails "fork/exec /usr/bin/bash: operation not permitted" without CAP_SYS_ADMIN
body:
## 现象

对 execd 的 `/command` 代理端点：

- 不带 `uid`：正常执行（execd 默认就是 root）
- 带 `{"uid":0,"gid":0}`：`CommandExecError: fork/exec /usr/bin/bash: operation not permitted`

## 根因

沙箱容器 capabilities 被 drop（无 `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`）时，**指定 uid 的命令会被路由到 bwrap/session gate 包装路径**（`components/execd/pkg/isolation/*`、`components/execd/pkg/runtime/bash_session.go`），而 bwrap 的 `pivot_root`/`mount` 需要 `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`，缺失即直接 EPERM。

问题是：

1. 报错不提示缺什么能力，"operation not permitted" 完全无法定位
2. 没有降级路径——`uid=0 && gid=0` 时语义上完全可以直接 exec，不必过 gate

调用方（例如 DeepSonar 在 provision 阶段注入 gateway hosts，`session.run(..., {uid:0,gid:0})`）在这个配置下 100% 失败。

## 修复建议（至少二选一）

1. `uid==0 && gid==0` 时跳过 bwrap gate，直接 exec（语义等价）；
2. 检测 `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` 缺失时给出可操作错误，例如：
   `bwrap gate requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN; grant via bootstrap.execd.isolation=enable or exclude SYS_ADMIN from drop_capabilities`

服务端目前只在沙箱创建请求带 `bootstrap.execd.isolation=enable` 时才 grant `CAP_SYS_ADMIN + apparmor/seccomp=unconfined`（`server/opensandbox_server/services/docker/docker_service.py` ~L914-930）。调用方一旦没带该 extension（见 DeepSonar 仓库同名 issue），gate 在标准 drop 配置下必 EPERM，而错误信息不会告诉它是这个原因。

## 影响

调用方在 `drop_capabilities=["ALL"]` 这类标准加固配置下 100% 卡死，且无法从报错定位到 isolation 授权缺失。

title: [Bug] Podman containers lack /.dockerenv — egress sidecar readiness probe falls back to 127.0.0.1 and always fails
body:
## 现象

Podman（含 rootless）部署 server 时，创建带 networkPolicy 的沙箱必失败：

```
Egress sidecar did not become ready within 30s for sandbox xxx:
<urlopen error [Errno 111] Connection refused> (500; DOCKER::SANDBOX_START_FAILED)
```

而 sidecar 本身完全正常（caps 到位、nft 规则成功、policy server 监听 :18080，退出 code=0）。

## 根因

`server/opensandbox_server/services/docker/networking.py` 中：

```python
def _running_inside_docker_container() -> bool:
    """Return True if the current process is running inside a Docker container."""
    return os.path.exists("/.dockerenv")     # L67-69
```

`_resolve_proxy_host()`（L347 起）用这个判断决定是否采用 `[docker].host_ip`，否则兜底 `127.0.0.1`（L360）：

```python
if _running_inside_docker_container():
    host_ip = self._get_docker_host_ip()
    if host_ip:
        return host_ip
return "127.0.0.1"
```

`/.dockerenv` 是 Docker 专属特征文件，**Podman 容器不创建它**（Podman 的等价物是 `/run/.containerenv`）。于是：

1. server 明明运行在容器内，却被判定为"非容器环境"
2. `[docker].host_ip`（本例 = `host.docker.internal`）被跳过
3. 探针落到 `127.0.0.1`，访问的是容器自身的 loopback 宿主映射端口 → 永远 refused（L575 的 `/healthz` 探针）

## 修复建议

```python
def _running_inside_docker_container() -> bool:
    return os.path.exists("/.dockerenv") or os.path.exists("/run/.containerenv")
```

建议同时覆盖 Podman rootless 的 `/run/.containerenv` 与 `CONTAINER` 类环境变量场景，避免只修一半。

## 临时绕过（已实测）

`docker exec <server-container> touch /.dockerenv`（或挂载持久化标记文件）。

Podman 4.9.4 rootless 实测：打标记后带 networkPolicy 的沙箱（egress sidecar + 主容器）完整创建成功。

## 环境

- `opensandbox/server @ sha256:ae8dfbb2…`
- Podman 4.9.4 rootless（非 Docker daemon，docker.sock → podman system service）
- Server 以容器方式部署（官方 compose 拓扑）

body:
# Summary

Continue the OSEP-0023 revision-transaction phase after #1775, #1777, and #1791 with an isolated Go coordinator. This PR separates coordinator correctness from authenticated IPC and live runtime integration.

- Allocate monotonic decision epochs independently of public Vault revision lifetimes, hashing exact serialized snapshot bytes.
- Serialize one subject's transactions and require the complete generation/epoch/digest identity in acknowledgements.
- Retire failed or ambiguous prepares with an acknowledged abort. Once commit is attempted, never infer rollback or abort the candidate: gate reads and subsequent mutations until exact readback or an idempotent commit retry confirms the outcome.
- Reconcile without resending snapshot payloads. Unexpected/foreign readback identities and transport failures remain indeterminate; transport errors cannot leak credential-bearing details.
- Cancel in-flight transport and fence local completion on close without waiting for the network.

The transport is injected and tested with an in-memory peer. No IPC endpoint, public API, SDK, live addon, or existing Vault/ETag path imports this package. The future adapter must validate complete snapshots, authenticate/fence the receiver session, coordinate policy/Vault preparation and public-store finalization under one mutation barrier, and perform remote teardown. Startup/recovery and selective TLS interception remain subsequent work. The OSEP progress note records these boundaries.

Related: #1713. This is the coordinator portion of the revision-transaction phase, not completion of that phase or the public interception mode.

title: feat(sdks): align Python sandbox pool warmup model with Kotlin

labels.name: size/XXL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 1000+ lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

Aligns the Python client pool (`SandboxPoolSync` + `SandboxPoolAsync`) with the Kotlin SDK's warmup execution model and cross-SDK behavior:

**Admission model (the core change)** — a reconcile tick now only reaps expired idle, shrinks excess, plans, and admits warmups through a submit callback before returning, mirroring Kotlin's `PoolReconciler`. Each admitted warmup task creates, validates, renews, and commits its sandbox independently of the tick, so a slow warmup no longer delays its peers, the idle buffer, or the next tick (previously the tick blocked on `as_completed` / `FIRST_COMPLETED` loops until the whole batch finished).

**Behavioral alignment**
- `warmup_create_qps` (default `10`) caps admissions per tick; in-flight admissions count toward `max_idle` alongside idle sandboxes, so concurrent replenish cannot overshoot the target.
- `warmup_concurrency` becomes a warmup-worker cap (asyncio semaphore / executor threads), matching the Kotlin warmup executor's role instead of a per-tick submission cap.
- New `warmup_post_prepare_health_check` + `warmup_post_prepare_health_check_timeout` (default `30s`): post-preparer validation polled at `warmup_health_check_polling_interval`; retries never rerun the preparer; timeouts raise `SandboxReadyTimeoutException` and kill instead of committing.
- Warmup commit renews the primary lock first — a lost lease drops and kills the sandbox (Kotlin leader-epoch commit fence).
- Independent primary-lock heartbeat at `min(reconcile_interval, primary_lock_ttl / 3)`; the tick now reports `primaryOwned`.
- Replenish exponential backoff removed (Kotlin design: fixed create admission is the pressure control); `degraded_threshold` still tracks `HEALTHY/DEGRADED`, `snapshot().backoff_active` is always `False`.
- `ReconcileState` is thread-safe for concurrent warmup accounting.

## Tests

- Reconciler tests assert admission counts (`submit_warmups`) instead of blocking on creates.
- Pool-level tests cover: slow warmup does not block fast peer's commit or the tick; in-flight warming prevents overshoot; post-prepare check success/timeout paths; heartbeat renewal and stop-on-lease-loss; shutdown cancels an in-flight warmup and kills its sandbox; config validation for the new knobs.
- Updated backoff-era tests to the aligned semantics.

## Verification

- `uv run ruff check` / `uv run pyright` — clean
- `uv run pytest tests/` — all green
- `cd docs && pnpm docs:build` — zero errors
- Docs updated: `docs/sdks/python.md`, `docs/guides/client-pool.md`

## Not aligned (intentional, follow-ups if wanted)

OTel warmup tracing, Kotlin's `RunContext` restart fencing, shared HTTP connection pool, fixed 1s reconcile cadence (Python keeps the configurable `reconcile_interval`; removing it would be a breaking change).

title: fix(kubernetes): trigger pool reconcile when poolRef changes

labels.name: size/XS
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 0-9   lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Problem

Follow-up to #1779. Comparing `Replicas` (`*int32`) by value was correct, but it removed an accidental catch-all trigger: previously every BatchSandbox update event passed the predicate because distinct informer copies always had different `Replicas` pointers. That masked a missing trigger condition — a change in `spec.poolRef` (most importantly auto-assign resolving `*` to a concrete Pool name) no longer enqueues a Pool reconcile.

As a result, after the BatchSandbox controller patches `poolRef: "*" -> "<pool>`, the Pool reconciler never runs again: no pods get allocated, the `alloc-status` annotation is never written, and `status.allocated` stays empty. This breaks the Core e2e on all Kubernetes versions:

```
[FAIL] Manager Pool Auto-Assign [It] should auto-assign BatchSandbox without template to the only Pool when poolRef is *
Timed out after 120.000s. Expected <string>:  to equal <string>: 2
```

Since #1779 was merged in 05a8d26a, main is currently red for `Controller E2E Core` (verified on runs 34347818431 and 34351472199).

## Fix

Trigger a Pool reconcile when `spec.poolRef` changes in `shouldReconcilePoolForBatchSandboxUpdate`:

- `"*" -> "<pool>"` — the auto-assign resolution path broken above
- `"<pool-a>" -> "<pool-b>"` — pool reassignment
- `"" -> "<pool>"` — attaching to a pool
- `"<pool>" -> ""` — still filtered here (new poolRef empty) and handled by the existing `filterBatchSandboxDetached` watch on the old pool

Adds two predicate test cases covering the auto-assign resolution and reassignment transitions.

## Verification

- `go test ./internal/controller/ -run TestPoolBatchSandboxUpdate -v` — all cases pass
- `go test ./internal/controller/ -run TestPool`, `go vet ./...`, `go build ./...` — clean
- Full envtest suite / Kind e2e not run locally (binary download blocked by network); relying on CI
