title: fleets: snapshot / pause / resume support on fast-sandbox (cross-host restore required)
body:
## Summary

The fleets (fast-sandbox) runtime currently rejects pause/resume and runtime snapshots. Fast-sandbox itself has no snapshot/pause/resume semantics today — the Firecracker golden-image pipeline produces build-time snapshots (rootfs.ext4 / vmstate.snap / memory.snap), but there is no mechanism to snapshot a **running** sandbox and restore it, and no pause/resume of a live microVM that survives process or node boundaries.

## Requirements

- **Pause / Resume**: freeze a running sandbox (microVM) and resume it, ideally transparently to in-guest execd sessions.
- **Snapshot**: capture a running sandbox's state (memory + device state + writable rootfs diff) as a restorable artifact.
- **Resume must work cross-host**: a snapshot taken on node A must restore on node B (different CPU is acceptable within the same microarchitecture family). This is the hard requirement — node-local restore is not enough:
  - memory + vmstate artifacts published to the object store (same channel as golden images, DART P2P delivery applies)
  - CPU feature compatibility check before restore (Firecracker requires matching CPU template; pin a CPU template per pool/template)
  - rootfs diff handling: the writable layer must be captured (overlay/reflink diff → artifact) and re-materialized on restore
  - clock/entropy: restored VMs need kvmclock + reseeded CRNG on resume (VMGenID, as the golden-image path already does)
- **Server API surface**: the existing OpenSandbox pause/resume/snapshot lifecycle routes (`POST /sandboxes/{id}/pause|resume`, `POST /sandboxes/{id}/snapshots`, snapshot create/restore) need fleets adapters; restore-from-snapshot as a create source (`snapshotId`).

## Out of scope (initial)

- Cross-cluster restore
- Live migration (pause-copy-resume is sufficient)

## Open questions

1. Snapshot consistency: Firecracker `SnapshotCreate` requires the VM paused — do we expose pause-on-snapshot semantics or an opaque atomic snapshot?
2. Rootfs diff format: reflink-based diff of the writable copy vs overlaybd layers (the builder already has OverlayBD tooling).
3. Pool interaction: should snapshot restore allocate from the same pool/template or allow a different pool on the same CPU family?
4. Fast-sandbox CRD shape: a new `SandboxSnapshot` CRD vs annotations on Sandbox (OpenSandbox's kubernetes runtime already has `SandboxSnapshot` semantics to mirror).

Reference: fast-sandbox golden-image pipeline (`SandboxTemplate` builder) already demonstrates snapshot capture/publish/restore mechanics — this issue is about doing it for **live** sandboxes with cross-host guarantees.

# Summary
- What is changing and why?

The agent-sandbox workload provider now honors `image.auth` in create requests, mirroring the existing batch-sandbox behavior: a per-sandbox `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` Secret is created right after the Sandbox CR and referenced in the pod template's `imagePullSecrets`, so sandboxes can pull images from private registries with request-supplied credentials. This also adds an `owner_name` parameter to `build_image_pull_secret`: agent-sandbox normalizes digit-leading ids to `sandbox-<id>` for DNS-1035, so the ownerReference must carry the actual CR name, or the K8s garbage collector deletes the Secret as an orphan while the sandbox is still running.

body:
## Why do you need it?

The create-sandbox API already defines `image.auth` (username/password) for pulling sandbox images from private registries, and the `batch-sandbox` provider honors it: it creates a per-sandbox `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` Secret, wires it into the pod spec via `imagePullSecrets`, and lets Kubernetes GC remove the Secret together with the owning CR.

The `agent-sandbox` provider rejects the same request with HTTP 400:

> `image.auth is not supported by the current workload provider. Use imagePullSecrets via Kubernetes ServiceAccount or sandbox template.`

(`_ensure_image_auth_support` in `server/opensandbox_server/services/k8s/kubernetes_service.py`)

The suggested alternatives are deployment-scoped: secrets bound to a ServiceAccount or baked into a sandbox template must be provisioned by the operator beforehand. They cannot carry credentials supplied per request (e.g. a caller's own registry account), so a multi-tenant deployment running `agent-sandbox` has no request-level path to private images at all.

## How could it be?

Same input batch-sandbox already accepts:

```json
{
  "image": {
    "uri": "registry.example.com/team/runtime:1.0",
    "auth": { "username": "user", "password": "pass" }
  }
}
```

Expected behavior — agent-sandbox mirrors batch-sandbox:

1. Create the `Sandbox` CR first.
2. Create a per-sandbox dockerconfigjson Secret named `opensandbox-image-auth-<sandbox_id>`, owned by the CR via ownerReference. The reference must use the **actual CR name**: agent-sandbox normalizes ids for DNS-1035 (digit-leading ids get a `sandbox-` prefix), so pointing the reference at the raw id would leave the Secret orphaned and immediately GC'd.
3. Add the Secret to the pod template's `imagePullSecrets`.
4. If Secret creation fails, roll back the CR.

## Other related information

I have a working implementation with unit tests and a manual e2e run (private-registry pull verified via pod events plus an anonymous-401 negative control; Secret GC verified on sandbox delete) ready to submit as a PR.

title: fix(execd): reclaim stale upper dirs under upper_root at startup

labels.name: size/M
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 30-99 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

execd never reconciled the on-disk `upper_root` tree with its in-memory session table (`UpperManager.entries`). Any upper/work directories left behind when execd exits were permanently orphaned: after a restart the new process knew nothing about them, never counted them, and never removed them.

This fixes all three impacts from #1780:

1. **Unbounded disk leak** — execd exiting mid-session (crash, OOM, container restart) orphaned that session's dirs forever.
2. **Cross-occupant data residue in pooled sandboxes** — session overlay contents written by occupant A stayed readable by occupant B.
3. **Quota accounting reset on restart** — `upper_max_bytes` usage started from zero while stale bytes were still on disk.

## Changes

- **`NewUpperManager` now runs a startup-only `reclaimStale()` sweep**: enumerate every child of `upper_root` and remove it. The session table lives only in memory and dies with the process, so at startup every existing child is stale by definition — no correct behavior depends on stale upper dirs surviving a restart. The sweep runs synchronously in the constructor, before any session can be allocated, so it cannot race live allocations.
- **Failed reclaims stay tracked**: children that cannot be removed yet (e.g. an upper still referenced by a leftover overlay mount from the previous lifetime) are registered as released entries, so the existing idle collector (`CollectWithErrors`) retries them once the blocker is gone, and `usageLocked` keeps counting their bytes toward `upper_max_bytes`.
- **`usageLocked` skips already-missing upper dirs** (contributes 0 instead of failing the whole sum) so partially-removed residue does not break `Usage()`.
- Startup summary log: `upper: reclaimed N stale session dir(s) under ... (M failed)`.

## Tests

- `TestNewUpperManager_ReclaimsStaleChildren` — session-layout residue, bare residue, and junk files are all removed at startup; `Usage()` is 0; nothing stays tracked.
- `TestUpperManager_ReclaimStaleFailureRetainedForGC` — a blocked reclaim is registered as released, counted by `Usage()`, and freed by a later `CollectWithErrors` retry.
- `TestUpperManager_UsageSkipsMissingUpper` — `Usage()` tolerates a tracked entry whose upper dir is already gone.

All existing `pkg/isolation` and `pkg/runtime` tests pass (`go test ./pkg/...`). One pre-existing failure on macOS dev machines (`TestMergedView_WriteFileReader`, symlink policy) also fails on unmodified `main` and is unrelated.

## Docs

`docs/guides/isolation-sessions.md` now documents the restart reclamation semantics in the Workspace Modes section.

Fixes #1780

title: Python SDK: health-probe 401/403 responses are masked as readiness timeouts
body:
## Problem

Python SDK readiness polling turns HTTP 401/403 from the sandbox health endpoint into `SandboxReadyTimeoutException` instead of returning the authentication/authorization error immediately.

This concerns the health request after endpoint resolution succeeds, not an invalid management API key on `POST /sandboxes`.

## Reproduction

1. Start an execd instance with access-token authentication enabled.
2. Resolve an existing sandbox endpoint successfully, but provide an invalid `X-EXECD-ACCESS-TOKEN` for that endpoint.
3. Call `Sandbox.connect()` (or the shared readiness check).
4. Observe repeated `GET /ping` responses with HTTP 401 until the readiness timeout expires.

The same classification issue applies to a proxy returning 401/403 during the health probe. It does not require a missing-header bug.

## Expected behavior

Stop after the first unauthorized/forbidden health response and propagate `SandboxApiException`, preserving the HTTP status and existing error details/request ID. Keep polling for transient startup failures. Preserve the boolean behavior of the public built-in `is_healthy()` probe.

## Cause

At upstream base `da268303`, the async and sync health adapters catch API exceptions and return `False`. The public health wrappers also suppress exceptions, and the readiness budget catches probe errors and continues polling. Fixing only the final polling loop therefore does not handle real HTTP failures.

## Related work

#1686 reported the timeout symptom when proxy requests omitted the management API key. #1687 fixed header propagation. This report addresses the remaining case where the health endpoint actually returns 401/403 even with header propagation fixed.

A focused Python async/sync fix is prepared with HTTP-transport regression tests covering connect/resume, 401/403 single-probe failure, transient 429/503 recovery, and compatibility of `is_healthy()`.

title: execd isolated sessions: stale upper dirs under upper_root are never reclaimed after execd restart (disk leak + cross-occupant residue)
body:
## Summary

execd never reconciles the on-disk `upper_root` tree with its in-memory session table. Any upper/work directories left behind when execd exits are permanently orphaned: after a restart the new process knows nothing about them, never counts them, and never removes them. This silently leaks disk and, in pooled / pre-provisioned sandboxes where the pod outlives individual occupants, leaks session data across occupants.

## Current behavior (current `main`)

`UpperManager` tracks sessions exclusively in the in-memory `entries` map:

- `NewUpperManager` (`components/execd/pkg/isolation/upper.go:44`) only does `os.MkdirAll(root)` — no scan of existing children.
- `Allocate` (`upper.go:65`) creates `<root>/<id>/{upper,work}` and registers the entry in `m.entries`.
- `Collect`/`CollectWithErrors` (`upper.go:137`) GC only entries present in `m.entries`.
- `usageLocked` (`upper.go:168`) sums `dirSize` over `m.entries` **only** — the filesystem is never walked.

After execd restarts, `entries` starts empty, so every directory under `upper_root` from the previous lifetime is invisible: not cleaned, and not even counted toward `upper_max_bytes`.

## Impact

1. **Unbounded disk leak.** execd exiting mid-session (crash, OOM, `restartPolicy: Always` container restart) orphans that session's dirs. Repeated restarts accumulate. With the recommended emptyDir backing, this either fills the node or trips kubelet ephemeral-storage eviction once a `sizeLimit`/`emptyDir` limit is in play.
2. **Cross-occupant data residue in pooled sandboxes.** In pool-mode / pre-provisioned sandboxes the pod (and its `upper_root` volume) outlives individual occupants while the agent process is restarted per occupant. Session overlay contents written by occupant A remain on disk and readable by occupant B — the upper root is a normal mount inside the container, so any later code in the pod can traverse it. This breaks the "session writes are private and die with the session" expectation for overlay workspaces.
3. **Quota accounting resets on restart.** Because `usageLocked` only counts tracked entries, `upper_max_bytes` starts from zero after a restart while stale bytes are still on disk — compounding #1773 (which is about enforcement being allocation-time-only; this issue is about stale data never being reclaimed or even observed at all).

## Why startup cleanup is safe

- The session table lives only in memory: after a restart, `GET /v1/isolated/session/{id}` 404s for every pre-restart ID, and attach (`feat/isolated-session-attach`) only reattaches within a single execd lifetime.
- Background runs die with the process; there is no persistence path that could resurrect a pre-restart session.

So no correct behavior depends on stale upper dirs surviving a restart.

## Suggested fix

At runner init (before or inside `NewUpperManager`, called from `components/execd/pkg/runtime/isolated_session_ctrl.go:68` / wired in `components/execd/main.go:103-160`):

1. Enumerate children of `upper_root`; since `entries` is empty at startup, every existing `<id>/{upper,work}` is stale by definition — remove them and log count + freed bytes.
2. Optionally: an age-grace knob (e.g. skip dirs younger than N seconds) for operators who want crash-scene forensics, defaulting to full wipe.
3. Optionally: the same reconciliation can run periodically (remove on-disk ids not present in `entries`) to also reclaim dirs orphaned by failed `Allocate` cleanup paths within a single lifetime.

## Repro sketch

```sh
# in a sandbox with execd isolation available
curl -X POST .../v1/isolated/session   # create session
# inside the session: write files to the overlay workspace
kill -9 <execd pid>                    # supervisor/container restarts execd
ls /var/lib/execd/isolation/           # default upper_root: previous <id> dirs still there
# they are never collected; Usage() reports 0; new sessions allocate fresh ids
```

## Environment

Observed while evaluating execd isolated sessions for warm-pooled sandboxes (Aone Sandbox / fast-sandbox style deployment where worker pods are recycled between occupants). Code references are against current `main` (`da268303`).

Related: #1773 (quota enforcement semantics — separate ask, same subsystem).

title: bug(kubernetes): Pool update predicate compares replica pointers instead of values
body:
## Summary

The BatchSandbox update predicate in `PoolReconciler.SetupWithManager` compares `Spec.Replicas` directly:

```go
if oldObj.Spec.Replicas != newObj.Spec.Replicas {
    return true
}
```

Since `Replicas` is `*int32`, this compares pointer addresses rather than replica counts. Old and new objects can both request one replica while holding different pointers, causing status-only or unrelated metadata updates to enqueue the associated Pool unnecessarily.

Source: [pool_controller.go](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/kubernetes/internal/controller/pool_controller.go), `filterBatchSandbox.UpdateFunc`.

## Reproduction

1. Construct a BatchSandbox with a non-empty `spec.poolRef` and `spec.replicas` set to `1`.
2. Deep-copy it to obtain the new object.
3. Change only a status field or unrelated annotation, keeping the release annotation and deletion timestamp unchanged.
4. Evaluate the update predicate.

The generated deep copy allocates a new `Replicas` pointer. Although both replica counts remain `1`, the pointer comparison returns `true`, and the predicate accepts the update.

This finding is based on source inspection; no live-cluster benchmark has been performed.

## Expected behavior

An unrelated update should not pass this predicate when the replica count, release annotation, and deletion state are unchanged.

## Impact

Each unnecessary Pool reconciliation can repeat listing and processing of the pool’s Pods and associated BatchSandboxes. Larger pools and frequent status updates can increase CPU, memory allocation, and logging overhead.

Duplicate requests for the same Pool may be coalesced by the work queue. This issue alone does not establish incorrect allocation or an infinite reconciliation loop, and the performance impact has not been measured.

## Suggested fix

Use a nil-safe value comparison:

- Both pointers are nil: equal.
- Only one pointer is nil: different.
- Both pointers are non-nil: compare their values.

Add regression tests covering equal values at different addresses, changed values, nil cases, and unrelated updates. Preserve the existing release-annotation and terminating-state triggers.

title: egress: make Credential Vault scoped-match enforcement default-on with explicit opt-out
body:
## Why do you need it?

PR #1762 added `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_CREDENTIAL_VAULT_REQUIRE_SCOPED_MATCH` as an opt-in guard: when enabled, vault create/patch operations reject bindings that omit `match.methods`, omit `match.paths`, or contain the host-wide `/*` path, instead of normalizing them to all common methods + `/*`.

Today the default remains fail-open: a control plane that projects higher-level API tool definitions into vault bindings can silently drop scoped endpoint metadata and create a host-wide credential injection binding. That is an easy projection mistake with a costly blast radius, and deployments have to discover the env var to protect themselves.

## How could it be?

In a future egress release, flip the default so scoped-match enforcement is **on by default, explicitly disableable** via the same env var (e.g. `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_CREDENTIAL_VAULT_REQUIRE_SCOPED_MATCH=false`), so new deployments get the stricter posture out of the box.

Considerations for the flip:

- Migration note / changelog entry for existing deployments that rely on implicit all-methods + `/*` defaults (they would need to either add explicit scopes to their bindings or set the env var to `false`).
- Whether the change should ship behind a deprecation window (e.g. warn in logs when defaults are implicitly applied) before the hard flip.

## Other related information

- PR that introduced the guard: #1762
- Discussion: https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/pull/1762#issuecomment-5596452302
- Docs: `docs/guides/credential-vault.md` (env var table), `docs/components/egress.md`

title: execd isolated sessions: upper_max_bytes enforced only at allocation — writes uncapped, then all new sessions wedge
body:
## Summary

`upper_max_bytes` (documented as "Hard limit on total upper directory size across all sessions") is enforced **only in `UpperManager.Allocate()`**: before creating a new session's upper dir, it walks the upper root and rejects the *new* session if current usage ≥ limit. Writes made by an already-running session are **not capped at all**, and once usage crosses the limit every subsequent session creation fails — so a single runaway session both escapes the quota and then wedges all new sessions in that sandbox.

## Observed behavior

Config: `upper_max_bytes = 33554432` (32 MiB), upper_root on an emptyDir.

```sh
# inside an isolated session with overlay workspace:
dd if=/dev/zero of=/workspace/big bs=1M count=45   # rc=0, 45 MiB lands on disk

# then every new session create fails:
{"code":"RUNTIME_ERROR","message":"allocate upper: upper: total usage exceeds configured limit: 47185920 >= 33554432 bytes"}
```

No ENOSPC is ever delivered to the writing process; the limit only gates *future* allocations.

## Code reference

- `components/execd/pkg/isolation/upper.go` — `Allocate()` is the only enforcement point: `usageLocked()` (a `filepath.Walk` size sum) compared against `maxBytes`; nothing else consumes the limit.
- `components/execd/pkg/isolation/config.go` — default 8 GiB; config comment says "Hard limit".

## Impact

1. The quota does not actually bound disk usage — a session can write until the backing emptyDir/node disk fills.
2. After the limit is crossed, all new isolated sessions in the sandbox fail (self-DoS), and the error does not identify the session that consumed the space.
3. Recovery requires killing/rebuilding the sandbox (Pod) since an in-session process owns the data.
4. A true write-time cap needs fs-level enforcement (project quota / overlay quota), which is silently absent on common ext4 nodes (no prjquota) — so even a future "hard" mode would need detection.

## Suggestions

1. Document the allocation-time-only semantics in the config comment and the isolation guide ("new sessions are rejected once usage ≥ limit; running sessions are not capped").
2. Expose `UpperManager.Usage()` (already implemented) via an endpoint or metric so operators can alert before the wedge happens.
3. Consider soft per-session enforcement: a periodic usage walk that flags/kills sessions disproportionately consuming the upper root, or project-quota-based hard enforcement with a startup check that warns when the backing filesystem cannot enforce it.
4. On `Allocate` rejection, include the top contributing session dirs in the error/message to speed up triage.

Happy to provide more environment details if useful.

title: execd isolated sessions: binds with non-existent dest always fail (opaque gate EOF) — bwrap mkdir on read-only root
body:
## Summary

`POST /v1/isolated/session` with a `binds` entry whose **dest does not already exist in the sandbox filesystem always fails** with an opaque runtime error:

```
{"code":"RUNTIME_ERROR","message":"start bwrap: wait for isolated workload identity: read native workload gate: read unixpacket @->@: EOF"}
```

The real failure is bwrap dying while creating the dest mountpoint on the read-only-bound root. `extra_writable` is unaffected because its dest always equals source (which is validated to exist).

## Affected

- execd v1.1.0 and `latest` (main build 2026-09-06) — reproduced on both
- bwrap v0.11.2 (the static build shipped in the execd image)
- k3s v1.30.5, kernel 6.17; container has `SYS_ADMIN`+`NET_ADMIN`, seccomp/apparmor unconfined, upper on emptyDir (so this is not the overlay-on-overlay or caps issue)

## Root cause

`buildArgvWithLifecycle` (components/execd/pkg/isolation/bwrap.go) emits the root mount first:

```
--ro-bind / /  ... --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run --dev /dev  [workspace overlay]  [--bind extra_writable...]  [--bind/--ro-bind binds...]
```

At that point `/` is read-only inside the namespace. For a `binds` entry whose dest path does not exist, bwrap must `mkdir` the dest mountpoint — which fails on the read-only root:

```
bwrap: Can't mkdir /hostdata-ro: Read-only file system
```

bwrap exits immediately, the session-gate control socket closes, and execd reports the identity handshake EOF above instead of the underlying cause. Source paths *are* validated (a missing source returns a clean `binds source "...": must be an existing path`), but dest creatability is never checked.

## Minimal repro (standalone bwrap, same container topology)

```sh
mkdir -p /upper/u /upper/w /workspace /tmp/osb-extra   # /upper is an emptyDir (non-overlay)
B="--unshare-pid --unshare-uts --hostname sandbox --unshare-ipc --unshare-cgroup
   --ro-bind / / --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run --dev /dev
   --overlay-src /workspace --overlay /upper/u /upper/w /workspace --proc /proc --die-with-parent"

# extra_writable shape: dest == source, exists → OK
/usr/local/bin/bwrap $B --bind /tmp/osb-extra /tmp/osb-extra -- echo A-ok          # A-ok

# binds shape: dest missing on ro root → FAILS
/usr/local/bin/bwrap $B --ro-bind /tmp/osb-extra /hostdata-ro -- echo B-ok
# bwrap: Can't mkdir /hostdata-ro: Read-only file system

# dest missing but parent is a tmpfs mounted earlier → mounts fine
/usr/local/bin/bwrap $B --ro-bind /tmp/osb-extra /tmp/hostdata -- echo C-ok         # C-ok

# dest exists → mounts fine
/usr/local/bin/bwrap $B --ro-bind /tmp/osb-extra /tmp -- echo D-ok                  # D-ok
```

## Suggested fixes (any of)

1. **Clear validation**: at session create, reject a binds dest that does not exist and is not creatable, with a 4xx naming the path (mirrors the existing source validation).
2. **Auto-provision**: for missing dests, emit `--tmpfs` for the missing parent chain before the bind so bwrap's mkdir succeeds (matches the empirical C case above).
3. **At minimum**, capture bwrap stderr and surface it in the API error instead of the generic gate EOF — today the message gives no hint that the cause is `Can't mkdir ...: Read-only file system`.

Happy to provide more environment details if useful.

title: feat(execd): add caller-bound command and PTY creation recovery

labels.name: size/XXL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 1000+ lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
# Summary

Related to #1547. If a command starts and its create response is lost before the caller saves the execution ID, an ordinary retry starts another process. This PR adds opt-in caller-bound command and PTY creation: callers persist an operation identity and immutable request before sending; matching retries recover the original handle, and conflicting requests return 409.

- Add `/command/operations`, `/pty/operations`, instance discovery and private operation lookup. Preserve legacy command SSE and PTY creation responses. Unsupported servers return an error instead of executing through a legacy fallback.
- Claim creation in the runtime Controller before launch. Both creation paths run under runtime ownership; `202 creating` reports the reserved handle. Command kernels and PTY sessions remain authoritative for execution state.
- Keep PTYs dormant until their first WebSocket connection and allow one launch attempt for a saved identity. `GET /pty/{id}` exposes optional `launch_attempted` and `launch_failed` fields, so a caller can distinguish dormant, failed launch and completed execution after losing a WebSocket error frame. Operation state remains `created` once the session exists. Replay, takeover and terminal reconnect preserve the original process.
- Preserve original command content and runtime errors through the existing authenticated command-status endpoint for keyed and unkeyed commands. Failed keyed command creation retains diagnostics under the reserved handle, including foreground startup/preparation failures. Foreground stdout/stderr is removed after execution; callers needing retained output choose background mode before creating the operation.
- Recover target records without sweeping unrelated records. Capacity pressure and the hourly janitor collect expired records; PTY lifecycle checks and resource closure run outside the registry mutex, with session locking and record identity checks protecting concurrent launch/expiry.
- Keep a uniform 24-hour recovery window, including failed creation. Configure capacity with `--operation-capacity` / `EXECD_OPERATION_CAPACITY` (default 4096), advertised by instance discovery. Export bounded request outcomes, occupancy, capacity and oldest creating age through existing OpenTelemetry.
- Cache instance discovery for up to 60 monotonic seconds in Python async/sync, JavaScript, Go, Kotlin and C#. Concurrent misses share a fetch and callers receive independent snapshots. Instance mismatch/expiry invalidates future discovery without replacing saved IDs or replaying creation; stale in-flight responses cannot repopulate the cache.
- Merge upstream main through `47ccb7af`. Resolve the flag, flag-test, command launch-error and execd documentation conflicts while preserving the upstream 200ms shutdown default and credential diagnostics alongside operation capacity and caller-bound logging. Preserve upstream negative log-cursor validation in Go and JavaScript. Preserve native `argv` execution and include the copied, ordered argument array in operation request matching. Strict creation decoding rejects unknown fields despite the upstream custom JSON decoder. Kotlin creation omits the unused command/argv alternative instead of sending a conflicting null field.
- Update the source spec, generated clients, recovery guide, configuration/metrics docs and provisional OSEP-0024. Recovery remains an optional capability for JavaScript/Python custom adapters implementing the current upstream command interface.

The guarantee is at-most-once creation for the saved identity within the authenticated principal, resource kind and one execd Controller lifetime. The window starts at the server timestamp encoded in the identity; creating and active records stay protected. Expired identities return 410; instance mismatch returns 409 with unknown outcome. Failed records retain their original result, and a full registry rejects new identities without evicting protected records. Cached instance time reduces a new identity's remaining window and must not become a permanent ID source.

This is an experimental implementation pending maintainer design review. Memory registration and OS spawn are not transactional. Cross-execd-restart recovery, command success and exactly-once business effects are outside the guarantee. Recovery uses the original persisted ID; refreshing identity components is not reconciliation. Callers sharing execd's access token share its trust boundary, including existing command status and logs. Operation lookup and errors expose no raw command inputs.

# Testing

- [x] Unit tests
- [x] Integration tests
- [x] e2e / manual verification

Validation of the September 15 merge revision (`a6ae1232`, macOS arm64):

- `go test -mod=readonly -race -count=1 -timeout=4m ./pkg/flag ./pkg/runtime ./pkg/web/... ./pkg/telemetry` passed, including command/PTY operation recovery, HTTP response loss, lifecycle, configuration and upstream credential tests.
- Go SDK full suite with `-race` passed. JavaScript API generation/build and all 171 tests passed; typecheck and lint passed. The generated lifecycle client drift from unrelated upstream schema changes was excluded from this update, and typecheck was repeated on the committed sources.
- Execd scoped `go vet`, Windows amd64 cross-compilation, VitePress build, rendered execd configuration values, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Used `-mod=readonly` because a local ignored vendor directory contains older dependencies. Docker was unavailable, so Linux container, privileged bwrap/eBPF, native Windows and deployment E2E checks were not rerun for this merge. Hosted CI and maintainer approval remain separate.

Earlier validation at `bce9df04` (September 10; not all checks below were rerun for the September 15 merge):

- macOS and Linux arm64: operation/runtime/web/config/telemetry, command/argv, PTY lifecycle and body-limit tests with `-race`. Real HTTP response-loss tests recover the same handle and one PID for foreground/background commands. PTY tests cover lost launch-error frames in PTY and pipe modes, status lookup, failed-launch reconnect, replay/takeover, nonzero exit and legacy restart state.
- Standalone compiled Linux execd: capacity environment/CLI precedence verified through instance discovery; real command response loss and daemon restart rejection with no second process. Containers use `--init` for child reaping.
- Regression coverage includes command failure diagnostics after response loss, unchanged diagnostics after retry, authenticated status access, native argument-order conflicts, strict unknown-field rejection with legacy decoding preserved, and Python generated-client handling of absent/false/true launch fields.
- Go SDK full suite with `-race`; Python 616 tests, Pyright and changed-file Ruff; JavaScript 166 tests, API generation/build/typecheck/lint; Kotlin API generation/compilation, 23 CommandsAdapter tests and Spotless; C# 33 CommandsAdapter tests and all-target-framework library build.
- Execd `go vet`, golangci-lint and Windows cross-compilation; OpenAPI schema regression test; VitePress build and rendered guide checks; changed-source license headers and `git diff --check` passed.
- Separate self-review covered lifecycle ownership/locking, failure retention, request fingerprinting, merge resolution and SDK wire compatibility. Hosted CI and maintainer approval are separate from these local checks.

Not run: unfiltered Linux suite, privileged bwrap/eBPF CI, Kubernetes/Jupyter deployment E2E, Windows native execution, production load or instruction-level crash injection. Retention tests use controlled clocks rather than a 24-hour soak. SDK tests use HTTP test transports; runtime/standalone-daemon tests use OS processes.

# Breaking Changes

- [x] None
- [ ] Yes (describe impact and migration path)

Recovery is opt-in through new methods and paths. PTY launch-status fields are optional for older-server compatibility; absent fields mean unavailable launch information. Wait for PTY operation state `created` before attaching. Command handle recovery does not replay foreground output; background mode uses the existing log cursor.

labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 500-999 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

Implements the phase 1 server telemetry contract from #1766: business metrics for the lifecycle control plane, emitted through the existing OTel setup.

- **Sandbox lifecycle**: create/delete/pause/resume/renew counters and durations via a `@instrument_lifecycle(operation)` decorator on the docker / composite / fleets services. Runtime label is resolved per call (`flt-*` ids route to fleets under the kubernetes composite); `create` records a bounded `error_type` (quota / pool_timeout / image / timeout / invalid_request / runtime / unknown) and `source` (image / snapshot / pool); `delete` records `trigger` (user / expiry / recovery).
- **Expiry & recovery**: TTL-timer and startup-recovery deletions recorded explicitly in the Docker backend, including 30s retry failures; orphan sidecar cleanups counted.
- **Snapshots**: counts at terminal state (READY/FAILED), not at 202; creation duration measured in the async worker, so recovery-resolved snapshots count without inflating durations.
- **Server proxy**: request count/duration for HTTP (up to response headers) and WebSocket (whole session, handshake status), via `@instrument_proxy_http` and explicit exit-point recording.
- **Access renew**: pipeline outcomes (extended / dropped / stale / throttled) from the controller and consumer.
- **`server.sandbox.active`**: observable gauge by lifecycle state and runtime, paging `list_sandboxes` on the export interval; registered only when `[otel]` enabled.
- **Spec**: telemetry contract documented in `server/docs/opentelemetry.md` (aligned with the execd/ingress/egress `docs/opentelemetry.md` convention); docs site page updated.

## Design notes

- Counters use the `.count` suffix and durations are `ms`, matching the ingress/execd convention; no `_total` (Prometheus exporters append it).
- Attribute values are closed sets; sandbox IDs, tenant IDs, API keys, and raw paths never become attributes.
- All recording functions never raise and no-op when `[otel]` is disabled; method bodies are untouched — instrumentation is one decorator line per service method.

## Testing

- New `server/tests/test_business_metrics.py`: instrument emission through a real provider, attribute shapes, decorator runtime routing, error-type mapping, gauge collection, noop-when-disabled.
- Full server suite: 1811 passed / 16 skipped; `ruff` clean; `pyright` delta clean; `docs` build clean.

Closes #1766 (metrics scope; traces integration tracked separately within the issue)

title: Systematically audit and clean up all-language SDKs: docs, tests, comments, logic fixes, deduplication
body:
## Summary

Systematically review and clean up all OpenSandbox SDKs across languages (`sdks/sandbox/{python,javascript,kotlin,csharp,go}`, `sdks/code-interpreter/*`, `sdks/mcp/sandbox/python`, `sandbox/kotlin/code-interpreter`), covering documentation, tests, comments, code logic, and duplicate-code abstraction.

## Motivation

The SDKs grew feature-by-feature and across five languages. Drift has accumulated: outdated docs, inconsistent test depth, noisy/stale comments, language-specific logic bugs, and repeated logic that should live in shared handwritten adapters. A systematic pass is needed to bring them to a consistent, maintainable baseline.

## Audit Dimensions

1. **Documentation fixes**
   - Correct outdated examples, wrong parameter descriptions, broken links in READMEs and docstrings
   - Align quick-start samples with current server behavior
   - Ensure each language SDK README documents the same feature set; note language gaps explicitly

2. **Test governance**
   - Inventory test coverage per language/SDK; identify and fill critical gaps
   - Remove flaky/duplicate/meaningless tests; standardize test structure and naming
   - Align cross-language behavioral coverage for identical capabilities (mirror tests in `tests/` where applicable)

3. **Comment governance**
   - Remove stale/misleading comments and commented-out dead code
   - Keep docstrings accurate and consistent in style per language conventions
   - No noisy inline comments restating the code

4. **Code logic fixes**
   - Fix language-specific bugs and behavior drift against `specs/` (auth, retry, timeout, error mapping, lifecycle methods)
   - Align error handling and typed exceptions/errors across languages

5. **Duplicate code abstraction**
   - Extract repeated logic (URL building, retry/backoff, pagination, auth refresh, multipart upload) into shared handwritten modules per language
   - Keep generated code untouched; abstractions live in handwritten adapters only
   - Where multiple languages repeat the same design, document the common pattern in `sdks/AGENTS.md`

## Guardrails

- Generated code paths (e.g. `sandbox/python/src/opensandbox/api/**`, `sandbox/javascript/src/api/*.ts`, `sandbox/kotlin/sandbox-api/build/generated/**`) must not be hand-edited as the fix
- No public API breaking changes; behavior changes must follow `specs/` and be aligned across languages
- Work should land as per-language incremental PRs, not one big-bang change

## Suggested Execution

- Phase 0: audit report (per language x dimension matrix of findings)
- Phase 1..N: per-language cleanup PRs, ordered by severity (logic fixes first, then tests, docs, comments, abstraction)

## Acceptance Criteria

- Audit report checklist fully triaged (fixed or explicitly wontfix with reason)
- All SDK unit tests pass per language with their standard toolchain
- Cross-language e2e tests in `tests/` pass
- READMEs/docstrings accurate; no dead code from this effort remains

title: Define core metrics/traces for BatchSandbox controller and systematically integrate OpenTelemetry
body:
## Summary

Define the core metrics and traces for the BatchSandbox controller (`kubernetes/internal/controller/batchsandbox_controller.go`) and systematically integrate OpenTelemetry (OTel) for instrumentation and export.

## Motivation

The BatchSandbox controller is the core of pool scheduling and sandbox lifecycle reconciliation, but it has no systematic telemetry. A minimal, well-defined set of metrics and traces is needed to answer production questions: reconcile health, batch allocation latency, pool fill rate, and pause/resume outcomes.

## Design Principles

- **Restrained by design**: metrics and traces must stay minimal; avoid over-engineering
- **Core-only first phase**: only the essential signals below; no speculative dashboards, exotic samplers, or per-subsystem metric sprawl in phase 1
- Reuse standard OTel semantic conventions (including K8s controller semantic conventions) where they exist

## Phase 1 Scope (core only)

1. **Core metrics**
   - Reconcile loop: reconcile count and duration per controller (by result: success/error/requeue)
   - BatchSandbox lifecycle: create/delete/snapshot counts and durations (success vs error), current BatchSandbox count by phase/state
   - Pool allocation: allocation latency and success/error counts from the scheduler path
   - Workqueue depth (via standard controller-runtime metrics if already exposed — reuse, don't duplicate)

2. **Core traces**
   - One span per reconcile attempt for BatchSandbox (and its sub-operations: allocation, pause/resume, snapshot) with name/namespace/phase attributes
   - Spans for downstream calls made by the controller (API server updates, server/runtime integration calls)

3. **OTel integration**
   - Consistent tracer/meter provider setup in `cmd/controller/main.go`, wired from controller flags/config
   - OTLP exporter (endpoint, headers, interval) configurable; graceful shutdown flushing
   - Do not double-instrument what controller-runtime already exposes (workqueue, client metrics) — integrate rather than duplicate

## Out of Scope (explicitly deferred)

- Metrics for scheduler internals (bin-packing details, strategy internals), eviction/recycle subsystems
- Per-node-agent or execd-side telemetry
- Dashboards, alerting definitions, tail-based sampling
- Traces for Pool/SandboxSnapshot controllers beyond minimal reuse of the same wiring (separate issue if needed)

## Acceptance Criteria

- Core metrics and traces are defined in a short telemetry spec under `kubernetes/docs/` (names, types, attributes, units)
- Controller emits the defined signals with standard OTel SDK setup configured via flags/config
- Unit/env tests cover instrumentation wiring and key metric emission
- Docs updated: how to enable/configure OTLP export for the controller, what signals to expect

- **Restrained by design**: metrics and traces must stay minimal; avoid over-engineering
- **Core-only first phase**: only the essential signals below; no speculative dashboards, custom samplers, or exotic exporters in phase 1
- Reuse standard OTel semantic conventions where they exist; no custom semantics when a standard one fits

## Phase 1 Scope (core only)

1. **Core metrics**
   - HTTP server: request count, latency histogram, active requests (by route/method/status)
   - Sandbox lifecycle operations: create/delete/snapshot counts and durations (success vs error)
   - Runtime integration: Docker/Kubernetes operation durations and error counts
   - execd/egress proxy call durations where the server acts as client
   - Basic process/runtime metrics via standard OTel runtime instrumentation

2. **Core traces**
   - Span per inbound HTTP request (root span) with route/method/status attributes
   - Span per sandbox lifecycle operation covering downstream calls (runtime, snapshot store)
   - Context propagation to execd/egress over HTTP where supported

3. **OTel integration**
   - Single, consistent tracer/meter provider setup wired from server config
   - OTLP exporter (endpoint, headers, interval) configurable via existing config system
   - Graceful shutdown flushing
   - Documented env/config switches to enable/disable telemetry

## Out of Scope (explicitly deferred)

- Full request-body / payload redaction pipelines
- Metrics for pool scheduling internals, per-tenant quotas, advanced sampling strategies
- Dashboards and alerting definitions
- Trace/metrics for components other than the server (execd, ingress, egress)

## Acceptance Criteria

- Core metrics and traces are defined in a short telemetry spec under `docs/` (names, types, attributes, units)
- Server emits the defined signals with standard OTel SDK setup configured through existing config
- Unit tests cover instrumentation wiring and key metric emission
- Docs updated: how to enable/configure OTLP export, what signals to expect

# Summary

Agent-sandbox v1.0.0 removes the alpha API that OpenSandbox's Server provider and ingress informer still request. Merely changing the version leaves newly created sandboxes Ready but unreachable through ingress because beta Service creation is opt-in.

This migrates both consumers to `agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1`, creates workloads with `operatingMode: Running` and `service: true`, and tests template overrides and the informer's actual beta list/watch path. Existing status readers remain applicable. The migration guide covers controller/CRD prerequisites, custom templates, and existing resources without a Service.

Closes #1649. This follows the maintainer's invitation to submit the migration and the reported `service: true` workaround in that issue.

# Testing

- [ ] Not run
- [x] Unit tests
- [x] Integration tests (isolated API server; limitations below)
- [ ] e2e / manual verification in a deployed cluster

Validation (based on upstream `75243b726562`)

```bash
cd server
PYTHONPATH="$PWD" .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/k8s tests/test_agent_sandbox_service.py
# 651 passed
.venv/bin/ruff check opensandbox_server/services/k8s/agent_sandbox_provider.py tests/k8s/test_agent_sandbox_provider.py tests/k8s/test_agent_sandbox_template.py
# passed
.venv/bin/pyright opensandbox_server/services/k8s/agent_sandbox_provider.py tests/k8s/test_agent_sandbox_provider.py tests/k8s/test_agent_sandbox_template.py --outputjson
# baseline and candidate: the same 45 existing errors; no added file/message/rule diagnostics

cd ../components/ingress
GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.25.8 go test ./pkg/sandbox -count=1
GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.25.8 go vet ./pkg/sandbox
# passed; touched Go files are gofmt-clean

cd ../../docs
pnpm docs:build
# passed with pnpm 9.15.0; existing chunk-size/syntax-highlighting warnings
```

The two new template-lifecycle regression cases fail on the unchanged upstream provider and pass with this change.

I also ran an evidence-only local Kubernetes 1.35 envtest harness (not added as a repository dependency): the actual Server provider/client, unmodified release controller managers, and actual ingress informer share one API server. The final candidate passes 13 grouped cases on v0.5.0 (including 46 real HTTPS conversion requests and alpha-created resource update/delete) and 8 on v1.0.0. Failure injection covers Pod readiness loss/recovery, Service deletion/recreation, missing FQDN, and informer invalidation after deletion. Upstream goleak and probe Go vet pass.

An additional v1.0.0 probe exercises `Proxy.ServeHTTP` and the real HTTP reverse proxy through both header and URI routing, with the live informer backed by that same controller/API server. All 8 lifecycle checkpoints pass in both routing modes: 200 while Ready, 503 with `Retry-After: 1` while pending or missing FQDN, and 404 after deletion. Rejected requests make zero upstream calls; successful POSTs preserve the body, encoded path/query and expected upstream Host, and remove the ingress routing header. This uses a loopback HTTP backend: the dial hook validates the exact controller-published FQDN and port before substituting loopback, so it does not test Kubernetes DNS or Service networking. No product code changes were needed for this probe.

**Uncovered boundaries**

Envtest has no scheduler/kubelet: Pod status is synthetic; Sandbox status is written only by the real controller. The conversion handler uses local TLS instead of in-cluster Service networking. These checks do not establish in-cluster DNS/Service networking, container execution, HTTP lifecycle endpoint behavior, a full deployed CRD/storage upgrade, or pre-v0.5 support. HTTP traffic through the ingress proxy is covered only by the loopback probe described above; WebSocket/SSE traffic is not covered by this probe. The integration starts at `AgentSandboxProvider`; the broader service callers are covered with mocked Kubernetes APIs. No performance claim is made.

# Breaking Changes

- [ ] None
- [x] Yes (agent-sandbox support floor and template migration)


This proposes agent-sandbox **>= v0.5.0** as the support floor. Server and ingress should be upgraded together. Discovery-based alpha fallback would preserve pre-0.5 installations but adds two manifest/informer paths for a removed upstream API; this change uses a single beta path and documents the upgrade sequence. The exact support floor was raised in #1649 and is still a review decision, not an already-agreed project policy. OpenSandbox BatchSandbox is unaffected.

`service: true` overrides a custom template's `false` for newly created OpenSandbox sandboxes because ingress requires an FQDN. Existing resources are not rewritten. On v0.5.0, conversion preserves an omitted Service field; an explicit per-resource Service patch can restore ingress without recreating the Sandbox. The guide distinguishes that migration from intentionally service-free resources.

title: fix(egress): require TLS SNI to match credential binding host scope

labels.name: size/M
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 30-99 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
# Summary
- Fixes #1758. Credential Vault selects a binding from `request.pretty_host` — the `Host` / HTTP/2 `:authority` header — which is unauthenticated input from the sandbox workload. Nothing checked it against the identity of the peer the request is delivered to, so a workload could open a TLS session to any host its egress policy allows, send `Host: <bound host>`, and have that binding's credential injected into a request delivered to a peer of its choosing.
- `requestheaders()` now requires the ClientHello SNI, when present, to fall inside the matched binding's `match.hosts` scope before anything is injected; mismatches go through the existing `_reject_request` path (403, or connection drop for streamed bodies).
- The SNI is the right anchor because mitmproxy propagates it to the upstream handshake and verifies the upstream certificate against it (`tlsconfig.py`: `server.sni = client.sni or server.address[0]`, then `X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_host`), so unlike the `Host` header it is an identity the peer must prove. The same asymmetry is already relied on by the `ignore_hosts` re-check in `tls_clienthello`.
- `Host`-header matching is kept for binding selection itself: it is per-request (HTTP/2 multiplexing, keep-alive), `http` bindings have no SNI at all, and transparent-mode `request.host` can be a bare IP. The new check is an additional condition, not a replacement.
- Flows without SNI keep previous behavior — plaintext HTTP carries none, and no-SNI TLS never reaches this hook because `tls_clienthello` passes it through. For `http` bindings the egress allow rules stay the only destination control; the guide now says so.

# Testing
- [x] Unit tests — `cd components/egress && python -m unittest discover -s tests -p "test_*.py"` (65 tests, OK; the 4 runtime tests skip locally because `mitmdump` is not installed). New `SystemAddonSniHostConsistencyTest` covers: spoofed `Host` on a foreign SNI rejected with 403 and no header injected, matching SNI still injects, SNI normalization (case + trailing dot), wildcard binding accepting a covered SNI with a differing `Host`, absent SNI falling back to previous behavior, and a streamed body being killed instead of 403.
- [ ] Not run: `docs` VitePress build (text-only edit to an existing page, no new links) and the egress e2e/smoke suites, which need the sidecar image.

# Breaking Changes
- [x] None for correctly configured clients: a normal HTTPS client sends SNI and `Host` for the same name. Two deliberate behavior changes worth calling out in review:
  - A client that coalesces an HTTP/2 connection across authorities (SNI `a.example.com`, `:authority` `b.example.com`) no longer receives an injected credential for a binding scoped to `b.example.com` alone, and gets a 403. This is fail-closed by design — the session is authenticated as a different name than the binding trusts. A binding whose `match.hosts` covers both names (for example `*.example.com`) keeps working; there is a test for that.
  - `http` bindings are unaffected.

# Checklist
- [x] Linked Issue or clearly described motivation
- [x] Added/updated docs (if needed) — `docs/guides/credential-vault.md`: how binding host matching relates to SNI, the new 403 reason, and the explicit statement that `http` bindings have no verifiable endpoint identity
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Security impact considered
- [x] Backward compatibility considered

Follow-up worth deciding separately: `oseps/0012-credential-vault.md` specifies `match.hosts` normalization and wildcard rules but never states which host of the request is matched, and carries no SNI/`Host` consistency requirement. Pinning that invariant down in the OSEP would keep it from being re-lost.

title: Credential Vault: binding match uses the Host header alone, letting a workload steer an injected credential to another TLS peer
body:
## Summary

Credential Vault decides which binding applies — and therefore which secret to inject — from `request.pretty_host`, which is the `Host` (HTTP/2 `:authority`) header. That value is unauthenticated input from the sandbox workload, and nothing later checks it against the identity of the peer the request is actually delivered to. A workload can therefore cause a vault credential to be injected into a request that is delivered to a host it controls.

`components/egress/mitmscripts/system.py`:

- `_request_host()` (L259) → `flow.request.pretty_host or flow.request.host`; mitmproxy's `pretty_host` prefers the `Host`/`:authority` header and only falls back to the connection target.
- `_binding_matches()` (L394) matches `match.hosts` against that value.
- `requestheaders()` (L702) injects `binding.headers` and applies substitutions once a binding matches.

## Impact

The credential leaves the sandbox boundary to a destination the workload picked, which is exactly what Credential Vault exists to prevent: the secret is never exposed to the workload as a value, but the workload can still decide who receives it. Affects header injection and every `substitutions` surface (path/query/header/body).

## Preconditions

The chosen destination must be reachable under the sandbox's effective egress policy. `defaultAction` parses to `deny` by default (`pkg/policy`), so a tightly scoped allowlist that contains only the bound hosts is not exploitable. It becomes exploitable when the policy allows anything the workload can also control, which is common in practice:

- `defaultAction: allow`
- wildcard allows covering provider domains where anyone can obtain a subdomain (tunnel/preview/pages style hosts)
- any allowed host whose request logs the workload can read

Note the guide already warns that default-allow "may allow credential destination bypass"; this report is that the same bypass exists for TLS destinations under a *deny*-default policy whenever the allowlist is wider than the set of bound hosts.

## Mechanism

Over an intercepted TLS session to an allowed host `H` (SNI `H`, so `tls_clienthello` does not pass it through and interception proceeds normally), the workload sends a request whose `Host` header is the bound host `B` and whose path is inside `B`'s binding scope. `_binding_matches` sees `B`, injects `B`'s credential, and the request is forwarded on the session established with `H`.

## Why SNI is different

The SNI is not just a second copy of the same claim — mitmproxy 11.0.2 turns it into a verified identity (`mitmproxy/addons/tlsconfig.py`):

```python
if server.sni is None:
    server.sni = client.sni or server.address[0]
...
if server.sni:
    # We need to set SNI + enable hostname verification.
    X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_host(param, host_name, len(host_name))
```

The client's ClientHello SNI becomes the hostname the upstream certificate is verified against. A workload cannot claim SNI `api.github.com` toward a server it controls and complete the upstream handshake. The `Host` header has no such anchor.

The same file already relies on this asymmetry elsewhere: the `ignore_hosts` re-check (`tls_clienthello`, L142-171) is deliberately done against the SNI. Only the injection path uses the header.

## Proposed fix

After binding selection and before injection, require the ClientHello SNI (when present) to fall inside the matched binding's `match.hosts` scope, and reject otherwise via the existing `_reject_request` path. Keep `Host`-header matching for the binding itself — it is the right key for per-request granularity (HTTP/2 multiplexing, keep-alive), for `http` bindings that have no SNI, and because transparent-mode `request.host` can be a bare IP.

Flows with no SNI keep current behavior: plaintext HTTP has none, and no-SNI TLS never reaches the hook (`tls_clienthello` passes it through). For `http` bindings the egress allow rules remain the only destination control, which is worth stating explicitly in the guide.

PR: #1759

## Note on OSEP 0012

`oseps/0012-credential-vault.md` specifies `match.hosts` normalization and wildcard rules but never says *which* host of the request is matched, and has no SNI/Host consistency requirement. Worth pinning down in the OSEP so the invariant is not re-lost.

title: Execd command execution cannot accept an argument list without a shell
body:
## Why do you need it?

Applications that already represent a command as an executable and an argument list must convert it into shell text before calling OpenSandbox. The `/command` API only accepts `command: string`, so callers must implement quoting for the sandbox's shell even when they do not need shell syntax.

For example, an application wants to execute:

```json
["python3", "-c", "import sys; print(sys.argv[1:])", "a b", "$HOME", "x'y", ""]
```

The last four arguments should reach Python unchanged, including the literal `$HOME` and the empty string.

To reproduce:

1. Start with the argument list above.
2. Call the SDK's command execution API; it requires a shell string.
3. Join the arguments into a string; argument boundaries and shell metacharacters now require escaping.
4. Add shell-specific quoting to preserve the arguments. Execution still depends on a shell, and POSIX quoting does not work for Windows shells.

This affects callers of the Go, Python, JavaScript, Kotlin, and C# SDKs. Correct quoting can preserve arguments for a particular shell, but it cannot request direct process execution.

## How could it be?

Accept an `argv` array as an alternative to `command`, with exactly one supplied per request. Execute the program directly and preserve its arguments without shell expansion. Keep shell strings available for pipelines, redirection, and other shell syntax.

Expose this mode in all five SDKs and support the existing foreground/background, output, timeout, and interruption behavior. Resolve executable paths using the command's environment and working directory, and document how `cwd` expansion differs from literal arguments and request environment values. Make Windows executable lookup and argument encoding rules explicit.

## Other related information

The current workaround is to quote each argument and join them into shell text. An additive `argv` mode would remove that conversion for callers that already have structured arguments.

title: fix(egress): make credential vault mutations immediately visible

labels.name: size/XL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 500-999 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

- make successful Credential Vault create, patch, and delete responses visible to the next intercepted flow
- replace the 0.5-second cache window with a private conditional lookup: `304` reuses the snapshot, `200` validates and replaces it, and `404` alone means no active vault
- use an opaque mutation tag because delete and recreate can reuse public revision `1`
- clear cached plaintext and fail closed on transport, status, ETag, revision, or deep-schema failures; buffered requests receive `503`, while streamed requests terminate before upstream forwarding

## Why

#1281 removes an unrelated one-second execd delay. An immediate request can therefore reuse the pre-mutation egress snapshot after the Credential Vault mutation returned success.

The Store publishes the tag with mutation state under one lock. Conditional comparison and snapshot rendering share one read lock, preventing mixed-version responses.

## Relationship to #1636

This overlaps #1636 only in fail-closed lookup handling. The main change is the ACK-visibility protocol across the Go Store, sidecar/fleet handlers, per-client fleet cache, and Python addon. It also covers malformed payloads, cache clearing, status preservation, streamed-body termination, and operator documentation. It stays separate from #1281 so its approved execd scope remains unchanged.

## Summary

Implements #482. `CodeInterpreter` creation now blocks until the interpreter is **strictly ready** instead of returning an unverified wrapper. An attempt is healthy only when both conditions pass:

1. **execd daemon**: `GET /ping` answers on the interpreter's own execd endpoint.
2. **Interpreter runtime**: the Jupyter kernel gateway is running inside the sandbox, verified by executing a process-check script (`ps aux | grep -v grep | grep jupyter`) through the execd command API.

The runtime leg is required because execd serves `/ping` **before** the sandbox entrypoint installs language kernels and launches Jupyter (`components/execd/pkg/runtime/initmode_linux.go` launches the user entrypoint after execd starts serving; `sandboxes/code-interpreter/scripts/code-interpreter.sh` starts Jupyter last) — a daemon ping alone cannot prove the runtime is ready.

The check applies regardless of how the wrapped sandbox was created (`skip_health_check`, pool acquire, resume). Each SDK exposes language-idiomatic opt-outs and knobs (default: 30s timeout, 200ms polling) plus an on-demand `is_healthy()` probe; `Codes` services gain a `ping()`.

- **Python** (async + sync): `CodeInterpreter.create(..., ready_timeout, health_check_polling_interval, skip_health_check)`, `ping()/is_healthy()/check_ready()`

body:
## Summary

Add a server-side `[egress]` setting, `otlp_endpoint`, that tells the egress sidecar where its OpenTelemetry collector is. The server injects it into every egress sidecar as `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`, on both the Docker and Kubernetes runtimes.

Fixes #1401 (server-side part; see follow-ups below).

## Why server-side only

The collector address is infrastructure config — identical for every sandbox. It is read only from the server config file and:

- is **not** added to `ALLOWED_EGRESS_ENV_VARS`, so `split_egress_env()` never forwards it from a create request;
- is injected **before** the request-derived sidecar env, so nothing per-request can shadow or override it.

This matches the design expectation stated in the review of #1402.

## Validation

- `otlp_endpoint` must be an `http://` or `https://` URL — the sidecar telemetry client (`components/internal/telemetry`) only speaks OTLP over HTTP/protobuf; a gRPC endpoint (4317) would silently not work. Empty string normalizes to `None` (unset).
- When unset, behavior is unchanged: sidecar metrics remain unexported.

## Changes

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `services/constants.py` | `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` constant (server-injected, not user-settable) |
| `config.py` | `EgressConfig.otlp_endpoint` (optional, http(s)-only validator) |
| `services/k8s/workload_provider.py` | `EgressWorkloadSettings.otlp_endpoint` |
| `services/k8s/create_helpers.py` | thread config → workload settings |
| `services/k8s/egress_helper.py` | append env to sidecar spec |
| `services/docker/networking.py` | append env in `_start_egress_sidecar` |
| `configuration.md` + 4 example configs | document the new key (incl. delta temporality note for Prometheus/GMP collectors) |

## Tests

- config: default `None`, http/https accepted, empty → `None`, non-http rejected (`grpc://`, bare host, `unix://`)
- K8s: `apply_egress_to_spec` injects/omits the env; create-path threads the config value into `EgressWorkloadSettings`
- Docker: `_start_egress_sidecar` injects/omits the env

`uv run ruff check`, `uv run pytest` (1693 passed / 16 skipped), `uv run pyright` — no new findings beyond pre-existing patterns.

## Known follow-ups (out of scope here)

- Under `mode = "dns+nft"` with default-deny, the sidecar's own OTLP export traffic is subject to the nftables policy it installs; the Go side needs an exporter client exempted from its own policy (e.g. the `SO_MARK` approach discussed in #1402) or the collector address must be allowed by policy.
- Telemetry-identity hardening discussed in #1402 (`OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_METRICS_EXTRA_ATTRS` re-attribution) is pre-existing and independent of this change.

Fixes #1750

## Summary

When a namespace ResourceQuota is exhausted, synchronous sandbox creation waits the full `sandbox_create_timeout_seconds` before failing with `504 KUBERNETES::POD_READY_TIMEOUT`, even though the real cause is visible on the Sandbox CR within ~1s:

- **Compute quotas** (`requests.cpu` / `limits.memory`): the Sandbox CR is created, the controller's Pod create is rejected asynchronously, and the rejection lands on the CR as `Ready=False, Reason=ReconcilerError` with the API server's message (`... is forbidden: exceeded quota: ...`). `_wait_for_sandbox_ready` polls this status but only inspects `state`, so it blind-waits to the timeout.
- **Count quotas** (`count/sandboxes.agents.x-k8s.io`): the synchronous CR create 403 falls into the generic handler and surfaces as `500 KUBERNETES::API_ERROR`.

## Changes

- `_wait_for_sandbox_ready` now raises `403 KUBERNETES::QUOTA_EXCEEDED` (carrying the K8s message) as soon as the workload condition reports `ReconcilerError` with `exceeded quota`. Other `ReconcilerError` messages keep polling — they can be transient (e.g. scheduler `Insufficient cpu` still polls, covered by an existing test).
- A synchronous 403 quota rejection on workload create maps to the same clean error after the existing rollback runs (instead of the generic 500).
- Coexists with the `Failed` fast-fail from #1722: a quota admission rejection happens before the Pod object exists, so that path does not fire here.

## Verification

- Unit: `tests/k8s/test_kubernetes_service.py` +3 (fail fast on quota / non-quota ReconcilerError keeps polling / count-quota 403 mapping). Full server suite on this branch: 1687 passed, 16 skipped.
- Live kind cluster (agent-sandbox provider): create with `requests.cpu` quota at limit went from 180.2s / 504 to **0.17s / 403**; create with count quota at limit went from 500 to **0.07s / 403**.

title: server/k8s: fail fast when ResourceQuota admission rejects the sandbox instead of timing out as POD_READY_TIMEOUT
body:
## Summary

When a namespace `ResourceQuota` is exhausted, synchronous sandbox creation hangs for the full `sandbox_create_timeout_seconds` (180s in our deployments) and eventually returns a generic `504 KUBERNETES::POD_READY_TIMEOUT` — even though the real cause is written onto the Sandbox CR within ~1 second.

Two variants, both observed on a live kind cluster with the agent-sandbox provider:

1. **Compute quotas** (`requests.cpu` / `limits.memory` / `pods`): the Sandbox CR is created successfully, the controller tries to create the Pod, and quota admission rejects it asynchronously. The rejection lands on the CR as:

   ```
   Ready=False, Reason=ReconcilerError
   Message: Error seen: pods "sandbox-…" is forbidden: exceeded quota: sandbox-quota,
            requested: requests.cpu=1, used: requests.cpu=0, limited: requests.cpu=10m
   ```

   `_wait_for_sandbox_ready` polls this status (we can see the message in the server log at t+1s) but only inspects `state`, so it keeps polling until the timeout.

2. **Count quotas** (`count/sandboxes.agents.x-k8s.io`): the CR create itself is rejected synchronously with 403, which falls into the generic `except` and surfaces as `500 KUBERNETES::API_ERROR` with the raw Kubernetes error string.

## Reproduction

kind cluster, agent-sandbox provider, quota `requests.cpu: 10m` in the sandbox namespace:

```
$ time curl -X POST $SERVER/v1/sandboxes -H 'OPEN-SANDBOX-API-KEY: …' \
    -d '{"image":{"uri":"…"},"resourceLimits":{"cpu":"1","memory":"2Gi"}}'

{"code":"KUBERNETES::POD_READY_TIMEOUT","message":"Timeout waiting for sandbox … Elapsed: 180.1s, Last state: Pending"}
HTTP 504 — 180.2s total

Server log at t+1s (the cause was already visible):
INFO Sandbox <id> state: Pending - Error seen: pods "…" is forbidden: exceeded quota: …
```

## Why #1722 doesn't cover this

#1722 (propagate terminal Pod failures) keys on Pod `phase=Failed` / container exit. A quota rejection happens **before the Pod object exists** — the CR stays `Ready=False/ReconcilerError`, which `agent_sandbox_provider.get_status` classifies as `Pending`, so the request still blind-waits to `POD_READY_TIMEOUT`.

This looks like the same family as #1175 (missing poolRef → fail fast) and #1578 (pool capacity exhaustion → surface instead of timeout); this variant (namespace ResourceQuota) is the remaining uncovered case we could find.

## Suggested fix

In `_wait_for_sandbox_ready`, treat `ReconcilerError` conditions whose message contains `exceeded quota` as terminal and fail fast with a structured 4xx (e.g. `403 KUBERNETES::QUOTA_EXCEEDED` carrying the K8s message). Other `ReconcilerError` messages should keep polling — they can be transient. Additionally, map the synchronous 403 quota rejection on CR create to the same clean error instead of 500.

## Evidence from our side

- Scanned upstream issues/PRs (open+closed) for quota / `exceeded quota` / `ReconcilerError` / `POD_READY_TIMEOUT` / fail-fast: no existing report of this variant (per CONTRIBUTING's search-first requirement).
- We have a working patch on our fork (unit tests + live-cluster verification: 180.2s/504 → 0.17s/403 for the compute variant; 500 → 0.07s/403 for the count variant) and are happy to open a PR if the maintainers agree with the approach — including the preferred error-code shape (`KUBERNETES::QUOTA_EXCEEDED` vs reusing an existing code).

title: SDK connect/resume fails before the readiness timeout when endpoints are not yet available
body:
## Why do you need it?

Connecting to a starting Kubernetes sandbox can fail immediately even when the caller provides a 30-second readiness timeout. The SDK resolves the required endpoints before starting health polling, so the timeout does not cover endpoint publication.

A sandbox may already exist, or even report `Running`, while its Pod IP is temporarily unavailable. During this window, the endpoint API returns HTTP 404 with:

```json
{
  "code": "KUBERNETES::POD_IP_NOT_AVAILABLE",
  "message": "Pod IP is not yet available. The Pod may still be starting."
}
```

This affects Python (async and sync), Go, JavaScript, Kotlin, and C#. It also occurs when reconnecting after resume, when endpoints may change.

To reproduce:

1. Create or resume a Kubernetes sandbox.
2. Call the SDK's connect method with a 30-second readiness timeout while the Pod IP is still unavailable.
3. If the first endpoint request returns `404 / KUBERNETES::POD_IP_NOT_AVAILABLE`, connect fails immediately instead of waiting within the configured timeout.
4. Retry manually after the Pod IP becomes available; the connection succeeds.

Callers consequently need their own retry loop around connect, matching a Kubernetes-specific error code. The SDK should handle this temporary startup condition within its existing readiness timeout.

## How could it be?

The configured readiness timeout should cover waiting for required endpoints as well as health checks. With a 30-second timeout, connect should tolerate temporary endpoint unavailability and succeed if the sandbox becomes ready within those 30 seconds.

The same behavior should apply when reconnecting after resume. Errors such as a missing sandbox or denied access should still fail immediately, and callers should be able to cancel the wait.

## Other related information

The current workaround is to catch `KUBERNETES::POD_IP_NOT_AVAILABLE` and retry connect in an application-level loop until an outer timeout expires. Every caller has to repeat this handling even though the SDK already exposes a readiness timeout.

title: fix(kubernetes): fail sandbox when main container terminates without restart

labels.name: size/M
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 30-99 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Problem

When a BatchSandbox pod's main container exits with a non-zero code while the pod stays in Kubernetes phase `Running` (e.g. an egress sidecar keeps the pod alive under `restartPolicy: Never`, so the pod can never reach phase `Failed`), the controller does not detect a terminal failure. With `status.Ready` at 0 and no failure classified, `applySteadyRuntimePhase` regresses the sandbox phase from `Succeed` back to `Pending` instead of `Failed`.

## Fix

`getTerminalPodFailureReasonAndMessage` now treats a non-zero termination of the sandbox's main container — the first regular container (`spec.containers[0]`, the server-side convention: main `sandbox` container with `execd-installer` as an init container and `egress` appended last) — as terminal when `restartPolicy: Never` will not restart it, even while the pod is still `Running`.

`Always`/`OnFailure` pods are excluded: the kubelet restarts the container there, and a transient termination must not brick the sandbox in the sticky `Failed` phase. The existing `PodFailed` condition reason `ContainerFailed` is reused, so the terminal-failure condition gate and server-side phase mapping are unaffected.

## Verification

- New unit tests: Running pod + terminated main container under `Never` → `Failed`; same pod under `""`/`Always`/`OnFailure` → not terminal.
- Existing terminal-failure / pause-resume unit tests pass.
- Docs updated (`docs/kubernetes/index.md` `Failed` phase row).

## What

Two logical commits to cut kubernetes CI runtime and remove dead test/comment cruft.

### 1. ci(kubernetes): trim PR e2e matrix and skip unused e2e assets

- **PR e2e matrix**: `controller-e2e-core` on PRs now runs only the boundary Kubernetes versions (`1.22.4 / 1.28.6 / 1.34.2`, was 8 versions). The full 7-version sweep (min `1.22.4`, `1.21.1` dropped) moved to a new nightly job `controller-e2e-core-matrix` in `kubernetes-nightly-build.yml` (schedule + workflow_dispatch only). PauseResume job untouched.
- **Unit test job**: dropped the redundant `make build`/`make task-executor-build` steps — `make test` already regenerates manifests and compiles every package (incl. `cmd/controller`, `cmd/task-executor`).
- **e2e BeforeSuite**: only provisions pause/resume assets (image-committer build, in-cluster registry, alpine) when the PauseResume label is in the run (`E2E_LABEL_FILTER` plumbed through the Makefile e2e targets). Core-only runs skip them.
