title: Readiness polling can overshoot the timeout by one full polling interval (Go, Kotlin, JS, C# SDKs)
body:
## Why do you need it?

The Python SDK used to wait for the full polling interval after the last unsuccessful health check, even when the readiness timeout had already expired. With a 10 ms timeout and a 200 ms polling interval, a failing sandbox took about 200 ms to report `SandboxReadyTimeoutException` instead of ~10 ms.

That was fixed for Python in https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/pull/1734 (bounded sleep + monotonic deadline), but the equivalent loops in the other SDKs still exhibit the same overshoot:

| SDK | Location | Deadline source | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Go | `sdks/sandbox/go/sandbox.go` `WaitUntilReady` (deadline at line ~345, `time.After(interval)` at ~375) | wall clock `time.Now()` | final failed check sleeps a full interval before the loop exits |
| Kotlin | `sdks/sandbox/kotlin/sandbox/src/main/kotlin/com/alibaba/opensandbox/sandbox/Sandbox.kt` `checkReady` (deadline ~701, `Thread.sleep(pollingInterval.toMillis())` at ~731) | wall clock `System.currentTimeMillis()` | final failed check sleeps a full interval before the loop exits |
| JavaScript | `sdks/sandbox/javascript/src/sandbox.ts` `waitUntilReady` (deadline ~794, `sleep(pollingIntervalMillis)` at ~832) | wall clock `Date.now()` | deadline is checked before each attempt; after the final failed check the full interval is slept before the deadline is re-checked |
| C# | `sdks/sandbox/csharp/src/OpenSandbox/Sandbox.cs` `WaitUntilReadyAsync` (deadline ~808, `Task.Delay(PollingIntervalMillis)` at ~850) | wall clock `DateTime.UtcNow` | deadline is checked before each attempt; after the final failed check the full interval is slept before the deadline is re-checked |

Note: these SDKs also use wall-clock deadlines; NTP/clock adjustments can make the wait effectively unbounded. The Python fix switched to a monotonic clock (`time.monotonic()`).

## How could it be?

Mirror the Python fix in each SDK, keeping the public signatures, success path, and timeout exception behavior unchanged:

1. Compute the deadline with a monotonic clock where the platform offers one (`time.Now()` in Go is not monotonic for comparisons with `time.Since`-style logic; use `time.Now()` + a `<-time.After(...)` bounded by the remaining budget, e.g. clamp the delay with `time.Until(deadline)`; JS: `performance.now()` or keep `Date.now()` but clamp the sleep; Kotlin: `System.nanoTime()`; C#: `Environment.TickCount64` or `Stopwatch`).
2. After each unsuccessful check, clamp the next sleep to the remaining budget: `min(polling_interval, deadline - now)`.
3. Keep the timeout exception message and attempt-count reporting compatible.
4. Add a regression test per SDK proving that with `timeout < polling_interval` the call fails in ~`timeout`, not `timeout + polling_interval`.

## Other related information

- Reference fix: https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/pull/1734 (`sdks/sandbox/python/src/opensandbox/sandbox.py`, `sdks/sandbox/python/src/opensandbox/sync/sandbox.py`)
- Behavior should stay aligned across languages per the repo's SDK guidelines (same readiness timeout semantics in every SDK).

title: dns+nft 下 OSSFS 连接超时是否与动态 DNS 放行有关？
body:
## 我们遇到的问题

### 域名与出口策略

我们在 `dns+nft`、`defaultAction=deny` 的出口策略下，通过域名规则允许 OSS 访问：

- allowlist 规则：`*.aliyuncs.com`
- OSSFS 配置的区域 endpoint：`oss-cn-zhangjiakou-internal.aliyuncs.com`
- 实际 Bucket 请求域名：`xxxx.oss-cn-zhangjiakou-internal.aliyuncs.com`

按照我们对 OpenSandbox 域名匹配逻辑的理解，这两个 OSS 域名应该都在 `*.aliyuncs.com` 的覆盖范围内。我们暂时没有发现还缺少其他 OSS 域名，但不确定这里的理解是否正确。

### OSSFS 现场表现

- OSSFS 挂载和初始访问能够成功，并不是从启动开始就完全不可用。
- 运行一段时间后，OSSFS 元数据查询开始长时间无响应，日志反复出现 `send header failed errno=110 (Connection timed out)`、重试以及 `connection timedout`。
- 调用方对 OSSFS 挂载目录执行同步 `stat` 时，我们看到线程停在 `vfs_statx -> fuse_lookup_name -> request_wait_answer`。从这个现象看，当时的文件查询似乎仍在等待 FUSE 用户态文件系统返回。
- 单次上层请求会先超时返回，但我们观察到底层 OSSFS 查询和重试仍可能继续数分钟；同一时期，依赖该挂载目录的后续请求也出现了等待或超时。
- 故障期间，我们主动触发了一次上述 OSS endpoint 的系统 DNS 解析。此后，到相同 OSS 地址的连接和已经阻塞的文件查询曾暂时恢复；没有继续触发 DNS 解析时，复用缓存地址的新连接稍后又出现超时。我们无法确认 DNS 查询与恢复之间是否存在直接因果关系。
- 现场 OSSFS 版本为 `2.0.7`。在我们抽样查看的日志里，没有看到 OSS 明确返回 `403` 等权限错误，主要看到的是连接和请求头发送超时；这不代表已经排除了所有权限或网络因素。

目前我们还没有取得对应时段动态 nftables 条目的添加、续租、过期和丢弃计数，也没有确认现场 egress 组件的准确版本。因此，上述内容只是我们观察到的现象，并不是已经闭环的根因结论。

## 我们的怀疑

我们怀疑，这个问题可能与 DNS 响应生成的动态 nftables IP 条目和 OSSFS 内部 DNS 缓存的生命周期不一致有关。一种可能性是：动态条目已经失效，但 OSSFS 仍在复用缓存 IP，没有再次发起 DNS 查询，因此后续新连接没有触发动态规则更新并发生超时。新的 DNS 查询可能重新填充了相关动态规则，从而解释暂时恢复的现象，但我们目前没有 nftables 记录可以验证这一点。

我们查看了 OSSFS `2.0.7` 及其 Photon HTTP 客户端的公开代码。我们的理解是，Photon 存在相对较长的 DNS 缓存；部分连接失败路径会清理 DNS 缓存，但请求头发送失败的重试路径似乎不一定触发同样的清理。不确定这一实现是否与我们观察到的现象有关：

- [OSSFS 2.0.7 依赖声明](https://github.com/aliyun/ossfs/blob/v2.0.7/dependencies/CMakeLists.txt)
- [Photon HTTP 客户端](https://github.com/alibaba/PhotonLibOS/blob/v0.9.3/net/http/client.cpp)
- [Photon DNS 缓存实现](https://github.com/alibaba/PhotonLibOS/blob/v0.9.3/net/utils.cpp)

我们注意到这个现象与 #1398 以及修复它的 #1399 比较相似。按照我们对 #1399 的理解，它会轮询活跃 TCP 连接并续租相应的 DNS 动态地址。我们不确定以下情况是否都在它的覆盖范围内：

- 客户端在较长空闲期内没有可被轮询到的活跃 TCP 连接，但仍保留 DNS 缓存；
- 短连接恰好在两次轮询之间建立并结束；
- 最后一次连接结束后的续租宽限期已经过去，但客户端 DNS 缓存仍未失效；
- 现场部署的 egress 组件可能尚未包含 #1399。

我们目前无法判断这是现场版本尚未包含 #1399，还是“没有活跃连接但客户端仍持有缓存地址”这一场景可能存在未覆盖的边界。希望确认我们的理解是否合理，以及这些现象是否可能由同一机制解释。

`RunCommandOpts.timeout` (used by `CommandsAdapter.run` / `Sandbox.run`) had no negative-timeout validation, unlike `run_in_session`'s `_resolve_run_in_session_timeout`. Negative `timedelta` values were silently converted to millisecond integers and sent to the server:

title: python-sdk: negative timedelta in RunCommandOpts.timeout is silently accepted and sent to server
body:
## Summary

The Python sandbox SDK validates negative timeouts for `run_in_session`, but the `run_command` path (`CommandsAdapter.run_command` / `Sandbox.run` via `RunCommandOpts.timeout`) has no negative-timeout validation at all. Negative `timedelta` values are silently converted to millisecond integers and sent to the server.

This is the sibling of the issue fixed in https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/pull/1726 (which only covered `run_in_session`).

## Location

`sdks/sandbox/python/src/opensandbox/adapters/converter/execution_converter.py` line ~62:

```python
timeout_milliseconds = UNSET
if opts.timeout is not None:
    timeout_milliseconds = int(opts.timeout.total_seconds() * 1000)
```

`RunCommandOpts.timeout` (`sdks/sandbox/python/src/opensandbox/models/execd.py`) is a free-form `timedelta | None` with no validator.

## Why it is a problem

1. `int(...)` truncates toward zero, so negative sub-millisecond durations such as `timedelta(microseconds=-1)` become `0` ms and are sent as if no/zero timeout.
2. Whole-millisecond negative durations such as `timedelta(milliseconds=-1)` are converted to `-1` ms and sent as-is to the server, which may reject the request server-side with a confusing error or behave unexpectedly.

Users get no client-side `InvalidArgumentException` explaining the mistake.

## Repro

```python
from datetime import timedelta
from opensandbox import RunCommandOpts  # or via CommandsAdapter.run_command opts

opts = RunCommandOpts(timeout=timedelta(milliseconds=-1))
# -> silently becomes timeout_ms = -1 in the API request
```

## Expected behavior

Match `_resolve_run_in_session_timeout` in `opensandbox/adapters/command_adapter.py` (and the sync counterpart): reject `timeout < timedelta(0)` with `InvalidArgumentException("timeout must be positive")` before converting to milliseconds, in both the async and sync adapters.

## Suggested approach

- Add a check in `ExecutionConverter.to_api_run_command_request` (or a model validator on `RunCommandOpts.timeout`) mirroring the fix in PR #1726.
- Add regression tests: `timedelta(microseconds=-1)`, `timedelta(microseconds=-999)`, `timedelta(milliseconds=-1)` should all raise `InvalidArgumentException` and no HTTP request should be sent.
- Verify async and sync paths (`test_command_service_adapter_streaming.py` / `test_sync_command_service_adapter_streaming.py` and the non-streaming command adapter tests).

## Notes

- Behavior should be mirrored in the sync adapter (`opensandbox/sync/adapters/command_adapter.py`).
- No impact on `None`, zero, or positive values.

title: fix(server): relay client websocket closes with a legal code

labels.name: size/S
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 10-29 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
# Summary

- Translate the ASGI `websocket.disconnect` code into a transmittable WebSocket close code before relaying it to the sandbox backend.
- Keep normal, application-defined and other externally valid codes exactly as the client sent them.
- Add regression tests for both the new boundary helper and the client relay loop.

## Problem

When a browser calls `ws.close()` with no status code, the Close frame it sends carries an empty payload. Uvicorn reports that to the app as `{"type": "websocket.disconnect", "code": 1005}`, and it reports a dropped connection as `1006`. RFC 6455 7.4.1 reserves both codes for local use and forbids them on the wire.

`_relay_client_messages()` in `server/opensandbox_server/api/proxy.py` passed that code straight into `backend.close()`. Serializing it fails, so `websockets` raises `ProtocolError: invalid status code`. The exception escaped the relay task, tore down the proxy task group, and came out the other side as an `Unexpected websocket proxy failure` traceback plus a `1011` close to a client that had already gone. The backend never learned why its peer disappeared, and the most common way a browser closes a WebSocket logged an error every time.

## Root cause

Two call sites relayed the raw code: the `websocket.disconnect` branch (`proxy.py:448`, `code=message.get("code", ...)`) and the `WebSocketDisconnect` handler (`proxy.py:454`, `code=exc.code`).

The mirrored direction was already fixed. `_relay_backend_messages()` runs every backend code through `_client_websocket_close_code()` before closing the client. The client-to-backend direction had no equivalent.

## Change

Add `_backend_websocket_close_code()` next to the existing helper and route both close paths through it.

- Codes in `EXTERNAL_CLOSE_CODES` and application codes `3000-4999` pass through unchanged.
- `1005` maps to `1000`: the client did send a Close frame, it just carried no status.
- Everything else reserved or out of range, including `1006` and `1015`, maps to `1001`, because from the backend's point of view the peer went away without a clean close.
- A missing code still maps to `1000`, as before.

## Testing

`_RecordingBackendWebSocket.close()` in the new tests calls `Close(code, reason).serialize()`, the same trick the existing backend-to-client test uses, so an illegal relayed code fails deterministically instead of silently passing.

- `uv run pytest tests/test_routes_proxy.py -q` gives `115 passed`. On `main` the two new relay cases fail with `websockets.exceptions.ProtocolError: invalid status code`.
- `uv run pytest -q --cov=opensandbox_server --cov-report=term --cov-fail-under=80` gives `1670 passed, 16 skipped`, total coverage `82.57%`.
- `uv run ruff check` gives `All checks passed!`.
- `uv run pyright opensandbox_server/api/proxy.py tests/test_routes_proxy.py` gives `0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 informations`.
- `./scripts/verify-license.sh` gives `License headers verified.`, and `git diff --check` is clean.
- Manual check against a real peer: I ran `_relay_client_messages()` against a live `websockets` server and fed it each disconnect code. Before the change, `1005`, `1006`, `1015` and `999` all raised `ProtocolError` and the server saw no Close frame. After it, the server observes `1000`, `1001`, `1001` and `1001`, while `1000`, `1001` and `4001` arrive unchanged.

`uv run ruff format --check` reports drift on both files, but it reports the same drift on `main`; the reformatting it wants is in unrelated lines, so this change leaves that baseline alone. CI runs `ruff check`, not `ruff format`.

No HTTP API, OpenAPI, SDK, config or Kubernetes change. Close codes that were already legal on the wire are relayed exactly as before; only the codes that could never be sent change.

title: fix(kubernetes): propagate terminal Pod failures

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
# Summary

- propagate a Kubernetes Pod in terminal `Failed` phase into `BatchSandbox.status.phase=Failed` with a stable `PodFailed` reason/message, including the failing init-container or container exit code
- keep initial scheduling waits and retryable image-pull states in `Pending`, and preserve `status.taskFailed` as the failed optional-task count
- stop standalone Pod replacement only after a terminal Pod failure has been recorded, while retaining normal expected-state replacement for other missing Pods
- make synchronous Server creation fail immediately with the existing `KUBERNETES::POD_FAILED` error instead of waiting for `KUBERNETES::POD_READY_TIMEOUT`

## Root cause and state-machine boundary

The Controller's failure detector only inspected `containerStatuses[*].state.waiting` for selected reasons. It did not inspect `pod.status.phase=Failed` or terminated init-container statuses. A Pod whose init container exited non-zero with `restartPolicy: Never` therefore left its owning BatchSandbox in `Pending` (`ready=0`) even though Kubernetes had already made the Pod terminal.

The Server already mapped `BatchSandbox.status.phase=Failed` to public state `Failed`, but its synchronous readiness loop only returned on Running/Allocated and special-cased platform scheduling failures. Generic terminal failures continued polling until the full readiness timeout.

This change uses Kubernetes Pod phase as the terminal boundary:

- `PodFailed`: terminal; surface `InitContainerFailed`, `ContainerFailed`, or `PodFailed` details and retain the failed state.
- ordinary Pending, scheduler waits, `ErrImagePull`, and `ImagePullBackOff` during initial provisioning: retryable; remain Pending.
- missing Pods without a recorded terminal failure: continue to reconcile toward `spec.replicas`.
- missing Pods after a recorded terminal failure: do not recreate and hide the original error; delete/recreate the BatchSandbox to retry.

`status.taskFailed` is intentionally not overloaded: it remains the number of failed optional tasks, while Pod failures use `status.phase` and the `PodFailed` condition.

## Minimal reproduction

Create a standalone BatchSandbox with one replica, `restartPolicy: Never`, and an init container that exits `1`. Before this change, the Pod reaches `phase: Failed` while the BatchSandbox remains `Pending`, and Server creation ends only at the readiness timeout. After this change, the BatchSandbox reports `Failed` with the init-container exit details and the Server returns `KUBERNETES::POD_FAILED` on the first failed-status observation.

## Why this is not a DELETE 204 leak

This PR does not change deletion, finalizers, owner references, or garbage collection. In the observed sequence, an unauthenticated DELETE was rejected; a subsequent authenticated DELETE returned 204, and follow-up reads found the Sandbox and owned Kubernetes resources gone. The defect addressed here is the pre-delete failure-status path and the replacement race while the owner CR still exists, not resource leakage after a successful DELETE.

title: Kubernetes snapshots should fail closed for gVisor RuntimeClasses
body:
## Description

The Kubernetes snapshot runtime currently reports `supports_create_snapshot() == true` for every Kubernetes-backed sandbox. The built-in `rootfs-v1` image committer then assumes that the source workload is compatible with containerd task pause/resume and writable-snapshot image creation.

That assumption does not hold for gVisor (`RuntimeClass` handler `runsc`). A gVisor sandbox can be healthy and `Running`, while the public snapshot request is accepted and only fails later in the commit Job.

Current `upstream/main` at `17b00f87281309db694da3e1fcec55a11d75dfed` still has the unconditional capability response, and the gVisor e2e suite covers RuntimeClass execution but not snapshot creation.

## Reproduction

1. Configure the Kubernetes Server to create sandboxes with a `RuntimeClass` whose handler is `runsc`.
2. Create a sandbox and wait for it to reach `Running`.
3. Call `POST /sandboxes/{sandboxId}/snapshots`.
4. Observe `202 Accepted` and a persisted snapshot in `Creating`.
5. The `SandboxSnapshot` commit Job retries and eventually fails. A representative committer error is:

   ```text
   no running task found
   ```

   The Job may reach `BackoffLimitExceeded`; cleanup of the source Pod can also be delayed while the runtime recovers from the failed pause/commit attempt.

The public snapshot metadata store and terminal `Failed` convergence can remain healthy, so this is a runtime data-plane compatibility gap rather than a persistence failure.

## Expected behavior

Before persisting a public snapshot record or creating a `SandboxSnapshot` CR, the Server should inspect the source workload's effective `RuntimeClass` and fail closed when the handler is `runsc`.

The rejection should:

- return a clear conflict/unsupported-runtime error;
- create no public snapshot record;
- create no `SandboxSnapshot` or commit Job;
- leave the running source sandbox untouched.

Non-gVisor Kubernetes workloads should keep the current snapshot behavior.

## Scope

This issue's minimal fix is a runtime capability/preflight guard. Native gVisor checkpoint/restore needs a separate backend design covering checkpoint format, restore semantics, kernel/runsc compatibility, artifact lifecycle, and dedicated e2e coverage; it is intentionally out of scope for the guard PR.

title: [MCP] opensandbox-mcp 0.1.1 is incompatible with mcp 2.x
body:
## Problem

Installing `opensandbox-mcp` from PyPI without an explicit MCP version constraint resolves `mcp==2.1.1`, but `opensandbox-mcp==0.1.1` imports the removed/changed MCP 1.x API:

```python
from mcp.server.fastmcp import Context, FastMCP
```

With `mcp==2.1.1`, running the CLI fails immediately with:

```text
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mcp.server.fastmcp'. This is mcp 2.x, where FastMCP was renamed to MCPServer...
```

## Environment

- macOS Apple Silicon
- Python 3.13
- `opensandbox-mcp==0.1.1`
- `opensandbox==0.1.16`
- `mcp==2.1.1` (resolved by default)
- Installed with `uv tool install opensandbox-mcp`

## Reproduction

```bash
uv tool install opensandbox-mcp
opensandbox-mcp --domain 172.18.82.40 --protocol http
```

This installs `mcp==2.1.1` and fails during import.

As a workaround, pinning MCP to v1 works:

```bash
uv tool install opensandbox-mcp --with 'mcp<2' --force
opensandbox-mcp --domain 172.18.82.40 --protocol http
```

This resolves to `mcp==1.29.1` and the server starts successfully.

## Questions

1. Is `opensandbox-mcp` planned to support MCP 2.x?
2. If yes, is there a target release/version for the migration?
3. Should `opensandbox-mcp==0.1.1` declare an upper bound such as `mcp<2` until MCP 2.x support is available, so a fresh installation does not resolve to an incompatible dependency?
4. Is the current GitHub `main` branch already migrated, while the PyPI `0.1.1` package is behind?

The current documentation shows `opensandbox-mcp` supports Streamable HTTP, so clarification on the supported MCP SDK version would also be helpful.

Thanks!

title: fix(server): coordinate snapshot recovery across replicas

labels.name: size/XXL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 1000+ lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
# Summary

- Add persistent operation generation, attempt, owner, and expiry fields to the PostgreSQL snapshot repository.
- Claim, renew, complete, and delete operations with short database transactions and owner/generation fencing; runtime work never holds a database transaction open.
- Run periodic recovery so an already-running standby Server can take over `Creating` and `Deleting` work after lease expiry.
- Make Kubernetes snapshot recovery observe the deterministic `SandboxSnapshot` before create, then validate and follow the winner of any create race.
- Fail closed in Helm unless `server.replicaCount > 1` explicitly declares the supported PostgreSQL-plus-Kubernetes topology, and change the safe default from two Server replicas to one.

Fixes #1654.

# Coordination model

Each snapshot operation is claimed before external runtime side effects. The repository atomically increments `operation_generation`, assigns `lease_owner`, and sets `lease_expires_at`; the fenced worker increments `operation_attempt` immediately before runtime side effects begin. Active workers renew their lease while runtime work is in progress. A terminal update or metadata delete succeeds only while the same owner and generation still hold an unexpired lease.

A periodic recovery scan allows another active Server to claim expired work. Within one process, work still executing locally is excluded from takeover even if its database lease has elapsed; after that worker exits, recovery reconciles the result. A stale cross-process worker can still finish an external call, but its database write is fenced out. This provides one current owner, takeover after expiry, observe-before-create runtime recovery, and one fenced terminal database result.

# Runtime boundaries

- PostgreSQL plus the Kubernetes runtime supports multiple active Server replicas for public snapshots.
- Kubernetes uses the stable snapshot ID-derived CR name. Recovery reads that CR first, follows an existing commit, and creates only after the live API confirms absence. A create race still validates the source sandbox.
- SQLite remains single-active and the chart prevents the unsafe default topology.
- Docker snapshot execution remains single-active. PostgreSQL fencing cannot safely fence Docker image or registry side effects across hosts.
- This is not an exactly-once claim across PostgreSQL, Kubernetes, the controller, and the OCI registry.
- No session affinity is added or required for the supported PostgreSQL and Kubernetes topology.

# Schema, migration, and rollback

The PostgreSQL schema upgrade is additive and serialized by the existing schema advisory lock. Existing rows receive zero generation and no owner; legacy unfinished `Creating` rows are conservatively assigned one attempt so recovery observes rather than repeats possible side effects. The SQLite-to-PostgreSQL migration preserves counters when present but clears source owner and expiry before cutover.

Older Server versions ignore the new columns. Before rolling back the Server version, operators must return to one active replica because older versions do not enforce operation ownership. The one-shot migration remains one-way.

# Testing

- [x] Unit tests: local full Server suite, `1681 passed, 26 skipped`.
- [x] Static checks: full Ruff and file-scoped Pyright for every changed Server source file, zero errors.
- [x] Kubernetes runtime tests: existing CR observation, confirmed-missing create, shared-deadline enforcement before create and existing-CR follow-up, create-race winner validation, deterministic name behavior.
- [x] Repository and service tests added for one-winner claim, fenced runtime-start marking, renew, expiry, takeover, queued never-started creation, stale completion and deletion rejection, legacy schema upgrade, two-Server get/list/restore, and already-running standby takeover of both `Creating` and `Deleting`.

# Summary

Closes #1688.

When running `opensandbox-server` with the Docker runtime in `bridge` network mode, `allocate_host_port()` probes port availability with `socket.bind()` inside the server's own process. When the server runs inside a container (e.g. standard `docker-compose` topology) or on hosts with excluded/reserved port ranges (such as Docker Desktop on Windows with WinNAT reservations), this in-process bind probe only verifies availability inside the server container's network namespace and cannot detect port conflicts on the Docker host.

If `container.start()` subsequently fails because the allocated host port is already bound on the host or forbidden, `_create_and_start_container` cleans up the failed container, but `create_sandbox` previously treated this as terminal and raised an HTTP 500 (`DOCKER::SANDBOX_START_FAILED`) immediately without retrying.

This PR adds:
- `is_port_publish_error(exc)` in `port_allocator.py` to identify Docker daemon port conflict and permission errors (`port is already allocated`, `ports are not available`, `bind: forbidden`, `bind: permission denied`, `address already in use`).
- Bounded retry (up to `MAX_PORT_PUBLISH_ATTEMPTS = 3`) during sandbox container creation in bridge mode when no egress sidecar is configured:
  - Releases previously reserved ports before drawing new ones.
  - Re-allocates fresh host ports and updates host configuration bindings and container port labels.
  - Retries container create and start.
- Unit tests covering:
  - `is_port_publish_error` pattern matching across various error formats (plain exception, chained `__cause__`, `HTTPException` detail).
  - Successful sandbox creation after retrying on host port conflict.
  - Raising `HTTPException` when retries are exhausted.
  - Immediate failure without retry on non-port errors.

title: Add credential-bound TLS interception for Credential Vault
body:
## Why do you need it?

Credential Proxy currently redirects every outbound connection on its configured HTTP(S) ports into mitmproxy. For HTTPS, binding selection runs in the system addon's `requestheaders` hook, after the TLS ClientHello and TLS termination. A request that matches no Credential Vault binding is forwarded unchanged, but its TLS session has already been decrypted and the client still has to trust the OpenSandbox-generated CA.

That scope is broader than credential injection requires. A sandbox may need a credential for one model API while also calling package registries, documentation sites, source hosts, or certificate-pinned services. Today those unrelated HTTPS destinations are decrypted even though no credential can be injected into them.

Static mitmproxy `ignore_hosts` can preserve opaque TLS, but it is operator-owned image/ConfigMap configuration. It cannot follow sandbox-local binding mutations or vary per subject in the fleet egress profile.

Current behavior is visible in:

- [configured-port interception](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/components/egress/pkg/iptables/transparent.go)
- [binding selection after TLS termination](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/components/egress/mitmscripts/system.py)
- [static `ignore_hosts` guidance](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/components/egress/docs/mitmproxy-transparent.md)
- [unmatched requests are forwarded unchanged](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/docs/guides/credential-vault.md)

## How could it be?

Add an opt-in create-time mode while preserving current behavior by default:

```json
{
  "credentialProxy": {
    "enabled": true,
    "interceptionMode": "credential-bound"
  }
}
```

- `all` (default): current intercept-all behavior.
- `credential-bound`: on HTTPS/443, decrypt only when visible SNI matches a host selector from an active binding that is eligible for HTTPS/443. Other visible-SNI TLS is passed through opaquely.
- Static `ignore_hosts` and existing no-SNI pass-through retain precedence.
- ECH-hidden/no-SNI traffic remains opaque and never receives credentials.
- SNI only decides whether decryption is needed. The existing full scheme/host/method/path binding selection must still authorize injection after decryption.

Before implementation, the design needs explicit contracts for:

1. **Authoritative state**: distinguish bootstrapping or control failure from an acknowledged empty binding revision; unknown state must not silently become pass-through.
2. **Atomic revisions**: install immutable TLS-decision and request-binding state together, with idempotent prepare/commit/abort/readback and an indeterminate-result recovery path.
3. **Runtime mutation**: close existing opaque connections when a host becomes bound; fence new requests and drain existing decrypted connections when the final binding is removed.
4. **Concurrency**: serialize policy, vault, replay, and unload changes per sandbox/subject; require `expectedRevision` for Credential Vault PATCH in this mode.
5. **Fleet isolation**: key snapshots and live connections by generation-fenced subject identity so the same SNI can decrypt for one subject and pass through for another.
6. **Destination identity**: complete the existing SNI/original-destination/HTTP-authority hardening before enabling the mode; SNI must never become credential-injection authorization.
7. **Telemetry**: bounded-cardinality decrypt/pass-through/deny and transition metrics, without credential values or hostname labels.
8. **Compatibility**: keep `all` as the default, make mode immutable for a runtime generation, reject unsupported extra-port/runtime combinations, and expose the public field only after HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, sidecar, and fleet semantics are complete.

## Other related information

- Transparent mitmproxy: #615
- Static YAML `ignore_hosts`: #975
- Credential Vault design and implementation: #955, #1009
- Dynamic HTTP credential source (separate concern): #1188
- No-SNI pass-through: #1469
- Destination-identity hardening: #1193
- Fail-closed active-vault lookup: #1636
- Fleet shared MITM data plane: #1633

I did not find an existing open or closed Issue, PR, Discussion, release note, or commit that derives the TLS decrypt/pass-through decision from the active sandbox-local or subject-local binding host set. A Draft OSEP will follow to define lifecycle, concurrency, revocation, telemetry, compatibility, security, and phased rollout before any data-plane behavior changes.

title: [Bug] Execd silently skips Chromium NSS trust when certutil is unavailable
body:
## Description

When transparent MITM is enabled, `components/execd/bootstrap.sh` calls `trust_mitm_ca_nss` so Chromium and Chrome can trust the exported CA through the per-user NSS database. If `certutil` is not on `PATH`, the helper currently returns success without any diagnostic.

The official execd Dockerfile also does not install Alpine's `nss-tools`, although #776 introduced the NSS import and its PR/release description stated that `nss-tools` would be installed.

## To reproduce

1. Use current `main` (`a8ad18fa741f9c50a552116c16d09ba4be385468`).
2. Run the `trust_mitm_ca_nss` path with an existing CA file and a valid `HOME`, but without `certutil` on `PATH`.
3. Observe that the helper returns success and writes nothing to stderr.

The same prerequisite gap is relevant to injected workload images: the Docker and Kubernetes runtime paths copy `execd`, `bootstrap.sh`, and static helpers from the execd image, but do not transfer distro-specific NSS packages or dynamic libraries into the workload image.

## Expected behavior

- The official execd image includes `certutil` for its Alpine base image.
- If an injected workload image does not provide `certutil`, bootstrap emits actionable package guidance while preserving best-effort startup.
- Documentation makes the image responsibility explicit.

## Actual behavior

NSS import is silently skipped. Chromium or Chrome can reject intercepted TLS even when system, Node, or JDK trust setup succeeds, leaving operators without a direct explanation.

## Suggested scope

- Install `nss-tools` in the official execd image.
- Warn when `certutil` is missing, while continuing startup.
- Document that custom workload images must install their native package (for example, `nss-tools` on Alpine or `libnss3-tools` on Debian/Ubuntu).
- Add focused bootstrap and image-contract regressions.

Non-goal: copying Alpine NSS dynamic libraries into arbitrary Debian/Ubuntu or other workload images.

title: execd: command output files and metadata grow without bound
body:
### Component

`execd` command runtime

### Version

Observed with execd 1.1.0 (`c39b814f36ded4c61d5ac6f9332ee4dfbab86c00`).

### Problem

Every foreground command creates `<command-id>.stdout` and `<command-id>.stderr` directly under the system temporary directory. The files remain after the SSE response completes. Background `.output` files and completed entries in `commandClientMap` also have no retention policy.

In a long-lived sandbox this accumulated to tens of thousands of files. Enumerating the temporary directory then took tens of seconds, while execd became intermittently slow or unresponsive. This is consistent with directory and metadata pressure, though the issue does not assume it is the only possible source of resource pressure.

### Reproduction

1. Start execd.
2. Execute many short foreground commands through `/code`.
3. After they finish, inspect the system temporary directory.
4. Observe one stdout/stderr pair per command and completed command metadata retained indefinitely.

### Expected behavior

- Remove foreground temporary output after streaming completes.
- Keep background output and completed status for a documented, bounded retention window.
- Never delete output for a running command.
- Clean up files left by older execd versions without scanning user directories.
- Keep command output in a dedicated temporary subdirectory so it does not inflate the shared temp-directory root.

I have a fix with tests and API documentation ready and will link the PR here.

title: fix(execd): clamp background log cursors to the end of the log

labels.name: size/S
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 10-29 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
# Summary

Refs #1010.

`SeekBackgroundCommandOutput` echoed a past-the-end cursor straight back to the caller: seeking past EOF succeeds on every platform, `io.ReadAll` returns nothing, and `Seek(0, io.SeekCurrent)` reports the *requested* offset rather than the real end of the log. A client that polls with a cursor at or beyond the tail therefore keeps an offset larger than the file, and every byte the command writes afterwards is skipped for good — the tail loop looks alive but never returns output again.

Case 3 of #1010 (`cursor = 10_000_000`) is exactly this. Cases 1 and 2 of that issue are the JS parser side, already fixed in 92094bdb.

This change:

- clamps the requested cursor to the current file size, so an overshooting poll returns empty output plus the real end offset, and the next poll picks up new output;
- rejects negative cursors with an explicit `cursor cannot be negative` error instead of leaking a platform-specific seek failure (`An attempt was made to move the file pointer before the beginning of the file`) through the 400 response;
- applies the same clamp to `SeekIsolatedBackgroundOutput`, which had the identical past-EOF behaviour (it already rejected negative cursors).

No API or contract change: `specs/execd-api.yaml` already documents `cursor` with `minimum: 0` and documents `EXECD-COMMANDS-TAIL-CURSOR` as the *highest available* index after applying the request cursor. Returning an offset past the end of the log contradicted that; this makes the implementation match the spec.

# Testing
- [x] Unit tests

```
# windows
go test ./pkg/runtime/ -run 'TestSeekBackgroundCommandOutput'
# linux (isolated tests are !windows)
go test ./pkg/runtime/ ./pkg/web/controller/
```

New cases:

- `TestSeekBackgroundCommandOutput_ClampsCursorPastEOF` — overshooting cursor returns `("", size)`, and output appended afterwards is still delivered on the next poll.
- `TestSeekBackgroundCommandOutput_RejectsNegativeCursor`
- `TestSeekIsolatedBackgroundOutput_ClampsCursorPastEOF`

Full `./pkg/runtime` and `./pkg/web/controller` pass, except the pre-existing `TestRunInIsolatedSessionBackground_RejectsUnwritableWorkspace` failure, which also fails on `main` in this environment (the workspace lives on a mount that does not enforce the unwritable bit).

# Breaking Changes
- [x] None

Clients that stored an out-of-range cursor now start receiving output again instead of silently starving; in-range cursors behave exactly as before.

# Checklist
- [x] Linked Issue or clearly described motivation
- [x] Added/updated docs (if needed) — behaviour now matches the existing spec wording, no spec change required
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Security impact considered — the clamp only narrows the read range; no new file access
- [x] Backward compatibility considered

## Follow-up (not in this PR)

`specs/execd-api.yaml` describes the `/command/{id}/logs` cursor as a "0-based line cursor" while the implementation (and the isolated-run endpoint) uses a byte offset. Worth correcting separately, since it also regenerates SDK typings.

body:
## Summary

When creating sandboxes with an egress sidecar on Docker Desktop for Windows (or other environments with OS-reserved excluded port ranges), `docker start` can fail with \`"ports are not available: ... bind: ... forbidden"\` even though the container-side port probe succeeded. The server currently raises a generic HTTP 500 without retrying — this PR adds a one-shot retry with freshly-allocated ports.

## Root Cause

`allocate_host_port()` in `port_allocator.py` probes availability with `socket.bind()` inside the server container (Linux network stack). On Docker Desktop/Windows the actual bind happens on the Windows host, where OS-reserved excluded port ranges (e.g. Hyper-V/WinNAT) make the bind fail with `WSAEACCES` — the container-side probe cannot see this.

`_start_egress_sidecar()` in `networking.py` only retried on the IPv6-sysctl rejection; any other `start()` failure (including `"ports are not available"`) cleaned up and raised HTTP 500 without re-allocating a new host port.

## Fix

- Added `_is_port_publish_error()` helper that detects `"ports are not available"` and `"bind:" + "forbidden"` patterns in Docker errors.
- When `start()` fails with a port-publish error and a `port_allocator` is wired in, re-allocate fresh ports, clean up the failed container, and retry create+start once.
- When the retry also fails with a port error, surface the real Docker error in the 500 detail instead of the generic message.
- Fixed a shallow-copy bug: `build_sidecar_host_config()` does `dict(base_sidecar_host_config_kwargs)`, which preserves the old `port_bindings` dict when `sidecar_port_bindings` is reassigned. The fix rebuilds `base_sidecar_host_config_kwargs` from scratch before the retry.

## Testing

- Added `test_egress_sidecar_retries_on_port_publish_error`: verifies that on a port-publish failure the sidecar is recreated with different ports and starts successfully.
- Added `test_egress_sidecar_raises_on_second_port_failure`: verifies that when both attempts fail, an HTTPException is raised with the real Docker error.
- All 146 tests in `test_docker_service.py` pass.
- `ruff check` passes on all changed files.

## Files Changed

- `server/opensandbox_server/services/docker/networking.py` — retry logic + `_is_port_publish_error`
- `server/opensandbox_server/services/docker/docker_service.py` — wire `port_allocator` at the call site
- `server/tests/test_docker_service.py` — two regression tests

Closes #1702

title: Port allocation race: concurrent sandbox creation fails with "port is already allocated"
body:
## Summary

With `runtime.type = "docker"` and `docker.network_mode = "bridge"`, concurrent sandbox creation
fails intermittently because the server hands out a host port that another in-flight creation is
already using. The failure surfaces to the caller as HTTP 500:

```
Failed to create or start container: 500 Server Error for
http+docker://localhost/v1.55/containers/<id>/start: Internal Server Error
("failed to set up container networking: driver failed programming external connectivity
 on endpoint sandbox-<uuid>: Bind for 0.0.0.0:41106 failed: port is already allocated")
```

The port appears to be **chosen at random from `docker.port_range_*` and then handed to Docker to
bind, with nothing reserving it in between**. Two creations racing between the pick and the bind get
the same port.

## Evidence: the failure rate follows the birthday paradox

Each sandbox consumes 2 host ports, so N concurrent creations draw 2N ports from the range. If the
draws are independent and unreserved, the expected number of collisions is `(2N)² / (2 · R)` for a
range of R ports. Measured on a single node, server `v0.2.3`, `secure_runtime.type = "gvisor"`:

| Concurrent creations | Draws | Range | Expected collisions | **Observed failures** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 20 | 1000 | 0.2 | 1 |
| 20 | 40 | 1000 | 0.8 | 1 |
| 30 | 60 | 1000 | 1.8 | 0 |
| 40 | 80 | 1000 | 3.2 | 2 |
| 60 | 120 | 1000 | 7.2 | **7** |
| 80 | 160 | 1000 | 12.8 | **15** |
| 80 | 160 | 7000 | 1.8 | **1** |

The model tracks the observations closely, including the drop after widening the range — which is
what one would expect if the allocator draws without reserving. At 80 concurrent creations on a
1000-port range, **19% of creations fail**.

Every failure carried the same message, with the port numbers spread across the whole range
(41011 … 41996) rather than clustered — consistent with random selection rather than
first-free scanning.

## Impact

Any workload that creates sandboxes concurrently. It is particularly visible in the
one-sandbox-per-conversation pattern, where several users starting at once each get a 500 with no
indication that a retry would succeed.

The server does clean up after a failed creation — no orphan containers were left behind in any of
the runs above.

## Suggested fix

Reserve the port between the pick and the bind. Two options, not exclusive:

1. **Track in-flight allocations.** Keep the set of ports handed out but not yet confirmed bound,
   guarded by the same lock that serves the allocation, and skip them when picking. Release on
   success or failure.
2. **Retry internally on the daemon's error.** When Docker returns
   `Bind for 0.0.0.0:<port> failed: port is already allocated`, pick another port and retry a
   bounded number of times, rather than surfacing a 500. This alone would make the symptom
   disappear, though option 1 is the actual fix.

## Workarounds available today

- **Widen `docker.port_range_min/max`.** Going from 1000 to 7000 ports took the failure rate from
  19% to 1.3% at 80 concurrent creations. Worth noting for anyone choosing a range: the upstream
  default `40000-60000` sits inside the Linux ephemeral port range
  (`net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range`, 32768-60999 by default), so published ports there can collide
  with the host's own outgoing connections. A range below 32768 avoids that.
- **Retry client-side on that specific error.** One retry draws a fresh port and is enough in
  practice. It should be matched on the message, not applied to every 500 — other create failures
  (missing image, resource limits) must not be retried.

title: egress fleet: replies to GUEST-originated (SNATed) flows intermittently lost while same-subject netns flows answer instantly
body:
### Title: egress fleet: replies to GUEST-originated (SNATed) flows intermittently lost while same-subject netns flows answer instantly

**Component**: components/egress (fleet profile)

**Environment**
- `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_PROFILE=fleet`, `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_MODE=dns+nft`, deployed host-process in a Kubernetes pod (fast-sandbox fastlet pod).
- Subjects are Firecracker guests (Alpine, `/etc/resolv.conf` → `nameserver <slot gateway>`). Guest traffic leaves the VM at `172.30.0.3`, is SNATed in the slot netns to the slot IP (e.g. `172.30.0.6`), and enters the egress plane via a veth on the egress bridge (`fsb0`, address `172.30.0.1`).
- Egress dispatches per-subject (`subj_s_<uid>`), redirects `gateway:53 -> :15353` (DNS proxy) and answers via upstream cluster DNS.

**Observed behavior (intermittent, minutes at a time; more likely right after whole-cluster / egress-instance recreation)**
- DNS (UDP:53) queries **originating inside the guest** reach the proxy and are REDIRECTed (pod-side conntrack shows the `src=.1 sport=15353` reply mapping), but **no reply ever arrives back in the slot/guest netns** for minutes: guest `nslookup`/`wget` hang until their own timeout.
- At the **same moment**, a query for the **same subject (same slot IP)** issued from the slot netns itself is answered immediately (deny → NXDOMAIN, allow → resolves). Deny subjects are equally silent during windows (deny also produces no NXDOMAIN), i.e. it is not an allow/deny logic issue.
- During the window the proxy keeps logging `egress outbound example.com target.ips=[...]` — **allow decisions are being made**.
- Both the egress-netns and slot-netns conntrack entries for the guest flow exist (with NAT/REDIRECT mappings) but stay **unassured** — the reply packet never enters the slot netns.
- Recovery is time-based (minutes); afterwards the full path works end-to-end (upstream resolution, reply delivered into the guest).
- Not reproducible on demand so far (several fresh-instance/subject attempts green); the only failing episodes followed whole-environment cold starts. A packet capture *during* an actual window has not yet been obtained.

**Code facts (read: fleetnft.go, refresh.go, gateway_dns.go, fleet_server.go, proxy.go)**
1. `serveDNS` replies to every handled query (deny → NXDOMAIN, nil selector → NXDOMAIN, upstream failure → SERVFAIL, success → answer). "Query received, no reply" therefore means either the query never reached `serveDNS`, or the reply dies in the kernel path between the proxy socket and the guest.
2. The dispatch chain accepts `ct state established,related` first; the query reached the proxy only after REDIRECT (nat table), which means its conntrack entry exists in the egress netns — so the reply cannot be dropped by the dispatch tail.
3. Combined with (1) and the outbound-event logs, the failure is between the proxy's reply write and the slot-netns ingress, and correlates with the **origin path of the query flow** (guest-originated: forwarded in from a sibling netns through the bridge after SNAT) vs netns-local (OUTPUT in the egress netns), both byte-identical at the egress netns.

**Minimal reproduction (standalone, no fast-sandbox)**
Topology of three netns on a Linux host:
```
netns G (guest) .3/29 ── veth(tap) ── netns S (slot) eth0 .6/24 ── veth ── bridge fsb0(.1) in netns E
                                        S: DNAT .6→.3, SNAT .3→.6       E: runs real egress (fleet, dns+nft)
                                        S: ip_forward, default via .1    E: resolv upstream = e.g. 223.5.5.5
```
Subject registration is the real protocol (captured from fast-sandbox → egress):
```json
POST /_fastlet/v1/actions
{"apiVersion":"sandbox.fast.io/actions/v1","operation":"SET_BINDING",
 "invocationId":"sha256:rep1",
 "sandbox":{"uid":"repro-uid-1","name":"sbx-r","namespace":"repro"},
 "revision":{"specGeneration":1,"runtimeInstanceId":"ri-1","attachmentId":"sha256:att1","routeGeneration":1},
 "attachment":{"network":{"ip":"172.30.0.6","gateway":"172.30.0.1","privateCidr":"172.30.0.0/24","hostVeth":"fh0"}},
 "binding":{"input":"{\"egress\":[{\"action\":\"allow\",\"target\":\"example.com\"}],\"defaultAction\":\"deny\"}"}}
```
followed by `LIFECYCLE_HOOK` `sandbox.runtime-ready` (sequence 1) and `sandbox.data-plane-ready` (sequence 2) — policy activates after the latter. `attachment.network.ip` is required (else 400 `attachment.network.ip is required`).

Repro loop (rebuild netns/egress between rounds to raise hit probability):
```
ip netns exec G timeout 6 nslookup example.com 172.30.0.1   # guest-origin
ip netns exec S timeout 6 nslookup example.com 172.30.0.1   # same subject, netns-local
# during a window: G times out, S answers; capture tcpdump + conntrack both sides + egress logs
```

**Fix suggestions (for discussion)**
1. Observability first: per-query logs in the DNS serve path (query id / subject / decision / reply-write ok|err) so windows are diagnosable in one shot.
2. Inspect the reply transmission path for flows whose first packet arrived via bridge forward (+ prior SNAT) vs OUTPUT: if replies are written via raw sockets (NET_RAW), prefer `connect()`ed UDP sockets (or otherwise let kernel NAT/route own delivery) so reply handling is symmetric regardless of origin hook path.
3. If subject "connection/refresh" state (30s buckets) gates answering, queue/hold first queries until state is ready instead of dropping them silently, and surface DNS-plane readiness separately from `status.ready` (today `ready=true` is not equivalent to "DNS serving").
4. fast-sandbox mitigation already applied: egress policy assertions now run from the subject netns (same subject identity, zero flakes); guest-executed end-to-end probes are gated until this is fixed.

title: egress sidecar start fails intermittently: host port probe misses OS-reserved ranges (Docker Desktop/Windows) and start failure is not retried with a new port
body:
## Summary

When creating sandboxes with an egress sidecar, the randomly allocated host publish port can land in an OS-reserved port range that is invisible from inside the server container. Docker then fails the `start` with `ports are not available` / `bind: ... forbidden by its access permissions`, the whole sandbox creation returns HTTP 500, and there is no retry with a different port.

## Environment

- OpenSandbox server 0.1.11 (Docker provider), running as a container
- Docker Desktop on Windows 11 (Linux containers) — host publish happens on the Windows host
- Multiple sandboxes created concurrently, `networkPolicy` requiring an egress sidecar (each sandbox needs 2+ host ports)

## Symptom

Sandbox creation intermittently fails (observed ~10–15% of concurrent batches), wrapped as:

```
Egress sidecar container failed to start.
```

Server logs (INFO/WARNING) show the real cause:

```
sandbox=44bee438-… | action=start egress sidecar | error=500 Server Error for http+docker://localhost/v1.55/containers/4e54dce2…/start:
Internal Server Error ("ports are not available: exposing port TCP 0.0.0.0:49870 -> 127.0.0.1:0:
listen tcp4 0.0.0.0:49870: bind: An attempt was made to access a socket in a way forbidden by its access permissions.")
```

On this host, `netsh interface ipv4 show excludedportrange protocol=tcp` shows Hyper-V/WinNAT reserved ranges such as `49845–49944`, `50060–50359` — and the failing ports (`49870`, `50103` on two different attempts) both fell exactly inside those ranges. Retrying the same request succeeds.

## Root cause

1. `allocate_host_port()` in `server/opensandbox_server/services/docker/port_allocator.py` probes availability with `socket.bind()` **inside the server container (Linux network stack)**. On Docker Desktop/Windows the actual bind happens on the **Windows host** during `docker start`, where OS-reserved excluded port ranges make the bind fail with `WSAEACCES` — the container-side probe cannot see this.
2. `_start_egress_sidecar()` in `networking.py` only retries when the failure is the IPv6-sysctl rejection; any other `start` failure (including `ports are not available`) cleans up and raises HTTP 500 without re-allocating a new host port.

## Suggested fix

- On `docker start` failure with a port-publish error (`ports are not available`, `bind:` permission errors), re-allocate a different host port and retry the create/start once or twice before giving up — port conflicts are probabilistic on hosts with dynamic reserved ranges.
- Longer term: make the probe Docker-publish-aware (or allow configuring the host port pool so it can be kept clear of reserved ranges).
- Consider surfacing the original Docker error instead of only the generic message, so callers can distinguish port conflicts from other start failures.

## Additional context

Host port allocation range is 40000–60000 (`allocate_host_port` defaults); OS-reserved ranges on Windows change between reboots, which is why the failure is intermittent and environment-dependent.

# Summary

Document the Server HTTP Proxy's existing transparent response behavior in generated OpenAPI. All 20 proxy operations now describe `200` and `default` with `*/*` and no fixed payload schema, while retaining the explicit validation `422` response.

## Problem

On `main@1eb8fffa0493fdfae4cf021580cdff61c9d1f50b`, the proxy forwards backend status, body, and Content-Type, but generated OpenAPI lists only JSON-only `200` and validation `422`. Valid backend responses such as HTML `200`, redirects, and binary error responses are not accurately described.

## Reproduction

Generate `app.openapi()` using the repository's mocked Server fixtures, or inspect `/openapi.json`. For each root/full-path route under both root and `/v1` prefixes, inspect GET/POST/PUT/DELETE/PATCH. All 20 operations have only `200/422`, and `200.content` contains only `application/json`.

Existing tests already demonstrate forwarded backend `201` and `302` responses.

## Root cause

The method-specific schema routes use FastAPI's default JSON response metadata and do not describe arbitrary backend responses. Declaring `responses.default` directly would also suppress FastAPI's automatic validation `422`; `openapi_extra` is merged after that validation response is generated.

## Change

- Add shared `200/default` response metadata with wildcard content and no payload model.
- Apply `StreamingResponse` and the metadata only to the existing method-specific schema routes.
- Retain hidden multi-method runtime routes and all current operation IDs from #1634.
- Add 20 schema cases, 20 backend status/body/media-type cases, and four invalid-port cases.
- Document the transparent response boundary in the architecture page.

# Testing

- [x] Unit tests
- [ ] External-service integration tests
- [ ] Live e2e / production verification

Local results on Python 3.10.20 with locked FastAPI 0.137.2:

- Before the fix: 20 schema failures (`KeyError: default`) and 24 passing runtime/validation cases.
- After the fix, identical selection: 44 passed.
- Full Proxy suite: 96 passed, including authentication, redirects, complete `405 Allow`, response streaming, and WebSockets.
- Full Server suite: 1649 passed, **16 PostgreSQL integration tests skipped** because no test DSN was configured. Coverage: **82.52%**, exceeding the 80% gate.

Docker host/bridge smoke tests, live Kubernetes/SDK E2E, the Windows/Linux CI matrix, and external client-generator compatibility were not run locally.

## Compatibility and security

Runtime paths, supported methods, authentication, endpoint resolution, response forwarding, redirects, `405 Allow`, and WebSocket behavior remain unchanged. Non-Proxy OpenAPI operations and components are unchanged.

Generated Proxy response metadata becomes broader and more accurate. Clients generated from Server OpenAPI may map wildcard/default responses differently and should treat backend payloads as opaque transport data; no runtime migration is required. The existing explicit `422` validation declaration is preserved; this narrow change does not redesign the schema overlap with a backend's own `422`.

No new dependencies, configuration, permissions, or forwarded headers. No lifecycle spec or SDK generation source changed.

Fixes #1700: https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/issues/1700

egress: forward-hook accept cannot allow IP-direct egress on the bridge topology (postrouting never reached)
body:
## Summary

In the fast-sandbox Firecracker integration, egress policy enforcement via the per-subject nft `dispatch` chain (hook `forward`) breaks **IP-direct egress for allowed subjects**: packets that should be accepted (`dyn_v4` / `allow_v4` set match) are silently dropped after the forward verdict, and never reach `postrouting` (the SNAT MASQUERADE counter stays at 0). DNS-domain policy works fine (the egress DNS proxy path is unaffected); the break is specific to the IP/forward path.

## Environment

- fast-sandbox Firecracker runtime: each slot netns's `eth0` veth is attached to a bridge (`fsb0`, IP `172.30.0.1/24`, the sandbox gateway); guest/netns traffic to the outside is forwarded through the bridge; `net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1`
- egress fleet profile, `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_MODE=dns+nft`, image `460b1cb`
- Sandbox policy: `{"egress":[{"action":"allow","target":"example.com"},{"action":"allow","target":"1.1.1.1"}],"defaultAction":"deny"}` — `allow_v4` set confirmed to contain `1.1.1.1`

## Repro

From the sandbox's slot netns (fastlet pod, `ip netns exec <ns>`):

```bash
timeout 4 nc -w 3 1.1.1.1 80 </dev/null   # hangs / no SYN-ACK
timeout 4 ping -c 1 -W 2 1.1.1.1          # 100% loss
```

`ip route get 1.1.1.1` resolves (`via 172.30.0.1 dev eth0 src <slot-ip>`); the gateway itself is reachable (ping/TCP to `172.30.0.1` works); the pod's own outbound connectivity works (curl to `1.1.1.1` from the pod returns HTTP 301).

## Evidence (nft counters inserted during the trace)

| hook / chain | packets | note |
|---|---|---|
| `prerouting` (probe chain) | 39 (4 from the sandbox) | packet arrives |
| `dispatch` (forward, jump to subject chain) | 2 | SYN reaches the forward hook |
| `input` (probe chain) | 0 | NOT a local-delivery path |
| `postrouting` MASQUERADE (table ip nat) | 0 | **packet disappears after the forward accept** |

## Root cause analysis

With `bridge-nf-call-iptables=1`, frames entering from a bridge port (`iifname = sandbox veth`) whose destination is the bridge itself (the ARP for the gateway `172.30.0.1` resolves to the bridge MAC) are processed on the IP path, but the verdict semantics of the forward hook are **"continue bridge L2 forwarding"**, not "continue IP routing":

- A frame with **no rule hit** in forward (the control case: a Firecracker pool without egress — no nft forward table, iptables FORWARD default ACCEPT) is **naturally passed** and continues to IP routing → `postrouting` SNAT → outbound works.
- A frame with an **explicit `accept` verdict** (egress `dispatch` `jump subj_<id>` → `dyn_v4`/`allow_v4` `accept`) is returned to the bridge L2 path → destination MAC = bridge → local delivery → destination IP is not local → dropped.

So on the bridge topology, an explicit forward-hook `accept` can never allow traffic; only "not matching a drop rule" passes. This also explains why `iptables -I FORWARD -s <slot-ip> -j ACCEPT` (tried as a control) still fails.

## Suggested fix: mark-based allow (no explicit accept)

Mark allowed destinations in `prerouting`, and let forward only drop unmarked traffic:

```
# new prerouting chain (per subject):
ip saddr <slot.IP> iifname "<veth>" ip daddr @subj_<id>_allow_v4  meta mark set 0x2
ip saddr <slot.IP> iifname "<veth>" ip daddr @subj_<id>_dyn_v4    meta mark set 0x2

# dispatch chain: policy drop -> policy accept, plus:
meta mark & 0x2 != 0x2 drop        # deny-first: unmarked outbound dropped

# subject chain: drop deny set + unmarked; remove the explicit accepts
# (marked packets fall through -> no rule hit -> natural pass -> IP routing)
```

Concrete touch points in `components/egress/pkg/fleetnft/fleetnft.go`:

1. `writeTableHeader` (line ~438): dispatch chain `policy drop` → `policy accept`; add the `prerouting` mark chain; add the unmarked-drop rule.
2. `writeDispatchRule` (line ~686): add the two per-subject mark rules (v4/v6) for `allow_v4` and `dyn_v4`.
3. `writeSubjectChain` (line ~660): keep `deny_v4/v6` drops + unmarked-drop; remove the explicit `dyn`/`allow` `accept` rules and the trailing default drop/accept.
4. Constants: new `markChain` / `markPriority` / allow-mark bit.

Note: do **not** reuse mark `0x1` — the egress DNS proxy already uses `SO_MARK 0x1` for its bypass; use a separate bit (e.g. `0x2`).

DNS-domain policy, the DNS proxy, gateway redirect, and MITM handling are unaffected by this change (verified separately: deny → NXDOMAIN, allow → resolution works end to end).

## Impact

Without this, allowed subjects can never make IP-direct (non-DNS) connections on the fast-sandbox bridge topology — DNS-domain allow works, but the follow-up TCP to resolved IPs is dropped by the dispatch fallback. The fix keeps deny-first semantics intact.

## Summary

Make the repository's Docker Compose example use host-mapped sandbox proxy
targets and make `host.docker.internal` resolve on Linux. Clarify the same
network-topology requirement in the server and single-host networking docs.

## Motivation

The Compose lifecycle server is attached to `opensandbox-net`, while sandboxes
created through the mounted Docker socket use Docker's separate default bridge.
With the historical/default `proxy.resolve_internal = true`, server-proxied
requests to a sandbox without an egress sidecar target its `172.17.x.x` address.
That address is not normally routable from the lifecycle server container on
Linux, so `/proxy/44772/ping` waits until the client times out.

This can be masked when a request includes `networkPolicy`: those sandboxes use
the egress sidecar path, for which Docker endpoint resolution already falls back
to a host-mapped port. Switching between the two sandbox shapes can therefore
look like an intermittent lifecycle or connection-pool failure.

`proxy.resolve_internal = false` is the existing supported control for this
topology. The example now selects it explicitly and supplies the Linux
`host-gateway` mapping required by its configured `docker.host_ip`.

This is a follow-up to #1631: that PR introduced the routing control; this PR selects the correct mode for the repository's shipped Compose topology.

Related: #252, #404, and #1631.

## Changes

- set `[proxy] resolve_internal = false` in `server/docker-compose.example.yaml`
- add `host.docker.internal:host-gateway` to both example containers
- document that Compose/user-defined and sandbox default bridges are separate
- point the server setup docs to `[proxy] resolve_internal`

## Validation

- `cd server && uv run pytest -q tests/test_docker_compose_example.py tests/test_config.py tests/test_docker_endpoint.py tests/test_routes_proxy.py` (241 passed)
- `cd server && uv run ruff check tests/test_docker_compose_example.py`
- `cd server && uv run pyright tests/test_docker_compose_example.py`
- `docker compose -f server/docker-compose.example.yaml config`
- `cd docs && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm docs:build`
- Linux A/B reproduction: the stock internal-IP path timed out, while the same
  sandbox passed after selecting host-mapped proxy targets:
  https://github.com/yanpgwang/mango/actions/runs/33511967527

## Breaking Changes

- [ ] Yes

## Security

This does not add a new published port or change the example's existing Docker

reach a sandbox. Deployments should continue to restrict host-published sandbox
ports with host firewall and network policy appropriate to their trust model.

title: execd: POST /command hangs on Firecracker guest (SSE never streams; /ping works)
body:
## Summary

`POST /command` on the execd HTTP API hangs in a Firecracker guest: the connection is established, but the SSE stream never emits a single byte (curl times out with `0 bytes received`). `GET /ping` on the same listener answers immediately, and the request definitely reaches execd — a malformed body returns `400 Bad Request` instantly.

## Environment

- Sandbox runtime: Firecracker microVM (fast-sandbox), guest = Alpine-based golden snapshot, per-instance rootfs
- execd image/version: `opensandbox/execd:1.1.0`
- Access path: the request goes through the fastlet proxy chain (port route) — but the same hang reproduces independent of the proxy, since `/ping` through the identical chain is instant

## Repro

```bash
curl -sS -m 10 -N \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Accept: text/event-stream' \
  -d '{"command":"echo probe-ok"}' \
  http://<guest-ip>:44772/command
# -> curl: (28) Operation timed out after 10000 milliseconds with 0 bytes received
```

Expected: SSE events (`stdout`, `execution_complete` with exit code). Actual: nothing, until the client times out. The same command works on non-Firecracker runtimes (container runtime e2e passes with the official Go SDK).

## Code pointer

`components/execd/pkg/web/controller/command.go` — `RunCommand()` calls `codeRunner.Execute(...)` synchronously (line 104) and only starts writing SSE after execution completes/errors. The hang is inside `components/execd/pkg/runtime/command.go` `runCommand()` during its synchronous init sequence:

1. `stdLogDescriptor(session)` / `stdoutFileName` / `stderrFileName` — stdout/stderr are redirected to files that are then tailed and streamed as SSE;
2. `getShell()` — the shell used for `bash -c`/`sh -c`;
3. `launchManaged(cmd)`.

One of these steps stalls in the Firecracker guest (no error, no event). The most suspicious candidate is the stdlog/file-pipe path or the shell dependency (the guest is Alpine/busybox; if execd requires `bash`, `launchManaged` would normally fail fast with an error event though, so a silent stall points more at the descriptor/tail pipeline).

## Impact

`fastctl exec` / the official Go SDK `RunCommand` are unusable on Firecracker-backed sandboxes. `GET /ping` (used by readiness probes) is unaffected.

## Expected

- `POST /command` either executes and streams, or fails fast with a structured error event (SSE or JSON) — never hang silently.
- Please investigate the stdlog descriptor / tail pipeline under the Firecracker guest (or confirm the shell requirement and surface a fast failure).

## Summary

Redesigns OSEP-0007 (fast-sandbox fleets runtime support) around a **template-based sandbox creation model**. The previous design (simplified subset of `CreateSandboxRequest` + phase 1a/1b split) is replaced by a native fleets contract.

## Key changes

- **Instance-level coexistence**: `fleets` runs alongside `docker`/`kubernetes` in one server; sandbox IDs use `flt-<uuid>` prefix routing for shared lifecycle endpoints (no registration store)
- **Distinct Create endpoint**: `POST /fleets/sandboxes` with its own request model — `templateId` + `poolRef` (required top-level) + `timeout` + `metadata` + `networkPolicy` + `extensions`; `image`/`entrypoint`/`env`/`resourceLimits`/`resourceRequests`/`credentialProxy` are absent from the contract (`additionalProperties: false`)
- **Template management API**: `POST/GET/DELETE /fleets/templates` — simplified build request, async 201 (`Pending`), server-persisted metadata, tenant-private isolation, mapped to fast-sandbox `SandboxTemplate` CRD (Firecracker golden-image builds)
- **DB schema**: full `fleets_templates` DDL for SQLite and PostgreSQL (aligned with existing snapshot repository pattern), phase state machine, lazy CRD status sync
- **Egress via Sandbox Actions**: `networkPolicy` serialized into an `egress` action binding; runtime policy CRUD through a server policy proxy (`/fleets/sandboxes/{id}/policy`) backed by `UpdateSandbox(ReplaceActionBindings)`; phase 1b split removed
- **Full spec contracts** documented: template API, fleets create mapping/status codes, policy proxy endpoints

## Scope

- Only `oseps/0007-fast-sandbox-runtime-support.md` changed (design doc)
- `specs/`, server implementation, and SDKs untouched — contract changes are deliberately kept in the OSEP until design approval

title: Is a pool-mode sandbox created without env/entrypoint expected to be unusable?
body:
## Scenario

Creating a sandbox from the official sample pool (`kubernetes/config/samples/sandbox_v1alpha1_pool.yaml`) via `POST /sandboxes` with only `extensions.poolRef` — no `env`, no `entrypoint` — succeeds and immediately reports Running/Ready, but the sandbox is unusable: no task is scheduled and execd (port 44772) is never started, so SDK interactive calls fail.

## Question

Is this expected? If yes, should the API reject no-args pool creation (or at least not report Ready)? If no, how do you get a usable sandbox from a pool without passing exec args?

## What I found

- `api/schema.py:495-507`: poolRef branch only rejects `snapshotId`; `entrypoint`/`env` are never required.
- `batchsandbox_provider.py:375`: no taskTemplate when both are empty → controller schedules no task, execd never launches; `get_status()` only checks pod Ready.

title: Support fenced durable materialization: metadata CAS, resolved image digest, and trusted setup
body:
## Why do you need it?

A durable sandbox consumer needs to reconnect after its client process restarts without allowing two stale workers to operate the same sandbox. With OpenSandbox server 0.1.14 and Python SDK 0.1.15, metadata can be patched and sandboxes can be listed by metadata, but metadata updates expose no resource version / ETag / expected-value precondition. The returned SandboxInfo also echoes the requested image reference without a separately reported resolved OCI digest. Finally, setup and final commands share the sandbox execution surface, so a consumer cannot establish root-owned or externally read-only material and then prove that final UID/GID 1000 commands cannot mutate it.

Without these primitives, clients can support ordinary remote execution but cannot honestly claim process-recoverable, immutable accepted-material execution.

## How could it be?

Please consider adding:

1. A conditional metadata or lease operation with an opaque revision (for example resourceVersion/ETag plus If-Match), atomic conflict behavior, monotonically changing ownership epochs, and conditional renewal/deletion.
2. A server-reported resolved OCI image digest that is distinct from the requested tag/reference and available from create/get/list responses.
3. A trusted setup mechanism separate from the final unprivileged execution principal, or a genuinely read-only volume/snapshot attachment. The final principal must be unable to write, chmod, rename, unlink, shadow, or mount over the published material.

These operations should remain discoverable by metadata after a client restart and should have explicit conflict/not-found responses suitable for reconciliation.

## Other related information

Observed against OpenSandbox server 0.1.14 and Python SDK 0.1.15. The lifecycle API PATCH `/sandboxes/{sandbox_id}/metadata` currently accepts only a metadata patch body, and `SandboxInfo.image` reports an image specification rather than an independently resolved digest.

title: JavaScript and C# SDKs send OPEN-SANDBOX-API-KEY to execd in direct mode (tenant credential exposed to untrusted sandbox code)
body:
## Description

In the JavaScript and C# SDKs the API key is attached to the connection's shared headers at construction time and is sent on **every** request — including execd-plane requests in **direct mode** (`useServerProxy=false`), where no server sits in the path to strip it.

The API key is a full-scope tenant credential. In direct mode the request terminates inside the sandbox pod, and execd shares the container with untrusted user code, so the header is readable by code running in the sandbox.

The Go SDK already implement the correct invariant: attach the key to execd-plane headers only when server-proxy mode is declared.

## To Reproduce

JavaScript, direct mode:

```js
const config = new ConnectionConfig({
  domain: "10.42.1.7:18080",   // sandbox pod address, no server in the path
  apiKey: "osb-...",
  useServerProxy: false,
});
// config.headers already contains OPEN-SANDBOX-API-KEY at this point, and
// every execd request built from this config (health, commands, files)
// carries it straight into the sandbox pod.
```

## Affected code paths

**JavaScript** (`sdks/sandbox/javascript`):
- `src/config/connection.ts:342-346` — constructor injects `OPEN-SANDBOX-API-KEY` into `this.headers` whenever `apiKey` is set, regardless of `useServerProxy`
- `src/factory/defaultAdapterFactory.ts:53-62` (`createExecdStack`) and the egress stack — build execd/egress clients from those shared headers

**C#** (`sdks/sandbox/csharp`):
- `Config/ConnectionConfig.cs:196-199` — API key header goes into `Headers`, applied as `DefaultRequestHeaders` (`:259-266`, `:296-302`)
- `Factory/DefaultAdapterFactory.cs:59` — execd headers fall back to `ConnectionConfig.Headers`

## Expected behavior

- `useServerProxy=true`: execd-plane requests carry `OPEN-SANDBOX-API-KEY` (they pass the server's auth gate, which strips it before forwarding).
- `useServerProxy=false` (direct): the key must **not** be sent — execd performs no authentication and the credential must never travel into the untrusted sandbox.
- Lifecycle/management requests keep the key in both modes.

## Additional Context

The expected behavior above matches what #1686 requested for the Python SDK. Surfaced by the Codex review on #1687.

## Suggested direction

Mirror the Go implementation (`sdks/sandbox/go/sandbox.go`, inject only when `UseServerProxy` is set): gate execd/egress header construction on the server-proxy declaration while keeping the key on lifecycle client headers.

title: Docker runtime: host-port probe cannot see the Docker host from a containerized server, and a failed publish kills the create with no retry
body:
## What happens

On the Docker runtime, `allocate_host_port()` (`server/opensandbox_server/services/docker/port_allocator.py`) picks a random port from `[docker].port_range_min..max` and checks availability with `sock.bind(("0.0.0.0", port))` in the server's own process. When the server itself runs in a container — the topology in `server/docker-compose.example.yaml` — that bind tests the server container's network namespace and says nothing about the Docker host. If the pick is unbindable on the host, `container.start()` fails and the create returns a terminal 500 (`DOCKER::SANDBOX_START_FAILED`): no retry with a fresh port, and no way to let Docker pick (`HostPort: 0`).

This bites hard on Docker Desktop for Windows, where WinNAT excluded port ranges (`netsh interface ipv4 show excludedportrange protocol=tcp`) sit inside the default 40000-60000 range — on one observed host they cover ~860 of those ports, so with 2-3 published ports per sandbox roughly one create in twelve fails with `bind: An attempt was made to access a socket in a way forbidden by its access permissions`. A port genuinely busy on the host fails the same way on any OS.

## Reproduction (server v0.2.3, any OS)

Occupy a port range on the host, give the server exactly that range, and create a sandbox — the probe passes (the ports are free inside the server container), the publish fails, the create dies:

```bash
cat > config.toml <<'EOF'
[server]
host = "0.0.0.0"
port = 8090

[runtime]
type = "docker"
execd_image = "opensandbox/execd:v1.1.0"

[docker]
network_mode = "bridge"
host_ip = "host.docker.internal"
port_range_min = 41000
port_range_max = 41199
EOF
docker run -d --name portblock -p 41000-41199:41000-41199 alpine:3 sleep 3600
docker run -d --name osx-server -p 18090:8090 \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  -v "$PWD/config.toml:/etc/opensandbox/config.toml:ro" \
  -e SANDBOX_CONFIG_PATH=/etc/opensandbox/config.toml \
  -e OPENSANDBOX_INSECURE_SERVER=YES \
  opensandbox/server:v0.2.3
```

```python
from datetime import timedelta
from opensandbox import SandboxSync
from opensandbox.config import ConnectionConfigSync

conn = ConnectionConfigSync(domain="localhost:18090", protocol="http", use_server_proxy=True)
SandboxSync.create(image="python:3.12-slim", timeout=timedelta(seconds=300), connection_config=conn)
```

Fails every time with:

```
opensandbox.exceptions.SandboxApiException: Create sandbox failed: Failed to create or start container: 500 Server Error for http+docker://localhost/v1.55/containers/.../start: Internal Server Error ("failed to set up container networking: driver failed programming external connectivity on endpoint sandbox-...: Bind for 0.0.0.0:41077 failed: port is already allocated") | [DOCKER::SANDBOX_START_FAILED]
```

Control: change the range to `42000`/`49151` (free on the host), restart the server — the same create succeeds. Verified with SDK 0.1.16 against server v0.2.3; the allocator and the start path are unchanged on current main (4ae41fd).

## Suggested fix

I realize the in-process bind is deliberate (the comment added in #797 describes it as mirroring the publish binding), but that mirror only holds when the server shares the host's network namespace. Either change would fix the containerized topology:

- on a `start()` failure caused by a port bind, retry the create with freshly allocated ports (bounded, say 3 attempts), or
- publish with `HostPort: 0` and read the assigned ports back from inspect, so the host's own allocator picks a bindable port.

Happy to open a PR for either shape if useful. (Related but distinct: #1666 reserves ports against same-process races and keeps the probe's scope.)

title: Multi-tenant servers: execd-plane requests omit OPEN-SANDBOX-API-KEY when use_server_proxy=True, surfacing as a 30s health-check timeout
body:
## Description

When the server runs in **multi-tenant mode** and the client sets `ConnectionConfig.use_server_proxy=True`, all execd-plane requests (health ping, commands, filesystem, metrics, egress, isolated) are sent **without** the `OPEN-SANDBOX-API-KEY` header.

The server's auth middleware rejects them with `401 MISSING_API_KEY`. The SDK's health check folds that failure into `False`, so `Sandbox.connect()` keeps polling until the 30s timeout and then raises `SandboxReadyTimeoutException` — with no hint that the real cause is authentication.

Management-plane requests on the same connection do carry the key and succeed, which makes the failure look like "the sandbox never became healthy".

## To Reproduce

Server: any deployment in multi-tenant mode (tenant provider configured). Client on current `main`:

```python
import asyncio

from opensandbox import Sandbox
from opensandbox.config import ConnectionConfig


async def main() -> None:
    config = ConnectionConfig(
        domain="my-server.example.com",  # multi-tenant server
        protocol="https",
        api_key="<tenant-api-key>",
        use_server_proxy=True,
    )
    sandbox = await Sandbox.connect("<existing-sandbox-id>", config)
    await sandbox.commands.run("echo ok")


asyncio.run(main())
```

Result after ~30s:

```
Sandbox health check timed out after 30.0s (147 attempts).
Health check returned false continuously.
```

The server access log shows what actually happened:

```
GET /sandboxes/<id>/proxy/18080/health -> 401 MISSING_API_KEY
```

Direct confirmation that only the header is missing:

```bash
# no key -> 401
curl -i "https://my-server.example.com/sandboxes/<id>/proxy/18080/health"

# with key -> 200
curl -i -H "OPEN-SANDBOX-API-KEY: <tenant-api-key>" \
  "https://my-server.example.com/sandboxes/<id>/proxy/18080/health"
```

## Expected Behavior

- `use_server_proxy=True`: execd-plane requests carry `OPEN-SANDBOX-API-KEY` (they pass the server's auth gate in both single- and multi-tenant mode).
- `use_server_proxy=False` (direct): the key must **not** be sent — execd performs no authentication and the API key must never travel into the untrusted sandbox.

## Environment

- Python SDK, current `main` (`OpenSandbox-Python-SDK/0.1.16`); async and sync clients are both affected
- Server in multi-tenant mode

## Additional Context

This is the client-side half of #248. #250 resolved that report by exempting `/sandboxes/{id}/proxy/...` paths from API-key validation on the server, which fixed single-tenant deployments. In multi-tenant mode the server must authenticate every request (tenant lookup), so the exemption cannot apply there and the client-side gap resurfaces.

# Summary

#1675 made the server proxy answer backend-connection failures on proxied routes with HTTP 502 and a structured body:
