labels.name: size/XXL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 1000+ lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

Implements [OSEP-0018](oseps/0018-execd-as-sandbox-init.md) "execd as Sandbox Init" — execd becomes the sandbox init (PID 1) and the privilege authorizer for all user code. 10 commits covering phases 1–5:

1. **Init mode (PID 1)** — single reaper (only wait4-family caller), managedProcess abstraction replacing `Cmd.Wait` on every launch path (command/bash/PTY/isolated session), signal forwarding (TERM/HUP/USR1/USR2/WINCH), entrypoint-owned container lifecycle (exit-code propagation), subreaper fallback for the Pool path, `bootstrap.sh` `EXECD_INIT` exec branch (default off, classic topology unchanged).
2. **Pre-exec hardening floor** — `opensandbox-launcher` native helper applies env strip → KEEPCAPS → bounding-set trim → no_new_privs → identity drop → ambient caps → seccomp (last) → execve; `[hardening] enabled`/`keep_capabilities`; `[seccomp] deny` reused with `execve` reserved; everything fail-open and reported on the capabilities endpoint.
3. **Landlock** — `[landlock] enabled` filesystem allowlist (system paths + `/proc/self` + device files + writable dirs), ABI probe with bit trimming; ABI < 1 → `unsupported` (fail-open).
4. **eBPF observation** — `execd-ebpf` variant (CGO + cilium/ebpf): exec/connect/privilege hooks (CO-RE), sandbox-cgroup scoped, rotating JSONL audit; kernel ≥5.10 with BTF; default image unchanged.
5. **Server switch + Pool** — `runtime.execd_run_as_init` injects `EXECD_INIT=1` across Docker/K8s Batch/Agent/Pool; Pool taskTemplate runs execd as the task root (reaping + exit-code propagation); `kill 1` recycle contract confirmed compatible.

**Contract**: `GET /v1/isolated/capabilities` gains a `hardening` object (init_mode/signal_shield + cap_drop/seccomp/landlock/ebpf layer states); spec, Go/Python/JS/Kotlin/C# SDKs aligned; docs updated.

**Tests**: unit tests for the reaper/lifecycle/hardening/landlock; ebpf event-decode tests; real-container regression (`tests/init_container.sh`: PID 1 handoff, zombie reaping, `kill -9 1` inert, exit-code propagation, SIGTERM graceful shutdown, hardening floor, landlock `/proc/1/environ` denial, subreaper) wired into the execd CI.

## Kernel compatibility

- Init mode / floor: any modern Linux (5.10+ fine)
- Landlock: requires ≥5.13; below it reports `unsupported` and skips (fail-open)
- eBPF: 5.10+ with `CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF`; the 5.16 trace-event layout change and the 6.3 `kernel_cap_t` change are handled via CO-RE discriminators

## Known limitations (tracked)

- In-namespace `kill 1` (SIGTERM) still stops the sandbox — same as pre-OSEP bootstrap behavior; the trusted out-of-band stop channel (OSEP §3) is follow-up work
- Pool pod-level PID 1 is operator template configuration (documented), not auto-injected
- Kernel 5.10 eBPF path pending validation on a real 5.10 node

title: fix(chart/server): roll the server Deployment when config.toml changes

labels.name: size/XS
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 0-9   lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
# Summary

- The server parses `config.toml` **once at startup**, but `opensandbox-server` mounts it from a ConfigMap with no content hash on the pod template. Helm (or a GitOps sync) updates the ConfigMap in place, so the running pod keeps serving the **previous** configuration — the mounted file shows the new values while the process does not.
- We hit this in production with `[kubernetes].sandbox_create_timeout_seconds`: the ConfigMap carried `180` for days while the server kept timing out sandbox creates at the `60` default (`KUBERNETES::POD_READY_TIMEOUT … Elapsed: 60.0s`), and the only reason it eventually picked the new value up was an unrelated node rotation. Our client's create-retry masked it, so the misconfiguration was invisible for four days.
- Fix: add a `checksum/config` pod annotation over the rendered TOML — `.Values.configToml` plus the `[ingress]` block the chart appends via `opensandbox-server.ingressConfigToml` — so any config change rolls the Deployment. `server.podAnnotations` still merge on top.

```diff
-      {{- with .Values.server.podAnnotations }}
       annotations:
+        checksum/config: {{ printf "%s%s" .Values.configToml (include "opensandbox-server.ingressConfigToml" .) | sha256sum }}
+        {{- with .Values.server.podAnnotations }}
         {{- toYaml . | nindent 8 }}
-      {{- end }}
+        {{- end }}
```

Scoped to the server Deployment: the ingress gateway does not mount the config ConfigMap, so it needs no equivalent. Secrets consumed as env (e.g. `server.gateway.secureAccess.existingSecret`) are out of scope — `values.yaml` already documents the manual restart for those.

Happy to swap this for an opt-in `server.deploymentAnnotations` value instead (so operators can wire Stakater Reloader themselves) if you prefer the chart not to force rollouts — just say which you'd rather have.

# Testing

- [x] e2e / manual verification
- `helm lint` passes.
- `helm template` renders the annotation on the server Deployment; the digest changes when `configToml` changes, and again when `server.gateway.enabled=true` alters the appended `[ingress]` section.
- `--set server.podAnnotations.foo=bar` renders alongside `checksum/config` (no override, correct indentation).
- Verified against the real failure mode: a server pod started before the ConfigMap change kept logging `Waiting for sandbox … (timeout: 60s)`; a restarted pod on the same ConfigMap logs `(timeout: 180s)`.

# Breaking Changes

- [x] None
- Behavioural note: a `configToml` change now rolls the server pod, which is the intended fix. Sandbox state lives in the CRs, so the stateless server can be rolled safely.

# Checklist

- [x] Linked Issue or clearly described motivation
- [x] Added/updated docs (if needed) — the annotation carries an inline comment; no user-facing values change
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed) — chart has no test suite; verified via `helm lint` / `helm template`

title: perf(sdks): releaseAllIdle kills idle sandboxes serially (500 sandboxes ≈ 8 min)
body:
## Problem

`SandboxPool.releaseAllIdle()` (and `Pool.release_all_idle()` in Python) drains idle sandboxes with a strictly serial loop: one `killSandbox` HTTP DELETE at a time. Teardown time grows linearly with pool size and can take minutes for large pools.

## Measurements (Kotlin SDK 1.0.18 / aone-sandbox-sdk 2.0.25, pre-production env)

- Serial `releaseAllIdle()`: **~480s for 500 idle sandboxes** (~1s per kill)
- Parallel kill (50 concurrent `DELETE /v1/sandboxes/{id}`): **~150s for 477 sandboxes, 0 failures** (env was partially degraded; healthy env should be much faster)

## Affected code

- Kotlin: `sdks/sandbox/kotlin/sandbox/src/main/kotlin/com/alibaba/opensandbox/sandbox/pool/SandboxPool.kt:440` — `while (true) { tryTakeIdle(); manager.killSandbox(id) }`
- Python async: `sdks/sandbox/python/src/opensandbox/pool_async.py:366` — same serial `while True` pattern
- Python sync / Go: likely same pattern, to be verified

## Suggested fix

Bound the parallelism instead of serializing:

- Kotlin: submit kills to a bounded executor (reuse `warmupExecutor` or a dedicated pool), keep best-effort semantics and per-sandbox error logging
- Python async: `asyncio.gather` in bounded batches (e.g. 50)
- Go: same with a worker pool

Semantics to preserve: best-effort kill, log per-failure, do not abort on a single failed kill, drain state store ids regardless of kill outcome.

title: fix(server): avoid duplicate proxy response headers

body:
## Problem

When a sandbox backend returns `Date` or `Server`, the HTTP server proxy forwards those values into the client-facing `StreamingResponse`. Uvicorn also generates both fields, so clients receive duplicate response headers.

## Minimal reproduction

Return a valid `Date` and a `Server` header from a sandbox HTTP service, then access it through `/v1/sandboxes/<sandbox-id>/proxy/<port>/`. With Uvicorn's default response headers enabled, the raw response contains both the proxy-generated and backend-provided values.

A focused route test injects those backend headers. A real Uvicorn socket reproduction verifies the duplicate fields at the protocol boundary.

## Root cause

`_proxy_http_request` filters hop-by-hop backend response headers but passes `Date` and `Server` to Starlette. Uvicorn prepends its defaults later at the protocol layer, even when the application already supplied those fields.

Dropping the backend `Date` avoids the duplicate but changes the origin timestamp and can alter HTTP cache freshness calculations. The proxy therefore needs to preserve an existing `Date` while preventing Uvicorn from adding another one.

## Change

- preserve an origin `Date` on HTTP server-proxy responses
- continue excluding the backend `Server` header
- disable Uvicorn's default `Date` in the supported server entry points
- add an application-managed current `Date` only when a response lacks one
- add regression coverage for preserved and generated `Date` behavior
- document the response-header behavior

## Testing

- [ ] Integration tests
- [x] e2e / manual verification

title: [Bug] Server proxy duplicates Date and Server response headers
body:
## Summary

When a sandbox backend returns `Date` or `Server` response headers, the HTTP server proxy forwards those values into the client-facing `StreamingResponse`. Uvicorn also generates its own `Date` and `Server` headers, so the raw response contains two values for each field.

## Affected versions

- OpenSandbox Server `v0.2.2`
- `upstream/main` at `601275f07fa085edb5ccc01caae9e83840c6793d`

## Minimal reproduction

1. Run an HTTP service in a sandbox that returns `Date: backend-date` and `Server: backend-server`.
2. Access it through `/v1/sandboxes/<sandbox-id>/proxy/<port>/`.
3. Inspect the raw response headers.

The response contains both the Uvicorn-generated and backend-provided values:

```http
Date: <proxy-generated date>
Server: uvicorn
Date: backend-date
Server: backend-server
```

The same behavior can be reproduced without a Kubernetes runtime by returning a Starlette `StreamingResponse` with backend `Date` and `Server` headers under the server's normal Uvicorn layer.

## Expected behavior

The client-facing response should contain only one `Date` and one `Server` value, generated by the OpenSandbox server layer. Application-level backend headers should remain unchanged.

## Root cause

`server/opensandbox_server/api/proxy.py::_proxy_http_request` filters hop-by-hop response headers before passing the remaining backend headers to `StreamingResponse`, but it does not exclude `Date` or `Server` even though Uvicorn adds those fields later.

## Impact

Duplicate single-valued response metadata is ambiguous for clients and intermediaries, and forwarding the backend `Server` value also exposes an implementation detail that the proxy does not otherwise need.

## Related history

PR #408 introduced hop-by-hop response-header filtering, but it does not cover server-generated `Date` or `Server` fields.

title: fix(egress): pass through TLS connections without SNI

labels.name: size/S
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 10-29 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

No-SNI TLS connections currently become broken MITM attempts: with no hostname available from the ClientHello, mitmproxy's upstream hostname verification falls back to the destination IP, which fails for any public certificate without an IP SAN (`hostname mismatch`), so the upstream connection is torn down.

This is a real-world issue: ossfs2 (and other embedded clients) connect to OSS by IP without SNI, so HTTPS egress to OSS fails under transparent MITM unless `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_MITMPROXY_SSL_INSECURE=1` is set — which Credential Vault rejects.

## Change

In `components/egress/mitmscripts/system.py`, `tls_clienthello` now sets `ignore_connection=True` when the ClientHello carries no SNI, passing such connections through untouched:

- Hostname-based `ignore_hosts` matching still applies to SNI-carrying connections (unchanged).
- TCP-layer enforcement (deny/allow rules) still applies to no-SNI flows.
- Credential Vault bindings match on host, which is unavailable for no-SNI flows, so pass-through creates no binding conflict.

## Tests

Added 5 unit tests in `components/egress/tests/test_mitmscripts_system.py` (no-SNI pass-through with/without patterns, SNI match/no-match, empty patterns). Full mitmscripts suite: 39 passed.

title: fix(egress): inject credential vault headers at requestheaders for streamed bodies

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## What

Fixes #1465. With Credential Vault enabled, requests with bodies above 1 MiB failed against the upstream with `403 invalid api-key`: `stream_large_bodies: 1m` streams such bodies upstream, and the `request` hook fires only after the streamed body has been forwarded — too late for auth header injection.

Split the credential proxy into two phases:

- **`requestheaders` hook**: binding match, ambiguous-path rejection, path/query/header substitutions, auth header injection, and response redaction metadata. Fires before the upstream connection is established, so it works for request bodies of any size.
- **`request` hook**: body substitutions only (need the full body); skipped for streamed requests whose body is no longer available or modifiable.

This also fixes a latent issue: redaction metadata was set in `request`, but with request streaming the `response` hook can fire before `request` (e.g. upstream returns 413 mid-upload), so response header redaction could be missed.

## Tests

- Unit (`components/egress/tests/test_mitmscripts_system.py`): existing cases split across the two hooks; new `SystemAddonStreamingTest` covering header injection at `requestheaders` for > 1 MiB bodies, streamed-request body substitution skip, body-only binding redaction timing, and `request`-without-`requestheaders` no-op. 38 tests pass.
- E2E regression at the 1 MiB boundary (1 MiB - 1, exactly 1 MiB, 1 MiB + 1, 2 MiB) in both `tests/go/credential_vault_e2e_test.go` and `tests/python/tests/test_credential_vault_e2e.py`, backed by a new `/large-body` route in the echo server.

> E2E suites were not run locally (require sandbox infra via `OPENSANDBOX_CREDENTIAL_VAULT_E2E_TARGET_IP`); `go vet` and unit tests are clean.

title: egress: Credential Vault fails to inject auth header for request bodies > 1 MiB (403 invalid api-key)
body:
## Summary

With Credential Vault enabled, requests with a body larger than 1 MiB fail against the upstream with `403 invalid api-key`. Small requests work fine, and the vault credentials themselves are valid (verified via the proxy control channel for small requests).

## Reproduction boundary

- `Content-Length = 1,048,575` (1 MiB - 1): HTTP 200
- `Content-Length = 1,048,577` (1 MiB + 1): HTTP 403 `invalid api-key`
- Both requests are identical except for body size (same auth headers, model, etc.)

## Root cause

The egress mitmproxy config sets `stream_large_bodies: 1m` (`components/egress/mitmproxy/config.yaml`). Bodies above the threshold are streamed upstream, and the `request` addon hook fires **only after the streamed body has been forwarded** (per mitmproxy docs, `response` may even fire before `request`). The Credential Proxy performs binding match and auth header injection in the `request` hook (`components/egress/mitmscripts/system.py`), so for streamed bodies the headers are modified too late — the upstream already received the request without credentials and returns 403.

An additional consequence: the response redaction metadata (`FLOW_REDACTIONS_KEY`) is also set in the `request` hook, so response header redaction can be missed on streamed flows where the response arrives before `request` fires.

## Affected component

- `components/egress/mitmscripts/system.py` — credential proxy header injection in the `request` hook
- `components/egress/mitmproxy/config.yaml` — `stream_large_bodies: 1m`

## Suggested fix

Split the credential proxy into two phases:

- **`requestheaders` hook**: binding match, ambiguous-path rejection, path/query/header substitutions, auth header injection, and redaction metadata. This hook fires before the upstream connection is established, so it works for request bodies of any size.
- **`request` hook**: body substitutions only (they need the full body); skipped for streamed requests since the body is no longer available or modifiable.

Add regression tests at the 1 MiB boundary (1 MiB - 1, exactly 1 MiB, 1 MiB + 1, and a larger streamed size).

A fix implementing this approach is available in branch `fix/egress-credential-vault-large-body` (fork: `Pangjiping/OpenSandbox`).

title: fix(execd): stop holding resultMutex across blocking resultChan sends

labels.name: size/M
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 30-99 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
# Summary

Fixes #1463: `handleExecuteResult`, `handleStreamOutput`, and `handleExecutionError` in `components/execd/pkg/jupyter/execute/execute.go` each send on `resultChan` while still holding `state.resultMutex`. When the channel's consumer falls behind draining it — realistic under bursty stdout (module imports, logging setup, an LLM streaming tokens) compounded by node/network contention from concurrent sandboxes — the send blocks while the lock is held.

Because `receiveMessages()` dispatches every incoming kernel message through these handlers synchronously on a single goroutine, a blocked send wedges that goroutine outright: no further kernel message — including the genuine `execute_reply`/`idle` completion signal — can ever be read off the websocket again, even if the kernel already sent it. Separately, `finalizeExecution` (the only code path that ever closes `resultChan`) needs the same mutex just to poll its completion condition, so it's starved too. The execution hangs permanently, with no output and no error, until an external timeout tears the sandbox down.

**Relationship to #1206 / #1321:** that work fixes a different failure mode in the same neighborhood — the real `execute_reply` being lost entirely (dropped WS message, kernel restart), against which `finalizeExecution`'s poll loop previously had no upper bound. This fix is orthogonal: no lost message is required here, an ordinary slow consumer is sufficient, because the deadlock is in the mutex itself. I verified PR #1321 does not already fix this — its new `trySend()` is still a blocking send, still called from inside the same held-lock scope in all three handlers (checked directly against its branch tip). Happy to rebase onto #1321 if it merges first; the same principle (send after releasing the lock, and before recording the completion-gating field) applies cleanly on top of `trySend`/`terminate`.

## Root cause

```go
state.resultMutex.Lock()
defer state.resultMutex.Unlock()
...
resultChan <- notify   // blocks here if the buffer is full, still holding the lock
```

`finalizeExecution`'s poll loop needs the same lock just to check `state.result.ExecutionCount > 0 || state.result.Error != nil`. If a handler is blocked mid-send holding the lock, that check can never run, `resultChan` is never closed, and — because `receiveMessages()` is strictly sequential — no further websocket message of any kind can be processed either.

## Fix

- Release `state.resultMutex` before sending on `resultChan` in `handleExecuteResult`, `handleStreamOutput`, `handleExecutionError`, and `finalizeExecution`'s own initial send.
- For `handleExecuteResult` and `handleExecutionError` specifically, additionally reorder the send to happen *before* the corresponding completion-gating field (`ExecutionCount` / `Error`) is recorded. Without this, `finalizeExecution`'s poll loop could observe "done" and close `resultChan` while that send was still in flight — a send/close race caught by `go test -race` during development of this fix (would otherwise risk a "send on closed channel" panic).

## Testing

- [x] Unit tests
- [ ] Integration tests
- [ ] e2e / manual verification

New test `TestResultMutexNotHeldAcrossBlockingChannelSend` in `components/execd/pkg/jupyter/execute/deadlock_repro_test.go`: a minimal, deterministic reproduction against `Client.handleStreamOutput` directly (no websocket/HTTP layer). Fills a 1-slot `resultChan`, forces a second call to block on the send, then asserts an unrelated goroutine can still acquire `resultMutex` within 500ms (standing in for `finalizeExecution`'s completion check).

- Fails against `main` (mutex still held after 500ms) — confirms the repro.
- Passes after this fix, 10/10 under `go test -race -count=10`.
- Full regression check: `go test -race ./...` across the entire `execd` module (`jupyter`, `execute`, `runtime`, `web/controller`, etc.) — all green, no new races.
- `gofmt -l`, `go vet ./...`, `golangci-lint run ./pkg/jupyter/...` all clean.

## Breaking Changes

- [x] None

Purely internal locking-order fix; no API, wire-protocol, or externally observable behavior change on the success path. The only observable difference is that executions which previously hung forever under this specific backpressure condition now complete normally.

## Checklist

- [x] Linked Issue or clearly described motivation (#<issue-number-from-step-3>)
- [ ] Added/updated docs (if needed) — not needed, internal fix only
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Security impact considered — none; concurrency/locking fix only, no new attack surface
- [x] Backward compatibility considered — no behavior change on any previously-succeeding path

title: [Bug] execd: handler goroutine deadlocks holding resultMutex during a blocked resultChan send
body:
**Description**

In `components/execd/pkg/jupyter/execute/execute.go`, three message handlers — `handleExecuteResult`, `handleStreamOutput`, and `handleExecutionError` — send on `resultChan` (a bounded, 10-slot buffered channel per `runtime.runJupyterCode`) while still holding `state.resultMutex`:

```go
state.resultMutex.Lock()
defer state.resultMutex.Unlock()
...
resultChan <- notify   // blocks here if the buffer is full
```

If the channel's consumer (which streams output back over the `/code` HTTP response) falls behind draining it — realistic under bursty stdout (module imports, logging setup, an LLM streaming tokens) compounded by node/network contention from concurrent sandboxes — this send blocks *while the lock is held*.

Because `receiveMessages()` dispatches every incoming kernel message through these handlers synchronously on a single goroutine, a blocked send wedges that goroutine outright: no further kernel message can be read off the websocket again, including the genuine `execute_reply`/`idle` completion signal — even if the kernel already sent it and it's sitting in the socket buffer. Separately, `finalizeExecution` — the only code path that ever closes `resultChan` — needs the same mutex just to poll its completion condition, so it's starved too. The execution hangs permanently with no output and no error until an external timeout (session TTL, caller-side deadline) tears the sandbox down.

Related to but distinct from #1206 / #1321: that work fixes the case where the real `execute_reply` is lost entirely (dropped WS message, kernel restart) and the poll loop had no upper bound. This bug requires no lost message — an ordinary slow/backpressured consumer is sufficient, since the deadlock is in the *mutex*, not in waiting for a message that never comes. I verified #1321's `trySend()` does not fix this: it's still a blocking send, still called from inside the same held-lock scope in all three handlers (checked directly against PR #1321's branch tip).

**To Reproduce**

Minimal, deterministic unit-level repro (no websocket needed) — fill a 1-slot `resultChan` via one `handleStreamOutput` call, then call it again from a goroutine (it blocks on the full channel, holding `resultMutex`), then show a second, unrelated goroutine cannot acquire `resultMutex` within 500ms even though it only needs the lock to check state, not to touch the channel. I have this written up as a `go test` and am happy to submit it as part of a fix PR.

**Expected Behavior**

A handler blocked on a full `resultChan` should not prevent unrelated goroutines (in particular `finalizeExecution`'s completion check) from acquiring `state.resultMutex`. Slow consumers should produce ordinary backpressure, not a total, unrecoverable stall of the connection's reader goroutine.

**Environment**

- OpenSandbox execd version: `docker/execd/v1.0.18` (commit `277262361e81bec91a0e696e02fcf8d6cafc58ad`)
- Runtime: Kubernetes-based OpenSandbox server, `use_server_proxy: true`
- Reproduced under: 5 concurrent sandbox sessions, each running a flow that invokes an LLM and streams reasoning/output tokens back through `codes.run()`

**Additional Context**

Observed as an intermittent (~1-in-5 under 5-way concurrency, not deterministic) production hang: sandbox creation and kernel handshake complete normally, the real code is submitted, and then the connection goes completely silent — no stdout, no error, no completion — until the caller's own timeout eventually tears the sandbox down. Confirmed via an instrumented rerun (stdout checkpoints written directly to the sandbox's raw stdout, bypassing any framework-level logging) that not even the first line of the submitted code's output was ever relayed, ruling out the application code, the LLM call, and the framework layer as the cause.

I proposed to fix this via [PR #1464](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/pull/1464)

title: egress: LLM SSE chunks >1MB truncated when TLS HTTP/1.1 upstream closes connection right after body
body:
**Component**: `components/egress` (mitmproxy transparent mode)
**Environment**: egress image (debian bookworm / Python 3.11, mitmproxy==11.0.2)

## Summary

LLM SSE chunks larger than ~1 MB get truncated at the tail when the upstream serves the response over **TLS + HTTP/1.1 and closes the connection immediately after the body**. Data loss is nondeterministic (from ~14 bytes up to several hundred KB), and the client's SSE stream is cut mid-event.

This is **not** caused by `stream_large_bodies: 1m` — it reproduces without that option. It is a race in mitmproxy's pure-asyncio `sslproto` (CPython) read path for TLS upstream connections: the connection EOF can be processed before the remaining plaintext is fed to the HTTP/1 layer. h11's `ChunkedReader.read_eof()` then raises `RemoteProtocolError`, mitmproxy kills the flow (`HttpErrorHook`: `HTTP/1 protocol error: peer closed connection without sending complete message body (incomplete chunked read)`), and the client connection is closed — silently truncating the SSE stream.

## Reproduction

Setup: `mitmdump --mode regular --listen-port 19080 --set ssl_insecure=true --set connection_strategy=lazy -s components/egress/mitmscripts/system.py` (config equivalent to egress transparent mode; `stream_large_bodies=1m` irrelevant).

1. Upstream: TLS (ALPN `http/1.1`) server that responds to `GET /stream` with:
   - `Content-Type: text/event-stream`, `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, `Connection: close`
   - a single chunk containing one SSE event with a 2 MiB `data:` line, then the terminating `0\r\n\r\n`
   - **closes the connection immediately** after the last byte
2. Client: `CONNECT` through the proxy + TLS + `GET /stream`, read until EOF.

Observed (8/8 runs): body truncated; mitmproxy logs
`PROBE ERROR hook fired: HTTP/1 protocol error: peer closed connection without sending complete message body (incomplete chunked read)`

| Upstream behavior | Result |
|---|---|
| TLS h1, close immediately after body (2 MiB) | Truncated, 8/8 |
| TLS h1, close immediately (256 KiB – 1.5 MiB) | Truncated, 8/8 |
| TLS h1, close immediately (≤ 64 KiB) | Mostly OK |
| TLS h1, delay ~1 s before close (2 MiB) | Complete |
| Plain TCP (no TLS) h1, close immediately (2 MiB) | Complete, 8/8 |
| HTTP/2 upstream (h2 client) 2 MiB | Complete |

## Root cause

In `mitmproxy/proxy/server.py::handle_connection`, the upstream read loop consumes `reader.read(65535)` over the asyncio SSL transport. When the peer sends the final bytes and a FIN back-to-back, EOF (`ConnectionClosed`) can be delivered while undelivered plaintext remains pending in the SSL read path. mitmproxy's HTTP/1 client (`_http1.py::read_body`) then calls h11 `ChunkedReader.read_eof()`, which hard-errors on an incomplete chunk:

```python
def read_eof(self) -> NoReturn:
    raise RemoteProtocolError(
        "peer closed connection without sending complete message body "
        "(incomplete chunked read)"
    )
```

`HttpStream.handle_protocol_error` then closes the client connection. Large SSE bodies span many SSL read batches, so the race is reliably hit; small bodies often fit into fewer batches and dodge it — matching the field report that only chunks > 1 MB truncate.

CPython 3.11 and 3.12 `asyncio/sslproto.py::_do_read__copied` are identical, so the egress image (Python 3.11) is affected.

## Impact

- Any sandbox calling an LLM API (or self-hosted gateway) that streams over TLS HTTP/1.1 and closes the connection after the response loses the tail of large SSE events; the SDK then reports malformed/truncated JSON or a dropped stream.
- HTTP/2 upstreams (e.g. OpenAI, Anthropic) are unaffected.
- Non-SSE large TLS HTTP/1 responses are affected as well (the buffered path errors out with a 502 to the client).

## Suggested actions

- Report upstream to mitmproxy with this minimal repro (mitmdump + TLS h1 chunked response + immediate close).
- Check newer mitmproxy versions / the `mitmproxy-rs` transport for a fix and consider unpinning.
- Add an egress e2e regression test covering "large SSE + TLS upstream + immediate connection close".

I can provide the full repro scripts (server/client) if useful.

title: Feature: Add Sandbox lifecycle hooks
body:
## Why do you need it?

Agent sandboxes may need to persist application or filesystem state before being paused or terminated, and restore state after resume.

OpenSandbox currently provides task-level `preStart` and `postStop` hooks, but no Sandbox lifecycle hooks.

## How could it be?

Provide optional lifecycle hooks such as:

- `prePause`
- `postResume`
- `preTerminate`

## Other related information

  - [OpenSandbox#1366](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/issues/1366) — Credentials need to be re-injected after resume.
  - [OpenSandbox#1355](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/issues/1355) — Filesystem state needs to be synchronized before pause and snapshot.
  - [OpenSandbox#1448](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/issues/1448) — Automatic idle-pause and resume-on-revisit.
  - [openkruise/agents#743](https://github.com/openkruise/agents/issues/743) — Similar proposal for extensible Sandbox lifecycle hooks.

title: Feature: Improve Kubernetes sandbox resume latency
body:
## Why do you need it?

Agent sandboxes are long-lived but bursty, so they need suspension and rapid resumption.

Currently, a Sandbox is effectively mapped 1:1 to a Pod. Resume recreates the Pod, introducing scheduling, image pulling, container startup, and Agent initialization latency.

## How could it be?

Is there any plan to optimize resume latency, for example by decoupling the Sandbox lifecycle from the Pod lifecycle, using pre-warmed runtimes, or supporting process/ memory hibernation?

Kubernetes P50/P95 resume latency benchmarks would also be helpful.

## Other related information

  - [#1448](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/issues/1448) — Auto idle-pause and resume-on-revisit for long-lived Agent sandboxes
  - [#1169](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/issues/1169) — Volume-based pause/resume as an alternative to OCI image commit
  - [#1354](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/issues/1354) — Clarification of cold-start and warm-start latency
  - [#1324](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/pull/1324) — Lifecycle latency metrics for pause, resume, and kill

title: feat(execd): support background runs in isolated sessions

labels.name: size/XXL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 1000+ lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

Adds detached background run support to isolated sessions (`bwrap` isolation, OSEP-0013), mirroring the existing background command support in the regular command API.

`POST /v1/isolated/session/{sessionId}/run` accepts `background: true`: the code is submitted detached inside the persistent session shell, and the endpoint returns immediately with a JSON run handle instead of an SSE stream. Combined stdout/stderr and exit code are captured to files under the workspace's `.execd/background-runs/` directory (upper layer for overlay workspaces, workspace itself for rw workspaces), visible to execd from the host side.

Two new endpoints enable polling:

- `GET /v1/isolated/session/{sessionId}/runs/{runId}` — run status (running, exit code, error, timestamps)
- `GET /v1/isolated/session/{sessionId}/runs/{runId}/logs` — plain-text log with byte-offset incremental reads via the `EXECD-ISOLATED-TAIL-CURSOR` header (same semantics as `EXECD-COMMANDS-TAIL-CURSOR`)

## Design notes

- Background jobs are wrapped as `( code ) </dev/null >log 2>&1; echo $? >code &`, so their output never pollutes the session stdout consumed by foreground end-marker scans, and stdin-reading commands cannot steal script lines from the shared pipe.
- Lifecycle: in-flight runs block idle GC (new per-session `activeBackgroundRuns` counter); the watcher marks runs finished on exit-code file or session death. Deleting a session reaps background processes via the bwrap process group kill and sweeps run records.
- `timeout_seconds` remains foreground-only; background runs are bounded by session lifetime.
- Read-only workspace sessions reject background runs (no host-visible writable log location).

## Contract changes

- `specs/execd-api.yaml`: `IsolatedRunRequest.background`, JSON response for the run endpoint, and two new paths + `IsolatedBackgroundRunResponse` / `IsolatedRunStatus` schemas.

## Verification

- `go build` (darwin + windows cross), `go vet`, `go test ./pkg/...` green. New runtime tests cover completion, exit codes, env injection, foreground-output isolation, stdin detachment, idle-GC protection, delete reaping, and read-only rejection; controller tests cover the HTTP flow and 404 mapping.
- Note: `pkg/isolation` MergedView tests fail on macOS (pre-existing, `/var` is a symlink); unrelated to this change.

## Follow-ups (not in this change)

- Regenerate Python/Go SDK clients and update `sdks/` alignment per `sdks/AGENTS.md`
- e2e tests in `tests/python/test_isolated_session_e2e.py` / `tests/go/isolated_session_e2e_test.go`
- docs update for the isolated session API

title: [Feature] Expose the resolved image digest on sandboxes and snapshots (and/or snapshot labels), so a snapshot cache can tell that a mutable tag was rebuilt
body:
## Why do you need it?

Since the exact-name filter landed in #1205 / #1301, a snapshot can be used as a warm cache: create the snapshot under a deterministic key derived from the image reference, and on the next run look it up with `GET /snapshots?name=<key>&state=Ready` and restore with `POST /v1/sandboxes` + `snapshotId` instead of provisioning and re-installing a toolchain from scratch. That works, and it turns a multi-minute cold start into seconds. Thank you for shipping it.

The problem is that the only identity the cache can key on is the image **reference**, and in practice image references are **mutable tags** — `myorg/toolchain:latest`, `myorg/toolchain:dev`, or any tag an internal CI job re-pushes on every build. When that tag is rebuilt, the reference string does not change, so the cache key does not change either. The lookup keeps hitting the same `Ready` snapshot, and every subsequent sandbox is restored with the **old** image content. Nothing surfaces the divergence:

- there is no error, no state change, and no warning — the restore succeeds and returns a healthy sandbox that simply contains stale software;
- and the failure is unbounded in time: once a stale snapshot exists, it is served forever, because nothing will ever invalidate it.

This is the quiet inverse of #1162 (registry GC deletes the snapshot's image, so restore fails loudly at pull time). Here the restore works perfectly and the answer is wrong, which is considerably harder to notice.

A client cannot fix this on its own, because nothing on the public contract carries **content** identity for the image a sandbox came from:

- `Sandbox.image` is an `ImageSpec`, and `ImageSpec` has exactly `uri` (plus optional `auth`). `uri` is the string that was *requested*; it is echoed back unchanged and says nothing about what content the runtime actually resolved and pulled.
- `Snapshot` carries no image information at all — `{id, sandboxId, name, status, createdAt}`, with `additionalProperties: false` in the spec.
- `Snapshot` has no labels, metadata, annotations, or any key-value map, and `GET /snapshots` filters only by `sandboxId`, `name`, `state`, `page`, `pageSize`. So a client cannot even attach a digest it computed itself and then filter on it.

There is an asymmetry here that also reads as a plain consistency gap: sandboxes already have a full custom key-value story — `CreateSandboxRequest.metadata` ("Custom key-value metadata for management, filtering, and tagging"), `GET /sandboxes?metadata=...` filtering, and `PATCH /sandboxes/{sandboxId}/metadata` (RFC 7396 merge patch). Snapshots are the *longer-lived* resource — they routinely outlive the sandbox that produced them — yet they are the one resource with no key-value map at all.

That leaves two workarounds, neither of which holds up as a general answer:

1. **Invalidate out of band — have whatever rebuilt the image delete the snapshots.** The natural version of this is a `DELETE` call bolted onto the image-publishing pipeline, and where the same team owns both the pipeline and the consumer it does work. It fails as a general answer for three reasons. First, the producer and the consumer are frequently not the same system: the image being cached is very often one this caller does not build at all — an upstream base image, a vendor or third-party toolchain image, a `:latest` published by another team or another repository — so there is no pipeline to bolt anything onto. Second, even when the producer is in-house, this makes correctness depend on a push notification arriving; every consumer must be discovered and told, new consumers are silently uncovered, and a missed or failed call leaves no trace — the cache simply keeps serving old content forever. Third, its failure mode is silent wrong content rather than an error, which is the worst property an invalidation scheme can have. A resolved digest inverts all of this into a pull-based check that needs no coordination between producer and consumer, and that is correct by construction for images this caller does not own.
2. **Keep an external tag-to-digest mapping in the client's own database.** This duplicates state the server already resolves internally on every pull, and it can drift from the server's view — the same objection #1205 raised against maintaining an external name-to-snapshot-id map, which #1301 accepted and fixed.

The server already has this information. Provisioning a sandbox necessarily resolves the reference to concrete image content: the Docker path pulls the image and can read its repo digest (or the image ID when the image is local-only), and the Kubernetes path has `status.containerStatuses[].imageID`. The value exists at pull time on every runtime; it is simply discarded rather than recorded, so callers cannot use it.

To be precise about one nearby field, since it is easy to conflate the two: the `SandboxSnapshot` CRD does already carry `ContainerSnapshot.ImageDigest`, but that is the digest of the *pushed snapshot* image ("ImageDigest is the digest of the pushed snapshot image") — the snapshot's own output, in the same forward-pointing family as #1272's `imageUri`, not the source image this request is about. It is cited here only as precedent that digest plumbing already exists internally and that the project is comfortable modeling a digest field; the source-image digest is a separate value that is currently recorded nowhere.

With a digest exposed, cache keys become content-addressed and the whole class of problem disappears: the key is derived from `sha256:...` rather than from a tag, a rebuild changes the key, the stale snapshot is never looked up again, and the new content is captured under a new key — automatically, with no operator step and no external database.

**On the obvious answer, "just pass a digest reference instead of a tag."** It is a fair first reaction, and it does not close the gap:

- It moves the resolution work to the client, which is precisely workaround 2 above. To send `myorg/toolchain@sha256:...` the client must first resolve `myorg/toolchain:latest` itself, which means a registry API round trip on the create path, plus registry credentials held client-side for that purpose. Those credentials are today handed to the *server* through `ImageSpec.auth` precisely so the client does not need its own registry access; requiring a client-side registry query to make snapshot caching correct inverts that design. The server, meanwhile, resolves the very same reference moments later, on the pull it was already going to perform.
- It does not help on the snapshot side at all. `Snapshot` carries no image information of any kind, so even a client that diligently pins every create by digest still cannot look at an existing snapshot and determine which image content it came from. Provenance is lost the moment the source sandbox is gone.
- It also changes deployment semantics that are not the client's to change: operators frequently *want* a tag such as `:latest` or `:dev` to mean "whatever CI last published", and pinning every create by digest opts the whole fleet out of that.

The narrow ask, then, is not "let me pin by digest" — that already works. It is "tell me what you resolved", so that a client can key a cache on content rather than on a name.

## How could it be?

Two independent options. **Either one alone unblocks this**; they compose well and doing both is the strongest outcome. Option A is the one we would prefer, because it puts the fact where it is actually known — in the server.

### Option A (preferred) — expose the resolved image digest end-to-end

- **Spec** (`specs/sandbox-lifecycle.yml`): add an optional, response-only `resolvedDigest` to the `ImageSpec` schema (or, if a request/response split is preferred, an optional `imageDigest` sibling field on `Sandbox`), and an optional `imageDigest` on the `Snapshot` schema, captured from the source sandbox at snapshot-creation time. Note that `Snapshot` is `additionalProperties: false`, so this genuinely has to be a spec change — a client cannot read the value out of an unmodeled extra property today.
- **Server**: populate it from the runtime's resolved image once the image has been pulled (Docker: the image's repo digest, or the image ID when the image is local-only and has no repo digest; Kubernetes: `imageID` from the container status). For `Snapshot`, copy the source sandbox's resolved digest onto the record when the snapshot is created, so the provenance survives the sandbox.
- **SDKs**: surface it on the public sandbox and snapshot models (`SandboxInfo`, `SnapshotInfo`) in the generated and hand-written clients.

**Input:** none — no new request fields. **Output:** `sha256:...` when the runtime can resolve it, omitted or null otherwise (for example while the sandbox is still `Pending`, or for a runtime that cannot report it). Optional and omitted-by-default means the change is additive and backward compatible.

A useful secondary consequence: `Snapshot.imageDigest` also makes a snapshot self-describing about its provenance, which helps any consumer that needs to reason about *what* a snapshot contains after the source sandbox is gone.

### Option B — arbitrary snapshot labels with selector filtering (Phase 2 of #1205)

This is the part that was explicitly descoped when #1205 was closed:

- add an optional `labels: map<string, string>` to `Snapshot` and `CreateSnapshotRequest`, persist it on the snapshot record;
- support label-selector filtering on `GET /snapshots`, for example `labelSelector=key1=value1,key2=value2`;
- surface both through the SDKs.

This closes the sandbox/snapshot consistency gap described above, and it independently solves a second problem #1205 raised: a single `name` string cannot express a **multi-dimensional** cache key (toolchain digest × repository revision × configuration hash). Today those dimensions have to be hashed together into one opaque name, which means the client can only ever ask for an exact full-key match — it can never ask "any snapshot for this toolchain digest, regardless of configuration".

Option B does not, by itself, tell a client *what* the digest is — the client would still have to resolve the tag out of band (for example by querying the registry) before it could label anything. That is why Option A is the preferred one and B is the complement: **A** supplies the fact, **B** supplies the general-purpose place to put facts and query them.

## Other related information

**Relationship to existing issues** — please note this is deliberately *not* a duplicate of any of these:

- **#1205 / #1301** — this is the direct parent. #1301 shipped Phase 1 (the exact `name` filter) and closed #1205 via `Fixes #1205`, while Phase 2 (labels) was explicitly set aside. From the implementer on #1205: *"I would like to work on Phase 1 of this issue: add the exact-match `name` filter to the lifecycle spec, server/repository path, and supported SDKs, with focused regression tests. I will keep snapshot labels out of scope for this PR."* Option B above picks that descoped piece back up, and Option A is the new part — #1205 asked for lookup keys, not for content identity, and it is content identity that turns out to be the missing piece for correct invalidation.
- **#1271 / #1272 (open)** — `imageUri` there is the OCI image the snapshot itself *produces*, so that the snapshot can be restored on another server or runtime. It is a forward pointer derived from the snapshot's own captured rootfs. This request is the opposite direction: the provenance of the *source* image the sandbox was provisioned from. A caller cannot compute a snapshot's restore-image URI in advance from a source tag, so `imageUri` cannot be used as a comparison key to detect that the source tag was rebuilt. The two are complementary and neither subsumes the other. Practically, they also do not conflict: #1272 adds an optional `imageUri` to the same `Snapshot` schema Option A would extend, so if #1272 lands first the source `imageDigest` simply sits alongside it as a second optional field — one describing what the snapshot *produces*, one describing what it *came from*. We are happy to rebase around #1272 in whichever order suits the maintainers. (History for context: #994 was closed as a duplicate of #1077, and #1077 was closed by its author in favor of #1271.)
- **#1162 (closed)** — same family, opposite failure mode: there, the snapshot's own image was garbage-collected by the registry so restore fails loudly; here, restore succeeds and silently returns stale content.
- **OSEP-0008** (pause/resume via rootfs snapshot) is where today's `Snapshot` shape comes from, and its minimalism was deliberate rather than a considered rejection of image identity. Its goals include *"Keep the design minimal by retaining only one snapshot per sandbox"*, and its non-goals include *"Supporting multiple historical snapshots per sandbox"* and *"Adding `GET /sandboxes/{sandboxId}/snapshots` in v1"* (<https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/47d85df848f957f5e7b3231e435ef9333a57537c/oseps/0008-pause-resume-rootfs-snapshot.md#L87-L98>). Snapshots have since grown past that scope into an independently listed, long-lived resource with its own lookup key (#1205 / #1301). The identity gap described here is the part that scope never had reason to cover.

**Verification performed today (2026-08-07).** Everything below was re-checked directly rather than recalled; only `GET` requests were made against the running server.

Versions exercised — both are the current latest at time of writing:

- Python SDK `opensandbox` **0.1.15** (tag `python/sandbox/v0.1.15`, released 2026-07-24 — the latest release on PyPI and the latest Python SDK tag).
- Server image **`opensandbox/server:v0.2.2`** (tag `server/v0.2.2`, released 2026-07-20 — the latest server tag). Note: this server's `GET /openapi.json` self-reports `info.version: 0.1.0`; that is the separately-reported staleness in #1436, not an older server.
- Docker runtime, Python 3.12.

**a. SDK model surface (`opensandbox` 0.1.15).** Full field sets, printed from `model_fields`:

```text
SandboxInfo   : ['created_at', 'entrypoint', 'expires_at', 'extensions', 'id', 'image', 'metadata', 'platform', 'snapshot_id', 'status']
SnapshotInfo  : ['created_at', 'id', 'name', 'sandbox_id', 'status']
SandboxImageSpec: ['auth', 'image']
SnapshotFilter: ['name', 'page', 'page_size', 'sandbox_id', 'states']

SandboxInfo     : digest-like field(s) -> NONE
SnapshotInfo    : digest-like field(s) -> NONE
SandboxImageSpec: digest-like field(s) -> NONE
SnapshotInfo    : labels/metadata field(s) -> NONE
SandboxInfo     : labels/metadata field(s) -> ['metadata']
SnapshotInfo    : image field(s)           -> NONE
```

The same holds for the generated wire models (`opensandbox.api.lifecycle.models`): `Snapshot` is `['created_at', 'id', 'name', 'sandbox_id', 'status']` and `ImageSpec` is `['auth', 'uri']`. A text scan of the entire installed SDK reports **0 occurrences of the string `digest`**.

**b. Live server schema (`GET /openapi.json` on `opensandbox/server:v0.2.2`).**

```json
"Snapshot": {
  "description": "Persistent point-in-time capture of a sandbox.",
  "properties": {
    "createdAt": {"format": "date-time", "type": "string"},
    "id":        {"type": "string"},
    "name":      {"anyOf": [{"type": "string"}, {"type": "null"}]},
    "sandboxId": {"type": "string"},
    "status":    {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/SnapshotStatus"}
  },
  "required": ["id", "sandboxId", "status", "createdAt"],
  "type": "object"
}
```

```json
"ImageSpec": {
  "properties": {
    "auth": {"anyOf": [{"$ref": "#/components/schemas/ImageAuth"}, {"type": "null"}]},
    "uri":  {"description": "Container image URI in standard format (e.g., 'python:3.11', ...)", "type": "string"}
  },
  "required": ["uri"],
  "type": "object"
}
```

And the complete filter surface the server advertises for `GET /v1/snapshots`:

```text
sandboxId (query) | name (query) | state (query, array) | page (query) | pageSize (query)
```

The evidence here is the **schema** the server advertises, not any particular instance's data: no `Snapshot` or `ImageSpec` response can carry a digest or a label map, because neither is modeled. `GET /v1/snapshots` and `GET /v1/sandboxes` were also exercised (`HTTP 200`) purely to confirm the live responses conform to exactly these schemas and add no undocumented fields.

**c. Current `main` — the gap is not already fixed.** Checked at commit `47d85df848f957f5e7b3231e435ef9333a57537c`:

- `Snapshot` schema, `{id, sandboxId, name, status, createdAt}` with `additionalProperties: false`: <https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/47d85df848f957f5e7b3231e435ef9333a57537c/specs/sandbox-lifecycle.yml#L966-L996>
- `Sandbox` schema, whose `image` is a plain `ImageSpec` ref: <https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/47d85df848f957f5e7b3231e435ef9333a57537c/specs/sandbox-lifecycle.yml#L1038-L1106>
- `ImageSpec` schema, `uri` + `auth` only: <https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/47d85df848f957f5e7b3231e435ef9333a57537c/specs/sandbox-lifecycle.yml#L1158-L1189>
- `GET /snapshots` parameters, `sandboxId` / `name` / `state` / `page` / `pageSize`: <https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/47d85df848f957f5e7b3231e435ef9333a57537c/specs/sandbox-lifecycle.yml#L275-L317>
- Server `Snapshot` response model: <https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/47d85df848f957f5e7b3231e435ef9333a57537c/server/opensandbox_server/api/schema.py#L651-L676>
- Server-side snapshot record — note `SnapshotRestoreConfig` is deliberately shaped so "future fields can be added without changing the top-level snapshot record shape", which is exactly where a source-image digest would sit: <https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/47d85df848f957f5e7b3231e435ef9333a57537c/server/opensandbox_server/services/snapshot_models.py#L39-L49>
- Kubernetes CRD already modeling a digest internally — again, this is the *pushed snapshot* image's digest, not the source image's, and is cited only as precedent: <https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/47d85df848f957f5e7b3231e435ef9333a57537c/kubernetes/apis/sandbox/v1alpha1/sandboxsnapshot_types.go#L43-L52>

The strings `digest`, `labelSelector`, and `labels:` do not occur anywhere in `specs/sandbox-lifecycle.yml` on `main`.

We are happy to help with the spec change, the server change, or the SDK plumbing if the direction is agreeable — and equally happy to adjust the shape (field naming, `ImageSpec.resolvedDigest` vs a `Sandbox`-level field, whether `Snapshot` carries the source digest or only labels) to whatever fits the project's conventions best.

title: docs(osep): propose exact request-header credential selectors

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

Address Issue #1373 

This draft adds OSEP-0020, a proposal for choosing between Credential Vault bindings that otherwise have the same scheme, host, method, and path.

Today, Credential Proxy fails closed when more than one binding matches. This makes two legitimate credentials for the same destination shape impossible, even when the client already sends a distinct non-secret placeholder or authentication form that could distinguish the request.

The OSEP proposes optional exact request-header selectors on a binding. A selector refines an existing destination match; it does not replace destination matching or become a general request-policy language.

## Proposed safety boundary

- A binding may require up to four exact request-header predicates, combined with AND.
- Header names are case-insensitive; values are exact after outer HTTP whitespace is trimmed.
- A selected header must occur exactly once. Missing or repeated headers do not match.
- Overlapping destination scopes remain valid only when static validation proves their selectors cannot both match a request.
- There is no generic-binding fallback or selector-precedence rule. If multiple bindings are eligible, selection remains fail closed.
- Selectors are non-secret routing hints, not proof of process identity or per-process authorization.
- Selector values are write-only and must not appear in reads, logs, metrics, diagnostics, or errors.

## What this does not propose

- Regex, prefix, wildcard, or case-insensitive value matching.
- Query, body, cookie, or process-identity selectors.
- Automatic migration of existing bindings.
- A change to existing bindings without selectors.

## Review focus

Feedback is particularly useful on the exact-match contract, duplicate-header handling, the conservative static overlap rule, sanitized read shape, and the cross-SDK compatibility rollout.

- [x] Documentation review
- [x] git diff --check
- [ ] Unit tests (proposal only)
- [ ] Integration tests (proposal only)

## Breaking Changes

- [x] None. The proposed contract is additive; existing bindings retain current behavior.

- [x] Security impact considered

title: docs(osep): add OSEP-0018 Auto Idle-Pause and Resume-on-Revisit

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

Adds **OSEP-0018: Auto Idle-Pause and Resume-on-Revisit** — the design proposal for a server-side `IdlePauseCoordinator` that automatically pauses sandboxes idle beyond a configurable threshold and resumes them on the next proxy access.

It is the symmetric counterpart of `renew_intent` (OSEP-0009):

- `renew_intent`: **on access → extend TTL**
- `idle_pause`: **no access beyond a threshold → pause; on next access → resume**

Motivation and full discussion: #1448.

## Why

Long-lived Agent workloads are bursty — real I/O in short windows, idle for the majority of their lifetime (LLM think time). On a memory-constrained namespace the resident concurrency ceiling is fixed by physics, yet these sandboxes must not lose filesystem state (short TTL destroys intermediate files → Agent hallucination). OSEP-0008 gives manual pause/resume (release memory, keep state); OSEP-0009 renews TTL on access but never releases memory. Nothing today **automatically** releases idle memory while preserving state, or wakes a paused sandbox on return. This proposal fills that gap, turning the memory constraint into a cheap storage constraint.

## What's in this PR

- `oseps/0018-auto-idle-pause-and-resume-on-revisit.md` — full proposal (status: `draft`).
- `oseps/README.md` — index entry for OSEP-0018.

**Documentation only.** No code, no schema, no behavior change. Implementation will follow in separate PRs once the design is reviewed.

## Key design points (for reviewers)

- **Activity signal**: reuses the single unified signal the server has — the proxy hook at `api/proxy.py:265` (HTTP) and `:431` (WS). Verified there are no `/exec` or `/files` endpoints; all Agent data-plane I/O flows through the proxy.
- **Core safety invariant**: `pause_sandbox` only patches `spec.pause` and the Go controller's expiration check is unconditional (runs before pause scheduling), so a paused sandbox with a short TTL is still deleted. The proposal pushes `renew_expiration` to a retention window **before** pausing — server-only, no Go change.
- **Auto-resume**: proxy `ConnectError` (Paused → Pod scaled to 0) → `ensure_resumed` → resume → poll to Running → reset TTL → retry.
- Global `[idle_pause]` config (default off); mirrors `[renew_intent]`. Server-only, no client/fork changes, no new dependencies.
- Complementary to #1422 (pause/resume the egress sidecar): this decides *when* to pause; #1422 makes a single pause operation complete. Orthogonal.

## Checklist

- [x] OSEP follows `oseps/osep-template.md.template` structure
- [x] `oseps/README.md` index updated
- [x] status set to `draft`
- [x] Related issue opened (#1448)

Looking for feedback on: the renew-before-pause invariant as the TTL-safety approach (vs. a Go controller change), the global-switch vs per-sandbox opt-in trade-off, and the resume-latency visibility story.

title: Feature: Auto idle-pause and resume-on-revisit for long-lived Agent sandboxes
body:
## Why do you need it?

Code-sandbox workloads — especially Agent tasks driving a code interpreter — are **long-lived but bursty**: they do real I/O for short windows and sit idle for the majority of their lifetime (waiting on the LLM). On a memory-constrained Kubernetes namespace (e.g. ~20 Gi allocatable, per-sandbox memory limit 500 Mi that cannot be lowered because of large-file reads), the resident concurrency ceiling is fixed by physics — roughly `allocatable / (active_ratio × limit + (1 − active_ratio) × idle_usage)`, on the order of tens of sandboxes — regardless of how the ResourceQuota or runtime is tuned.

These workloads also **must not lose state**: an Agent writes many intermediate files into the sandbox, and reclaiming the sandbox (short TTL) destroys that state, causing the Agent to hallucinate missing artifacts. So short TTL is not an acceptable lever.

What's missing today:
- **OSEP-0008** provides manual pause/resume (rootfs snapshot → Pod scales to 0, memory freed, filesystem preserved, `sandboxId` stable). But nothing decides *when* to pause.
- **OSEP-0009** provides auto-renew-on-access (extends TTL while the sandbox is being used). But it never releases memory — an idle-but-renewed sandbox still occupies resident memory.

There is no mechanism to **automatically release the memory of idle sandboxes while preserving their state**, and none to **wake a paused sandbox when traffic returns**. Without it, the only way to run more long-lived Agent tasks than the memory ceiling allows is to add memory — the constraint can't be converted into the cheap storage cost that OSEP-0008 was designed to enable.

## How could it be?

A server-side `IdlePauseCoordinator` that is the symmetric counterpart of `renew_intent`:

- `renew_intent`: **on access → extend TTL.**
- `idle_pause`: **no access beyond a threshold → pause; on next access → resume.**

Concretely (server-only, no Go changes, no client/fork changes, default off):

1. **Activity tracking** — reuse the single unified activity signal the server already has: the proxy hook at `api/proxy.py:265` (HTTP) and `:431` (WS), where `_schedule_proxy_renew` already lives. A new `_touch_idle` refreshes a per-sandbox `last_activity` timestamp. (There are no `/exec` or `/files` endpoints; all Agent data-plane I/O flows through the proxy.)
2. **Idle scanner** — a background task lists `Running` sandboxes every `scan_interval_seconds`; any idle longer than `idle_threshold_seconds` is paused.
3. **Auto-resume on revisit** — when a proxy request hits a Paused sandbox, the Pod is scaled to 0, so `client.send` raises `ConnectError` (currently surfaces as 502). On that error, call `ensure_resumed(sandbox_id)` → `resume_sandbox` → poll until `Running` → retry the send once. Transparent to the caller (one slow request, no data loss).

**Critical safety invariant (the reason this isn't trivial):** `pause_sandbox` only patches `spec.pause=True` and does **not** touch `spec.expireTime`; the Go controller's expiration check runs unconditionally *before* pause scheduling, so a paused sandbox with a short TTL is still deleted — files lost, hallucination problem returns. The fix is server-side: **before pausing, renew the expiration to `now + paused_retention_seconds`** (verified that `renew_expiration` does not check sandbox state, so renew-while-Running is valid). After resume, reset TTL to a fresh `resume_ttl_seconds`.

Global config, mirroring `[renew_intent]`:

```toml
[idle_pause]
enabled = false
scan_interval_seconds = 60
idle_threshold_seconds = 600        # MUST be >= scan_interval (anti-flapping)
min_sandbox_age_seconds = 120       # don't pause during bootstrap
paused_retention_seconds = 86400    # TTL pushed before pause; protects files while Paused
resume_ttl_seconds = 3600           # TTL reset after resume
```

With this, total concurrent tasks (resident + paused) can far exceed the resident memory ceiling, because paused sandboxes occupy object storage (a committed OCI snapshot), not node memory.

## Other related information

- Full design drafted as **OSEP-0018: Auto Idle-Pause and Resume-on-Revisit** (to be submitted as a PR to `oseps/`).
- Builds directly on **OSEP-0008** (pause/resume via rootfs snapshot) and **OSEP-0009** (auto-renew on ingress access) — it is the automation layer between them.
- Complementary to **#1422** (pause/resume the egress sidecar together with the sandbox): #1422 makes a single pause operation complete; this proposal decides *when* to pause and *when* to resume. They are orthogonal and compose.
- Scope: standard Kubernetes backend only. The `fleets` (fast-sandbox) runtime rejects pause/resume and is intentionally out of scope.

title: [Bug] SandboxErrorCodes has no attribute 'INTERNAL_ERROR' when PVC auto-create fails
body:
### Summary

  `kubernetes_service.py` references `SandboxErrorCodes.INTERNAL_ERROR` when raising
  a 500 error for PVC auto-create failure, but the `INTERNAL_ERROR` attribute is not
  defined on the `SandboxErrorCodes` class in `constants.py`. This causes an
  `AttributeError` to be raised instead of the intended `HTTPException`.

  ### Location

  - **File**: `server/opensandbox_server/services/k8s/kubernetes_service.py`
  - **Line**: 658
  - **Class**: `server/opensandbox_server/services/constants.py:71`

  ### Reproduction

  1. Configure kubernetes runtime with a sandbox that mounts a PVC whose
     `claimName` does not exist in the namespace.
  2. Trigger PVC auto-create failure (e.g. insufficient RBAC, or namespace missing).
  3. Server raises `AttributeError` instead of returning a 500 response with the
     `INTERNAL_ERROR` code.

  ### Error

  ERROR: opensandbox_server.services.k8s.kubernetes_service: Error creating sandbox:
  type object 'SandboxErrorCodes' has no attribute 'INTERNAL_ERROR'

  HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
  {
    "detail": "type object 'SandboxErrorCodes' has no attribute 'INTERNAL_ERROR'"
  }

  ### Root Cause

  `kubernetes_service.py:658`:

  ```python
  raise HTTPException(
      status_code=status.HTTP_500_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,
      detail={
          "code": SandboxErrorCodes.INTERNAL_ERROR,  # ← attribute missing
          "message": f"Failed to auto-create PVC '{claim_name}': {e.reason}",
      },
  ) from e

title: feat(server,chart): source OSEP-0011 secure-access keys from a Secret

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Problem

The `opensandbox-server` chart only accepts the OSEP-0011 signing keys through `server.gateway.secureAccess.keys` — plaintext in values. The chart renders them into the gateway `--secure-access-keys` arg and the server's ConfigMap-mounted `config.toml`, so there is no way to source the keys from a k8s Secret: the kubelet `$(VAR)` expansion trick works for container args (gateway) but not for file contents (server). Anyone running the chart from a GitOps flow must either commit the signing key in plaintext or forgo signed routes.

## Changes

- **server**: `OPENSANDBOX_SECURE_ACCESS_KEYS` (`key_id=base64,...` ring) and `OPENSANDBOX_SECURE_ACCESS_ACTIVE_KEY` env overrides, mirroring the existing `OPENSANDBOX_SERVER_API_KEY` override. Both must be set together, require `ingress.mode = "gateway"`, and win over the `[ingress.secure_access]` TOML block. Parsing/validation reuses `SecureAccessKey`/`SecureAccessConfig`.
- **chart**: `server.gateway.secureAccess.existingSecret` (mutually exclusive with `keys`, enforced by a template `fail`). The named Secret carries `keys` (`a=<b64>[,b=<b64>...]`) and `active-key` entries, wired as env vars into both containers: the server reads them via the new overrides; the gateway via `$(OPENSANDBOX_SECURE_ACCESS_KEYS)` expansion in `--secure-access-keys`. Key material never appears in values, the ConfigMap, or pod specs.
- **docs**: chart README + secure-access guide.

Default behavior is unchanged: no `secureAccess` config renders exactly what main renders, and plaintext `keys` render identically to before.

## Test plan

- `cd server && uv run pytest tests/test_config.py` — 7 new env-override tests (populates config without TOML block, env wins over TOML, both-vars pairing, gateway-mode requirement, malformed entry, invalid base64, active key not in ring); full file: 88 passed.
- `uv run pytest tests/test_config.py tests/test_signing.py tests/test_ingress.py tests/test_endpoint_auth.py` — 146 passed.
- `uv run ruff check` — clean.
- `helm template` matrix: default (no secureAccess references), plaintext keys (byte-identical arg + TOML block to main), `existingSecret` (gateway arg `$(OPENSANDBOX_SECURE_ACCESS_KEYS)` + `secretKeyRef` env on both Deployments, no `[ingress.secure_access]` in the ConfigMap), keys+existingSecret (render fails with the validation message), `gateway.env` alone and combined with `existingSecret` (env lists merge correctly).
- `helm lint` — clean with and without `existingSecret`.

# Summary

- parse standard SSE with the focused httpx-sse 0.4.3 library instead of HTTPX universal line splitting
- preserve compatibility with current and older execd versions by normalizing legacy bare JSON frames into standard data events before parsing
- apply the shared parser to command and isolated execution streams in both async and sync Python Sandbox SDK adapters
- cover U+0085, U+2028, U+2029, CRLF, multiline data fields, one-byte chunk boundaries, legacy framing, and compressed responses

HTTPX iter_lines/aiter_lines treat additional Unicode separators as line endings, splitting valid JSON strings and causing decode failures. httpx-sse 0.4.3 implements SSE-specific CR/LF framing and full event parsing.

## Compatibility

No execd wire-format change is required. Standard data events pass through unchanged; legacy JSON followed by two LF bytes is normalized locally. Code Interpreter SDK and CLI are independently released packages and remain outside this package-scoped fix.

Fixes #1429.

title: fix(server): report correct version across API, package metadata, and chart

labels.name: size/M
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 30-99 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Problem

The server reports a stale version everywhere a client can read it programmatically， regardless of the deployed release. On a deployment running `v0.2.2`：

| Channel | Reported | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `/openapi.json` & `/docs` | `0.1.0` | hardcoded in `main.py` |
| installed package metadata （`importlib.metadata`） | `0.1.0.dev0` | hatch-vcs `fallback_version` |
| `helm list` / chart `appVersion` | `0.1.0` | stale `Chart.yaml` |

Only the container image tag is correct， and it is not reachable through the API. This makes upgrade verification and support harder than it needs to be.

## Root cause & fix

Three independent root causes， each tied to a different channel， fixed in three commits：

1. **`main.py` hardcodes the version** → read it from installed package metadata at runtime via `importlib.metadata`， mirroring `opensandbox-cli`. Falls back to `0.0.0-dev` for source checkouts without installed metadata. （`server/opensandbox_server/main.py`）
2. **hatch-vcs falls back to `0.1.0.dev0`** because the `.git`-less image build （and the shallow， tag-less PyPI checkout） never feed a version in → derive `pkg_version` from the release tag and export `SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION` for **both** the Docker build （`build.sh` `--build-arg` → `Dockerfile` `ARG`/`ENV`， honored by the editable install） and the PyPI `uv build`. （`server/Dockerfile`， `server/build.sh`， `.github/workflows/publish-server.yml`）
3. **`Chart.yaml` `appVersion` stays stale** — it was only patched at chart-package time by `publish-helm-chart.yml`， while the `server/v*` release only bumped the `values.yaml` image tag → extend `scripts/bump-server-chart.sh` to also set `appVersion` （bare SemVer， no leading `v`） and have the release workflow `git add Chart.yaml` next to `values.yaml`. （`scripts/bump-server-chart.sh`， `.github/workflows/publish-server.yml`）

## Commits

- `fix(server): resolve version from package metadata at runtime`
- `fix(server): inject SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION into build to resolve real version`
- `fix(chart): bump Chart.yaml appVersion on server release`

## Validation （local prototype）

- **（1）** `main.py` compiles. With a synthetic `opensandbox_server-0.2.2.dist-info`， `importlib.metadata.version("opensandbox-server")` returns `0.2.2`； with no metadata it falls back to `0.0.0-dev`.
- **（2）** `SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION=9.9.9 uv build --wheel` produces `opensandbox_server-9.9.9-py3-none-any.whl`， confirming the whole chain （uv → hatchling → hatch-vcs） honors the env end-to-end. At release time the same path with the real tag yields `0.2.2`.
- **（3）** `scripts/bump-server-chart.sh 0.2.2` sets `values.yaml` image tag → `v0.2.2` and `Chart.yaml` `appVersion` → `0.2.2`， leaving chart `version` unchanged.

The actual Docker build/push was not exercised locally （needs registry credentials）； it runs at release time.

## Notes

- **（1） and （2） must land together**： with only the `main.py` change， `/openapi.json` would move from `0.1.0` to `0.1.0.dev0`， still not the real version.
- **（3）** is an independent code path （the Helm chart）； its fix lives in the release process， not the server package. Chart `version` is intentionally left to the existing helm release process.
- No duplicate found. #758 is about the chart package version under a release branch — a different code path； this PR is about the version the running server reports.
