title: Feature Request / Question: Is secure credential injection for SSH on the roadmap?
body:
## Why do you need it?

While some tasks (like repository cloning) can be pivoted to Git-over-HTTPS, many real-world AI agent workflows absolutely require native outbound SSH connections where HTTPS is not an option:

1. **Remote Infrastructure Orchestration & Administration:** Agents doing systems engineering or DevOps tasks (using tools like Ansible, Rsync, SFTP, or raw SSH) to provision, patch, or configure remote Linux VMs (AWS EC2, bare-metal, etc.). These environments do not expose HTTP endpoints for OS-level management.
2. **Secure Database and Protocol Tunneling:** Establishing secure SSH tunnels to query remote databases (e.g., Postgres, MySQL) that are not exposed to the public internet.
3. **Restricted Enterprise Environments:** Corporate networks where code hosting platforms (like internal GitLab or Bitbucket instances) strictly block Port 443 (HTTPS) for git operations and only permit Port 22 (SSH) for security and auditing compliance.

Currently, if an agent needs to perform these tasks, we must write the raw SSH private key (`id_rsa`) to the sandbox filesystem. Because the AI agent has shell access inside the sandbox, it can easily read, exfiltrate, or leak the private key. There is currently no way to allow an agent to use an SSH key without giving it read access to the key.


## Other related information

We would love to know:
1. Is securing or vaulting outbound SSH credentials (via an SSH-Agent socket or similar mechanism) currently on your roadmap?
2. If this is not on the roadmap, what are your currently recommended best practices for isolating or securing SSH-based workloads without exposing raw private keys to the sandbox container?

Thank you for building OpenSandbox!

title: feat(egress): use native nftables for DNS and transparent redirects (gVisor support) [DO NOT MERGE YET]

labels.name: size/XL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 500-999 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
> ⚠️ **DO NOT MERGE YET.** This PR depends on four upstream gVisor PRs that add the nftables features the new rulesets rely on. Until those land in gVisor **and** a runsc release ships with them, the native-nft redirect will not install under gVisor (GKE Sandbox). On `runc` and Kata the change works today. Please hold until the gVisor side is merged and released — see **Dependency** below.

## Why

The egress sidecar programs its dataplane with nftables, but the two NAT redirects — the **DNS redirect** (→ local DNS proxy) and the **transparent-HTTP MITM redirect** — were still shelling out to `iptables`/`iptables-nft`. Under **gVisor (runsc)** the iptables `nat` table is unavailable (gvisor#170), so the egress sidecar could not run under GKE Sandbox at all. These two redirects were the last part of the egress that was not native nftables.

## What

Rewrite both redirects to emit **native nftables** (a `nat`/`output` chain with `redirect to :port`), consolidated into `pkg/nftables` alongside the existing filter-policy manager. The egress dataplane is now 100% native nftables — no `iptables`/xt-compat dependency.

- `pkg/nftables/redirect.go` — DNS redirect: `OUTPUT :53 (udp/tcp) → :15353`, with a `meta mark 0x1` bypass for the proxy's own SO_MARK'd upstream queries and per-destination `RETURN` for the exempt nameserver list (`ip` + `ip6`).
- `pkg/nftables/transparent.go` — MITM transparent redirect: loopback `RETURN`, then `meta skuid != <mitm uid> tcp dport 80/443 redirect to :<port>` (IPv4, mirroring the previous behavior).
- `pkg/nftables/nat_common.go` — idempotent per-table cleanup helper.
- Delete `pkg/iptables/` (redirect + transparent + tests).
- `Dockerfile` — drop the `iptables` package (keep `nftables`).
- `scripts/cleanup.sh` — crash recovery now deletes the native-nft redirect tables (`opensandbox_dns_redirect`, `opensandbox_transparent`) instead of iptables rules; leaves the `inet opensandbox` filter table in place so filtering stays fail-closed across restarts.
- Update call sites (`main.go`, `shutdown.go`, `mitmproxy_transparent.go`), comments and docs.

No behavior change on `runc`/Kata: the rendered rules are equivalent to the previous iptables REDIRECT rules.

## Dependency: gVisor nftables support

The native-nft rulesets use nftables features runsc did not implement. These upstream gVisor PRs add them (tracking issue **google/gvisor#13796**, which also documents this OpenSandbox use case):

| gVisor PR | Feature the egress needs |
|---|---|
| google/gvisor#13797 | `meta mark` load (SO_MARK bypass) |
| google/gvisor#13799 | interval sets (CIDR allow/deny) |
| google/gvisor#13800 | timeout sets (expiring dynamic allow) |
| google/gvisor#13801 | `redir` / REDIRECT (this PR's DNS + MITM redirect) |

**This PR must not be merged until those are merged and a runsc release includes them.**

## Testing

- `go build ./...`, `go vet`, `gofmt` — clean.
- Full egress module test suite (`go test ./...`) — pass. New unit tests in `pkg/nftables` cover both redirect script builders, the missing-table cleanup path, and the apply-error path.
- **End-to-end under a patched runsc** (built from the four gVisor PRs above, `--TESTONLY-nftables`): the exact rulesets this code emits install cleanly and `nft list ruleset` renders them correctly — `redirect to :port`, `meta mark`, `meta skuid !=`, and exact `tcp dport` all evaluate under gVisor's netstack.

title: CredentialMatch can't disambiguate two credentials bound to an identical destination shape
body:
- `CredentialBinding.match` selects by scheme, host, method, and path only. 
- `CredentialAuth` is a `oneOf` where one binding carries exactly one auth rendering. 

If two different real credentials legitimately need to reach the same destination shape, there's currently no way to express that. Two bindings with an overlapping match fail closed as ambiguous (OSEP-0012 names this as an intentional simplification).

The problem is that "same destination shape" doesn't imply "same credential." 

When adopting credential vault (and thanks for the implementation !), we've found at least two concrete cases that we can't solve in the current form of the vault:
1. A single SaaS API exposes multiple logical environments/regions behind identical hostname and path where the differentiator is different API keys.  A sandbox that needs access to both at the same time has only one binding slot but two real credentials to place in it.
2. Two different clients in the same sandbox (say, an npm-compatible package manager and a Yarn-compatible one) both resolve packages from the same private registry host and path, but authenticate with different schemes - one sends a bearer token, the other sends Basic auth from a `user:pass` pair.  Both are legitimate and both hit the same `scheme+host+method+path` but only one binding can occupy that space.

In both cases, the fake placeholder value each client sends before injection could already be distinct - it's derived from whatever env var or config field that specific client reads.  The credential match rule collides on destination host, but the requests themselves could be differentiated.

I suggest a narrow fix along those lines: 
- Let `CredentialMatch` optionally match on the content of a header the client already sends (e.g. an existing `Authorization` prefix or a specific already-known placeholder value), used only to disambiguate otherwise-overlapping bindings, not as a replacement for the existing scheme/host/method/path match.
- `_binding_matches`/`_select_binding` in `mitmscripts/system.py` already have precedence handling for the ambiguous-match case; this would slot in as an additional, higher-precedence dimension rather than a re-architecture.

I haven't found this discussed in the OSEP-0012 review thread or in an existing issue - flagging this as a problem statement first, before writing anything resembling a design proposal.  

I'm happy to draft an OSEP if that's the right next step, or if there's a simpler solution I'm missing, I'd be happy to try it out first.

title: feat(sdks/python): resilient SDK transport (OSEP-0016)

labels.name: size/XXL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 1000+ lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

Python landing of [OSEP-0016 Resilient SDK Transport](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/pull/1368) for both `sdks/sandbox/python` and `sdks/code-interpreter/python`. Client-only; no spec change, no server change, no wire-format change.

Draft while OSEP-0016 is still under review; will be marked ready once the design lands (or updated to track any decision changes on the OSEP first).

## What it adds

**Retry policy** (`opensandbox.transport.RetryPolicy`)
- New value type on `ConnectionConfig` / `ConnectionConfigSync`.
- Defaults retry idempotent methods only; `POST` / `PATCH` status-code retry is opt-in through `retryable_status_codes_non_idempotent`.
- Default idempotent retryable set: `{HTTPStatus.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS, HTTPStatus.BAD_GATEWAY, HTTPStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE}` — narrower than the OSEP draft; happy to widen back to `{408, 425, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504}` if the OSEP thread lands there.
- Decorrelated jitter (default), full jitter, and deterministic exponential.
- `Retry-After` honored with a fixed 60s ceiling to prevent pathological server headers from stalling the client.
- `RetryPolicy.disabled()` for end-to-end fast-fail (also suppresses fresh-conn recovery).
- Public API uses `frozenset[HTTPStatus]` so callers get type checking and IDE completion.

**Exception hierarchy**
- Extend `SandboxException` with an `is_retryable` accessor reflecting the SDK's actual retry decision at emission time (budget exhaustion / deadline / cancellation all force `False` even for transient causes). In practice, because the retry transport exhausts its budget before surfacing an exception, the boundary value is almost always `False`; the accessor exists for forward compatibility and explicit fast-fail paths.
- New subclasses: `SandboxRateLimitException` (carries `retry_after`), `SandboxTimeoutException`, `SandboxConnectionException`.
- Existing classes and their public fields are unchanged; `except SandboxApiException` continues to catch rate-limit and API errors.

**Transport wrappers**
- `RetryAsyncTransport` (`httpx.AsyncBaseTransport`) and `RetrySyncTransport` (`httpx.BaseTransport`).
- `ConnectionConfig` / `ConnectionConfigSync` build a retry-wrapped `httpx.*HTTPTransport` by default and share it across all HTTP clients within a Sandbox/Manager instance. A user-supplied `transport` is passed through verbatim (retry wrapping is then the caller's job).
- SSE bootstraps must not go through the retry wrapper (request bodies are not replayable). The `opensandbox.transport.unwrap_retry_transport()` helper returns the raw inner transport, and the command / isolated / code-interpreter SSE clients call it so they share the underlying connection pool while bypassing retry.
- Generated OpenAPI code is not touched.
- `lifecycle_metrics` deliberately does **not** reuse the shared transport: its best-effort `httpx.Client` / `httpx.AsyncClient` is closed after each report, and closing it would also tear down the shared transport used by every other adapter on the same `connection_config`.

## Behavior change to call out

- `RetryPolicy` is enabled by default. Callers that rely on fast-fail semantics on `GET/HEAD/PUT/DELETE` must opt out via `ConnectionConfig(retry_policy=RetryPolicy.disabled())`.
- Under the default policy, `POST/PATCH` are never retried on any status code; pre-send transport failures (DNS, TCP connect, TLS handshake, fresh-conn RST) are still retried on `POST/PATCH`.

## Non-goals

Matches OSEP-0016 non-goals: no server-side idempotency store, no per-request override, no SSE stream resume, no client-side circuit breaker.

## Tests

- Retry policy defaults, validation, `HTTPStatus` usage.
- Pure decision function: status matrix, transport branch (pre-send vs. post-send), budget/deadline/cancellation predicates, opt-in rules, jitter algorithms, `Retry-After` parsing and clamping.
- Async + sync httpx transport integration via scripted mock transports: success, 4xx pass-through, budget exhaustion, pre-send vs. post-send classification, opt-in, observability callback invariants.
- `ConnectionConfig` wiring: default wraps, `disabled()` skips wrapping, user-supplied transports pass through verbatim.
- SSE client uses the raw inner transport (end-to-end assertion that the SSE client's transport is the unwrapped inner transport, not the retry wrapper).

Local verification (macOS, Python 3.12), after merging latest `main`:

- `sdks/sandbox/python`: `uv run ruff check` clean, `uv run pyright` clean on this PR's files, `uv run pytest` 451 passed.
- `sdks/code-interpreter/python`: `uv run ruff check` clean, `uv run pyright` clean, `uv run pytest` 15 passed.

## Follow-ups

- JS/TS, Kotlin, Go, C# SDKs — separate PRs.
- SSE stream resume with `Last-Event-ID` — deferred to a follow-up OSEP as noted in OSEP-0016.

## Related

- OSEP: #1368

title: fix(egress): purge stale mitmproxy CA on startup

labels.name: size/M
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 30-99 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

Fixes part of #1370.

mitmproxy's CA lives in the egress container's ephemeral confdir (`/var/lib/mitmproxy/.mitmproxy/`). Every time the egress container restarts, a fresh CA is generated with a new fingerprint. The previous generation's public cert, however, may still be on the pod-scoped shared volume at `/opt/opensandbox/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem` (an `emptyDir` under Kubernetes / a docker named volume, both survive container restarts).

Without any purge, an agent container starting or restarting alongside egress passes its bootstrap readiness check `[ -f "$MITM_CA" ] && [ -s "$MITM_CA" ]` on the stale file *before* egress has had a chance to overwrite it, and installs a CA that no longer matches what mitmproxy will sign with. Subsequent HTTPS from agent then fails with `unable to get local issuer certificate`.

## What this change does

Erase `/opt/opensandbox/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem` as early as possible in `egress` `main()` — immediately after logger initialization, before any telemetry / policy / dnsproxy / iptables / mitmproxy setup. This forces the agent's bootstrap wait-loop to block until *this* generation's `SyncRootCA` writes the current CA back to the shared volume.

Log level is `warn`: on a healthy first pod startup the file does not exist and nothing is logged; a `removed stale exported CA` warning is real signal that egress just restarted, which is useful when diagnosing HTTPS-from-agent problems.

## Scope

**Fixes**: pod-container co-restart (both containers restarting together within the same pod, with `emptyDir` surviving). This is scenario C in #1370.

**Does NOT fix**: egress-alone container restart (scenario B in #1370). In that case, the agent's bootstrap has long finished and never re-reads the file, so no amount of egress-side purging helps. That case still requires an agent-side reload path (watcher in `execd`), which is intentionally out of scope for this PR.

**Not affected**: whole-pod recreation (scenario A) already goes through a fresh shared volume and works correctly.

## In-place egress process restart (uncommon)

If the egress process is somehow restarted while its container stays up (uncommon under normal K8s / Docker lifecycles, since egress is PID 1), mitmproxy will reuse the CA already in confdir. The purge deletes the shared-volume copy, `SyncRootCA` writes back the same bytes moments later, and any agent bootstrap running concurrently only blocks for the duration of that gap. Functionally a no-op; the `warn` line correctly reports "previous egress generation left it behind".

## Tests

Added unit tests for the pure helper `purgeStaleExportedCAFrom` covering:

- Existing file is removed.
- Absent file is a no-op (first-boot path).
- Unrelated files (e.g. `merged-ca-certificates.pem`) are left untouched.

Local verification:

```
cd components/egress
go build -mod=mod ./...
go vet -mod=mod ./...
go test -mod=mod ./...
```

All pass.

## Files changed

- `components/egress/main.go` — call `mitmproxy.PurgeStaleExportedCA()` after `withLogger`, before telemetry init.
- `components/egress/pkg/mitmproxy/cacert_export.go` — new exported `PurgeStaleExportedCA()` and internal testable `purgeStaleExportedCAFrom`.
- `components/egress/pkg/mitmproxy/cacert_export_test.go` — three focused unit tests.

title: egress sidecar restart rotates mitmproxy CA and breaks HTTPS from the agent container
body:
## Summary

When the `egress` sidecar container restarts (while the sandbox pod itself is **not** recreated), the main (`agent`) container loses the ability to make HTTPS requests through the transparent mitmproxy interception. TLS handshakes fail with:

```
SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate
```

The `egress` container itself continues to work correctly against the same targets.

## Reproduction

1. Deploy a sandbox pod with transparent mitmproxy enabled (`OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_MITMPROXY_TRANSPARENT=true`).
2. Wait for the pod to become Ready — HTTPS works from the `agent` container.
3. Force the `egress` container (only) to restart, e.g. `kubectl exec` into it and kill the mitmdump / init process, or wait for a liveness restart. The pod is **not** recreated; only the `egress` container's `restartCount` increments.
4. From the `agent` container: `curl -v https://www.baidu.com` → fails with `unable to get local issuer certificate`.
5. From the `egress` container: the same `curl` succeeds; the presented certificate's issuer is `CN=mitmproxy; O=mitmproxy`, and the fingerprint differs from before the restart.

## Root Cause

The mitmproxy root CA is regenerated whenever the `egress` container restarts, but the `agent` only installs the CA once at bootstrap and never reloads it. The CA-sync path between the two containers is asymmetric.

### mitmproxy CA lives in the container's ephemeral writable layer

`components/egress/pkg/mitmproxy/launch.go` sets `HOME=/var/lib/mitmproxy` and does not pass `--set confdir=...`. mitmproxy therefore uses `/var/lib/mitmproxy/.mitmproxy/` as its confdir.

`components/egress/Dockerfile` creates `/var/lib/mitmproxy` as the mitmproxy user's home and bakes `config.yaml` into `/var/lib/mitmproxy/.mitmproxy/config.yaml`, but the CA files (`mitmproxy-ca.pem`, `mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem`) are generated by mitmproxy at first startup, not shipped in the image.

The path `/var/lib/mitmproxy` is **not** on any shared volume — the sidecar's only `volumeMount` is the shared `emptyDir` at `/opt/opensandbox` (see `server/opensandbox_server/services/k8s/egress_helper.py`). It is not on a PVC either. It is the container's ephemeral overlay writable layer.

When the `egress` container restarts, the overlay upper layer is discarded and confdir is reset to the image state: `config.yaml` is present, but the CA files are gone. mitmproxy's behavior in this state is to **generate a fresh self-signed root CA + key** (with a new fingerprint), since none exist in confdir.

### CA is only pushed to the `agent` at first startup

`components/egress/pkg/mitmproxy/cacert_export.go` `SyncRootCA`:
- Copies the mitmproxy CA to the shared volume at `/opt/opensandbox/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem`.
- Installs it into the `egress` container's system trust store via `update-ca-certificates`.
- Is called only once, from `startMitmproxyTransparentIfEnabled` in `components/egress/mitmproxy_transparent.go`. It is not re-invoked when the mitmproxy process is restarted by `restartWithBackoff`, and it is obviously not re-invoked across `egress` container restarts (the process starts over from `main`).

`components/execd/bootstrap.sh`:
- Waits (up to 300s) for `/opt/opensandbox/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem` to appear, then runs `trust_mitm_ca` to install it into the `agent` container's system trust store, NSS DB, JDK cacerts, and export env vars (`NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`, `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE`, `SSL_CERT_FILE`, etc.).
- Runs once, then `exec`s `execd`. There is no watcher for the CA file and no re-load mechanism.

### Scenario breakdown

Three scenarios need to be distinguished. The bug title mentions "pod restart", but the pod-lifecycle boundary matters:

**A — Whole pod is recreated** (node failure, eviction, `kubectl delete pod`, rollout, …)
- `opensandbox-bin` is a pod-scoped `emptyDir`, so recreating the pod gives both containers a completely empty shared volume.
- `agent` bootstrap blocks on the `while` loop until `egress` writes the CA. It installs the CA generated by this generation of mitmproxy.
- **Not affected.**

**B — Only the `egress` container restarts** (pod is unchanged, only its `restartCount` increments)
- New `egress` → mitmproxy confdir is empty → generates a **new** root CA (different fingerprint).
- `SyncRootCA` overwrites `/opt/opensandbox/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem` with the new CA and installs it into the `egress` container's trust store.
- `agent` is still running with the **old** CA in its trust store; no re-install ever happens.
- All subsequent HTTPS requests from `agent` fail: mitmproxy presents certs signed by the new CA, `agent` verifies against the old CA.
- **Main scenario. Reliably reproduces the bug.**

**C — `agent` and `egress` restart together at the container level** (pod unchanged, `emptyDir` preserved)
- Both containers start fresh, but the shared volume still holds the **previous generation's** `mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem`.
- New `egress` will regenerate CA as in B and eventually overwrite the file.
- New `agent` bootstrap's guard is only "file exists and is non-empty" — it cannot tell which generation the file belongs to. It reaches the `while` check essentially instantly; `egress` needs to bring mitmdump up and pass a `WaitListenPort(15s)` gate before running `SyncRootCA`.
- `agent` therefore very likely grabs the stale CA and installs it. New mitmproxy is signing with the new CA. **Same failure mode as B, via a narrow race.**

### Why `egress` still works in scenario B

`egress` shares the pod's network namespace with `agent`, and the transparent iptables redirect (`components/egress/pkg/iptables/transparent.go`, `OUTPUT tcp 80,443 → 18081`) applies to both. `egress`'s own HTTPS is also intercepted by mitmproxy, but `SyncRootCA` on the new `egress` container also installs the new CA into `egress`'s own system trust store, so verification succeeds locally.

## Impact

Every sandbox pod that has transparent MITM enabled AND has experienced an independent `egress` container restart at any point after `agent` bootstrap: HTTPS from the `agent` container is broken until the `agent` container itself is restarted so it re-runs bootstrap.

The Docker runtime is affected in the same way: `server/opensandbox_server/services/docker/networking.py` and `docker_service.py` only mount the shared `/opt/opensandbox` volume; they do not persist `/var/lib/mitmproxy` either. An independent `egress` container restart under Docker triggers the same behavior.

## Suggested fix directions

Non-exhaustive; happy to discuss which one to pursue before sending a PR.

1. **Persist mitmproxy confdir on the shared volume** (recommended, root fix). Point mitmproxy confdir at a path under the shared volume (e.g. `/opt/opensandbox/.mitmproxy`), either by setting `HOME` accordingly or by passing `--set confdir=...`. The CA is then reused across `egress` container restarts and never rotates unexpectedly. One thing to handle: `config.yaml` is currently baked at `/var/lib/mitmproxy/.mitmproxy/config.yaml`; if the whole confdir moves to the shared volume, the launch path needs to either copy `config.yaml` there on start or keep it separate and reference it via `--set` / a distinct flag.
2. **Watch the shared CA file from the agent side and re-install on change.** This belongs in `execd`, not in `bootstrap.sh` (bootstrap is one-shot and exits into `exec execd`). Reinstall into the system trust store, NSS DB, JDK cacerts, and re-export env-var bundles when the file's fingerprint changes.
3. **Lower-cost patch on top of the above:** have `egress` delete any stale `mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem` from the shared volume very early at startup, before mitmdump comes up. This makes `agent` bootstrap's `while` loop actually block on the new generation and eliminates scenario C's race, but does not by itself fix scenario B — scenario B still needs (1) or (2).

## Detection

- In `agent`: compare CA on disk against what mitmproxy is actually serving.
  - `openssl x509 -in /opt/opensandbox/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem -noout -subject -fingerprint -dates`
  - `echo | openssl s_client -connect www.baidu.com:443 -servername www.baidu.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -fingerprint`
  - Different fingerprints while both are mitmproxy-issued confirms rotation.
- Pod state: `kubectl describe pod` — `egress` container's `restartCount` higher than `agent`'s, or its `lastState.terminated.finishedAt` more recent, points at scenario B.

## Environment

- OpenSandbox with `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_MITMPROXY_TRANSPARENT=true` (Credential Vault injection scenarios).
- Both Kubernetes and Docker runtimes are affected.

title: fix(egress): allow single-layer %2f in raw request path (npm scoped packages)

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
# Summary
`_path_is_ambiguous()` in the egress credential proxy rejected every request whose raw path contained `%2f`. npm scoped packages are required by the registry protocol to send `/@scope%2fname` on the wire, so with Credential Vault active, `npm install @scope/pkg` in sandboxes was returning 403 (reported in Aone workitem 84550489 for `@ali/orion-claude-plugin`).

Split the two concerns:

- **Raw-request check (`request()`)** — tolerate a single-layer `%2f` (`allow_single_encoded_slash=True`). Nested encodings (`%252f`, `%252e%252e`), raw backslash `\`, encoded backslash `%5c`, and dot-segments still trip the guard.
- **New `_path_encoded_slash_changes_binding()`** — re-runs binding path matching against `unquote(raw_path)`. If the encoded slash would move the request across a credential binding boundary, the request is still rejected with 403. Legit `/@scope%2fname` decodes into the same binding → allowed; a crafted `/api/v8/projects/123%2f..%2f456/...` decodes into a different scope → rejected (also caught by the pre-existing dot-segment check).
- **Post-substitution check (`_apply_path_query_substitutions()`)** — keeps the strict semantics (`allow_single_encoded_slash=False`), because a `%2f` injected by the credential proxy itself always shifts the canonical path relative to what the client sent.

Also wire mitmscripts unit tests into `egress-test.yml` — the tests already existed but weren't being run in CI, so this class of regression had no signal.

# Testing
- [x] Unit tests — `python -m unittest discover -s components/egress/tests` → **34 passed** (28 existing + 6 new)

New tests cover:
- npm scoped registry path `/@scope%2fname` (lowercase and uppercase `%2F`) receives credential injection.
- Encoded `%2f` that stays inside a single binding scope is allowed.
- Encoded `%2f` that spans two bindings (broad vs. narrow) is rejected with 403.
- Double-encoded `%252f` and encoded backslash `%5c` remain rejected.

- [ ] Integration tests
- [ ] e2e / manual verification

# Breaking Changes
- [x] None

The credential-proxy 403 semantics only change for a single-layer `%2f` that does **not** cross a binding boundary. That path previously always returned 403 and now succeeds — this is the intended fix. All other rejection paths (`..`, `%252f`, `%5c`, `\`, `%2f` crossing bindings, substitution introducing `%2f`) still return 403.

# Checklist
- [x] Linked Issue or clearly described motivation
- [ ] Added/updated docs (if needed) — behavior change is internal to credential proxy; no user-visible doc surface
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Security impact considered — see the "Split the two concerns" section above; the binding-consistency guard preserves the original threat model
- [x] Backward compatibility considered

title: docs(oseps): add OSEP-0016 resilient SDK transport

labels.name: size/XL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 500-999 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

Adds OSEP-0016 proposing a client-only resilience layer for all five OpenSandbox SDKs (Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Kotlin, Go, C#) to absorb routine network infrastructure blips without any server-side change.

## Context

An audit of the five SDKs shows that, aside from Go, none has any HTTP-level retry. Even the Go SDK retries `POST` blindly on `429/502/503/504`, which is unsafe once the network fault produces a "sent request but lost response" race.

## Proposal in one paragraph

Every SDK ships a shared `RetryPolicy` contract with identical semantics across languages, an extended exception hierarchy with a machine-checkable `is_retryable` accessor, decorrelated jitter, and `Retry-After` handling with a bounded cap. The retry engine is injected at the same layer each SDK already uses for transport concerns (httpx transport, openapi-fetch middleware, OkHttp `Interceptor`, `net/http.RoundTripper`, `DelegatingHandler`). Generated OpenAPI code is not touched.

## Safety invariant

The `POST/PATCH` retry set is deliberately narrow: only conditions that can be locally proven side-effect free. Specifically pre-send transport failures (DNS, TCP connect, TLS handshake, fresh-conn RST), plus `429` and `502`. Read timeouts, `500`, `503`, `504` are **not** retried on `POST/PATCH`. This preserves at-most-once semantics without requiring any server-side idempotency store.

Idempotent methods (`GET/HEAD/PUT/DELETE/OPTIONS`) retry on the full transient set `{408, 425, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504}` plus all transport errors.

## Zero cross-cutting cost

- No spec change
- No wire-format change
- No server-side change
- No new external dependency
- Fresh-conn retry for idempotent methods works even when `RetryPolicy.disabled()`

## Behavior change to call out

`RetryPolicy` is enabled by default. Callers that rely on fast-fail semantics must explicitly opt out via `ConnectionConfig(retry_policy=RetryPolicy.disabled())`. The Go SDK's existing `RetryConfig` is preserved as a deprecated alias for one minor version; its `POST` behavior on `503/504` narrows from "retry" to "fail-fast" as a safety fix.

## What comes next (out of scope for this OSEP)

- SSE stream resume with `Last-Event-ID`
- Client-side circuit breaker / hedging / adaptive rate limiting
- `Idempotency-Key` protocol with a server-side dedup store

The SSE Resume follow-up is unblocked by this OSEP's requirement that every SDK's SSE parser stop discarding `id:` and `retry:` fields.

## Files

- `oseps/0016-resilient-sdk-transport.md` — new proposal

The `oseps/README.md` index entry will be added in a follow-up once the proposal is accepted.

## Reviewer notes

- Non-Goals, Risks and Mitigations, and the Retry Decision Algorithm are the three sections most worth reviewing first.
- Configuration Surface section includes six Python examples covering default, disabled, tuned attempts/backoff, tightened POST set, deadline caps, and per-request override.

body:
# Summary

Follow-ups from PR #1361 review, split into three logically independent commits:

1. **`fix(execd): parse sh export -p output using dash/ash quote convention`**
   PR #1361 added a POSIX single-quoted branch to `parseExportLine` that only handled the `'\''` escape emitted by bash / zsh / BSD sh, but **dash and BusyBox ash** — the default `sh` on Alpine / Debian slim images this fallback exists for — emit embedded single quotes as `'"'"'` instead. `shellEscape` also writes the `'"'"'` form, so on a bash-less image any session variable containing a single quote was silently corrupted on the next `/session` run.

   Accepted both escape forms in the parser and locked the invariant with:
   - New dash / BusyBox ash rows in `TestParseExportLine_BashAndShFormats`
   - New `TestShellEscapeParseExportLine_RoundTrip` fuzz-style round-trip
   - New `TestBashSession_FallsBackToSh_PersistsSingleQuotedValue` end-to-end

2. **`refactor(execd): unify shell launch via shellCommand helper and cache getShell`**
   The five shell-launch sites in `pkg/runtime` were each hand-rolling the same "preferred shell + optional `--noprofile --norc`" logic, with drift in flag ordering. Extract `shellCommand()` so bash-session, PTY, and isolated-session launches share the same code path. The two `Controller.runCommand*` sites keep their inline `getShell` + explicit `-c` invocation because `--noprofile/--norc` are no-ops for one-shot `bash -c`.

   Cache `getShell()` with `sync.Once` — execd's PATH is fixed at startup, so re-running `exec.LookPath` on every request is pure overhead. `resetShellCacheForTest` is exposed for tests that mutate PATH (wired into `useShOnlyPath`).

3. **`test(execd): replace inline bash lookups with requireBash helper`**
   25+ tests inlined the same `exec.LookPath("bash"); err != nil { t.Skip }` guard with two divergent skip messages. Extract `requireBash(t)` (in both `pkg/runtime` and `pkg/web/controller`) so future bash-dependent tests can opt in with one line and a consistent reason.

Each commit builds and passes tests standalone (bisect-safe).

# Testing

- [ ] Integration tests
- [ ] e2e / manual verification

Passed on darwin/arm64:
- `cd components/execd && go build ./...`

- Reverse-verified the parser fix: temporarily reverting only the `parseExportLine` hunk while keeping the new tests reproduces the failure on the dash/ash quote-escape cases, confirming the tests actually gate the fix.

title: Egress credential vault is lost on pause/resume (in-memory, not re-injected on resume)
body:
## Summary

The egress **credential vault** is in-memory state in the egress sidecar process. When a sandbox is **paused**, the pod (and the egress process) is deleted, so the vault is lost; on **resume** a fresh egress sidecar starts with an empty vault, and nothing re-populates it. Any credentials that were injected into the vault silently disappear across a pause/resume cycle.

Checked against `main` @ `883079bc8c4d12678a9a3668cfe5de1306f7642f`.

## Why this matters

The credential vault exists precisely so the **user/agent container never sees the secrets** — the egress sidecar injects them into outbound traffic (mitmproxy) on the sandbox's behalf. That isolation is important when the sandbox runs untrusted / arbitrary AI-generated code. But combined with pause/resume, a resumed sandbox comes back with **no credentials in the vault**, so outbound credential injection silently stops working until something re-pushes them — and there is no re-push.

## Where the behavior comes from

**1. The vault is purely in-memory, created empty at startup, populated only at runtime.**

- `components/egress/policy_server.go`: `handler.credentialVault = credentialvault.NewStore(...)` — created **empty** on egress startup (no file/env seed).
- `components/egress/pkg/credentialvault/vault.go`: `Store` holds `credentials map[string]record` and `bindings map[string]Binding` — **no disk persistence** anywhere in the `credentialvault` package.
- It is populated only via the runtime HTTP API `POST /credential-vault` (`handleCredentialVault`), i.e. after the pod is running.

**2. Pause deletes the pod (egress process dies → vault gone).**

- `kubernetes/internal/controller/batchsandbox_pause_resume.go` → `completePause` deletes the pods (`r.Delete(ctx, pod)` for non-pooled) after snapshotting container rootfs images. The `BatchSandbox.spec.Template` (env, sidecars) is retained, but the vault is *not* part of the template — it was runtime state.

**3. Resume only swaps container images; it never touches the vault.**

- `continueResume` reads the snapshot image URIs and rewrites `latest.Spec.Template.Spec.Containers[i].Image = img`, then normal reconciliation recreates the pod. The env/sidecars are preserved from the template, but the credential vault (runtime-only) is neither snapshotted nor re-injected.
- Neither the controller nor the server re-populates the vault on resume (the server doesn't call `POST /credential-vault` at all — the vault is pushed by an external client at runtime).

## Net effect

| Injected into egress sidecar | Survives pause/resume? |
|---|---|
| Env vars in the pod template (`EGRESS_RULES` policy, `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_*`, egress token) | ✅ yes (template is retained; resume only swaps images) |
| Credential vault entries (runtime `POST /credential-vault`, in-memory) | ❌ no (in-memory, lost on pod deletion, not re-injected on resume) |

So the *env-based* egress config survives, but the *credential vault* — the mechanism designed to keep secrets out of the untrusted container — does not.

## Suggestions (happy to send a PR)

Any of these would address it; I'd like to know which direction you prefer:

1. **Re-inject on resume** — have the resume flow (or the server) re-push the vault after the resumed pod is ready, from a persisted (encrypted) copy of the vault create requests.
2. **Persist + restore the vault** — snapshot the vault state (encrypted) alongside the sandbox and restore it into the fresh egress sidecar on resume.
3. **At minimum, document + surface it** — make the limitation explicit (docs + a warning/condition), so operators relying on the vault know they must re-inject credentials after a resume.

## Repro (outline)

1. Create a sandbox with an egress credential vault entry (`POST /credential-vault`); confirm outbound credential injection works.
2. Pause the sandbox, then resume it.
3. Observe the resumed sandbox's egress sidecar has an empty vault (`GET /credential-vault` sanitized state) and outbound injection no longer applies.

# Summary

Add **OSEP-0015: Unified Umbrella Release Governance** — a proposal to
replace the current per-component versioning model with a single
umbrella release where every OpenSandbox artifact (server, component
images, Kubernetes operator, Helm chart, CLI, and every language SDK)
carries the same `X.Y.Z` per release.

**Motivation.** OpenSandbox today ships 19+ independently versioned
targets (`server/v0.2.1`, `docker/execd/v1.0.21`, `docker/ingress/v1.0.10`,
`java/sandbox/v1.0.16`, `python/sandbox/v0.1.14`, …). There is no
single OpenSandbox version a user can install, audit, or roll back to,
no assertion that any given combination has been e2e-tested together,
and no clear client-vs-server compatibility story.

**Proposal (highlights).**

- Umbrella git tag: `opensandbox/X.Y.Z` (v-less; distinct namespace
  from every existing component tag).
- Container image tag: `release-X.Y.Z` (prefix chosen to be visually
  unmistakable next to legacy `opensandbox/execd:v1.0.21`-style tags).
- Helm chart, CLI, all language SDKs: bare semver `X.Y.Z`.
- **First release: `opensandbox/1.0.0` = OpenSandbox GA** (release
  governance only; API stability contract is deferred to a follow-up
  OSEP).
- Cadence: new line every 2 weeks; latest-only support; no LTS during
  the 1.x train; one N-1 emergency CVE window per line.
- Immutable BOM at `releases/opensandbox/X.Y.Z.yaml` pins the exact
  image digest for every artifact, signed via existing Sigstore /
  `actions/attest` infrastructure.
- Historical per-component tags are frozen at `1.0.0` (never deleted,
  never extended) so pinned users see no regression.

Full prior-model consideration, cadence trade-offs, image/tag naming
rationale, BOM schema, release workflow (fan-out with atomicity
guard), migration plan, and Alternatives (A: keep per-component
tags; B: no BOM; C: two-tier umbrella; D: longer cadence + LTS) are
documented in the proposal.

title: README: Star History chart no longer renders for public visitors
body:
## Background

The Star History chart embedded at the bottom of README.md no longer renders for most visitors:

```markdown
[![Star History Chart](https://api.star-history.com/svg?repos=opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox&type=date&legend=top-left)](https://www.star-history.com/#opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox&type=date&legend=top-left)
```

## Root Cause

GitHub has restricted the Stargazers API (`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/stargazers` with the `application/vnd.github.v3.star+json` accept header) to repository admins and collaborators only. Without an authenticated token with sufficient permissions, the API returns empty or error responses.

Since star-history.com generates the SVG by calling this endpoint server-side without repo-level credentials, the chart fails to render for unauthenticated/public viewers — which is everyone reading the README on GitHub.

## Suggestion

Remove the Star History section from README.md. Reasons:

1. **Broken UX** — A broken image or empty chart gives a poor first impression to new visitors.
2. **No simple fix** — The restriction is on GitHub's side; there's no way to make the embedded SVG work for anonymous viewers without a privileged token baked into the URL (which would be a security concern).
3. **Low information value** — Star count is already visible in the GitHub UI and in the badges at the top of the README.

Alternatively, if the team wants to keep it, a static screenshot updated periodically could work — but that adds maintenance overhead.

title: fix(execd): fall back to sh in bash-session and isolated-session launch paths
body:
## Why do you need it?

#1359 fixed the hard-coded `bash` in `StartPTY()` / `StartPipe()` so PTY sessions now fall back to `sh` on minimal images (e.g. Alpine) that ship `sh` but not Bash. The same hard-coding still exists in two other execd shell launch paths, so those code paths will keep failing on such images:

- `components/execd/pkg/runtime/bash_session.go:208` — the language-`bash` session runner:

  ```go
  cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "bash", "--noprofile", "--norc", scriptPath)
  ```

  This is used for the pipe-based bash session API (`CreateBashSession` / `run`). On an Alpine-only image the session fails to start with `exec: "bash": executable file not found in $PATH`.

- `components/execd/pkg/runtime/isolated_session.go:77` — the long-running shell inside a `bwrap` namespace used by `/v1/isolated/session`:

  ```go
  cmd := exec.Command("bash", "--noprofile", "--norc")
  ```

  Same failure mode when the host image only has `sh`.

There is also a stale wording issue: `docs/components/execd.md` still says *"Isolated sessions run a bash process inside a per-execution bubblewrap namespace"*. After a fallback lands, this should say "shell" (or explicitly mention the fallback).

## How could it be?

Apply the same pattern introduced by #1359:

- Reuse the existing `getShell()` helper (`components/execd/pkg/runtime/command.go`) — prefer `bash`, fall back to `sh`.
- Pass `--noprofile --norc` only when the selected shell is `bash`; they are not portable to POSIX `sh`.
- For `bash_session.go`, the script path continues to be passed positionally and is portable across bash / sh.
- For `isolated_session.go`, evaluate separately whether the bwrap namespace actually needs Bash semantics; if yes, keep hard-coded `bash` and document the image requirement instead of falling back. If no, apply the same fallback.

Two things to decide up front (worth calling out in the PR):

1. **Isolated sessions** — the shell here runs inside bwrap, and downstream tests (`bwrap_test/*`) exercise bash features (aliases, builtins). The fallback may quietly change semantics for isolated sessions on `sh`-only hosts. Options: (a) fallback + document the caveat, same as PTY; (b) do **not** fall back, keep requiring bash, and document that requirement; (c) probe at startup and expose the choice through `/v1/isolated/capabilities`.
2. **Bash language session** — the language is literally named `bash` in `runtime/language.go`. If we fall back to `sh` we should also decide whether that is still the same "language" from the SDK's point of view, or whether an `sh`-only host should report the `bash` language as unavailable.

Expected behavior after the fix (assuming option (a) for isolated sessions):

- Images with Bash: no behavior change.
- Images with only `sh`: bash-session runs and isolated sessions start successfully; commands using Bash-specific syntax may still fail under `sh`, same caveat as PTY.

## Other related information

- Follow-up to #1358 / #1359 — the PTY paths are already fixed; this issue tracks the remaining two shell launch sites in the same package.
- Relevant code:
  - `components/execd/pkg/runtime/bash_session.go` (`run`)
  - `components/execd/pkg/runtime/isolated_session.go` (`start`)
  - `components/execd/pkg/runtime/command.go` (`getShell`)
  - `components/execd/pkg/runtime/bash_session_test.go`
  - `components/execd/pkg/runtime/isolated_session_test.go`
- Docs to touch: `docs/components/execd.md` ("Isolated Sessions" paragraph).

## Why do you need it?

PTY sessions currently hard-code `bash` in both `StartPTY()` and `StartPipe()`. As a result, `/pty` sessions fail to start in minimal images such as Alpine images that provide `sh` but do not install Bash.

title: bug(kubernetes): snapshots may miss recent guest filesystem writes under Kata
body:
## Why do you need it?

When a Kubernetes sandbox uses a VM-isolated runtime such as Kata Containers, recent root filesystem writes may remain in the guest kernel page cache when a pause snapshot is committed. Host-side filesystem synchronization does not flush the guest filesystem.

As a result, pause, snapshot push, and resume can all succeed while files written immediately before pause are absent from the restored sandbox. Running `sync` inside the sandbox before pausing preserves the files, which indicates that guest filesystem synchronization is required.

## How could it be?

The snapshot workflow should attempt to synchronize the guest filesystem of every running container included in the snapshot before pausing and committing it.

Guest synchronization should be best effort so that stopped containers and images without a `sync` utility retain existing snapshot behavior. Failures should produce a clear warning that recent guest writes may be missing. The workflow should also report per-container and total synchronization duration.

Expected flow:

```text
discover containers
attempt guest filesystem sync for each running container
pause containers
commit containers
resume containers
push snapshot images
```

## Other related information

This affects Kubernetes pause/resume snapshots for runtimes with a separate guest kernel. A host-side `sync(2)` remains useful for shared-kernel runtimes but is not sufficient for a guest filesystem.

A regression test should write a file immediately before pause, without an explicit client-side sync, and verify that the file survives pause/resume under Kata Containers.

## Why do you need it？

I'm benchmarking OpenSandbox sandbox startup latency （`opensandbox.sandbox.create.duration` from #1307） across runtimes， and I need to interpret the OSEP-0004 performance numbers correctly before reporting them. The relationship between the two tables is currently ambiguous.

OSEP-0004 lists two performance tables under the "Performance Overhead" caveat. **Table A — "Startup Overhead"** （[L116](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/oseps/0004-secure-container-runtime.md#L116)） is introduced by this sentence （[L114](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/oseps/0004-secure-container-runtime.md#L114)）：

> "Secure runtimes add latency and resource overhead **compared to runc**："

| Runtime | Startup Overhead |
|---|---|
| runc | ~0ms |
| gVisor | ~10-50ms |
| Kata （QEMU） | ~500ms |
| Kata （Firecracker） | ~125ms |

**Table B — Cold Start / Warm Start** （[L126](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/oseps/0004-secure-container-runtime.md#L126)）：

| Runtime | Cold Start | Warm Start （from Pool） |
|---|---|---|
| runc | ~500ms | ~50ms |
| gVisor | ~550ms | ~100ms |
| Kata （QEMU） | ~1000ms | ~200ms |
| Kata （Firecracker） | ~625ms | ~125ms |

The Cold Start values in Table B happen to equal `runc Cold Start (~500ms) + Startup Overhead` from Table A：

| Runtime | 500ms + Startup Overhead | Table B Cold Start |
|---|---|---|
| gVisor | 500 + 50 = 550 | ~550ms ✅ |
| Kata （QEMU） | 500 + 500 = 1000 | ~1000ms ✅ |
| Kata （Firecracker） | 500 + 125 = 625 | ~625ms ✅ |

…but this relationship is never stated in the OSEP， and the "Startup Overhead" column isn't explicitly labeled as "relative to runc". I'd rather not report benchmark numbers under a wrong interpretation.

## How could it be？

Three clarifications would unblock the benchmark：

1. Is **"Startup Overhead"** （Table A） the *incremental overhead relative to runc* （i.e. how much slower this runtime is vs. the runc baseline）？
2. Is **`Cold Start ≈ runc baseline (~500ms) + Startup Overhead`** the intended model， or is the match coincidental？
3. What does **"Cold Start"** measure end-to-end （image pull？ execd injection？ health check？ API round-trip？）， and does **"Warm Start （from Pool）"** measure pool-acquire latency or full ready-to-serve latency？

Happy to send a PR adding a one-line clarification （and the `Cold = baseline + overhead` note） to OSEP-0004 once the definitions are confirmed.

## Other related information

- Related metrics work this benchmark depends on： #1307 （`opensandbox.sandbox.create.duration`， merged） and #1324 （resume/pause/kill latency， open）， both under the #870 SDK Metrics umbrella — these are how I plan to measure Cold vs Warm start empirically.
- Searched open/closed issues for `cold start`， `warm`， `startup`， `latency`， `overhead` — no existing issue discusses the *semantics* of these two OSEP-0004 tables. Several issues discuss pool pre-warming （#268 / #780 / #834） and secure runtimes （#281 / #934）， but not the table definitions themselves.

## Environment

Documentation question — reading [OSEP-0004](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/oseps/0004-secure-container-runtime.md) on `main`. Benchmarking `opensandbox.sandbox.create.duration` （#1307） across `runc` / `gVisor` / `Kata` （QEMU / Firecracker） on a local kind cluster.

---

<details>
<summary>📖 中文版（点击展开）</summary>

## 为什么需要它？

我在对 OpenSandbox 的沙箱启动延迟做性能测试（测 #1307 引入的 `opensandbox.sandbox.create.duration` 指标，跨多种 runtime），需要在汇报数据前正确理解 OSEP-0004 里的性能数字。目前两张表之间的关系表述是模糊的。

OSEP-0004 在 "Performance Overhead" 一节列了两张表。**表 A — "Startup Overhead"**（[L116](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/oseps/0004-secure-container-runtime.md#L116)）的引导句是（[L114](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/oseps/0004-secure-container-runtime.md#L114)）：

> "Secure runtimes add latency and resource overhead **compared to runc**："

| Runtime | Startup Overhead |
|---|---|
| runc | ~0ms |
| gVisor | ~10-50ms |
| Kata （QEMU） | ~500ms |
| Kata （Firecracker） | ~125ms |

**表 B — Cold Start / Warm Start**（[L126](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/oseps/0004-secure-container-runtime.md#L126)）：

| Runtime | Cold Start | Warm Start （from Pool） |
|---|---|---|
| runc | ~500ms | ~50ms |
| gVisor | ~550ms | ~100ms |
| Kata （QEMU） | ~1000ms | ~200ms |
| Kata （Firecracker） | ~625ms | ~125ms |

表 B 的 Cold Start 数值恰好等于 `runc 的 Cold Start（~500ms） + 表 A 的 Startup Overhead`：

| Runtime | 500ms + Startup Overhead | 表 B Cold Start |
|---|---|---|
| gVisor | 500 + 50 = 550 | ~550ms ✅ |
| Kata （QEMU） | 500 + 500 = 1000 | ~1000ms ✅ |
| Kata （Firecracker） | 500 + 125 = 625 | ~625ms ✅ |

……但这个关系在 OSEP 里从未明说，"Startup Overhead" 这一列也没有显式标注"相对 runc"。我不想在错误的解读下汇报性能数据。

## 希望怎样？

澄清以下三点即可推进性能测试：

1. **"Startup Overhead"**（表 A）是否为*相对 runc 的增量开销*（即这个 runtime 比 runc 基线慢多少）？
2. **`Cold Start ≈ runc 基线（~500ms） + Startup Overhead`** 是否为有意设计，还是数字巧合吻合？
3. **"Cold Start"** 端到端到底测了什么（镜像拉取？execd 注入？health check？API 往返？），**"Warm Start （from Pool）"** 测的是池分配延迟，还是完全就绪可用的延迟？

定义确认后，我愿意提一个 PR，给 OSEP-0004 补一句说明（以及 `Cold = baseline + overhead` 这条关系）。

## 其他相关信息

- 本次性能测试依赖的指标相关工作：#1307（`opensandbox.sandbox.create.duration`，已合并）和 #1324（resume/pause/kill latency，进行中），都在 #870 SDK Metrics 这条线下——我打算用它们实测 Cold vs Warm start。

## 环境

title: feat(sdk/go): add SandboxPoolManager with fence/tombstone parity with Python and Kotlin
body:
Discovered while reviewing #1352 (client pool guide). Codex flagged that the guide cannot cleanly recommend a cross-SDK "retire an old pool namespace" procedure, because the safe API exists in Python and Kotlin but not in Go.

## Current state

**Python** (`sdks/sandbox/python/src/opensandbox/pool_manager.py`) and **Kotlin** (`sdks/sandbox/kotlin/sandbox/src/main/kotlin/com/alibaba/opensandbox/sandbox/pool/SandboxPoolManager.kt`) both ship a `SandboxPoolManager.destroy(poolName, options)` API that applies a full protocol:

1. Short-circuit if `getDestroyState(poolName) == DESTROYED`
2. `beginDestroy(poolName, ownerId)` — write a `DESTROYING` fence into the state store, observable by any still-running peer pool instance
3. Loop `tryTakeIdle(poolName)` + `killSandbox(id)` up to `drainTimeout`, best-effort
4. `clearPoolState(poolName)` — wipe `max_idle`, idle TTL, etc.
5. `markDestroyed(poolName, ownerId, tombstoneTtl)` — write a `DESTROYED` tombstone (default 7 days) so future callers cannot silently rebind

Options: `strategy` (only `FORCE` currently), `drainTimeout` (default 30s), `tombstoneTtl` (default 7d).

**Go** (`sdks/sandbox/go/**`) has none of this:

- `grep -rE PoolManager|Destroy|Tombstone|Fence|DESTROYING|DESTROYED sdks/sandbox/go` → zero matches
- `PoolStateStore` interface at `sdks/sandbox/go/pool_store.go:25-74` has 15 methods; none of `GetDestroyState`, `BeginDestroy`, `ClearPoolState`, `MarkDestroyed`
- `RedisPoolStateStore` at `sdks/sandbox/go/poolredis/store.go` mirrors the same 15 methods, no extra destroy Lua / helpers
- `DefaultSandboxPool.Shutdown` (`sdks/sandbox/go/pool.go:548`) only stops the local reconciler and releases the primary lock; it does not kill idle sandboxes (guarded by `TestPool_Shutdown_DoesNotReleaseIdle` at `pool_test.go:803` and `TestPool_Shutdown_NonGraceful_DoesNotReleaseIdle` at `:841`)

The guide documents the gap explicitly at [`docs/guides/client-pool.md` "Retiring an old pool namespace"](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/docs/guides/client-pool.md) — Go users are told they must stop every writer first, manually loop `ReleaseAllIdle` + `SetMaxIdle(ctx, poolName, 0)`, rotate `PoolName`, and (for Redis) clean up keys with `DEL`/`SCAN`. Without a shared fence there is no way to safely retire a namespace while any peer pool instance is still writing.

## Why this matters

- Real gap in cross-language SDK parity for a public capability (pool retirement).
- Docs guide the affected users to an operator-driven manual sequence that races with any surviving peer node — the exact race that the Python/Kotlin `DESTROYING` fence closes.
- Users cannot safely swap a pool template on the same `pool_name` in Go under multi-process / multi-Pod deployment.

## Proposed direction

Port the Python/Kotlin design to Go. Rough scope:

1. **Extend `PoolStateStore` interface** (`sdks/sandbox/go/pool_store.go`) with four methods:
   - `GetDestroyState(ctx, poolName) (PoolDestroyState, error)`
   - `BeginDestroy(ctx, poolName, ownerID) error` — returns `ErrPoolDestroyed` if already tombstoned
   - `ClearPoolState(ctx, poolName) error`
   - `MarkDestroyed(ctx, poolName, ownerID, tombstoneTTL time.Duration) error`
2. **Implement in both stores**:
   - `sdks/sandbox/go/pool_store_memory.go`
   - `sdks/sandbox/go/poolredis/store.go` (with matching Lua / atomic ops as needed, mirroring the Python Redis store)
3. **Add types**: `PoolDestroyState` (`ACTIVE` / `DESTROYING` / `DESTROYED`), `PoolDestroyOptions`, `PoolDestroyResult`, `PoolDestroyStrategy` (start with just `FORCE`).
4. **Add `SandboxPoolManager` and `NewSandboxPoolManagerBuilder(...)`** in a new `pool_manager.go`, exposing `Destroy(ctx, poolName, options) (*PoolDestroyResult, error)` and following the same 5-step protocol as Python/Kotlin.
5. **Make `DefaultSandboxPool` observe the fence**: `Start()` and the reconcile loop should check `GetDestroyState` and refuse to warm up when the namespace is `DESTROYING` / `DESTROYED`.
6. **Tests**: port the corresponding Python/Kotlin test files. At minimum a table-driven `TestSandboxPoolManager_Destroy_*` covering idempotency, drain timeout, tombstone TTL expiry, and fence observation from a concurrent live pool.
7. **Docs**: once shipped, update `docs/guides/client-pool.md` "Retiring an old pool namespace" so the Go subsection collapses down to `pool_manager.Destroy(...)` with a note on `PoolDestroyOptions`.

## Compatibility

- All new interface methods on `PoolStateStore` are a breaking change for anyone with a custom store implementation. Options: (a) add them to the interface directly and cut a minor SDK version, or (b) add them via a narrower `PoolDestroyStore` optional interface and have `SandboxPoolManager` type-assert. Python and Kotlin took route (a); happy to discuss trade-offs.
- No changes to specs or server behavior — this is entirely in the Go client pool layer.

## References

- Python implementation: `sdks/sandbox/python/src/opensandbox/pool_manager.py`, `sdks/sandbox/python/src/opensandbox/_pool_store.py`
- Kotlin implementation: `sdks/sandbox/kotlin/sandbox/src/main/kotlin/com/alibaba/opensandbox/sandbox/pool/SandboxPoolManager.kt`, `sdks/sandbox/kotlin/sandbox/src/main/kotlin/com/alibaba/opensandbox/sandbox/domain/pool/PoolDestroyModels.kt`
- Docs surfacing the gap: PR #1352 (`docs/guides/client-pool.md`, "Retiring an old pool namespace")
- Related SDK AGENTS guidance on cross-language behavior parity: `sdks/AGENTS.md`

title: docs: add client pool guide with architecture diagrams
body:
## Summary

Adds a new cross-SDK guide at `docs/guides/client-pool.md` that documents the experimental client-side sandbox pool available in the Python, Kotlin/Java, and Go SDKs.

## Why a new guide

Client-pool coverage today is split across three per-SDK reference pages (`docs/sdks/python.md`, `docs/sdks/kotlin.md`, `docs/sdks/go.md`). The concept, semantics, and deployment model are cross-language, so this guide follows the repository docs rule of putting cross-cutting long-form content under `docs/` while leaving per-language surface in `docs/sdks/`.

## Contents

- **What the pool actually pools** — sandbox IDs on the server, not HTTP connections and not SDK client objects
- **Warmup vs acquire paths** — leader-only reconcile with a small warmup worker pool; acquire runs on every node
- **AcquirePolicy** — `FAIL_FAST` vs `DIRECT_CREATE` (the two policies currently on `main`; the retry variants on the feature branch aren't included)
- **Configuration** — canonical parameter table with defaults, matching current SDK source of truth
- **State stores** — `InMemoryPoolStateStore` vs Redis-backed store, with the distributed-deployment invariants
- **Minimal usage** — one runnable example each for Python sync, Python asyncio, Kotlin/Java, and Go
- **Diagnostics** — `snapshot`, `snapshot_idle_entries`, `resize`, `release_all_idle`, and `SandboxPoolManager.destroy`

## Diagrams

Five hand-drawn SVGs under `docs/public/images/client-pool-*.svg`, matching the visual style of the existing `architecture-overview.svg` (monospace font, same palette, `<title>`/`<desc>` for accessibility):

| File | Illustrates |
|---|---|
| `client-pool-architecture.svg` | Application nodes ↔ SandboxPool ↔ shared PoolStateStore ↔ Lifecycle API |
| `client-pool-warmup-sequence.svg` | Leader-only reconcile tick: lock → count → dispatch → create → ready → push |
| `client-pool-acquire-decision.svg` | pop → TTL check → connect/health/renew → success, with FAIL_FAST / DIRECT_CREATE branches |
| `client-pool-lifecycle.svg` | `NOT_STARTED → STARTING → RUNNING → DRAINING → STOPPED` with the `HEALTHY ↔ DEGRADED` substates |
| `client-pool-topology.svg` | Single-node in-memory pool vs multi-Pod Redis-backed pool |

## Files changed

- **New**: `docs/guides/client-pool.md`
- **New**: 5 SVGs under `docs/public/images/`
- **Edit**: `docs/.vitepress/config.mts` — register the new page in the guides sidebar

When that branch lands, the AcquirePolicy section and configuration table can be extended in a follow-up.

title: opensandbox-controller Helm chart grants cluster-wide RBAC via ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding
body:
## Summary

The `opensandbox-controller` Helm chart's "Manager" role ([`templates/clusterrole.yaml`](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/kubernetes/charts/opensandbox-controller/templates/clusterrole.yaml)) is a `ClusterRole` bound cluster-wide via a `ClusterRoleBinding`, granting the controller's ServiceAccount:

- `create/delete/get/list/patch/update/watch` on `pods` and `batch/jobs`
- `get/list/watch` on `secrets` and `configmaps`
- full CRUD on the `sandbox.opensandbox.io` CRDs (`batchsandboxes`, `pools`, `sandboxsnapshots`) and their `finalizers`/`status` subresources

**across every namespace in the cluster** — even though `batchsandboxes`, `pools`, and `sandboxsnapshots` are all declared `scope: Namespaced` in the CRDs themselves, implying the controller is only ever expected to operate against sandbox resources in one (or a small, known) namespace.

## Why this matters

Since OpenSandbox's purpose is running less-trusted/arbitrary workloads inside sandboxes, a compromised or buggy controller pod currently has:
- cluster-wide `secrets` read access (any Secret in any namespace — other apps' credentials, TLS keys, registry pulls, etc.)
- cluster-wide ability to create/delete `pods` and `batch/jobs` in any namespace, which is a well-known path to further privilege escalation (e.g. mounting a privileged `securityContext` or a sensitive ServiceAccount token in another namespace)

This significantly widens the blast radius of any controller compromise or bug beyond the namespace(s) it's actually meant to manage.

## Suggested fix

Scope the "Manager" role to a `Role`/`RoleBinding` in a configurable namespace (e.g. a new `sandboxNamespace` value, defaulting to wherever `BatchSandbox`/`Pool`/`SandboxSnapshot` resources are expected to live), rather than a cluster-wide `ClusterRole`/`ClusterRoleBinding`. The leader-election `Role`/`RoleBinding` in the same file is already namespace-scoped and wouldn't need to change.

Happy to open a PR with this change if that's useful — wanted to raise it as an issue first in case there's a reason (e.g. multi-namespace sandbox support) that the current cluster-wide scope is intentional.

title: feat(sdks/pool): add RETRY_NEXT_IDLE acquire policies

labels.name: size/XXL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 1000+ lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
# Summary

Adds two new \`AcquirePolicy\` values across Kotlin, Go, and Python SDKs so \`acquire\` can skip a stale idle candidate and retry the next one. This addresses the case where the pool contains a mix of healthy and unreachable idles — custom templates with long cold-start, or leftover unhealthy idles after a network flap — where a single bad idle used to force either \`FAIL_FAST\` or a slow \`DIRECT_CREATE\`.

**New policies:**
- \`RETRY_NEXT_IDLE\`: try up to \`maxAcquireRetries\` idle candidates; if all fail, raise \`PoolAcquireFailedException\` (fail-fast semantics on exhaustion).
- \`RETRY_NEXT_IDLE_THEN_CREATE\`: same retry loop, but fall through to direct-create instead of raising.

\`FAIL_FAST\` / \`DIRECT_CREATE\` keep single-shot semantics unchanged.

| Policy | Retry across idles | Fallback on exhaustion |
|---|---|---|
| \`FAIL_FAST\` | no | throw \`PoolEmptyException\` / \`PoolAcquireFailedException\` |
| \`DIRECT_CREATE\` (default) | no | lifecycle create |
| \`RETRY_NEXT_IDLE\` | up to \`maxAcquireRetries\` | throw |
| \`RETRY_NEXT_IDLE_THEN_CREATE\` | up to \`maxAcquireRetries\` | lifecycle create |

**New config field:** \`maxAcquireRetries\` / \`MaxAcquireRetries\` / \`max_acquire_retries\` (default 3, must be \`>= 1\`). Only takes effect under the retry policies. Bound is required because each failed candidate still pays up to \`acquireReadyTimeout\`; without a cap, mass-stale idle would freeze all acquires.

## Implementation notes

- Pool store contract is unchanged. \`tryTakeIdle\` is atomic pop, so the loop advances via repeated take calls without a new store API.
- Discarded-alive sandbox ids are accumulated across retry iterations and cleaned up asynchronously in a single batch after acquire returns/throws — same async cleanup path as before, just fed once instead of once per attempt.
- Loop re-checks pool lifecycle between iterations so an in-flight shutdown / namespace destroy short-circuits the retry loop instead of paying additional ready-timeouts.
- Go \`Acquire\` additionally honours \`ctx\` cancellation between iterations.
- Enum ordering: Go uses \`iota\`, new values are appended so \`AcquirePolicyDirectCreate == 0\` still holds.

## Design decisions

- **Fallback via enum combinations** (not an orthogonal \`fallbackToDirectCreate: bool\`). Keeps the acquire signature unchanged; users get four discrete, self-describing choices.
- **Retry bound is a count** (not a wall-clock deadline). Simpler to reason about; a deadline can be layered on later if operators need it.
- **OSEP-0005 not updated** — the enum extension is additive and the retry loop is a client-side implementation detail; can follow up in a separate PR if the OSEP maintainer wants it in the spec.

## Not in scope (possible follow-ups)

- No \`PoolSnapshot\` counter for evicted stale idles. The retry policies will amplify silent stale churn; \`bad_idle_evicted_total\` on the snapshot would help operators distinguish "pool healthy" from "pool churning" but is additive and can ship separately.
- JS / C# SDKs have no pool today, so no changes there.

# Testing

- [x] Unit tests
  - Kotlin: 6 new tests (\`SandboxPoolTest\`) — empty idle raise, all-stale bounded retries, drained-mid-loop, \`_THEN_CREATE\` fallthrough (with exhaustion / with empty), config validation. Full suite: **33 passed** (\`./gradlew :sandbox:test\`).
  - Go: 9 new tests in a new \`pool_retry_test.go\` — includes a \`staleAwareLifecycleServer\` mock, \`ctx\` cancellation, and helper-function unit tests. Full suite: **PASS** (\`go test -count=1 ./...\`).
  - Python: 14 new tests (7 sync + 7 async) mirroring Kotlin coverage. Full suite: **315 passed** (\`uv run pytest tests/\`). \`ruff\` clean; \`pyright\` clean on source, no new errors on tests (8 pre-existing \`FakeSandbox\` type-cast warnings unchanged).
- [ ] Integration tests
- [ ] e2e / manual verification

# Breaking Changes

title: Shade kotlinx.serialization in Kotlin SDK
body:
## Summary
- shade kotlinx.serialization into com.alibaba.opensandbox.shaded.kotlinx.serialization for sandbox-api, sandbox, and code-interpreter
- keep published GAVs unchanged while removing kotlinx.serialization from published POM/BOM dependencies
- bundle the relocated serialization runtime only in sandbox-api; sandbox and code-interpreter relocate their bytecode and reuse sandbox-api runtime
- make sandbox jsonParser internal/JvmSynthetic and keep code-interpreter on its own parser to avoid leaking serialization types across public/module APIs

## Background
Server-side response evolution can expose a runtime ABI conflict when older generated Kotlin serializers run with a user-forced older kotlinx.serialization runtime. In particular, an SDK version that does not know a newly-added response field may enter the unknown-key slow path, where older generated serializers can fail against newer GeneratedSerializer ABI expectations with AbstractMethodError. Shading removes the SDK's serialization runtime from the application dependency graph and makes future response field additions independent from user-selected kotlinx.serialization versions.

## Verification
- ./gradlew --no-configuration-cache spotlessCheck
- ./gradlew --no-configuration-cache :sandbox-api:publishToMavenLocal :sandbox:publishToMavenLocal :code-interpreter:publishToMavenLocal :sandbox-bom:publishToMavenLocal :sandbox:test :code-interpreter:test
- Maven repro with aone-sandbox-sdk 2.0.18 + OpenSandbox 1.0.16 local artifacts, with explicit user-side kotlinx.serialization runtime versions 1.3.2, 1.6.3, 1.7.3, 1.8.0, and 1.9.0
- Maven repro covers create sandbox and getInfo mock responses with added unknown fields
- Published POMs verified to no longer expose org.jetbrains.kotlinx serialization dependencies
- Published jar contents verified: sandbox-api contains relocated serialization classes; sandbox/code-interpreter do not bundle duplicate serialization runtime

## WIP notes
- This is intentionally opened as draft for CI/e2e signal and review of the publishing approach.
- Gradle module metadata is disabled for shaded SDK modules because the main Maven artifact is replaced by the shadow artifact; Maven POM remains the compatibility contract.

title: fix(docker): avoid TOCTOU race when listing sandboxes
body:
## Problem

The JavaScript E2E job `02 metadata filter uses AND semantics` in [run 29499569663](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/actions/runs/29499569663/job/87624812947) failed with:

```
SandboxApiException: Failed to query sandbox containers:
  404 Client Error for /v1.55/containers/{id}/json:
  Not Found ("No such container: {id}")
```

The failure originates in `docker_service.list_sandboxes` (`server/opensandbox_server/services/docker/docker_service.py:927`).

### Root cause: TOCTOU race in docker-py's high-level list

`docker_client.containers.list(all=True, filters=...)` calls Docker Engine `GET /containers/json`, then **for every matched container** issues a follow-up `GET /containers/{id}/json` to populate `container.attrs`. If a sandbox is removed between the summary listing and any of those inspects (e.g. sibling test cleanup, auto-removal, expiration timer), docker-py raises `NotFound`, the outer `except DockerException` catches it, and the whole listing fails with a 500 `CONTAINER_QUERY_FAILED`.

This is the pattern behind the recurring JS-E2E flake.

## Fix

Switch `list_sandboxes` to the low-level Docker Engine endpoint via `docker_client.api.containers(...)`, which returns a self-contained summary dict per container. Build the list-view `Sandbox` from that summary alone via the new `_summary_to_sandbox` helper — no follow-up inspect, no race.

Additionally, wrap `docker.errors.NotFound` in both single-container helpers (`DockerSandboxService._get_container_by_sandbox_id` and `DockerSnapshotRuntime._get_container_by_sandbox_id`) so that a container disappearing mid-inspect is reported as 404 `SANDBOX_NOT_FOUND` instead of 500 `CONTAINER_QUERY_FAILED`.

## Trade-offs (list view only)

The Docker summary does not expose `Config.Cmd`, `State.ExitCode`, or `State.FinishedAt`. For the list-view Sandbox we therefore accept these documented downgrades:

- `entrypoint` is reported as `[]`. Summary only exposes `Command` as a joined shell string, which is not round-trip safe. `Sandbox.entrypoint` is declared required in `specs/sandbox-lifecycle.yml`; returning `[]` preserves the schema contract at the type level. Callers that need the real entrypoint must use `getSandbox`.
- `exited` / `dead` are mapped to `Terminated` + `CONTAINER_EXITED`. Summary lacks `ExitCode`, so exit=0 vs exit!=0 cannot be distinguished here. Callers that need exit-code fidelity must use `getSandbox`.
- `last_transition_at` in the list view is derived from `created_at` (summary lacks `FinishedAt`).

`getSandbox` is unchanged and continues to inspect the container for full fidelity.

## Tests

Added unit tests in `server/tests/test_docker_service.py`:

- `test_list_sandboxes_uses_low_level_containers_and_skips_inspect` — verifies `docker_client.api.containers` is used with the sandbox-id label filter and that entrypoint/image/state are populated from the summary.
- `test_list_sandboxes_survives_concurrent_container_deletion` — regression: exited containers do not require a follow-up inspect and the listing succeeds.
- `test_list_sandboxes_summary_state_mappings` — every Docker `State` string maps to a defined Sandbox `(state, reason)`.
- `test_list_sandboxes_wraps_docker_exception` — `DockerException` from the low-level endpoint is wrapped as 500 `CONTAINER_QUERY_FAILED`.
- `test_get_container_by_sandbox_id_maps_notfound_to_404` — the single-container lookup treats `docker.errors.NotFound` from the inner inspect as 404 instead of 500.

## Verification

```
cd server
uv run ruff check                   # clean
uv run pytest --ignore=tests/k8s    # 746 passed
uv run pytest tests/k8s             # 541 passed
```

## Scope

Docker runtime only. No spec, SDK, CLI, or Kubernetes changes. `entrypoint=[]` in list view is compatible with the current `specs/sandbox-lifecycle.yml` `Sandbox` schema.

title: feat(sdk): report sandbox.create metrics from csharp and kotlin SDKs
body:
## Summary

Extends #1307 to cover the two sandbox SDKs it left out: **csharp** and **kotlin**. After this, all five sandbox SDKs (python, go, javascript, csharp, kotlin) report `sandbox.create` latency to the lifecycle server on the same `POST /v1/metrics/events` endpoint with the same wire format and opt-out semantics.

This PR is based on `main` and is independent of #1307 at the code level — the SDKs post fire-and-forget, so nothing here depends on the server route existing at compile/test time. Order of merge does not matter.

## Changes

### C# (`sdks/sandbox/csharp`)
- `Config/ConnectionConfig`: new `DisableMetrics` option; honored together with `OPENSANDBOX_DISABLE_METRICS=1` env var.
- `Internal/LifecycleMetricsReporter`: fire-and-forget POST to `{baseUrl}/metrics/events`, never blocks the caller, drains the response, includes API key + User-Agent + configured headers.
- `Sandbox.CreateAsync`: measures create duration and reports on success / failure paths (adapter-init failure and create/wait/dispose failure both covered).
- New `LifecycleMetricsReporterTests` (xUnit + a small loopback TCP stub server) verifies request line, headers, and JSON payload plus the `DisableMetrics` opt-out.

### Kotlin (`sdks/sandbox/kotlin/sandbox`)
- `config.ConnectionConfig`: new `disableMetrics` builder option and `isMetricsDisabled()` helper honoring `OPENSANDBOX_DISABLE_METRICS=1`.
- `internal.LifecycleMetricsReporter`: OkHttp `enqueue` fire-and-forget POST; drains the response body.
- `Sandbox.Companion.create`: wraps the create flow with a nanoTime timer and reports success / failure. Captures the created sandbox ID when available on the failure path.
- New `LifecycleMetricsReporterTest` (JUnit 5 + MockWebServer) verifies request path, headers, JSON payload, and the `disableMetrics` opt-out; also exercises the unreachable-server path.

### Wire format (unchanged from #1307)
```json
{
  "eventType": "sandbox.create",
  "sandboxId": "sbx_...",
  "image": "python:3.12",
  "createDurationMs": 1842,
  "success": true
}
```
`sandboxId` / `image` are omitted when unavailable. Failure events may omit `sandboxId`. SDK identity is derived from `User-Agent` on the server side (matches #1307's post-review behavior).

## Testing
- [x] Kotlin: `./gradlew clean :sandbox:test :code-interpreter:test --no-build-cache --rerun-tasks` — passing locally on this branch (based on main).
- [ ] C#: no local `dotnet` toolchain available on my machine. Tests target `net10.0` and rely only on `xunit` + `FluentAssertions` (already in the test csproj). Please run `dotnet test` in CI to confirm.
- [ ] e2e — not added in this PR; suggestion is to extend the tests added in #1307 for csharp/kotlin in a follow-up if desired.

## Breaking changes
None. `DisableMetrics` / `disableMetrics` default to `false`, matching the other SDKs.

## Checklist
- [x] Follows the pattern established by #1307 for Python/Go/JS
- [x] Adds unit tests for reporter payload, headers, opt-out, and error handling
- [x] No changes to generated code
- [x] Public API is additive (new opt-in options only)
