title: [helm] Pool CRD missing scaleStrategy/updateStrategy/recycleStrategy
body:
> 📖 Bilingual issue：
> English below；
> 中文版见文末折叠区 （Chinese version in the collapsible section at the bottom）.

## Why do you need it？

Installing the controller via the published Helm chart （v0.2.0） installs a `Pool` CRD that is missing three spec fields — `scaleStrategy`， `updateStrategy`， `recycleStrategy` — so Helm users cannot configure scaling throttling， rolling-update pace， or pod recycle policy on a Pool.

Reproduction （after `helm install` from the 0.2.0 release）：
```bash
$ kubectl explain pool.spec.scaleStrategy
GROUP:      sandbox.opensandbox.io
KIND:       Pool
VERSION:    v1alpha1

error: field "scaleStrategy" does not exist

$ kubectl explain pool.spec.updateStrategy
GROUP:      sandbox.opensandbox.io
KIND:       Pool
VERSION:    v1alpha1

error: field "updateStrategy" does not exist

$ kubectl explain pool.spec.recycleStrategy.type
GROUP:      sandbox.opensandbox.io
KIND:       Pool
VERSION:    v1alpha1

error: field "type" does not exist
```

The CRD is genuinely from the 0.2.0 chart （not a stale install）：

```bash
$ kubectl get crd pools.sandbox.opensandbox.io -o yaml | grep -iE "helm.sh/chart|app.kubernetes.io/version|release-name|scaleStrategy|updateStrategy|recycleStrategy"
    meta.helm.sh/release-name: opensandbox-controller
    meta.helm.sh/release-namespace: opensandbox-system
    app.kubernetes.io/version: 0.2.0
    helm.sh/chart: opensandbox-controller-0.2.0
```

The controller binary （v0.2.0） still understands these fields and falls back to defaults （`recycleStrategy: Delete`， etc.）， so nothing crashes — the knobs are just silently unavailable to Helm users.

## How could it be？

The chart-installed Pool CRD should match the code-generated one and expose all three fields. Two options：

1. **Short term：** copy the three field schemas from `kubernetes/config/crd/bases/sandbox.opensandbox.io_pools.yaml` into `kubernetes/charts/opensandbox-controller/templates/crds/pools.yaml`.
2. **Long term：** generate the chart CRDs from `config/crd/bases` （single source of truth）， or add a CI check that asserts the chart CRD schemas match the generated ones.

Happy to open a PR for option 1 if there's a preferred direction.

## Other related information

**Root cause — two CRD copies have diverged.** Field-level diff of `spec.properties`：

| CRD | fields in chart template | missing vs `config/crd/bases` |
|---|---|---|
| pools | `capacitySpec`， `template` | `scaleStrategy`， `updateStrategy`， `recycleStrategy` |
| batchsandboxes | （all 9） | none — in sync |
| sandboxsnapshots | `sandboxName` | none — in sync |

Verified on both `k8s/controller/v0.2.0` and `main` — the drift still exists on `main`.

The three fields were added to the Go types / generated CRD by [5c5926d3](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/commit/5c5926d350e0e6e2f3a603a5582f250d06fe7a41) (scaleStrategy)， [342576a9](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/commit/342576a96de6335925801e52409364ad551c1394) (updateStrategy)， [30b0b69a](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/commit/30b0b69aa48b6e73e66f3d02a319dca3b2f44c0f) (recycleStrategy)， but the chart's CRD template was never updated to match.

## Environment

chart `opensandbox-controller-0.2.0`， Kubernetes v1.35.6， controller image `sandbox-registry.cn-zhangjiakou.cr.aliyuncs.com/opensandbox/controller:v0.2.0`.

```bash
$ kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.nodeInfo.kubeletVersion}{"\n"}'
v1.35.6

$ helm list -n opensandbox-system
NAME                  	NAMESPACE         	REVISION	UPDATED                                	STATUS  	CHART                       	APP VERSION
opensandbox-controller	opensandbox-system	1       	2026-07-17 20:49:17.967556348 +0800 CST	deployed	opensandbox-controller-0.2.0	0.2.0      

$ kubectl -n opensandbox-system get deploy opensandbox-controller-manager \
-o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}{"\n"}'
sandbox-registry.cn-zhangjiakou.cr.aliyuncs.com/opensandbox/controller:v0.2.0
```

（No duplicate found — #1079 is about the `kubernetes/PROJECT` file， a different kind of drift.）

---

<details>
<summary>📖 中文版（点击展开）</summary>

## 为什么需要它？

通过官方发布的 Helm chart（v0.2.0）安装控制器后，落地到集群的 `Pool` CRD 缺失三个 spec 字段——`scaleStrategy`、`updateStrategy`、`recycleStrategy`——导致 Helm 用户无法在 Pool 上配置扩缩容节流、滚动更新节奏、Pod 回收策略。

复现（从 0.2.0 release 执行 `helm install` 之后）：

```bash
$ kubectl explain pool.spec.scaleStrategy
GROUP:      sandbox.opensandbox.io
KIND:       Pool
VERSION:    v1alpha1

error: field "scaleStrategy" does not exist

$ kubectl explain pool.spec.updateStrategy
GROUP:      sandbox.opensandbox.io
KIND:       Pool
VERSION:    v1alpha1

error: field "updateStrategy" does not exist

$ kubectl explain pool.spec.recycleStrategy.type
GROUP:      sandbox.opensandbox.io
KIND:       Pool
VERSION:    v1alpha1

error: field "type" does not exist
```

这个 CRD 确实来自 0.2.0 chart（不是旧版本残留）：

```bash
$ kubectl get crd pools.sandbox.opensandbox.io -o yaml | grep -iE "helm.sh/chart|app.kubernetes.io/version|release-name|scaleStrategy|updateStrategy|recycleStrategy"
    meta.helm.sh/release-name: opensandbox-controller
    meta.helm.sh/release-namespace: opensandbox-system
    app.kubernetes.io/version: 0.2.0
    helm.sh/chart: opensandbox-controller-0.2.0
```

控制器二进制（v0.2.0）仍然认识这些字段，并回退到默认值（如 `recycleStrategy: Delete`），所以不会崩溃——只是这些配置项对 Helm 用户静默不可用。

## 希望怎样？

chart 安装的 Pool CRD 应当与代码生成的那份一致，并暴露这三个字段。两个方案：

1. **短期**：把三个字段的 schema 从 `kubernetes/config/crd/bases/sandbox.opensandbox.io_pools.yaml` 复制到 `kubernetes/charts/opensandbox-controller/templates/crds/pools.yaml`。
2. **长期**：让 chart 的 CRD 从 `config/crd/bases` 生成（单一数据源），或加一个 CI 检查，断言 chart CRD 的 schema 与生成的一致。

如果有倾向的方向，我愿意为方案 1 提一个 PR。

## 其他相关信息

**根因——两份 CRD 副本已经不同步。** `spec.properties` 字段级对比：

| CRD | chart 模板里的字段 | 相比 `config/crd/bases` 缺失 |
|---|---|---|
| pools | `capacitySpec`、`template` | `scaleStrategy`、`updateStrategy`、`recycleStrategy` |
| batchsandboxes | （全部 9 个） | 无——已同步 |
| sandboxsnapshots | `sandboxName` | 无——已同步 |

已在 `k8s/controller/v0.2.0` 和 `main` 两处验证——`main` 上这个差异仍然存在。

这三个字段由 [5c5926d3](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/commit/5c5926d350e0e6e2f3a603a5582f250d06fe7a41) (scaleStrategy)， [342576a9](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/commit/342576a96de6335925801e52409364ad551c1394) (updateStrategy)， [30b0b69a](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/commit/30b0b69aa48b6e73e66f3d02a319dca3b2f44c0f) (recycleStrategy)添加进 Go 类型 / 生成的 CRD，但 chart 的 CRD 模板从未同步更新。

##  环境

chart `opensandbox-controller-0.2.0`， Kubernetes v1.35.6， controller 镜像 `sandbox-registry.cn-zhangjiakou.cr.aliyuncs.com/opensandbox/controller:v0.2.0`.

title: fix(server): allow OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_SANDBOX_ID through the egress env allowlist
body:
## What

Adds `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_SANDBOX_ID` to `ALLOWED_EGRESS_ENV_VARS`.

## Why

Part of #1334. OSEP-0010 documents `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_SANDBOX_ID` as the variable that sets `sandbox_id` on the egress OTLP Resource, on every metric measurement, and on the structured logs. But it was missing from the allowlist, so `split_egress_env` dropped it and it never reached the egress sidecar — the documented per-sandbox attribution was impossible.

This lands the attribution var. The **remaining** part of #1334 — giving the egress sidecar a way to reach an OTLP endpoint (it currently has none: no `OTEL_*` endpoint, no `HOST_IP` downward-API injection, no `/etc/hostinfo`) — is a design choice discussed in the issue; happy to follow up with whichever direction you prefer.

## Changes

- `server/opensandbox_server/services/constants.py`: add `"OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_SANDBOX_ID"` to `ALLOWED_EGRESS_ENV_VARS` (next to `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_METRICS_EXTRA_ATTRS`).

## Testing

`tests/k8s/test_egress_helper.py` round-trips the entire allowlist dynamically (`{key: "val" for key in ALLOWED_EGRESS_ENV_VARS}` → asserts `split_egress_env` returns the same set), so it already covers the new key. Module parses cleanly.

title: egress sidecar OTel metrics can't be configured (SANDBOX_ID not allow-listed; no OTLP endpoint / HOST_IP reaches the sidecar)
body:
## Summary

For sandboxes created by the server on Kubernetes, the **egress sidecar's OpenTelemetry metrics (OSEP-0010) cannot be configured**. There are two independent gaps in the server:

### 1. The attribution var is not allow-listed

`ALLOWED_EGRESS_ENV_VARS` (`server/opensandbox_server/services/constants.py`) includes `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_METRICS_EXTRA_ATTRS` but **not** `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_SANDBOX_ID`, which OSEP-0010 documents as setting `sandbox_id` on the OTLP Resource, on every metric measurement, and on the structured logs. Because `split_egress_env` only forwards allow-listed `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_`-prefixed vars, `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_SANDBOX_ID` is silently dropped and never reaches the sidecar.

### 2. There is no way to set the sidecar's OTLP endpoint

The Go telemetry (`components/internal/telemetry/init.go`) resolves the export endpoint as:
`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT` / `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` → `HOST_IP` → `/etc/hostinfo`.

But `apply_egress_to_spec` (`server/opensandbox_server/services/k8s/egress_helper.py`) builds the sidecar env only from `EGRESS_RULES`/`EGRESS_MODE` + the allow-listed `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_` request vars. It never:
- sets any `OTEL_*` endpoint env,
- injects `HOST_IP` via downward API (`valueFrom.fieldRef: status.hostIP`) — there is no `valueFrom`/fieldRef anywhere in the k8s provider,
- mounts `/etc/hostinfo`.

And `OTEL_*` vars don't carry the `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_` prefix, so `split_egress_env` filters them out too.

**Net effect:** when deployed via the server on k8s, the egress sidecar can never reach an OTLP collector — the OSEP-0010 egress metrics are unreachable.

> For comparison, **execd** runs inside the main `sandbox` container, so its env (including `OTEL_*`) can already be set through the sandbox creation request (`sandbox_env`). The egress **sidecar** is the one with no path.

## Proposed fixes

1. **Add `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_SANDBOX_ID` to `ALLOWED_EGRESS_ENV_VARS`** — clearly an oversight; the var is documented and consumed by egress. I'll open a PR for this part.
2. **Provide a way to set the sidecar's OTLP endpoint.** Options:
   - **(a) Forward `OTEL_`-prefixed request env to the egress sidecar** (in addition to `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_`). Explicit and opt-in: nothing exports unless the caller sets the endpoint.
   - **(b) Inject `HOST_IP` via downward API** (`valueFrom.fieldRef: status.hostIP`) into the sidecar, matching the Go `HOST_IP` fallback (enables the node-local collector pattern). Note this makes export effectively "on by default" whenever a collector listens on the node, which relates to the default-export behavior raised in #1329 — so it may want a config gate.

Happy to implement whichever direction you prefer for the endpoint (2).

Related: OSEP-0010, #1329 (default-export / endpoint precedence in `internal/telemetry`).

title: feat(chart): allow extra env vars on the ingress-gateway container
body:
## What

Adds `server.gateway.env` (a list, default `[]`) to the `opensandbox-server` chart and templates it onto the **ingress-gateway** container, mirroring the existing `server.env` pattern.

```yaml
server:
  gateway:
    env:
      - name: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT
        value: http://otel-collector:4318
      - name: OTEL_SERVICE_NAME
        value: opensandbox-ingress
```

## Why

Fixes #1332. The chart already lets you set env on the server container (`server.env`), but the ingress-gateway container had no equivalent — so there was no way, via Helm, to pass env vars to it. In particular, the ingress OpenTelemetry metrics (OSEP-0010) are configured via env (`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`, `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME`, …), which was unreachable for chart users.

## Changes

- `values.yaml`: new `server.gateway.env` (default `[]`).
- `templates/ingress-gateway.yaml`: render an `env:` block on the ingress-gateway container, gated by `{{- with .Values.server.gateway.env }}` (no block when empty).
- `README.md`: values table row for `server.gateway.env`.

## Testing

`helm template` / `helm lint`:

- default (`server.gateway.env` unset) → the ingress-gateway container renders **no** `env:` block (behavior unchanged).
- with `server.gateway.env[0]=OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=...` → the var is rendered on the ingress-gateway container.
- `helm lint`: 0 failures.

title: Helm chart: ingress-gateway container has no way to set env vars (blocks OTLP metrics config)
body:
## Summary

The `opensandbox-server` Helm chart lets you set extra env vars on the **server** container (`server.env`), but the **ingress-gateway** container has no equivalent — `templates/ingress-gateway.yaml` renders no `env:` block and `values.yaml` has no `server.gateway.env`. So there is no way, via Helm, to pass environment variables to the ingress-gateway pod without patching the template.

## Why it matters

The ingress component emits OpenTelemetry metrics (OSEP-0010) that are configured **via environment variables** (`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` / `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT`, `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME`, `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES`, …). Without a way to set env on the ingress-gateway container, a Helm-based deployment cannot point the ingress metrics at an OTLP endpoint / collector — the metrics feature is effectively unreachable for chart users.

The `server` container already supports this via `server.env`; the gateway just needs the same.

## Proposal

Add `server.gateway.env` (a list, default `[]`) and template it onto the ingress-gateway container, mirroring the existing `server.env` pattern:

```yaml
server:
  gateway:
    env:
      - name: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT
        value: http://otel-collector:4318
      - name: OTEL_SERVICE_NAME
        value: opensandbox-ingress
```

I'll open a PR for this.

title: feat(chart): expose controller-runtime metrics endpoint in opensandbox-controller chart
body:
## What

Adds a `controller.metrics` block to the `opensandbox-controller` Helm chart so operators can enable the controller-runtime metrics endpoint without patching the chart.

```yaml
controller:
  metrics:
    enabled: false   # when true -> --metrics-bind-address=:<port>
    port: 8080
    secure: false    # --metrics-secure; false = plain HTTP for scraping
```

When `enabled: true`, the deployment gets `--metrics-bind-address=:<port>` + `--metrics-secure=<secure>` and a named `metrics` container port. Default is **disabled**, so existing installs are unchanged.

## Why

Fixes #1330. The controller binary already supports controller-runtime metrics (`--metrics-bind-address` / `--metrics-secure`, default `0` = disabled) and the kustomize config ships a Prometheus `ServiceMonitor` scaffold, but the Helm chart exposed none of it — and there is no `extraArgs` escape hatch for the `manager` container. So a Helm-based deployment had no way to enable `/metrics` (reconcile rate/latency, workqueue depth, `rest_client_*`, Go runtime) without editing the templates.

## Changes

- `values.yaml`: new `controller.metrics.{enabled,port,secure}` (disabled by default).
- `templates/deployment.yaml`: template the two flags + a named `metrics` container port, gated by `controller.metrics.enabled`. The `controller.metrics` map is read nil-safely (`… | default dict`) with defaulted `port`/`secure`, so it's optional (works under `helm upgrade --reuse-values` from a chart version that predates it).
- `templates/clusterrole.yaml` + `templates/clusterrolebinding.yaml` + `_helpers.tpl`, gated by `metrics.enabled && metrics.secure` (secure mode only):
  - `opensandbox-metrics-auth-role` ClusterRole (`create` on `tokenreviews`/`subjectaccessreviews`) **+ binding to the manager SA** — lets the controller-runtime auth filter run TokenReview/SubjectAccessReview. Mirrors `config/rbac/metrics_auth_role.yaml`.
  - `opensandbox-metrics-reader` ClusterRole (`get` on the `/metrics` non-resource URL) — for the scraper identity. Mirrors `config/rbac/metrics_reader_role.yaml`. **Not** bound by the chart (the scraper's ServiceAccount lives outside the release); the docs explain binding it.
  - No extra RBAC is created for the default `secure: false` path.
- `docs/kubernetes/deployment.md`: new "Operator Metrics" section documenting the values, plain-HTTP vs secure modes, and the RBAC provisioned in secure mode (per `AGENTS.md`, operations-visible settings are documented under `docs/`).
- `README.md`: values table rows for the new keys.

## Testing

`helm template` / `helm lint`:

- `--set controller.metrics=null` (simulating a reused-values upgrade without the key) → renders with **no** nil-pointer error.
- default (`enabled: false`) → no metrics flags/port and no metrics RBAC (behavior unchanged).
- `enabled=true, secure=false` → `--metrics-bind-address=:8080`, `--metrics-secure=false`, `name: metrics / containerPort: 8080`, and **no** extra RBAC.
- `enabled=true, secure=true` → additionally renders `opensandbox-metrics-auth-role` (ClusterRole + binding) and `opensandbox-metrics-reader` (ClusterRole).
- `helm lint`: 0 failures.

Verified end-to-end on a live cluster: with `--metrics-bind-address=:8080 --metrics-secure=false` the controller serves the full controller-runtime metric set over HTTP and is scraped successfully.

## Notes / follow-ups (happy to add if you want)

- An `extraArgs` list for the `manager` container as a general escape hatch.
- An optional `ServiceMonitor` (+ `Service`) template behind a toggle for Prometheus-Operator users.

title: Helm chart opensandbox-controller does not expose the controller-runtime metrics endpoint
body:
## Summary

The `opensandbox-controller` **Helm chart** (`kubernetes/charts/opensandbox-controller`) does not expose the controller-runtime **metrics endpoint** in any way, even though:

- the controller binary already supports it via the standard controller-runtime flags `--metrics-bind-address` and `--metrics-secure` (default `--metrics-bind-address=0`, i.e. **disabled**), and
- the kubebuilder **kustomize** config already ships a metrics/Prometheus scaffold (`kubernetes/config/prometheus/monitor.yaml` ServiceMonitor, plus the commented `PROMETHEUS` sections in `kubernetes/config/default/kustomization.yaml`).

So there is an inconsistency: the metrics story exists for the kustomize path but is completely absent from the Helm chart.

## Problem

For a Helm-based deployment there is **no way to enable the controller metrics** without editing the chart templates:

- `values.yaml` has no `metrics` block.
- `templates/deployment.yaml` never templates `--metrics-bind-address` / `--metrics-secure`, and declares no `metrics` container port.
- there is **no `extraArgs`** escape hatch for the `manager` container (only `extraEnv`, `extraContainers`, `extraVolumes`, `extraVolumeMounts`, `extraInitContainers`).
- there is no `Service` / `ServiceMonitor` / `PodMonitoring` template.

As a result, when deploying via Helm the controller exposes **no metrics at all** — reconcile rate/latency (`controller_runtime_reconcile_*`), workqueue depth, `rest_client_*`, and Go runtime metrics are all unavailable out of the box.

## Proposal

Add a `controller.metrics` block to the chart, disabled by default (preserving current behavior):

```yaml
controller:
  metrics:
    enabled: false      # when true, sets --metrics-bind-address=:<port>
    port: 8080
    secure: false       # --metrics-secure=false serves plain HTTP for scraping
```

which, when enabled, adds `--metrics-bind-address=:<port>` + `--metrics-secure=<secure>` and a named `metrics` container port.

Optionally (happy to include if you want them):
- an `extraArgs` list for the `manager` container as a general escape hatch, and
- an optional `ServiceMonitor` (+ `Service`) template behind a toggle for Prometheus-Operator users.

I'll open a PR with the core `controller.metrics.*` toggle. Verified locally: with `--metrics-bind-address=:8080 --metrics-secure=false` the controller serves the full controller-runtime metric set over HTTP and is scraped successfully.

title: OSEP-0010 telemetry: implementation in internal/telemetry diverges from spec (default-export contradicts R5, HTTP-only transport, delta temporality)
body:
## Summary

While integrating the OSEP-0010 telemetry into a Prometheus/OTel-collector pipeline, I found several places where the current implementation in **`components/internal/telemetry/init.go`** diverges from the OSEP-0010 spec (`oseps/0010-opentelemetry-instrumentation.md`). Some are likely just spec drift after later PRs (#1181, #1209), but **one contradicts a "Must Have" requirement (R5)** and can cause unexpected network traffic, so I wanted to flag them together.

Checked against `main` @ `518cad23422d3335e322ae35c58ded2560f824f2`.

---

### 1. Default behavior contradicts R5 (export happens without any `OTEL_*` config) — likely a bug

The OSEP is explicit that, with no OTLP config, nothing should be exported:

> **R5** | Default or unset OTLP config results in no export to avoid impacting deployments without observability | **Must Have**

> *Configuration*: … default to no export so deployments without observability backends are unaffected.

> Test Plan → *Configuration*: When `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_*` is unset, no connection is made and no error is raised.

But the current code enables export whenever a **node IP** can be resolved, even if no `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_*` env var is set:

```go
// Endpoint precedence: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_*_ENDPOINT -> HOST_IP -> /etc/hostinfo.
func metricsEnabled() bool {
	if otlpEndpointFromEnv() != "" {
		return true
	}
	_, ok := resolveNodeIP()   // <- HOST_IP env or /etc/hostinfo
	return ok
}

func metricsClientOptions() []otlpmetrichttp.Option {
	if otlpEndpointFromEnv() != "" {
		return nil
	}
	ip, ok := resolveNodeIP()
	if !ok {
		return nil
	}
	return []otlpmetrichttp.Option{
		otlpmetrichttp.WithEndpoint(net.JoinHostPort(ip, otlpHTTPPort)), // HOST_IP:4318
		otlpmetrichttp.WithInsecure(),
	}
}
```

**Impact:** In Kubernetes it is very common to inject `HOST_IP` via the downward API (`status.hostIP`). Any deployment that does so — for reasons unrelated to telemetry — will make execd/egress/ingress start pushing OTLP metrics to `HOST_IP:4318` (plaintext) with **no OTLP env configured at all**, which is exactly what R5 says must not happen. It also means there is **no clean way to disable export**: unsetting `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_*` is not enough if a node IP is resolvable.

**Suggestions (either is fine):**
- Make node-IP fallback **opt-in** (e.g. require an explicit flag/env like `OPENSANDBOX_OTEL_USE_NODE_IP=true`) so the true default is "no export", or
- Honor a standard disable switch (`OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=none` / `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true`) that short-circuits `metricsEnabled()`, and
- Update OSEP-0010 to document the node-IP fallback precedence explicitly.

---

### 2. Transport is HTTP-only, but the spec says HTTP and gRPC

The OSEP:

> Support **HTTP and gRPC** OTLP endpoints via environment variables

> `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/...` (metrics and logs, **HTTP or gRPC** as needed)

The implementation only ever constructs an HTTP exporter (`otlpmetrichttp`, port `4318`); there is no `otlpmetricgrpc` path:

```go
"go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlpmetric/otlpmetrichttp"
...
mexp, err := otlpmetrichttp.New(ctx, opts...)
```

**Suggestion:** either add a gRPC path (selectable via `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc|http/protobuf`, the standard OTel env var) or update the OSEP to state HTTP-only.

---

### 3. Delta temporality for Counter/Histogram — interop note worth documenting

`deltaTemporalitySelector` sets **delta** temporality for `Counter` and `Histogram` (gauges / up-down counters stay cumulative):

```go
func deltaTemporalitySelector(kind sdkmetric.InstrumentKind) metricdata.Temporality {
	switch kind {
	case sdkmetric.InstrumentKindCounter,
		sdkmetric.InstrumentKindHistogram:
		return metricdata.DeltaTemporality
	default:
		return metricdata.CumulativeTemporality
	}
}
```

This is a valid choice, but the OSEP lists **Prometheus/Grafana** as target integrations, and Prometheus-model backends assume **cumulative** temporality. Consumers therefore need a converting step (e.g. the collector `deltatocumulative` processor, or a backend that natively ingests delta) — otherwise counters/histograms won't behave as expected on a plain Prometheus/GMP pipeline.

**Suggestion:** document the temporality choice and its Prometheus implications in OSEP-0010, and/or honor the standard `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_TEMPORALITY_PREFERENCE` env var so operators can select `cumulative` when their backend needs it.

---

### 4. Minor: attribute keys renamed dot → underscore (#1209)

#1209 renamed attribute keys to underscore convention (`http_method`, `http_status_code`, `routing_result`). The OSEP prose and examples still use the dotted form in places. Worth a quick doc pass so the spec matches the emitted attributes.

---

### Question

For each of these: is the intent to **update OSEP-0010** to match the implementation, or to **change the code** to match the spec? Happy to send a PR for whichever direction you prefer (the R5 default-export one seems the most impactful).

title: feat(sdk): send client IP via OPEN-SANDBOX-CLIENT-IP header across all SDKs
body:
# Summary
- **What/why:** All five sandbox SDKs (Go, Python, JavaScript, Kotlin, C#) best-effort detect the host's own **intranet IPv4** and attach it to every request as a custom header **`OPEN-SANDBOX-CLIENT-IP`**, so the server can identify the calling device (primary use case: uniquely identifying machines on a corporate intranet).
- **Why a custom header name:** standard forwarded headers such as `X-Forwarded-For` are rewritten or stripped by intermediaries, so a dedicated name conveys the value reliably.
- **How detection works (reads a real NIC):** the SDK enumerates network interfaces and reads the IPv4 configured on one, rather than opening an outbound socket. Selection is a single pure, unit-tested `selectClientIp`: skip virtual/container/VPN NICs (`docker/veth/br-/virbr/vmnet/vbox/utun/tun/tap/zt/cni/flannel/cali`), then prefer known NIC names (`en0` > `eth0` > `eth*` > `en*` > `bond*` > others, case-insensitive) and RFC1918 private addresses, skipping loopback / link-local / unspecified. Per-interface enumeration errors are isolated so one bad NIC never aborts the scan.
- **Enumeration per language (stdlib, no new dependency):** Go `net.Interfaces`, Kotlin `NetworkInterface`, C# `NetworkInterface`, JS `os.networkInterfaces` (loaded via a guarded async dynamic import to stay browser/CJS-safe; the transport awaits detection so even the first request carries the header). Python is stdlib-only: Linux reads `/sys/class/net` + `SIOCGIFADDR` ioctl (full NIC-name priority); other platforms fall back to `gethostname()`/`getaddrinfo` + private-segment filter (degraded, may return empty).
- **Aligned behavior across languages:** best-effort (skip the header silently if the IP can't be determined — never error/block), never overwrite a user-provided value (case-insensitive), detect once and cache.
- **Injection points (all outbound paths covered):** Go connection headers + the create-metrics telemetry request; Python `ConnectionConfig.headers`; Kotlin OkHttp interceptor; C# `CreateHttpClient`/`CreateSseHttpClient` default headers (covers wrapper, raw, SSE, and code-interpreter); JS fetch wrapper (merges headers without dropping any). `code-interpreter`/MCP SDKs inherit via the shared transport.
- **Server is unchanged** — this is a client-side, additive request header; the server neither reads nor echoes it.

# Testing
- [ ] Not run (explain why)
- [x] Unit tests
- [ ] Integration tests
- [x] e2e / manual verification

Details:
- Unit tests added per language: pure `selectClientIp` cases (named-NIC priority, private-segment fallback, skip virtual/loopback/link-local, empty when nothing usable), injection, case-insensitive no-overwrite, best-effort omission. All green: Go `go test ./...`; Python `ruff`+`pyright`+full `pytest`; JS `tsc`+`eslint`+`tsup`+`node --test` (74); C# `dotnet test` (151 sandbox + 22 code-interpreter); Kotlin `spotlessCheck`+`:sandbox:test`+`:code-interpreter:test`.
- e2e / manual: ran the real lifecycle server from source against Docker; C# `SandboxManagerE2ETests` passed (3/3) with real sandbox create/list/kill. Verified all five SDKs detect the same address as `ifconfig en0` (the host's real intranet IP), and captured the exact header on the wire via a header-echo endpoint (`OPEN-SANDBOX-CLIENT-IP: <en0 IP>`).

# Breaking Changes
- [x] None
- [ ] Yes (describe impact and migration path)

Additive, backward-compatible request header. Existing behavior is unaffected; a user-supplied same-named header always wins.

# Checklist
- [x] Linked Issue or clearly described motivation
- [ ] Added/updated docs (if needed) — not needed; internal transport behavior with no public API/config surface
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Security impact considered — sends the host's own intranet IP (not a secret); never overwrites a user-provided value; best-effort and non-blocking
- [x] Backward compatibility considered

title: Informer cache has no periodic relist causes persistent 404 POD_IP_NOT_AVAILABLE for Running sandboxes
body:
## Informer cache has no periodic relist when watch is enabled → stale empty endpoints annotation causes persistent 404 POD_IP_NOT_AVAILABLE for Running sandboxes

Component: server — opensandbox_server/services/k8s/informer.py
Affected versions: server/v0.2.0 and server/v0.2.1
Severity: High under multi-replica + high sandbox-churn deployments; degrades over pod lifetime

### Summary

When the workload informer runs with enable_watch=True (the production default), there is no periodic full relist. The per-replica cache is refreshed only by (a) the live watch event stream and (b) a full list forced by an exception escaping the watch loop (410 "too old", any other ApiException, or an unexpected exception) or a process restart. There is no time-based safety-net resync on the watch path.

As a result, if a replica's cached BatchSandbox object ends up with a stale/empty sandbox.opensandbox.io/endpoints annotation and no subsequent watch event or error corrects it, that replica returns HTTP 404 KUBERNETES::POD_IP_NOT_AVAILABLE on /v1/sandboxes/<id>/proxy/<port>/command for a sandbox whose pod is actually Running — indefinitely, until the next relist-triggering error or a pod restart. Because the server runs many replicas behind a Service, a single lagging replica poisons a fraction of all traffic while peers serve the same sandbox fine.

### Where it manifests

get_endpoint(...) resolves the pod IP from the informer-cached CR. A falsy endpoint (empty endpoints annotation) leads directly to:

raise HTTPException(
    status_code=404,
    detail={"code": "KUBERNETES::POD_IP_NOT_AVAILABLE",
            "message": "Pod IP is not yet available. The Pod may still be starting."},
)

The error message implies "still starting," but in practice the sandbox has been Running and serving execs for minutes.

### Root cause (confirmed in code)

In informer.py::_run(), resync_period_seconds is used only in the enable_watch=False branch:

if not self.enable_watch:
    self._stop_event.wait(self.resync_period_seconds)
    self._has_synced = False   # trigger a fresh list on next loop
    continue
self._run_watch_loop()          # watch path: loops forever, no time-based relist

- _run_watch_loop() calls w.stream(list_fn, resource_version=self._resource_version, timeout_seconds=self.watch_timeout_seconds). A normal watch timeout (default 60s) returns without an exception, so _run() simply re-enters the watch loop resuming from the preserved resourceVersion — no relist.
- The only relist triggers are: 410 ApiException (also clears _resource_version=None), any other ApiException, any unexpected Exception, or a process restart. All set _has_synced=False.
- informer_resync_seconds (config default 300, described as "Full resync interval for informer cache… Shorter intervals refresh the cache more eagerly") is therefore dead config whenever watch is enabled — an operator who lowers it to mitigate staleness will see no effect. This is a config/behavior contract bug in its own right.

Production configuration that hits this (from config.py defaults + client.py construction): informer_enabled=True, enable_watch=True (constructor default; not overridable via config), informer_resync_seconds=300 (unused on watch path), informer_watch_timeout_seconds=60.

### Observed behavior (production, ap-south-1, ~40 replicas)

- POD_IP_NOT_AVAILABLE rate accumulates with replica age and resets on rolling restart: e.g. ~42/h immediately after a fleet restart, climbing monotonically to ~550/h over the following ~6h; the scheduled rolling restart resets it to the floor again.
- For an individual sandbox: created → Running with IP → ~30 successful proxy/command execs (HTTP 200) across many replicas → a single replica returns 404 POD_IP_NOT_AVAILABLE while peers had served 200 for the same sandbox seconds earlier.
- The lagging replica subset rotates over time; per-replica request totals are otherwise uniform, so this is fleet-wide aging rather than a few permanently-bad pods.

The age-correlation + reset-on-restart pattern is the signature of state that accumulates inside each replica's informer and is only cleared by a relist/restart — consistent with the missing periodic resync.

title: fix(execd): bound idle-post wait and fail streams on WS teardown (#1206)
body:
# Summary

Fixes #1206: \`CodeInterpreter.codes.run()\` intermittently hangs while the Jupyter kernel is idle, and secondarily fails with \`RemoteProtocolError: peer closed connection without sending complete message body\`.

## Root cause

Two related silent-hang paths in \`components/execd/pkg/jupyter/execute\`:

1. **\`finalizeExecution\` polled without an upper bound.** After the kernel published \`status: idle\`, the code waited for a late \`execute_reply\`/\`error\` by looping \`state.result.ExecutionCount > 0 || state.result.Error != nil\` with a \`time.Sleep(pollInterval)\` and **no deadline**. If the shell-channel reply was lost (WS re-connect, kernel drop, out-of-order delivery, etc.), \`ExecutionCount\` stayed 0 forever, \`resultChan\` was never closed, \`runJupyterCode\` blocked on \`<-results\`, \`RunCode\` never returned, and the SDK's chunked SSE stream was never terminated.
2. **\`receiveMessages\` break-ed silently on WS read errors.** If the kernel WebSocket died mid-execution, the read loop exited without notifying the in-flight stream, so callers of \`ExecuteCodeStream\` waited on \`resultChan\` forever.

Once either path stalled long enough, the server-side proxy's 180s read timeout would eventually tear the chunked response down mid-flight, surfacing as \`incomplete chunked read\` on the SDK — matching the second failure mode in the issue.

## Fix

- Introduce \`JupyterIdleGracePeriod\` (default \`5s\`, env \`EXECD_JUPYTER_IDLE_GRACE_PERIOD\`, flag \`--jupyter-idle-grace-period\`) to bound the post-idle wait. When it expires, \`finalizeExecution\` injects a \`KernelReplyTimeout\` \`ErrorOutput\` and closes the stream so the SDK gets a typed error instead of hanging.
- Track the currently in-flight stream on \`Client.activeStream\`. \`receiveMessages\` and \`Disconnect\` fail it explicitly with \`KernelStreamAborted\` / \`KernelDisconnected\` when the WS goes away **before** idle. When idle has already been observed, \`finalizeExecution\` owns the terminal close within its grace period, so the disconnect path stands down to avoid racing it.
- Add \`streamExecutionState.terminate\` / \`trySend\` to guarantee \`resultChan\` is closed exactly once and to make concurrent handler sends safe under \`-race\`.

# Testing

- [x] Unit tests
- [ ] Integration tests
- [ ] e2e / manual verification

New tests in \`components/execd/pkg/jupyter/execute/execute_test.go\`:

- \`TestExecuteCodeStreamGivesUpWhenExecuteReplyNeverArrives\` — mock kernel publishes only \`idle\`; asserts \`KernelReplyTimeout\` within grace period.
- \`TestExecuteCodeStreamFailsWhenWebSocketDiesBeforeIdle\` — kernel drops WS after reading the request; asserts \`KernelStreamAborted\` and stream close.
- \`TestExecuteCodeStreamFailsWhenDisconnectedMidExecution\` — client \`Disconnect()\` mid-execution releases the caller with a typed error.

Existing tests still pass:

\`\`\`
go test ./pkg/jupyter/execute/... ./pkg/flag/... ./pkg/runtime/... ./pkg/web/controller/... -race -count=5
ok
\`\`\`

(\`pkg/isolation\` failures on macOS reproduce on \`main\` — unrelated \`/var\` symlink issue.)

# Breaking Changes

- [x] None

Additive only: new flag/env with a safe default. Existing behavior for successful executions is unchanged. Callers that previously would have hung now get a typed terminal error, which the SDK already surfaces via the normal error path.

# Checklist

- [x] Linked Issue or clearly described motivation (#1206)
- [ ] Added/updated docs (if needed) — new flag documented via \`flag.DurationVar\` help text; can add to \`docs/components/execd\` on request
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Security impact considered — none; only affects execution stream shutdown semantics
- [x] Backward compatibility considered — additive, safe defaults

# Not included (happy to follow up in separate PRs)

- Map \`httpx.RemoteProtocolError\` to \`HTTPX_NETWORK_ERROR_TYPES\` in the Python SDK for a clearer typed error
- Relax the server-side proxy's 180s read timeout for SSE routes
- SSE ping goroutine race (see #1216)
- Wire \`runtime/ctrl.go\` to the request context so client disconnects propagate

title: egress: in-place worker restart inverts nat OUTPUT order, breaks redirected TCP DNS (UDP unaffected)
body:
## Summary

After an **in-place egress-worker restart** (worker process killed, supervisor restarts it without recreating the container/pod), the iptables `nat` `OUTPUT` chain is rebuilt with a **broken rule order**: the transparent-proxy loopback exemption `-A OUTPUT -p tcp -d 127.0.0.0/8 -j RETURN` ends up **above** the DNS redirect `-A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 53 -j REDIRECT --to-ports 15353`.

Consequence: redirected **TCP** DNS to the loopback resolver is `RETURN`ed instead of redirected and hits no listener → `connection refused`. **UDP DNS is unaffected** (the errant rule is `-p tcp` only), and the resolver itself is healthy on both protocols. Allowlisted egress that relies only on UDP DNS keeps working, so the regression is easy to miss; anything that needs TCP DNS (large responses, truncation/`TC` retry, resolvers that force TCP) breaks after a worker restart until the container is fully recreated.

## Reproduction (runc, deterministic)

Kill the egress worker in-place and let the supervisor restart it, then probe loopback DNS from inside the netns:

```
# pre-restart (healthy)
nat OUTPUT:
  ... 
  -A OUTPUT -p tcp -m tcp --dport 53 -j REDIRECT --to-ports 15353
  -A OUTPUT -d 127.0.0.0/8 -p tcp -j RETURN            # below the redirect
DNS: udp:127.0.0.1:53=OK  tcp:127.0.0.1:53=OK  15353 udp=OK tcp=OK

# after in-place worker restart (broken)
nat OUTPUT:
  -A OUTPUT -d 127.0.0.0/8 -p tcp -j RETURN            # PREPENDED, above the redirect
  ...
  -A OUTPUT -p tcp -m tcp --dport 53 -j REDIRECT --to-ports 15353
  -A OUTPUT -d 127.0.0.0/8 -p tcp -j RETURN            # stale duplicate, never flushed
DNS: udp:127.0.0.1:53=OK  tcp:127.0.0.1:53=ERR:ConnectionRefused  15353 udp=OK tcp=OK
```

A subsequent **full container restart** rebuilds the chain cleanly (`tcp:53=OK`), confirming the defect is specific to in-place, supervisor-managed worker restart — not container recreation.

Independently reproduced twice: on preprod (Kata/GKE) and on a local runc lab. It is **not** Kata-specific.

## Root cause (two coupled defects)

1. **`components/egress/scripts/cleanup.sh` — incomplete stale-rule flush.** `remove_stale_iptables()` deletes only rules matching `--dport 53` and `--dports 80,443`. It does **not** delete the transparent-proxy loopback exemption `-A OUTPUT -p tcp -d 127.0.0.0/8 -j RETURN` (installed by `transparentHTTPRules`, `components/egress/pkg/iptables/transparent.go:31`), because it matches neither pattern. That stale rule survives the pre-start cleanup.

2. **`components/egress/pkg/iptables/transparent.go` — append + no crash-time removal.** `SetupTransparentHTTP` installs the loopback `RETURN` with `-A` (`transparent.go:57`) and does not dedupe. `RemoveTransparentHTTP` only runs on graceful teardown, not on `SIGKILL`. On restart, the surviving loopback `RETURN` (from #1) plus the DNS redirect rules being deleted and **re-appended below it** leaves `RETURN -d 127.0.0.0/8 -p tcp` above `REDIRECT --dport 53`, and a duplicate loopback `RETURN` is appended as well.

Net: DNS `--dport 53` redirect and the loopback `RETURN` are installed by two different routines with no shared ordering guarantee across a restart, and the pre-start cleanup does not fully reset the block.

## Suggested fix directions (not yet implemented)

- **`cleanup.sh`:** also flush the transparent-proxy rules (the `-d 127.0.0.0/8 -p tcp -j RETURN` loopback exemption and any `--dports 80,443` REDIRECT), so nothing survives to invert ordering. i.e. fully reset the OUTPUT redirect block pre-start.
- **`redirect.go` / `transparent.go`:** make (re)install atomic and order-preserving — flush and rebuild the whole `nat OUTPUT` redirect block in a single pass so the DNS `--dport 53 REDIRECT` deterministically precedes the loopback `RETURN` (or scope the loopback `RETURN` so it cannot shadow the DNS redirect, e.g. exclude `--dport 53`). Consider `-C`/insert-at-fixed-index or an nft atomic ruleset swap.
- **supervisor pre-start:** the hook does run on crash-restart; the gap is that its cleanup is incomplete (see #1), not that it fails to run. Verify and add a regression around it.

## Validation harness

The local lab's L5 `go_egress_kill` recovery check currently stays green because it only does a single allowlisted HTTPS GET (UDP-DNS-backed) and never asserts TCP DNS redirect recovery. Strengthening that check to assert redirected TCP `:53` recovery reproduces the red locally under runc and will confirm the fix without a Kata round-trip.

## Evidence

Full frozen bundle (nat-chain time series with rule order + per-protocol DNS reachability, before/after worker restart), captured on both preprod and runc lab:
`~/.local/state/objective-10a-validation/task6-preprod-f5309414fcd9ebf1/task6-red-f5309414fcd9ebf1/` — `ROOT-CAUSE.md`, `LAB-REPRODUCIBILITY.md`, `lab-runc-repro-capture.log`, `telemetry/`.

title: feat(sdks/kotlin): shade kotlinx-serialization to isolate downstream classpath
body:
## Summary

Downstream consumers of the Kotlin SDK have been hitting `AbstractMethodError` inside kotlinx.serialization when their runtime classpath resolves `kotlinx-serialization-core` to a version older than 1.4. The SDK is compiled against kotlinx-serialization 1.9.0 and its generated `$$serializer` classes rely on the default implementation of `GeneratedSerializer.typeParametersSerializers()` introduced in 1.4. Against a pre-1.4 runtime that method is still abstract, so any call site (e.g. name-based JSON decoding) explodes with:

```
AbstractMethodError: Receiver class …$$serializer does not define or inherit an implementation
of the resolved method typeParametersSerializers() of interface
kotlinx.serialization.internal.GeneratedSerializer
```

Downstream applications often cannot pin kotlinx-serialization to 1.4+ themselves because their classpath is dictated by higher-priority BOMs (Spring Boot dependency management, internal component BOMs, etc.). Fix by **shading the kotlinx-serialization runtime into the SDK jars and relocating it** to `com.alibaba.opensandbox.shaded.kotlinx.serialization` so downstream classpath versions no longer matter.

## Changes

- Add the Gradle Shadow plugin (`com.gradleup.shadow` 9.5.1) to each module that references kotlinx-serialization (`sandbox`, `sandbox-api`, `code-interpreter`), wired via an isolated `shadedDependencies` configuration so the plugin's Maven publication does not declare kotlinx-serialization as a runtime dependency.
- Move kotlinx-serialization to `compileOnly` in those modules so the SDK still compiles against the vanilla API but the dependency is not leaked into the published pom. Test classpaths keep it via `testImplementation`.
- Relocate `kotlinx.serialization` → `com.alibaba.opensandbox.shaded.kotlinx.serialization` in the shadowJar output. Verified: `CreateSandboxResponse$$serializer.class` in the published `sandbox-api` jar `implements com.alibaba.opensandbox.shaded.kotlinx.serialization.internal.GeneratedSerializer`.
- Publish `shadowJar` as the primary Maven artifact (classifier=null). The plain `jar` output keeps a `plain` classifier and is used only by intra-project compile classpaths so `:sandbox` / `:code-interpreter` still see un-relocated kotlinx types at compile time (which matches the kotlinx types on their own `compileOnly` classpath).
- Disable Gradle module metadata (`.module`) for the shaded modules. Maven pom is the source of truth; pointing `runtimeElements` at the shaded jar while `apiElements` stays on the plain jar would otherwise leave GMM inconsistent with the pom. Our published audience is Maven-based.
- Drop the `kotlinx-serialization-json` constraint from `sandbox-bom`, since the SDK no longer exposes kotlinx-serialization to consumers. The bom still manages the sandbox artifacts + `kotlin-stdlib` + `okhttp` + `slf4j-api`.

No source code or public API changes; the shade is entirely a build/packaging concern.

## Verification

- `./gradlew clean :sandbox:test :code-interpreter:test` — all green.
- `./gradlew publishToMavenLocal` — published `sandbox`, `sandbox-api`, `code-interpreter`, `sandbox-pool-redis`, `sandbox-bom` locally.
- Published `sandbox-<v>.pom` no longer declares any `kotlinx-serialization*` dependency.
- `CreateSandboxResponse$$serializer.class` in the published `sandbox-api` jar was inspected via `javap -v`: all references to `kotlinx.serialization.**` are rewritten to the shaded package.
- Downstream `agent-sandbox` project upgraded to this SDK version locally: full build + test suite green, `mvn dependency:tree` shows only `com.alibaba.opensandbox:sandbox` / `sandbox-api` with no `kotlinx-serialization*` transitive dependency.

## Not included

- Version bump. Kept at `1.0.16` intentionally; release manager to bump when cutting the next release.
- Consumers of the SDK need to upgrade to a version containing this change to benefit; no source-side workaround is possible for the older releases.

title: Fix/go sdk stale conn
body:
# Summary

Fix intermittent timeouts hitting Go SDK users doing direct sandbox exec. Two customer-facing symptoms:

1. `sse read: context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout exceeded while
   reading body)` — any streamed command whose SSE output lasts longer than
   `RequestTimeout` (default 30s) was killed mid-stream.
2. `resolve execd: ... Get ".../endpoints/xxxxx?use_server_proxy=false":
   context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)`
   — `GetEndpoint` occasionally stalled on a dead pooled keep-alive
   connection.

**Root cause:** the SDK applied `http.Client.Timeout` (= `RequestTimeout`) to
*all* requests, including long-lived SSE streams, and reused pooled keep-alive
connections that could go stale behind NAT/LB idle-timeouts.

**Changes (Go SDK only):**
- `http.go`: SSE now uses a dedicated, lazily-created client
  (`Timeout: 0`, cloned transport with `DisableKeepAlives=true`) so streaming
  is never bounded by a total-request deadline and never reuses a pooled
  connection. Non-streaming requests are unchanged.
- `http.go`: idempotent `GET`/`HEAD` requests retry once on a fresh
  connection (`CloseIdleConnections`) when they fail with a network
  timeout/reset/EOF, the context is not done, and the error is not an
  `APIError`.
- `transport.go`: `DefaultTransportConfig.IdleConnTimeout` 90s → 30s, matching
  the Python/JS/Kotlin SDKs and reducing the stale-connection window.

**Cross-SDK alignment:** `IdleConnTimeout=30s` and "no total timeout on SSE"
now match the Python (`read=None`), JS, and Kotlin SDKs. The
"non-pooled SSE" and "fresh-connection GET retry" hardening is Go-first;
tracked as a follow-up to port to the other SDKs.

# Testing

- [x] Unit tests — `go test -race -count=1 ./...` passes (incl. new
  `staleconn_diag_test.go`, `staleconn_fix_test.go`,
  `streaming_timeout_test.go`); `gofmt`/`go vet` clean.
- [x] e2e / manual verification — `tests/go/streaming_timeout_e2e_test.go`
  passes (11s stream completes under a 5s `RequestTimeout`). Full local Go
  e2e suite: relevant lifecycle/command/filesystem/pool/pause-resume/network
  tests pass.

# Breaking Changes

- [x] None — no public API changes; non-streaming request behavior unchanged.

# Checklist

- [x] Linked Issue or clearly described motivation
- [ ] Added/updated docs (if needed) — N/A (internal transport behavior)
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Security impact considered — no auth/secret handling changed
- [x] Backward compatibility considered

title: `networkPolicy` is silently ignored when a sandbox is created with `extensions.poolRef` (K8s pool mode) — a security control is dropped with no error
body:
## Summary

On the Kubernetes runtime, creating a sandbox from a pre-warmed `Pool` (via `extensions.poolRef`) **silently discards** the `networkPolicy` passed on the create request. No error, no warning, no log. The egress sidecar is never attached, so the requested egress policy (including a strict `defaultAction: deny`) has **zero effect** — the sandbox has fully open network access.

This is inconsistent with the sibling per-request fields: `volumes`, `credentialProxy`, and `platform` are **rejected with an explicit error** in pool mode; `networkPolicy` is neither honored nor rejected.

## Environment

- Runtime: `runtime.type = kubernetes`, `workload_provider = batchsandbox`
- `[egress] mode = "dns+nft"`, valid egress image configured
- Sandbox created with `extensions={"poolRef": "<pool>"}` + `network_policy=NetworkPolicy(defaultAction="deny", egress=[])`

## Steps to reproduce

1. Create a `Pool` and let it warm up.
2. Create a sandbox referencing it, **with a deny-all network policy**:
   ```python
   SandboxSync.create(
       image="...",  # ignored in pool mode
       extensions={"poolRef": "<pool>"},
       network_policy=NetworkPolicy(default_action="deny", egress=[]),  # should block ALL egress
   )
   ```
3. Observe: create **succeeds** (no rejection).
4. Inspect the allocated pod: it has **only the `sandbox` container — no `egress` sidecar**.
5. From inside the sandbox, reach any external host.

## Expected vs Actual

- **Expected**: either (a) the egress policy is enforced (deny-all → external blocked), or (b) the request is rejected like `volumes`/`credentialProxy` are (fail loud).
- **Actual**: create succeeds, no egress sidecar is attached, and a `defaultAction: deny` policy blocks nothing:
  ```
  CREATE_OK (no rejection for networkPolicy+poolRef)
  allocated pod containers = [sandbox]        # no egress sidecar
  curl https://github.com  -> http=200        # should be blocked under deny-all
  curl https://example.com -> http=200        # should be blocked under deny-all
  ```
  (A non-pool sandbox with the same policy correctly gets an `egress` sidecar and blocks external.)

## Evidence (code)

- `server/opensandbox_server/services/k8s/batchsandbox_provider.py`:
  - `create_workload` accepts `network_policy`, but the `if extensions.get("poolRef"):` branch (~L133) rejects only `platform` and `volumes`, then `return`s `_create_workload_from_pool(...)` (~L144) **without passing `network_policy`**.
  - `apply_egress_to_spec(...)` — the only call site that attaches the egress sidecar — is at ~L234, in the template-mode path **after** the pool branch already returned. The pool path structurally cannot reach it.
  - `_create_workload_from_pool` (~L347) does not accept or use `network_policy`; the built BatchSandbox spec is just `{replicas, poolRef, [taskTemplate], [expireTime]}`.
- `server/opensandbox_server/api/schema.py` — `CreateSandboxRequest.validate_source_and_entrypoint` pool-mode branch checks `snapshot_id` and `credential_proxy.enabled` (rejects the latter), but **never references `network_policy`**. The governing comment is *"Reject conflicting fields that would be ignored in pool mode"* — a rule that was not applied to `network_policy`.
- No test asserts the ignore behavior (there are `..._poolref_ignores_image_spec` / `..._ignores_resource_limits` and `..._rejects_platform` / `..._rejects_volumes`, but nothing for `network_policy`).
- Docs: `docs/architecture/network-isolation.md` (the egress-isolation doc) has zero mentions of pool; no callout in `docs/components/egress.md`; the `networkPolicy` field description has no poolRef cross-reference.

## Impact

**Security.** A platform that relies on server-side `Pool` + per-request `networkPolicy` for tenant isolation will believe sandboxes are isolated while they are fully open — able to reach other sandboxes' pod IPs (cross-tenant RCE via the unauthenticated execd port) and arbitrary external hosts. The failure is silent.

## Suggested fix

1. **Minimum / consistency**: reject `network_policy` + `poolRef` with an explicit error (mirror the existing `credentialProxy` / `volumes` rejections), honoring the code's own "reject fields that would be ignored" principle.
2. **Better**: support egress for pooled sandboxes — either apply the egress overlay to the allocated pod, or document that the egress sidecar must be baked into the `Pool` template and provide a helper/example.
3. **Docs**: state the pool-mode limitations (volumes/credentialProxy/networkPolicy) in `docs/architecture/network-isolation.md`, `docs/components/egress.md`, the Pool docs, and the `networkPolicy` field description.

title: execd(isolation): always strip execd's own config env in bwrap
body:
## Summary

Previously bwrap inherited execd's process env by default. In particular, the default `EnvPassthrough` mode (deny with empty keys) only stripped a generic secret-name blacklist (`*_TOKEN`, `AWS_*`, etc.), so credentials configured on execd itself leaked into sandbox processes.

This change unconditionally strips execd's own configuration env vars in every `EnvPassthrough` mode:

- \`EXECD_ACCESS_TOKEN\`
- \`JUPYTER_HOST\`
- \`JUPYTER_TOKEN\`
- \`EXECD_ISOLATION_CONFIG\`

In \`EnvModeAllow\`, even if the caller explicitly allow-lists one of these keys, we refuse to re-inject its value via \`--setenv\`.

## Behavior change

- Sandbox processes can no longer read the four env vars above.
- User business env (\`PATH\`, \`HOME\`, \`LANG\`, custom app env, etc.) is untouched.
- Existing \`envPassthroughMode\` semantics (\`deny\` with explicit keys, \`allow\` with allow-list) are preserved; the four blacklisted keys are simply unset in addition.

## Tests

- Updated \`empty_mode_no_env_args\` → \`empty_mode_strips_execd_config_env\`: default mode must emit \`--unsetenv\` for all four keys and must not emit \`--clearenv\`.
- Added \`TestBuildArgv_ExecdConfigEnvAlwaysStripped\`: covers empty / deny(empty keys) / deny(with keys) modes, and verifies allow mode does not re-inject blacklisted values.
- \`go build ./...\`, \`go vet ./pkg/isolation/...\`, \`GOOS=linux go test -c ./pkg/isolation/\` all pass.

## Note

If new \`EXECD_*\` / \`JUPYTER_*\` configuration env vars are added to execd, remember to add them to \`execdConfigEnvBlacklist\` in \`components/execd/pkg/isolation/bwrap.go\`.

title: ci: make self-hosted E2E setup portable
body:
## Summary

- install `uv` explicitly with `astral-sh/setup-uv@v7` in every self-hosted Real E2E job
- use standard setup actions and runner-local cache paths instead of paths tied to the former `admin` user
- remove the remaining `/home/admin` fallback from the shared Docker cleanup script and use the runner's actual `$HOME`
- keep explicit `uv` and Python availability checks before running tests

## Root cause

The Real E2E workflow assumed that self-hosted runners had `uv` and language runtimes preinstalled under `/home/admin`. Newly registered runners execute as `ecs-user`, so jobs failed before tests started.

## Impact

Self-hosted Real E2E jobs now provision `uv`, Node.js, and .NET consistently. Go caches and the .NET install directory use `RUNNER_TEMP`, while Docker's buildx state is cleaned under the current runner user's home directory.

## Validation

- `bash -n scripts/ci-docker-cleanup.sh`
- `bash scripts/verify-license.sh`
- `git diff --check`
- parsed `.github/workflows/real-e2e.yml` with Ruby YAML
- verified all five self-hosted Real E2E jobs use `astral-sh/setup-uv@v7`
- verified the repository no longer contains hard-coded `/home/admin` paths
- latest CI confirms `setup-uv`, Node.js, .NET, Go, and the shared cleanup step all succeed under `/home/ecs-user`

## Current runner prerequisite

The workflow now reaches the Docker image build, but the newly registered runner service user cannot access `/var/run/docker.sock`. The runner host must grant `ecs-user` Docker access and restart the GitHub Runner service so the service process inherits the updated group membership.

title: feat(execd): add bounded command inventory

labels.name: size/XXL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 1000+ lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

- add additive, bounded `GET /command` inventory for commands retained by the current `execd` controller
- provide `running` filtering, opaque filter-bound cursor pagination, terminal-entry cap/TTL retention, and bounded JSON responses
- publish the OpenAPI contract and C#, Go, JavaScript, Kotlin, and Python SDK surfaces
- add deterministic smoke helpers, CI gates, runtime/controller/router coverage, and operational documentation

Closes #1308

## Contract

This is a runtime-local observation API, not durable command history or audit storage. It exposes no command content, environment, stdin, output, or log paths.

- Cursors are opaque, tied to the exact `running` filter and current controller instance. Preserve the filter for every page; after restart/controller replacement or a different instance, omit the cursor and restart pagination.
- Pagination is weakly consistent. Retention bounds terminal observations; it does not replace existing status/log endpoints.
- All inventory responses, including handler and authentication errors, use `Cache-Control: no-store`.
- No SSE/subscription/replay/backpressure surface and no process-group remediation are included.

## Retention boundary

The inventory TTL/cap applies only to its metadata index. It is independent of the known-ID command status and background-output retention introduced on main: completed command status and background output are retained for at least 24 hours and then removed by an hourly cleanup.

Inventory eviction does not remove those resources, and their cleanup does not remove inventory summaries. With an inventory TTL longer than 24 hours, a retained summary may outlive its detailed status and background logs. Foreground temporary output files are removed after streaming completes.

## Verification

Latest local verification: September 14 SSE-drain refresh, rebased onto main at `07f0a68d`:

- [x] Execd flags, runtime, web/controller/model package tests; flags/runtime/controller race selection covering inventory, recovery configuration, initialization, SSE and cleanup
- [x] Linux build, Windows runtime test cross-compilation, and actual CLI help exposing the 200ms drain default together with the inventory flags
- [x] Real Linux inventory smoke for default lifecycle, cap eviction and TTL expiry using the new 200ms default. A temporary copy of the existing smoke script removed only its 500ms environment override; the repository smoke script was not changed
- [x] Updated JS dependency lock installed with `--frozen-lockfile`; Sandbox typecheck, lint, build and command/inventory/native-argv tests (24)
- [x] Server Docker-service unit tests, including the incoming sidecar pause/resume changes (200; Docker is mocked, not a live container test)
- [x] Documentation build and diff-whitespace checks
- [ ] Native Windows execution and full upstream CI

The conflict resolution preserves the new 200ms graceful-shutdown default and its upstream regression test while retaining inventory TTL/cap initialization and configuration-validation coverage. Five of seven PR patches remain patch-equivalent; the other two differ only where they integrate with the upstream timeout change and test placement. No feature scope was added.

The Python, C#, Kotlin, Go and code-interpreter SDK source trees and execd OpenAPI spec are unchanged from the preceding verified branch. Earlier September 14 checks were not rerun wholesale: Python Sandbox 715 / code-interpreter 21, JavaScript Sandbox 171 / code-interpreter 10, Go test/vet/build, and real inventory smoke. Earlier C# results were 248 / 27 and Kotlin results were 398 / 22 on the final full rerun. This refresh rebuilt and retested the runtime against the new Go dependency versions and exercised the affected JavaScript dependency update as listed above.

Historical caveats remain recorded: the unchanged upstream Kotlin pool snapshot test failed once (expected 3, observed 4) on September 11, then the full suite passed without modifying that test or pool; the repository-wide license check failed on upstream `test_readiness_auth_fail_fast.py` missing a header. That repository-wide license check was not rerun in this refresh. No fresh independent review or full-project CI pass is claimed.

Generated Python OpenAPI models remain excluded from canonical Ruff/Pyright checks. The execd spec and generated execd clients were unchanged by this baseline update.

- [x] No breaking changes

title: feat(execd): expose runtime-local command status snapshots
body:
## Motivation

`execd` retains command state in the current controller process. Clients that lose a command ID after a transient failure need a bounded way to discover still-observable command state without exposing command content or creating a durable audit service.

## Delivered contract

The linked implementation adds additive `GET /command` as a bounded, runtime-local JSON inventory:

- `running` filtering and opaque, filter-bound cursor pagination;
- terminal-entry cap and TTL retention;
- cursor validity limited to the active controller instance; after a restart/replacement or different instance, clients restart pagination without a cursor;
- OpenAPI plus C#, Go, JavaScript, Kotlin, and Python SDK support;
- deterministic smoke coverage, CI gates, and operational documentation.

The endpoint deliberately excludes command content, arguments, environment, stdin, stdout/stderr, output, and log paths. Pagination is weakly consistent, and inventory retention is not a substitute for existing known-ID status/log APIs.

## Explicit non-goals

- Durable command history, audit storage, or cross-sandbox query.
- SSE/subscription/replay/backpressure APIs.
- POSIX process-group remediation.

This issue supersedes its original no-pagination/no-retention proposal; the linked PR implements the bounded contract above.

## Deferred compatibility follow-up

The inventory TTL/cap applies to the new metadata index only. Legacy known-ID command kernels remain in `commandClientMap` for compatibility and can retain command content for the controller lifetime. This is explicitly tracked separately in #1403 and is not claimed as solved by this issue or its linked PR.

title: fix(sdks/sandbox/go): survive silently-dropped LB connections and long SSE streams
body:
## Summary

Three related transport-layer fixes to the Go sandbox SDK, motivated by the intermittent `Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers` and `context canceled` failures observed when a long-running CLI (aenv) calls `GetEndpoint` through an enterprise load balancer.

Root cause (confirmed by local isolation experiments with `httptrace`):

- SDK transport keeps idle connections in the pool for **90s** (`IdleConnTimeout` default).
- Enterprise LBs commonly drop idle TCP connections after ~**60s** without FIN/RST.
- When the idle interval falls in the LB-already-dropped-but-SDK-still-cached window, the next request reuses a black-holed connection. `WroteRequest` succeeds locally, but `GotFirstResponseByte` never fires, and the request hangs until `http.Client.Timeout` fires — producing the Go net/http-specific `Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers` signature.
- The SDK's custom `DialContext` and `TLSClientConfig` also disable Go's automatic HTTP/2, so requests are HTTP/1.1 only with no PING-level liveness probing that could evict a black-holed connection.

Separately discovered while investigating: `http.Client.Timeout` is applied uniformly to all clients (lifecycle **and** execd streaming). Because that timeout is an overall wall-clock deadline that includes body reads, **any SSE stream running past `RequestTimeout` (default 30s) is cut off mid-flight**. This diverges from the Python SDK, which uses `httpx.Timeout(read=None, connect=…, write=…)` for streaming endpoints. Independent bug, fixed here in the same commit.

## Changes

### 1. Route SSE requests through a stream client with `Timeout=0`

`http.go`: `Client` now holds a `streamClient` that shares the same `Transport` as `httpClient` (so the connection pool is not split) but always has `Timeout=0`. `doStreamRequest` uses it. Callers control total SSE duration via their `context.Context`, matching the Python SDK.

### 2. Lower `DefaultTransportConfig.IdleConnTimeout` from 90s to 25s

`transport.go`: 25s comfortably beats the typical 60s LB idle timeout, so the SDK evicts potentially stale connections before the LB drops them silently. Users on reliable internal links can override via `TransportConfig`.

### 3. Retry stale-connection failures once on a fresh connection

`http.go`: `doRequestOnce` now transparently `CloseIdleConnections()` and retries once when:

- Method is `GET`/`HEAD`/`OPTIONS` (idempotent only — `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE` never retried, they may already have been applied server-side).
- Error is not an `APIError` (i.e. we never got response headers).
- Error signature matches `Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers` **or** a generic `net.Error` with `Timeout()==true`.
- Error is not a plain caller-driven `context.Canceled` / `context.DeadlineExceeded` (checked **after** the awaiting-headers suffix, because `http.Client.Timeout` wraps `DeadlineExceeded` and would otherwise be misclassified as caller-driven).

This is deliberately kept separate from the existing status-code-based `withRetry`, to keep policy semantics unambiguous.

## Tests

New file `http_retry_test.go` with 6 tests, all passing (`go test ./...` green):

- `TestStreamClient_NoOverallTimeoutOnLongStream` — SSE stream running longer than the client's `WithTimeout(100ms)` still receives all 3 events over 600ms.
- `TestStreamClient_SharesTransportWithHTTPClient` — invariant: stream client shares Transport, `Timeout=0`.
- `TestStreamClient_TimeoutOverrideStillYieldsZeroOnStreamClient` — user-set `WithTimeout(15s)` does not leak onto the stream client.
- `TestStaleConnectionRetry_GETRetriesOnFreshConnection` — `httptest` server hijacks and black-holes the first connection; GET transparently succeeds on retry.
- `TestStaleConnectionRetry_POSTNotRetried` — same black-hole scenario, POST returns the timeout error, server sees exactly 1 hit.
- `TestShouldRetryStaleConnection_TableDriven` — full policy matrix (method × error type → retry?).

Pre-existing `TestDefaultTransport` assertion updated from 90s to 25s.

## Compatibility

Two user-visible default behavior changes:

1. **`DefaultTransportConfig().IdleConnTimeout`: 90s → 25s.** Safe (only affects idle eviction). Users depending on longer idle reuse can override via `TransportConfig`.
2. **`GET`/`HEAD`/`OPTIONS` may retry once on `Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers`.** Safe (only idempotent methods). Callers that assert a single request per call in mocks may see one extra hit in the specific timeout-before-headers scenario.

Cross-language stance: this bug pattern is Go-specific (HTTP/1.1-only pool with 90s idle window and no liveness probe). Other language SDKs (Python `httpx`, JS `fetch`, Kotlin OkHttp, C#) have different pooling defaults and are not affected. Not synchronizing default values across languages.

## Verification still recommended

Consumer (`aenv`) should confirm on real infrastructure with `httptrace`:

- Failing request: `GotConn reused=true wasIdle=true`, `idleTime` near LB idle timeout, `WroteRequest err=<nil>`, no `GotFirstResponseByte`.
- Immediate retry succeeds.

If those hold, this PR is a full mitigation. If not, we regroup on the root cause.

## Related

- Independent finding fixed here: SSE streams being cut by `http.Client.Timeout` (matches Python SDK behavior).

title: bug(server): diagnostics endpoints ignore tenant namespace, return 404 for tenant sandboxes in multi-tenant mode
body:
## Summary

  When multi-tenancy (`[tenants]`) is enabled, the DevOps diagnostics endpoints
  (`GET /v1/sandboxes/{id}/diagnostics/logs`, `/diagnostics/inspect`, `/diagnostics/events`)
  always return `404 KUBERNETES::SANDBOX_NOT_FOUND` for any sandbox that lives in a
  tenant namespace. Only sandboxes in the server's default `[kubernetes].namespace`
  can be diagnosed.

  ## Environment

  - opensandbox-server: built from main (multi-tenancy per `docs/guides/multi-tenancy.md`, requires >= 0.2.2)
  - Runtime: Kubernetes, `workload_provider = "batchsandbox"`
  - Multi-tenancy: file provider, tenant namespace differs from `[kubernetes].namespace`

  ## Steps to reproduce

  1. Enable multi-tenancy with a tenant whose `namespace` is not the server's default
     `[kubernetes].namespace`.
  2. Create a sandbox using that tenant's API key — the pod is correctly created in the
     tenant namespace, and lifecycle endpoints (get/list/delete) work as expected.
  3. Call the diagnostics endpoint with the same API key:

     ```bash
     curl -H "OPEN-SANDBOX-API-KEY: <tenant-key>" \
       "http://<server>/v1/sandboxes/<sandbox-id>/diagnostics/logs"
     ```

  **Actual result:**

  ```json
  {"code":"KUBERNETES::SANDBOX_NOT_FOUND","message":"No pod found for sandbox '<sandbox-id>'"}
  ```

  **Expected result:** logs of the sandbox pod in the tenant's namespace, consistent with
  how lifecycle endpoints resolve the namespace.

  ## Root cause

  The auth middleware resolves the tenant and injects it into the request-scoped
  ContextVar, and lifecycle operations correctly resolve the namespace via
  `KubernetesSandboxService._resolve_namespace()`
  (`server/opensandbox_server/services/k8s/kubernetes_service.py:194`).

  However, `K8sDiagnosticsMixin` never consults the tenant context — it uses the static
  default namespace in all three places
  (`server/opensandbox_server/services/k8s/k8s_diagnostics.py`):

  - `_find_pod_for_sandbox()` — `list_pods(namespace=self.namespace, ...)` (line 60)
  - `get_sandbox_logs()` — `"namespace": self.namespace` in the pod-log kwargs (line 97)
  - `get_sandbox_events()` — `list_namespaced_event(namespace=self.namespace, ...)` (line 244)

  `get_sandbox_inspect()` is affected as well since it goes through
  `_find_pod_for_sandbox()`. So the pod lookup targets the wrong namespace and the
  endpoints 404 for every tenant sandbox.

  ## Suggested fix

  - In `_find_pod_for_sandbox()`, resolve the namespace via `self._resolve_namespace()`
    (the mixin is mixed into `KubernetesSandboxService`, so the method is available).
  - In `get_sandbox_logs()` / `get_sandbox_events()`, use the namespace of the pod that
    was actually found (`pod.metadata.namespace`) instead of `self.namespace`.

title: feat(server): docker runtime sandbox_env / sandbox_binds config

labels.name: size/M
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 30-99 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
## Summary

Add two `DockerConfig` fields applied to **every** sandbox container created by the docker runtime:

- `sandbox_env`: environment variables merged under the request's `env` (request keys win)
- `sandbox_binds`: host bind mounts in Docker `-v` syntax, prepended to the binds derived from a request's `volumes`

## Motivation

The Kubernetes runtime has a deployment-side pod template (`batchsandbox_template_file`) where operators can add fleet-wide mounts and environment variables. The docker runtime has no equivalent: sandbox env/mounts come only from each creation request, which the calling application controls.

The concrete case: when the services a sandbox calls back into present certificates from a **private/corporate CA**, tools inside the sandbox reject TLS (`SELF_SIGNED_CERT_IN_CHAIN` etc.). On Kubernetes this is solved in the pod template (mount the root CA + set `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`); on docker there was no operator-side hook at all. With this change:

```toml
[docker]
sandbox_binds = ["/opt/certs/root-ca.crt:/etc/ssl/private-ca/root-ca.crt:ro"]
sandbox_env = { NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS = "/etc/ssl/private-ca/root-ca.crt" }
```

## Test plan

- [x] `test_create_sandbox_applies_config_sandbox_env_and_binds`: config env lands in the container, request env overrides same-named keys, config binds precede request volume binds
- [x] full `server` test suite passes

title: OSEP-0015: Declarative Sandbox Features

- add OSEP-0015 defining the public API and lifecycle for declarative sandbox features

title: feat(controller): add --image-committer-pull-secret for authenticated registry proxies (e.g. Artifactory virtual repos mirroring Docker Hub)
body:
Fixes #1299.

## Problem

In corporate environments, direct access to Docker Hub is blocked and all images are pulled through a **private virtual repository** (e.g. JFrog Artifactory, Nexus) that proxies Docker Hub and requires authentication. Even though `image-committer` is a public image, pulling it through such a proxy fails because the commit Job has no `ImagePullSecrets`:

```
Failed to pull image "artifactory.corp.example.com/docker/opensandbox/image-committer:v0.1.1":
failed to authorize: unexpected status 401
```

```
Kubernetes node
  └─► pull "artifactory.corp.example.com/docker/image-committer:v0.1.1"
            │
            ▼
    Artifactory virtual repo   ← requires auth — no ImagePullSecret → 401
            │
            ▼ proxy / mirror
      Docker Hub (public image, but unreachable directly)
```

The controller already has `--snapshot-push-secret` and `--resume-pull-secret` for the same credential-injection pattern. This PR adds the missing equivalent for the image-committer pull.

## Changes

- **`sandboxsnapshot_controller.go`** — add `ImageCommitterPullSecret string` to `SandboxSnapshotReconciler`
- **`sandboxsnapshot_lifecycle.go`** — new `imageCommitterPullSecrets()` helper; set `PodSpec.ImagePullSecrets` in both `buildCommitJob` and `ensureUnpauseJob`
- **`cmd/controller/main.go`** — parse `--image-committer-pull-secret` and wire it to the reconciler
- **`charts/opensandbox-controller/values.yaml`** — add `controller.snapshot.imageCommitterPullSecret: ""`
- **`charts/opensandbox-controller/templates/deployment.yaml`** — pass the new flag when set

## Backwards compatibility

When `imageCommitterPullSecret` is empty (default), `imageCommitterPullSecrets()` returns `nil` — the Job `PodSpec` is identical to before. No behaviour change for existing deployments.

## Test plan

- [x] `go build ./...` passes
- [x] Empty `imageCommitterPullSecret` → `nil` ImagePullSecrets (no regression)
- [ ] Deploy with `imageCommitterImage` behind a private Artifactory virtual repo and `imageCommitterPullSecret` pointing to a valid dockerconfigjson Secret → commit Job pulls the image and snapshot completes successfully

Co-authored-by: Atenea Agent <svc_atenea_gitlab@ofidona.net>

title: feat(controller): add --image-committer-pull-secret for authenticated registry proxies (e.g. Artifactory virtual repos mirroring Docker Hub)
body:
## Problem

In corporate environments, direct access to Docker Hub is typically blocked. Images are pulled through a **private virtual repository** (e.g. JFrog Artifactory, Nexus) that proxies/mirrors Docker Hub and requires authentication. Even though `image-committer` is a public image on Docker Hub, pulling it through such a proxy fails with `401 Unauthorized` / `ImagePullBackOff` because the commit Job has no `imagePullSecrets`:

```
Failed to pull image "artifactory.corp.example.com/docker/opensandbox/image-committer:v0.1.1":
failed to authorize: failed to fetch anonymous token:
  unexpected status from GET request to https://...: 401
```

This is a common deployment pattern in enterprise clusters:

```
Kubernetes node
  └─► pull "artifactory.corp.example.com/docker/opensandbox/image-committer:v0.1.1"
            │
            ▼
    Artifactory virtual repo   ← requires auth (imagePullSecret)
            │
            ▼ proxy / mirror
      Docker Hub (public)      ← image is public, but unreachable directly
```

The controller already supports `--snapshot-push-secret` (credentials to push snapshots) and `--resume-pull-secret` (credentials to pull snapshot images during resume), but there is no equivalent for pulling the `image-committer` image into the commit Job pod.

## Root cause

`buildCommitJob()` in `kubernetes/internal/controller/sandboxsnapshot_lifecycle.go` constructs the `batchv1.Job` `PodSpec` without any `ImagePullSecrets`:

```go
Spec: corev1.PodSpec{
    RestartPolicy: corev1.RestartPolicyNever,
    // no ImagePullSecrets — anonymous pull only
    Containers: []corev1.Container{{
        Image: r.ImageCommitterImage,
        ...
    }},
}
```

## Proposed fix

Add a new `--image-committer-pull-secret` flag (mirrors the existing `--snapshot-push-secret` / `--resume-pull-secret` pattern):

1. Add `ImageCommitterPullSecret string` to `SandboxSnapshotReconciler`
2. In `buildCommitJob()` and `ensureUnpauseJob()`: if set, add it to `PodSpec.ImagePullSecrets`
3. In `main.go`: parse `--image-committer-pull-secret` and wire it to the reconciler
4. In the Helm chart: add `controller.snapshot.imageCommitterPullSecret` value

## Impact

Any production or enterprise cluster that proxies Docker Hub through an authenticated registry (Artifactory, Nexus, ECR pull-through cache, GCR mirror, etc.) cannot use the snapshot feature today. The operator must mirror `image-committer` to a separate unauthenticated registry or hack around it — neither is acceptable in a secure environment.

## Related

- `--snapshot-push-secret` — same pattern, already implemented
- `--resume-pull-secret` — same pattern, already implemented
