title: fix(server): preserve API mount prefix in server-proxied endpoint URLs
body:
## Problem

The lifecycle API is mounted both bare and under `/v1` (`main.py` includes every router twice), but the `use_server_proxy=true` endpoint rewrite builds the proxied URL from `request.base_url` only, dropping the mount prefix the client actually came through:

```
GET /v1/sandboxes/{id}/endpoints/{port}?use_server_proxy=true
->  "endpoint": "host/sandboxes/{id}/proxy/{port}"     # /v1 lost
```

On deployments where the server is published behind a path split (e.g. an ingress/reverse proxy routing `/v1/*` to opensandbox-server while `/` belongs to another backend), every proxied request then hits the wrong backend: plain HTTP runs into that backend's redirects, and WebSocket handshakes fail outright since WS clients do not follow redirects. This effectively breaks `use_server_proxy` — the option designed exactly for clients that cannot reach sandbox subdomains directly.

## Fix

Derive the mount prefix from the request path and keep it in the rewritten endpoint. `server.eip` is left verbatim: it is the operator-specified full external base and may already carry its own path prefix (existing test covers that semantic).

## Testing

- Updated the `/v1`-mounted expectation and added a bare-mount case in `test_routes_endpoint_behavior.py`
- Full server suite passes: 1126 passed

title: SDK: widen uid/gid types across Isolated* models to match spec's uint32
body:
## Background

`specs/execd-api.yaml` declares `uid` and `gid` on `CreateIsolatedSessionRequest` / `IsolatedSessionInfo` / `SessionState` as `type: integer, format: uint32`. execd stores them as `*uint32` internally.

Several SDKs currently type these fields as `int` / `Int?`:

| SDK | Type | Files |
|---|---|---|
| C# | `int?` | `sdks/sandbox/csharp/src/OpenSandbox/Models/Isolated.cs` (`CreateIsolatedSessionRequest` line 42-43, `IsolatedSessionInfo` line 58-59, `IsolatedSessionState` line 76-77) |
| Kotlin | `Int?` | `sdks/sandbox/kotlin/.../IsolatedModels.kt` (`CreateIsolatedSessionRequest` line 44-45, `IsolatedSessionInfo` line 60-61, `IsolatedSessionState` line 78-79); also the wire DTO `IsolatedSessionStateResponse` at `IsolatedSessionsAdapter.kt` line 106-107 |
| TypeScript | `number?` (works — 53-bit safe integer covers uint32) | `sdks/sandbox/javascript/src/models/isolated.ts` |
| Go | `*uint32` (correct) | `sdks/sandbox/go/isolated.go` |
| Python | `int` (works — arbitrary precision) | `sdks/sandbox/python/src/opensandbox/models/isolated.py` |

## Problem

For C# and Kotlin, `int` / `Int` cannot hold `uid`/`gid` above `2^31 - 1`, even though the spec advertises the full `uint32` range up to `2^32 - 1`. If a session is created (through Go / raw API) with a uid in that upper half, the C#/Kotlin `System.Text.Json` / `kotlinx.serialization` deserializer will fail before `AttachAsync`/`GetAsync` can return.

Raised by codex on PR #1295 (comments r3577375975 for C# and r3577375984 for Kotlin). Not fixed there because:

1. Practical Linux uid_t values are well within `Int32.MaxValue` — kernel default `UID_MAX` is 60000; systemd/LDAP/AD deployments virtually never allocate ≥ 2^31.
2. Widening only the state/info sides would create an asymmetry with `CreateIsolatedSessionRequest`, so the fix needs to be spec/SDK-wide.

## Proposed fix

For C# and Kotlin, widen all three types (`CreateIsolatedSessionRequest`, `IsolatedSessionInfo`, `IsolatedSessionState`) plus the private wire DTO (Kotlin only) to `long? / Long?`. Add a regression test with `uid > Int32.MaxValue` deserialization.

## Non-goals

- Go and Python are already fine — no change.
- TypeScript's `number` covers `uint32` losslessly (max safe integer is `2^53 - 1`) — no change.

## Priority

Low. No known real-world sandbox deployment allocates uid ≥ 2^31, and the failure mode (deserialize error at attach time) is loud rather than silent-corrupt. Filing to keep the compat gap visible.

title: feat(isolated-session): support attach(sessionId) for stateless recovery
body:
## Problem

execd's `/v1/isolated/*` HTTP endpoints are all keyed by `sessionId`
(the map lookup is stateless), but the SDKs today only expose
`create(...)`. A caller that only has a `sessionId` — for example a
serverless worker that restarted mid-flight, or a job runner that
persists the id in a queue — has no way to rebuild a session handle
without also having retained the original `CreateIsolatedSessionRequest`.

This PR adds `attach(sessionId)` across all five sandbox SDKs, plus the
spec/server changes needed to make the returned handle carry the same
info a `create(...)` handle would.

## Design

Purely additive and backward-compatible:

**Spec** (`specs/execd-api.yaml`)

`SessionState` echoes back the creation parameters of the session
(`profile`, `workspace`, `extra_writable`, `binds`, `share_net`,
`env_passthrough`, `uid`, `gid`, `uid_mode`, `idle_timeout_seconds`).
All fields are optional; older execd builds omit them and clients must
tolerate absence.

**execd**

- `runtime.IsolatedSessionState` and `model.SessionState` gain the echo
  fields.
- `GetIsolatedSession` snapshots the params from `s.opts` (already
  stored on the in-memory session struct).
- The `Get` handler fills them into the response.

**SDKs (Kotlin / TypeScript / Python / Go / C#)**

Each `IsolationService` gets a new `attach(sessionId)` method:

1. GET `/v1/isolated/session/{id}`
2. Build an `IsolatedSessionInfo` from the response
3. Return the same handle type `create(...)` returns

Handles built via `attach` are fully functional (`run/get/delete/files`)
because those operations only need the sessionId. On an older execd that
omits the echo fields, the returned handle still works — just with the
echo fields left null/empty.

`404` propagates as each SDK's usual not-found error; a blank sessionId
is rejected locally without hitting the wire.

## Tests

- **execd**
  - `TestGetIsolatedSession_ReturnsCreationParams` covers the runtime echo.
  - `TestSessionState_JSONRoundtrip` locks the wire keys against the spec.
- **Each SDK** ships three unit tests (full-info, older-execd tolerance,
  404) plus a blank-sessionId guard.
- **Cross-language e2e (Python, Go)**: create → drop original handle →
  attach by sessionId → run/get/delete against the same bwrap session.

All package-local checks pass locally:

| SDK | Tests |
|---|---|
| Kotlin (`./gradlew :sandbox:test`) | 206 |
| TS (`pnpm run test`) | 51 |
| Python (`uv run pytest`) | 283 |
| Go (`go test ./...`) | 214 |
| C# (`dotnet test`) | 136 |
| execd (`go test ./pkg/...`) | pass |

E2E was not run locally (needs a real sandbox environment); please
verify in CI.

## Non-Goals / Limits

- **Not a durable-recovery mechanism.** The isolated session lives in
  execd's in-memory `sync.Map`; attach only works while the sessionId is
  still valid there. execd restart / Pod migration / idle_timeout expiry
  all invalidate the sessionId as before.
- For long recovery windows, callers should set
  `idle_timeout_seconds=0` at create time and take responsibility for
  explicit delete.
- `diff` / `commit` remain Phase 2 stubs (unchanged by this PR).

## Compatibility

- Old SDK + new execd: unchanged behavior (new fields are ignored).
- New SDK + old execd: `attach` returns a functional handle with the
  echo fields left null/empty; `run/get/delete/files` still work.
- No public API removed or renamed anywhere.

title: OSEP-0015: Named-Element Template Merge for Admin-Defined Sidecar and Volume Injection
body:
## Summary

The server already supports admin-provided sandbox templates (`batchsandbox_template_file` / `template_file`), but `BaseSandboxTemplateManager._deep_merge` replaces lists wholesale, and the workload providers always populate `spec.template.spec.containers` and `volumes` in the runtime manifest — so containers and volumes declared in an admin template can never take effect.

This OSEP proposes an opt-in `merge-by-name` strategy (mirroring the Kubernetes strategic-merge-patch `mergeKey: name` convention): named list elements are merged element-wise, runtime wins on conflict, template-only elements are appended after runtime elements (preserving `containers[0] == main`).

## Why

Platform teams embedding OpenSandbox need to attach a platform-owned sidecar (log shipper, workspace sync agent, etc.) plus a shared volume to every sandbox pod:

- request-level sidecar/secret injection is a security risk in shared namespaces;
- mutating admission webhooks need cluster-scoped permissions many managed platforms don't grant;
- the existing template mechanism is the natural, admin-controlled place — it just silently drops template containers/volumes today.

Default behavior is unchanged (`replace`); the new strategy is explicit operator opt-in, so existing deployments are unaffected.

Happy to iterate on naming, config shape, or scope — and to implement it if the direction is accepted.

title: feat(sdk): declarative sandbox "features" - one-line add (git, jupyter, …) or ban tools
body:
## Why do you need it?

> **Scope note / prior art.** Tools get into a sandbox today only by: (a) baking a custom Docker image, (b) passing `env` / `entrypoint` at create, or (c) running `commands.run("apt install …")` manually. The `extensions` create field is reserved for internal / experimental flags (annotation codec) - **not** a user toolchain. Verified: there is no declarative "add git + jupyter" one-liner, and **no** way to *disable / ban* specific tools or capabilities inside a sandbox (no seccomp / apparmor field, no command blocklist, no read-only-rootfs option in the API/SDK; **OSEP-0004** is about isolation *runtimes*, not per-tool policy).

Two directions of one missing primitive:

- **Add** common toolchains without a custom image or manual install - `git`, `jupyter`, `node`, `playwright`, `uv`, … (devcontainer-"features" style).
- **Ban** tools / capabilities for safety - disable `git`, package managers, network tools, or a command blocklist - so an untrusted agent can't reach them.

## How could it be?

- **Add**: SDK create option `features=["git", "jupyter"]` → the server resolves each to a cached setup layer / script applied at provision (or as a lifecycle hook), instead of a bespoke image.
- **Ban**: `deny_tools=["git", "curl"]` / `command_policy={ block: [...] }` → enforced by execd (reject matching commands, strip from `PATH`, or remove the binary), optionally backed by seccomp / apparmor profiles for capability bans.
- Features are **named, versioned, cache-shared, and community-extensible** (a small feature registry - relates to the skill/recipe and template ideas).
- **CLI**: `osb sandbox create --feature git --feature jupyter --ban curl`.

**Output:**
`Sandbox.create(image="python:3.12", features=["git", "jupyter"], deny_tools=["curl"])`- reproducible toolchains and safety bans without building images.

## Other related information

- Relates to earlier brainstorm ideas: lifecycle hooks, skill/recipe registry, and template/blueprint marketplace - this is the concrete **SDK-level "features" slice**.
- Provisioning / behavior change → likely an **OSEP**. Additive / backward-compatible: no features or bans = today's behavior.

title: feat: human-in-the-loop approval gate for commands and egress
body:
## Why do you need it?

> **Scope note / prior art.** Policy today is **static and non-interactive**:
> - Egress uses static allow/deny lists (nft rules, `deny.always`) and fires an **async deny webhook** (`OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_DENY_WEBHOOK`) that only *notifies* subscribers of an **already-denied** request - it does not pause and ask.
> - Command execution has no approval concept at all.
> - The server's only "confirmation" is `startup_guard.py` prompting when no `api_key` is configured.

Missing: a **blocking** gate - hold a risky action (a command matching a rule, an egress to a not-yet-approved domain, a destructive operation) and await an approve/deny decision **before** it proceeds. This is the key primitive for supervising autonomous agents: let them run, but stop at defined risk boundaries.

## How could it be?

- **Declarative gate policy** at create/session time, e.g. `approval: { commands: ["rm -rf*", "curl*"], egress: "new-domains" }`.
- On a match, execd / egress **pauses** the action and raises a *pending-approval* event carrying context (the command, the target domain, a file diff, etc.).
- **Decision channel**: `POST /approvals/{id} { decision: allow | deny, ttl }`. On `allow`, the action proceeds; on `deny`, it's rejected with a clear error. Optional "remember for this session / domain."
- **Reviewer UX**: approve via SDK/CLI (`osb approvals ls | allow | deny`) or via a scoped **share link** (see draft #1) so a human can approve from a browser.
- **Timeout → default deny** (fail-closed).

**Output:** an agent runs autonomously but stops for a human at defined risk boundaries, then resumes on approval.

## Other related information

- Upgrades the egress **deny webhook** from notify-only to an optional *blocking* approval; integrates with the Credential Vault (**OSEP-0012**) for approve-before-credential-use.
- Security / UX change → **OSEP**. Additive: no policy configured = today's behavior.

title: feat(sdk/server): first-class agent runtime inside a sandbox (spawn / stream / stop)
body:
## Why do you need it?

> **Scope note / prior art.**
>
> Agents can already run *inside* OpenSandbox today, but there is no built-in
> agent runtime. Every existing approach requires developers to implement the
> same lifecycle management themselves.
>
> Current patterns include:
>
> - **Coding CLIs** installed inside the sandbox and invoked via `commands.run` (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, Qwen Code, Kimi CLI, etc.).
> - **Agent gateways** started as long-running processes inside the sandbox and exposed over HTTP (OpenClaw, NullClaw, etc.).
> - **Client-side orchestrators** (LangGraph, Google ADK, etc.) where the agent runs outside the sandbox and only uses the sandbox as a tool.

What is missing is a **first-class primitive for spawning and managing an agent inside the sandbox**.

Today, every implementation has to re-create the same workflow:

1. Install the agent.
2. Launch the process.
3. Wait until it is ready.
4. Connect to its output or endpoint.
5. Stream or parse events.
6. Stop or interrupt it.
7. Collect logs and artifacts.

This plumbing is repeated across every integration.

Instead, OpenSandbox could provide a managed agent runtime that:

- spawns an agent with a prompt and configuration,
- streams its steps, tool calls, and output,
- supports interruption and cancellation,
- gives the agent a scoped identity,
- collects logs and artifacts,

without every integration having to implement the same lifecycle management.

## How could it be?

### SDK

```python
handle = sandbox.agents.spawn(
    kind="claude-code" | "codex" | <custom>,
    prompt=...,
    env=...,
    tools=...,
)

async for step in handle.stream():
    ...

await handle.stop()
```

The SDK would expose a managed handle instead of requiring developers to launch and monitor processes manually.

### Server / execd

Manage the agent as a first-class session by:

- reusing the existing execd session model,
- reusing the SSE streaming infrastructure already defined in `specs/execd-api.yaml`,
- tracking lifecycle and status,
- exposing logs and generated artifacts.

### Scoped identity (optional)

Integrate with the Credential Vault (OSEP-0012) so an agent receives scoped, least-privilege credentials instead of long-lived account secrets.

### Pluggable agent adapters

Support different agent implementations through adapters, for example:

- coding CLIs,
- agent gateways,
- custom implementations.

This would promote today's example scripts into reusable first-class adapters.

## Output

Instead of manually installing, starting, polling, and parsing an agent:

```python
handle = sandbox.agents.spawn(...)

async for step in handle.stream():
    ...
```

The SDK manages the lifecycle while providing a consistent streaming interface.

## Other related information

- Builds on the existing coding-CLI and OpenClaw/NullClaw examples by promoting the pattern into a platform primitive.
- Builds on execd sessions.
- Integrates with Credential Vault (**OSEP-0012**) for scoped identity.
- Complements the planned **agent audit trail** by attributing agent actions.
- Composes naturally with:
  - human-in-the-loop approval gates,
  - session recording and replay.
- Introduces a new public API surface, so it would likely require an **OSEP**. The proposal is additive and backward compatible.

title: feat: record sandbox sessions and replay them as a shareable artifact
body:
## Why do you need it?

There is no way to capture a sandbox session - the ordered stream of commands, terminal output, file operations, and (optionally) network events - and replay or share it afterward. Verified: "record" in the codebase refers only to DB `SnapshotRecord` rows and log records; there is no session recording / replay / asciinema / playback surface.

This blocks:

- Reproducing exactly what a coding or GUI agent did during a run.
- Sharing a self-contained "here's what happened" artifact for a bug report or an eval result.
- Reviewing an agent trajectory offline.

It is also the concrete consumer that the roadmap's planned **agent in-sandbox audit trail** needs.

## How could it be?

Add opt-in session recording plus a replay artifact:

- Enable at create/session time (`record: true`) or via `osb session record <sandbox> <session>`.
- execd captures a timestamped event stream: terminal I/O (an asciinema/ttyrec-compatible cast), executed commands + exit codes, file write/read metadata, and - where egress proxying is on - outbound request summaries.
- Store the recording as a downloadable artifact (`GET /sandboxes/{id}/recordings/{recId}`), independent of the sandbox lifecycle (it may outlive the sandbox, like snapshots).
- **Replay**: `osb session replay <file>` renders the terminal cast; the structured events are consumable programmatically for eval / diffing.

**Output:** a portable, shareable recording that reproduces a session visually and as structured events.

## Other related information

- Natural building block for the roadmap's planned **agent audit trail**, and complementary to **OSEP-0010 (OpenTelemetry)** - telemetry is aggregate metrics/traces; this is a replayable per-session capture.
- Pairs with a "deterministic record-and-replay" proposal (byte-reproducible evals) and "flaky-run bisection."
- Privacy / retention sensitive (captures I/O, possibly secrets) → must define redaction, retention, and consent; likely an **OSEP**.
- Additive / backward-compatible; off by default.

title: feat(server): transfer ownership of a running sandbox between principals
body:
## Why do you need it?

A sandbox is bound to the identity / API key that created it, and there is no supported way to transfer a **live** sandbox to another user, API key, or tenant while preserving its state and lifecycle. Verified: "ownership" in the current code refers only to Kubernetes PVC ownerReferences and file uid/gid - there is no principal-to-principal sandbox transfer.

This blocks handing a running debugging or agent session from an automated agent identity to a human operator (or between teammates / shifts) **without** killing and recreating it - which loses all in-memory and on-disk working state.

## How could it be?

Add an ownership-transfer op:

- `POST /sandboxes/{id}/transfer` with a target principal (user id / API key id / tenant), optionally requiring the target to accept.
- After transfer: the sandbox's owner metadata, access control, quota accounting, and endpoint auth move to the new owner; the sandbox keeps running with the same id and state.
- **Auditable**: emit an ownership-change event (ties to the roadmap's planned agent audit trail).
- SDK/CLI: `osb sandbox transfer <id> --to <principal>`.

**Output:** continuity of a live sandbox across a change of responsible principal, with correct auth / quota re-binding.

## Other related information

- Tightly coupled to **OSEP-0014 (Multi-Tenancy)** - transfer semantics must respect tenant boundaries, quotas, and RBAC; this may fold into or extend that OSEP.
- Distinct from the "share links" proposal: sharing grants *temporary access*; handoff is a *permanent responsibility/ownership* change. Both may share an access-control substrate.
- Security-model change → **OSEP required** per `CONTRIBUTING.md`.
- Additive / backward-compatible: no transfer = today's behavior.

title: feat(server): fork a running sandbox into a divergent copy
body:
## Why do you need it?

The snapshot lifecycle (OSEP-0008) already supports `POST /snapshots` to capture a sandbox and creating a new sandbox from a `snapshotId`. But there is no single **fork** operation that captures the *current live state* and immediately spins up an independent, divergent copy. To get N parallel explorations from the same expensive setup state (installed deps, warmed caches, an agent mid-task), users must manually orchestrate snapshot → wait → create-from-snapshot, and there is no first-class notion of "fork this running box right now." Verified: zero `fork` / `clone-sandbox` references in `specs/`, `server/`, the SDKs, or the CLI.

Use cases:

- Branch an agent's exploration into several candidate directions from one point.
- Give each of several reviewers their own live copy of a reproduction.
- A/B two fixes from an identical starting state.

## How could it be?

Add a fork op that composes the existing snapshot + restore primitives as one step:

- `POST /sandboxes/{id}/fork` → snapshot the source (optionally with a brief pause for a consistent rootfs, reusing OSEP-0008), then provision a **new** sandbox restored from it; return the new sandbox id.
- **Options**: `count` (fork into N copies), `pause_source` (momentary pause vs best-effort live), and inherit-vs-override for env / resource limits / egress policy.
- The fork is fully independent: separate id, identity, and endpoints; the source keeps running.
- SDK/CLI: `osb sandbox fork <id> --count 3`.

**Output:** one call yields independent, divergent sandbox(es) that start from
the source's current state.

## Other related information

- Directly reuses **OSEP-0008 (Pause and Resume via Rootfs Snapshot)** - this is largely an orchestration + API-ergonomics layer over existing snapshot/restore.
- Volume forking is related but separate - see **OSEP-0003 (Volume Support)**. An initial fork could snapshot rootfs only and document volume-sharing/branching semantics (pairs with a future "copy-on-write volume branching" proposal).
- Additive; changes the lifecycle API surface, so likely a small **OSEP** or design note. Backward-compatible.

title: feat(execd): multi-client session attach ("sandbox rooms") with a shared terminal
body:
## Why do you need it?

execd sessions today are single-consumer: `create_session` / bash exec streams output over Server-Sent Events to the one caller (verified in `specs/execd-api.yaml` — sessions/contexts stream to a single client; there is no attach / multiplex / broadcast / presence surface). There is no way for two clients - e.g. a coding agent and a human, or two teammates - to see and drive the **same** live shell at once.

That blocks:

- Pair-programming with an agent (human watches and occasionally takes the keys).
- Live debugging handovers where a second person joins an in-progress session.
- Teaching / demo scenarios and "watch what the agent is typing" oversight.

## How could it be?

Extend the session model to support multiple concurrent attachments to one PTY-backed session:

- `POST /session/{id}/attach` returning a bidirectional stream. Output SSE already exists; add an input channel (WebSocket or chunked input endpoint) so N clients share one terminal buffer, tmux-style broadcast.
- **Roles** per attachment: `driver` (may write) vs `observer` (read-only), with the owner able to grant / revoke write.
- **Presence**: list currently-attached clients and emit a lightweight event when clients join or leave.
- **Scrollback on attach**: a late joiner receives recent output so they have context.

**Output:** multiple SDK/CLI clients (e.g. `osb session attach <sandbox> <session>`) sharing one live terminal, with clear driver/observer roles.

## Other related information

- Non-trivial change to the execution API surface → likely needs an **OSEP**.
- Backward-compatible: single-client sessions keep working unchanged.

title: execd: RunCommand doesn't terminate its chunked SSE response cleanly (missing completeCh/waitForExecutionComplete pattern used by RunCode/RunInSession)
body:
## `execd`: `RunCommand` doesn't terminate its chunked SSE response cleanly (missing the `completeCh`/`waitForExecutionComplete` pattern used by `RunCode`/`RunInSession`)

### Summary

`POST /command`'s HTTP response is not terminated correctly for HTTP/1.1 chunked transfer-encoding. After the command finishes and the `execution_complete`/`error` SSE event has been written and flushed, the handler does a fixed `time.Sleep(flag.ApiGracefulShutdownTimeout)` and then returns, letting `net/http` close the connection without ever writing chunked-encoding's terminating zero-length chunk. Strict HTTP/1.1 clients correctly treat this as a protocol violation. Python's `httpx`, for example, raises:

```
httpx.RemoteProtocolError: peer closed connection without sending complete message body (incomplete chunked read)
```

### Where

`components/execd/pkg/web/controller/command.go`, `RunCommand` handler, around line 97 — the `time.Sleep(flag.ApiGracefulShutdownTimeout)` call immediately after `codeRunner.Execute(runCodeRequest)` completes.

### Why this happens

`RunCommand` is inconsistent with its two siblings in the same package. `RunCode` and `RunInSession` both terminate their responses correctly: they open a `completeCh`, have their `OnExecuteComplete`/`OnExecuteError` hooks call `signalComplete()` into that channel, and then call `waitForExecutionComplete(ctx, completeCh)` — which returns as soon as the completion event is actually flushed (or the request context is cancelled, or `ApiGracefulShutdownTimeout` elapses as a fallback). Once that returns, the handler itself returns and the chunked response is finished properly.

`RunCommand` instead does a blind `time.Sleep(flag.ApiGracefulShutdownTimeout)` with no completion-channel wiring at all. Two consequences fall out of this one gap:

1. **Incomplete chunked read** — the response isn't terminated the way `RunCode`/`RunInSession` terminate theirs, which is what strict clients/proxies flag.
2. **Artificial latency on every command** — since the sleep is unconditional (not "wait until complete, capped at the timeout" like its siblings), every `/command` call holds the connection open for the *full* `ApiGracefulShutdownTimeout` (~1s by default) after the command has already finished, regardless of how fast the command itself ran. A trivial `true` takes ~1s wall-clock for this reason alone.

Fixing `RunCommand` to use the same pattern its siblings already use would resolve both issues at once.

### Reproduction

```bash
curl -s -N -w "\ntime_total=%{time_total}s\n" -X POST http://<execd-host>:44772/command \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"command":"true"}'
```

Direct requests straight to execd don't surface a visible error — most HTTP clients tolerate the malformed chunk termination silently and just treat the abrupt close as end-of-stream. But `time_total` shows ~1s even though the SSE events themselves (visible in the streamed output) arrive within single-digit milliseconds of each other — confirming the extra time is the fixed sleep, not real work.

The termination bug becomes a hard error once anything strict relays that response onward — e.g. the OpenSandbox control server's own Python (`httpx`-based) reverse proxy, in `opensandbox_server/api/proxy.py`'s `_stream_backend_response` (`async for chunk in resp.aiter_raw()`), throws `RemoteProtocolError` on essentially every `/command` call once traffic goes through `use_server_proxy=true`. Routing the identical exec directly to execd (bypassing that proxy) produces no error — same execd response, different strictness on the reading side.

### Suggested fix

Bring `RunCommand` in line with `RunCode`/`RunInSession`:

1. Initialize a `completeCh` and `signalComplete` before starting execution.
2. Have `OnExecuteComplete`/`OnExecuteError` call `signalComplete()`.
3. Replace `time.Sleep(flag.ApiGracefulShutdownTimeout)` with `waitForExecutionComplete(ctx, completeCh)` (already implemented and used by the other two handlers, timeout fallback included).

### Environment

- `opensandbox/execd:v1.0.19`
- Observed via `uvx opensandbox-server` (Python control plane, Docker runtime) with `use_server_proxy=true`, and confirmed absent with `use_server_proxy=false`

title: feat(egress): dynamic per-user credential management — lifecycle, storage and multi-tenancy
body:
## Problem

The credential vault (egress sidecar) already solves credential **isolation** per sandbox: each sandbox gets its own in-memory `Store` with its own credentials and bindings. That part works.

What is **not** addressed is how an operator manages credentials when there are **multiple users**, each with their own set of credentials (API keys, tokens, etc.). Concretely:

- **Where do user credentials live** before/between sandboxes? Currently the only durable storage is whatever the orchestrator has at sandbox-creation time. There is no user-scoped credential store outside the sandbox lifecycle.
- **How are credentials provisioned at creation?** The orchestrator must pass credentials in the `CreateRequest`. For multiple users, the orchestrator needs to know each user's credentials — but nothing in the platform defines how those are kept, rotated, or scoped.
- **How are credentials updated on running sandboxes?** The `Mutate` API exists, but who calls it, when, and authenticated as whom? There is no lifecycle contract for credential updates (e.g., token rotation mid-session).
- **How are credentials deleted/invalidated** when a user is offboarded or a token is revoked?

The `http` source type (PR #1188) is a step forward — instead of inline values, the egress fetches credentials from an HTTP endpoint at injection time. But it shifts the problem: now the operator must build and maintain that per-user HTTP credential endpoint themselves, with no guidance or standard interface from OpenSandbox.

## Current architecture (what exists)

```
orchestrator
  └─ CreateRequest { credentials: [{name, source: {type:"inline", value:"<token>"}}], bindings: [...] }
        └─► egress sidecar Store (singleton per sandbox, in-memory, lost on pod death)
```

Everything lives in the sidecar. Nothing is persisted. Nothing knows about users.

## What is needed

A first-class concept of **user credential sets** with a defined lifecycle:

### 1. User credential store (outside sandbox lifecycle)
A place to keep `(user → credentials)` mappings that persists across sandboxes. Could be:
- A new API on the OpenSandbox **server** (e.g. `POST /users/{userId}/credentials`)
- A Kubernetes Secret or external secret manager reference
- A pluggable backend (inline, K8s secret, Vault, HTTP endpoint)

### 2. Credential provisioning at sandbox creation
The server/orchestrator should be able to resolve a user's credentials by user ID and inject them into the `CreateRequest` automatically — without the caller embedding raw credential values in the API call.

### 3. Credential mutation lifecycle
Define who can call `Mutate` on a running sandbox's vault and when:
- Token rotation: update credential value without restarting the sandbox
- Revocation: remove a credential and its bindings immediately
- Audit: who changed what and when

### 4. Multi-tenancy boundary
Guarantee that user A's credentials cannot be read or injected into user B's sandbox, even if both run on the same node. The current per-sidecar isolation helps, but there is no access-control layer at the credential provisioning level.

## Considered approaches

| Approach | Pros | Cons |
|----------|------|------|
| **`http` source (PR #1188)** | No server-side state; operator controls the endpoint | Operator must build & secure the per-user HTTP service; no standard |
| **Server-side user credential store** | Single source of truth; lifecycle managed by OpenSandbox | New API surface, migration cost |
| **K8s Secret per user, referenced by name** | Leverages existing K8s RBAC | Couples OpenSandbox to K8s; credential rotation needs pod-level access |
| **Pluggable CredentialProvider interface** | Flexible; operators can bring their own backend | More surface area; needs a reference implementation |

## Questions for maintainers

1. Is a server-side user credential store in scope for OpenSandbox, or is it intentionally left to the operator?

title: Design discussion: snapshot-to-replacement contract for recovery
body:
Hi OpenSandbox maintainers,

### The problem we are trying to solve

An external control plane may need to recover after a sandbox runtime becomes unavailable:

1. keep a previously created snapshot whose public status is `Ready`;
2. use the existing `snapshotId`-based sandbox creation flow to create a replacement sandbox;
3. wait until the replacement reaches the documented request-serving state; and
4. route future requests to the replacement.

### Concrete recovery case

A sandbox can contain application work state. While it is healthy, a client has a `Ready` snapshot. If the underlying runtime later becomes unavailable, the control plane needs to know whether it can safely create exactly one replacement from that snapshot.

This recovery can restore only the state captured by the selected snapshot. It does not request zero data loss for writes made after snapshot capture, and it does not request restoration of data outside the documented snapshot contents.

A concrete unknown-result failure case is:

1. `GET /snapshots/{snapshotId}` returns `Ready`;
2. the client sends `POST /sandboxes` with that `snapshotId`;
3. the server may successfully create sandbox A and prepare the `202` response containing A's ID, but the client loses that response because of a timeout, restart, or network failure; and
4. retrying the same request may create sandbox B because the current public API documents no replay identity or request-result lookup.

The Lifecycle OpenAPI defines snapshot-based sandbox creation and lifecycle states, but it does not currently define filesystem consistency, compatibility rejection, or unknown-result reconciliation for this recovery case.

### Current boundary and context

The current Lifecycle API exposes snapshot creation/status and sandbox creation from `snapshotId`. OSEP-0008 also defines the pause/resume use of Rootfs snapshots. Pause/resume preserves one sandbox lifecycle and stable `sandboxId`; this discussion is about using an addressable `Ready` snapshot to create a replacement sandbox lifecycle after the original runtime is unavailable.

This discussion is based on the current `main` branch documentation and lifecycle specification reviewed on 2026-07-11. No local code changes or runtime mutation are being requested.

### Contract questions

Could maintainers clarify:

1. **Capture contract:** What state and consistency does public snapshot status `Ready` guarantee? In particular, does it cover the root filesystem and application workspace when that workspace is inside the captured filesystem, and what content may be omitted or in flight?
2. **Compatibility contract:** Can the server reject an incompatible snapshot before accepting sandbox creation, with a stable error that callers can handle?
3. **Unknown-result contract:** After a timeout, server restart, or lost response, what supported mechanism lets a caller determine whether snapshot-based creation was not accepted, is still progressing, succeeded, or failed without creating a duplicate sandbox?

The Lifecycle OpenAPI documents `Running` as ready to accept requests. This issue does not request a second readiness state; it asks whether the snapshot-to-sandbox contract above is sufficient for a caller to rely on that existing lifecycle state after replacement creation.

### Related work

- [Lifecycle OpenAPI](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/specs/sandbox-lifecycle.yml)
- [OSEP-0008: Pause and Resume via Rootfs Snapshot](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/oseps/0008-pause-resume-rootfs-snapshot.md)
- [Pause and Resume Guide](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/blob/main/docs/guides/pause-resume.md)
- [Public snapshot image URI selection and stable snapshot-ID-derived tagging change](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/commit/73ab862822b82bc060891274a45141ea11682bbf)

### Non-goals

This issue does not ask OpenSandbox to:

- detect runtime failure or decide when a replacement should be created;
- own external logical identities, generations, routing, or failover policy;
- change existing pause/resume behavior;
- define storage-backend-specific snapshot behavior or metadata-based locking;
- prescribe a new route, request schema, or general-purpose lifecycle operation framework; or
- restore process memory, active connections, terminals, sessions, or in-flight commands.

### Desired outcome

Please confirm whether these snapshot-to-sandbox guarantees belong in the public Lifecycle contract. If they do, should the missing semantics be documented directly or developed in a focused OSEP?

If a focused OSEP or documentation update is appropriate, I would be happy to draft it after the intended boundary is confirmed.

title: feat(snapshots): expose imageUri end-to-end (spec, server, all SDKs)
body:
# Summary

Closes #1271.

In our organization we integrate with OpenSandbox through the official SDKs rather than calling the REST API directly — the typed client is our integration contract. When a field is missing from the SDK we are forced to drop down to raw HTTP, which adds complexity and couples our code to the wire protocol, hurting maintainability.

A `Ready` snapshot already produces a portable OCI restore image internally, but it is never surfaced on the public snapshot contract, so callers cannot restore a sandbox from that image (e.g. to move a sandbox across clusters) through the SDK without bypassing it. This exposes it end-to-end as `imageUri`, across the spec, the server, and **all SDKs**.

> Per the Codex review on the earlier revision (which flagged that only the server + Kotlin were updated, leaving the other SDK snapshot models inconsistent), this now regenerates/updates **every** SDK. Commits are split by concern — one for spec + server, then one per SDK.

**Spec**

- Add the optional `imageUri` to the `Snapshot` schema in `specs/sandbox-lifecycle.yml`.

**Server**

- Add `image_uri`/`imageUri` to the `Snapshot` response model and populate it from the record's restore image in `_to_snapshot_response`, only once the snapshot is `Ready`.

**Generated clients** (regenerated from the spec, not hand-edited)

- **python**: regenerated the lifecycle `Snapshot` model with `scripts/generate_api.py` (openapi-python-client); mapped onto the domain `SnapshotInfo` in the converter.
- **javascript**: regenerated `api/lifecycle.ts` with `pnpm gen:api` (openapi-typescript); added `imageUri` to the domain snapshot model.
- **kotlin**: the lifecycle client regenerates from the spec at build time (`sandbox-api` OpenAPI generator); added `imageUri` to the domain `SnapshotInfo` and mapped it in `SandboxModelConverter`.

**Hand-written clients** (no spec codegen — field added by hand)

- **go**: the lifecycle types are hand-written, so the field was added directly to `types.go` (`ImageURI string` with `json:"imageUri,omitempty"`).
- **csharp**: the snapshot model is hand-written, so `Models/Sandboxes.cs` gets `string? ImageUri` and `Adapters/SandboxesAdapter.cs` parses `imageUri` from the response JSON.

`imageUri` is optional and only populated once the snapshot is `Ready` (null/omitted otherwise), so the change is additive and backward compatible.

## Commits

1. `feat(snapshots): expose snapshot imageUri in spec and server`
2. `feat(python): expose snapshot imageUri in the Python SDK`

4. `feat(kotlin): expose snapshot imageUri in the Kotlin SDK`

- **csharp**: `dotnet build` + `dotnet test` — 132 passed.

- **go**: hand-written field; the SDK has no codegen step.

# Breaking Changes

Additive optional field; null/omitted unless the snapshot is `Ready`.

title: Expose the snapshot restore image (imageUri) across all SDKs
body:
## Why do you need it?

In our organization we integrate with OpenSandbox through the official SDKs rather than calling the REST API directly — the typed client is our integration contract. Whenever an operation or field is missing from the SDK we are forced to drop down to raw HTTP alongside it, which adds complexity and couples our code to the wire protocol, making it harder to maintain.

A `Ready` snapshot already produces a portable OCI restore image internally, but it is never surfaced on the public snapshot contract — so it is absent from every SDK's snapshot model too. As a result, callers cannot restore a sandbox from that image (e.g. to move a sandbox across clusters, where the `snapshotId` is cluster-local but the OCI image reference is portable) through the SDK. The information exists server-side; it is just not exposed, which forces a consumer to bypass the SDK and read an internal/raw field.

## How could it be?

Expose the restore image reference end-to-end as `imageUri`, consistently across **all SDKs**:

- **spec**: add an optional `imageUri` to the `Snapshot` schema in `specs/sandbox-lifecycle.yml` (the source of truth the spec-driven clients generate from).
- **server**: add `imageUri` to the `Snapshot` response, populated from the record's restore image, only once the snapshot is `Ready`.
- **SDKs**: surface it through to the public snapshot model in every SDK — regenerating the spec-driven clients (Python, JavaScript, Kotlin) from the updated spec and updating the hand-written ones (Go, C#) to match.

**Input**: none (no new request fields).
**Output**: `snapshot.imageUri` populated when the snapshot is `Ready`, null/omitted otherwise.

## Other related information

`imageUri` is optional and only populated once the snapshot is `Ready`, so the change is additive and backward compatible.

This supersedes the earlier all-SDKs proposal (#1077 / #1053). Implementation: #1272.

title: fix(sdk/python): defer annotations in isolated service Protocols
body:
## Problem

The main branch CI (SDK Tests) is red. Run [29004692407](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox/actions/runs/29004692407) has 4 failing jobs, all with the same root cause:

- Python SDK Tests (sandbox)
- Python SDK Tests (code-interpreter)
- CLI Tests
- Python SDK Quality (sandbox) — pyright

All fail at import time with:

```
src/opensandbox/services/isolated.py:89: in IsolationService
    binds: list[BindMount] | None = None,
E   TypeError: 'function' object is not subscriptable
```

## Root cause

Introduced by f31696b4 (#1264). The `IsolationService` / `IsolationServiceSync` Protocols declare both:

- an `async def list(...)` method, and
- a `binds: list[BindMount] | None = None` parameter annotation on `run_once`.

Because these modules lack `from __future__ import annotations`, the annotation is evaluated at class-definition time. In the class body scope, the name `list` resolves to the class-scoped `list` method instead of the builtin, so `list[BindMount]` raises `TypeError: 'function' object is not subscriptable`. pyright reports the equivalent `Expected class but received ... -> list[...]`.

## Fix

Add `from __future__ import annotations` to both modules so annotations are evaluated lazily (PEP 563), restoring `list` to the builtin.

- `sdks/sandbox/python/src/opensandbox/services/isolated.py`
- `sdks/sandbox/python/src/opensandbox/sync/services/isolated.py`

Also adds a regression test that imports both service modules.

## Verification (local)

- `uv run pytest tests/` — all pass (Python sandbox SDK)
- `uv run pyright` — 0 errors
- `uv run ruff check` — passed
- CLI `uv run pytest tests/` — all pass

title: docs(security): make official container image provenance discoverable (DockerHub trust signals + README pointer)
body:
## Summary

The official container images are published to `docker.io/opensandbox/*` (verified: `publish-components.yml` / `publish-server.yml` push there and cosign-sign the digest, cross-published to Aliyun ACR and GHCR). The verification guide at `docs/community/release-verification.md` is excellent and covers `cosign verify` for the images.

However, there are two **discoverability** gaps that make it hard for a new user to confirm the images are official *before* deploying them:

## Gap 1 — DockerHub account has no trust signals

`https://hub.docker.com/u/opensandbox` is a plain **User** account (not an Organization), created 2025-12-03, with:
- No profile description, company, or link back to the GitHub repo
- No **Verified Publisher** / **Sponsored OSS** badge

A user landing there has no on-DockerHub way to tell it's the official project account — the only proof is cross-referencing the GitHub release notes and cosign signatures. Someone could squat a similar name and users couldn't easily distinguish it.

**Suggestions (any of):**
- Convert to a DockerHub **Organization** and apply for **Verified Publisher** / OSS program
- At minimum, populate the account profile: description, link to `github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox`, and per-repo "official image" descriptions

## Gap 2 — README doesn't point to official images or verification

The main `README.md` has no section telling users:
- Which registries host the official images (`docker.io/opensandbox/*`, Aliyun ACR, `ghcr.io/...`)
- That images are cosign-signed and how to verify (link to `docs/community/release-verification.md`)

A short "Container Images" section in the README with the registry list + a link to the verification guide would close the loop for users who never read `SECURITY.md`.

## Why this matters

For teams mirroring these images into a controlled/corporate registry (a common enterprise pattern), the first question in review is "are these the official images and can we verify them?". The infrastructure to answer that already exists — it's just not surfaced where users look first.

## Not a bug

Provenance itself is solid (keyless cosign, triple-registry, digest-pinned). This is purely about making that provenance **discoverable**.

title: feat: add explicit bind mounts to execd bwrap isolation
body:
# Summary

Add support for arbitrary **source→destination bind mounts** in execd isolated (bwrap) sessions, complementing the existing `extra_writable` (which only supports `source==destination`, always read-write). Each bind maps a host source to an in-namespace destination and may be mounted read-only.

This is an additive, backward-compatible change across the full stack: spec → execd server → all five sandbox SDKs → e2e tests.

## What changed

**Server (execd)**
- New `BindMount{source, dest, readonly}` and `WrapOptions.Binds`; the bwrap argv builder renders `--bind` / `--ro-bind` with distinct `src→dst`.
- Bind sources are validated against the writable allowlist (read-only binds included) to prevent mapping arbitrary host paths into the sandbox.
- Seed a non-empty default allowlist (`/workspace`, `/mnt`, `/media`, `/data`) so common sandbox data volumes and their subdirectories work out of the box. The allowlist is prefix-based, so subpaths (e.g. `/data/foo`) are allowed; `..` traversal is blocked via `filepath.Clean`.
- `Binds` threaded through runtime options and the web model/controller (and the Windows stub).

**Spec**
- Added the `BindMount` schema and `binds` field to `CreateIsolatedSessionRequest` in `specs/execd-api.yaml`.

**SDKs (python, javascript, kotlin, go, csharp)**
- Added `BindMount` and `binds` (plus the previously missing `uid_mode`) to the handwritten `CreateIsolatedSessionRequest` model.
- Threaded `binds` through the `run_once` convenience helper (Go already accepted the full request).
- Regenerated the python and javascript execd API models from the spec.

## Usage

```python
await sandbox.isolation.run_once(
    "cat /mnt/in/data.txt",
    workspace="/tmp",
    binds=[BindMount(source="/data/in", dest="/mnt/in", readonly=True)],
)
```

> Note: a bind must target an **existing** destination mount point — bwrap cannot create one under the read-only root. Create the destination directory first (e.g. `mkdir -p`).

# Testing
- [x] Unit tests — argv builder binds (rw/ro/default-dest/validation), request-mapping regression tests across SDKs.
- [x] Integration tests — `bwrap_binds_test.go` (src→dst write-through, read-only read + write-denied, source-not-in-allowlist rejected).
- [x] e2e / manual verification — three bind scenarios (legal read-write visible on host, illegal source rejected, read-only readable) for go, python, javascript, java, and csharp. All CI checks (5 language e2e suites, execd test, bwrap-smoke, ubuntu/windows smoke) pass.

# Breaking Changes
- [x] None — additive field on the request; existing `extra_writable` and all current callers are unaffected. The default allowlist changes from empty (reject-all) to `/workspace, /mnt, /media, /data`; the feature is unreleased.

# Checklist
- [x] Linked Issue or clearly described motivation
- [ ] Added/updated docs (if needed) — no user-facing docs page yet; spec updated
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Security impact considered — bind sources are allowlist-validated (read-only included); path traversal blocked via `filepath.Clean`
- [x] Backward compatibility considered

title: feat(charts): add hand-crafted values.schema.json to all three charts
body:
## Summary

Adds `values.schema.json` to `opensandbox-controller`, `opensandbox-server` and `opensandbox` charts, providing input validation at `helm install` / `helm upgrade` time.

Closes #1262

## Approach: hand-crafted (not auto-generated)

Auto-generators infer types from YAML values and produce incorrect results for edge cases. This PR uses an auto-generated base and manually corrects the known issues:

| Field | Auto-generated (wrong) | Hand-corrected | Reason |
|-------|----------------------|----------------|--------|
| `controller.kubeClient.qps` | `integer` | `number` | Go flag is `Float64` — accepts `12.5` |
| `opensandbox.global` | `null` | `anyOf: [object, null]` | See below |

### Why `global` needed two fixes

In YAML, a key with only comments as children has a `null` value:

```yaml
# BEFORE — global is null (comments are not a value)
global:
  # Example: imagePullSecrets:
  #   - name: my-registry-secret
```

This caused `helm lint` to fail even against the chart's own default values because the schema expected `object` but got `null`.

Two changes were needed:
1. **`opensandbox/values.yaml`**: `global:` → `global: {}` — makes the default an explicit empty object instead of null.
2. **Schema**: `anyOf: [object, null]` — allows null for users who install without passing any `global` override (Helm sends null when the key is not provided).

## Validated locally

```bash
# All three charts lint cleanly
helm lint kubernetes/charts/opensandbox-controller  # ✓
helm lint kubernetes/charts/opensandbox-server      # ✓
helm lint kubernetes/charts/opensandbox             # ✓

# Invalid values are rejected with a clear error
helm lint kubernetes/charts/opensandbox-controller \
  --set controller.replicaCount=abc
# [ERROR] at '/controller/replicaCount': got string, want integer ✓

# qps accepts floats (correct, it's Float64 in Go)
helm lint kubernetes/charts/opensandbox-controller \
  --set-json 'controller.kubeClient.qps=12.5'  # ✓ passes
```

## Notes

- No CI regeneration workflow — schemas are maintained manually alongside `values.yaml`.
- All integer probe fields (`initialDelaySeconds`, `periodSeconds`, etc.) are correctly typed as `integer`.
- `global.additionalProperties: true` allows arbitrary sub-chart global overrides without validation errors.

body:
## Summary

Add `values.schema.json` to `opensandbox-controller`, `opensandbox-server` and `opensandbox` charts to provide input validation at `helm install` / `helm upgrade` time.

## Why hand-crafted instead of auto-generated

Auto-generators (e.g. `helm-values-schema-json`) infer types from the YAML values and get several cases wrong:

| Field | Inferred (wrong) | Correct |
|-------|-----------------|---------|
| `global: {}` | `null` | `object` (with `additionalProperties: true`) |
| `controller.kubeClient.qps` | `integer` | `number` (the Go flag is `Float64`) |
| `controller.kubeClient.burst` | `integer` | `number` (same reason) |

A hand-crafted schema avoids these issues and does not require a CI regeneration step that would overwrite manual fixes.

## Expected benefits

```bash
# Type mismatch caught at install time
helm install opensandbox-controller . --set controller.replicaCount=abc
# Error: controller.replicaCount: Invalid type. Expected: integer, given: string

# Typo caught immediately
helm install opensandbox-controller . --set controller.logLevl=debug
# Error: additional properties 'logLevl' not allowed
```

## Scope

- `opensandbox-controller/values.schema.json`
- `opensandbox-server/values.schema.json`
- `opensandbox/values.schema.json`

No CI regeneration workflow — schemas are maintained manually alongside `values.yaml`.

title: chore(charts): add values.schema.json for Helm input validation
body:
## Summary

The charts have no `values.schema.json`, so `helm install` does not validate user-provided values. Invalid or mistyped values (wrong types, unexpected keys) are silently ignored until the chart fails to render or the pod fails to start.

Closes #1255

## Changes

- Adds `values.schema.json` to `opensandbox-controller`, `opensandbox-server` and `opensandbox` charts, generated from their respective `values.yaml` using the [`helm-schema`](https://github.com/losisin/helm-values-schema-json) plugin
- Adds `.github/workflows/helm-schema.yml` — triggers on PRs that touch `values.yaml`, regenerates the schema and auto-commits it

## How it works

The JSON Schema is derived directly from `values.yaml`. Helm validates user-provided `--set` flags and `-f values.yaml` overrides against it at install/upgrade time. Examples of what gets caught:

```bash
# Type mismatch — caught at install time instead of runtime
helm install opensandbox-controller . --set controller.replicaCount=abc
# Error: values don't meet the specifications of the schema(s) in the following chart(s):
#   opensandbox-controller: controller.replicaCount: Invalid type. Expected: integer, given: string

# Unknown key typo — caught immediately
helm install opensandbox-controller . --set controller.replicaCont=2
# Error: additional properties 'replicaCont' not allowed
```

## Verified locally

```bash
# All schemas are valid JSON
python3 -c "import json; json.load(open('values.schema.json'))"  # ✓ each chart

# helm lint passes with schemas present
helm lint kubernetes/charts/opensandbox-controller  # 1 chart(s) linted, 0 chart(s) failed
helm lint kubernetes/charts/opensandbox-server      # 1 chart(s) linted, 0 chart(s) failed
```

## Notes
- No breaking change — users who don't pass invalid values are unaffected.
- Consistent with Helm best practices for production charts.

title: chore(charts): add chart-testing (ct) CI for lint validation
body:
## Summary

Adds automated linting **and** template/schema validation for the Helm charts on every PR that touches a chart, closing the gap that let issues like #1233, #1235, #1236 and #1240 through.

Closes #1254

## What it does

`.github/workflows/chart-testing.yml` with two jobs:

1. **`ct lint`** — `helm lint` + `yamllint` over all three charts, run for the default values **and** each `ci/*-values.yaml` value set.
2. **`kubeconform`** — renders every chart (default + each `ci/` value set) and validates the produced manifests against **explicit, pinned Kubernetes schema versions** (`1.21.1`, `1.28.6`, `1.34.2`) — the charts' `kubeVersion` floor plus a mid and a recent release, mirroring `kubernetes-test.yml`.

## Values matrix (the important part)

A single default-values render misses the conditional branches — which is exactly where the referenced regressions lived. Each chart ships a `ci/` value set so those branches are the ones being linted and validated:

| Chart | Value set | Exercises |
|---|---|---|
| opensandbox-server | `ci/gateway-enabled-values.yaml` | Full ingress-gateway block (SA, ClusterRole/Binding, Deployment, Service) + secure-access signing (#1233/#1235/#1236) |
| opensandbox-server | `ci/volumes-and-env-values.yaml` | Non-empty `server.volumes`/`volumeMounts`/`env` (#1240, non-empty side) |
| opensandbox-controller | `ci/full-features-values.yaml` | Non-empty extra volumes/mounts, sidecars, init containers, env, pull secrets, scheduling, snapshot secrets |
| opensandbox-controller | `ci/minimal-values.yaml` | Disabled SA/RBAC/CRDs/probes/leader-election |
| opensandbox | `ci/full-values.yaml` | Both sub-charts' optional branches together |

## Notes

- `CustomResourceDefinition` is skipped in kubeconform (the CRDs are static definitions and the default schema set carries no CRD meta-schema); the workload manifests stay `-strict`.
- `--validate-maintainers=false` / `--check-version-increment=false` on `ct lint` (team email, no per-PR version bump).
- Strips trailing whitespace from `opensandbox-controller` / `opensandbox-server` `values.yaml`, which `yamllint` (run by `ct`) flags.

## Verified locally

- `ct lint` — all charts green, incl. every `ci/` value set.
- `kubeconform` — green across all three Kubernetes versions × all charts × every value set.

title: chore(charts): add helm-docs CI to auto-generate chart READMEs
body:
## Summary

The chart `values.yaml` files already follow the `helm-docs` comment convention (`# --` prefix on field descriptions), but `helm-docs` is not run in CI. This means chart READMEs are either missing or manually maintained and can drift from the actual values.

Closes #1253

## Changes

- Adds `.github/workflows/helm-docs.yml` — triggers on PRs that touch `values.yaml` or `Chart.yaml`, regenerates READMEs and auto-commits them
- Generates initial `README.md` for all three charts (`opensandbox-controller`, `opensandbox-server`, `opensandbox`)

## How it works

`helm-docs` reads `Chart.yaml` for metadata and the `# --` annotations in `values.yaml` to produce a Markdown table of all values. Since the charts already use this convention, no changes to `values.yaml` are needed — this works immediately.

Example of an existing annotation that gets picked up:
```yaml
# -- Tolerations for the controller pod
tolerations: []
```

## Notes
- No changes to chart logic or values — documentation only.
- READMEs are auto-committed on each PR by the workflow, so they stay in sync without manual effort.
- The `stefanzweifel/git-auto-commit-action` action is widely used for this pattern.

title: chore(charts): add values.schema.json to validate chart inputs
body:
## Summary

The charts have no `values.schema.json`, so `helm install` does not validate user-provided values. Invalid or mistyped values (wrong types, unexpected keys) are silently ignored until the chart fails to render or the pod fails to start.

## Proposed change

Add a `values.schema.json` to each chart, generated from `values.yaml` using a tool like [`helm-schema`](https://github.com/losisin/helm-values-schema-json):

```bash
helm plugin install https://github.com/losisin/helm-values-schema-json
helm schema -input kubernetes/charts/opensandbox-controller/values.yaml \
            -output kubernetes/charts/opensandbox-controller/values.schema.json
```

This can be run as part of CI (generate + commit, or fail if out of date).

## Benefits
- `helm install --set controller.replicaCount=abc` fails fast with a clear error instead of a broken deployment
- Type mismatches (string vs int, object vs array) caught at install time
- Consistent with Helm best practices for production charts

title: chore(charts): add chart-testing (ct) to CI for lint and template validation
body:
## Summary

The charts currently have no automated linting or template validation in CI (beyond what `helm package` catches at publish time). Several issues have been found in PRs that would have been caught earlier by `helm lint --strict` or `helm template`:

- Dead `networkPolicy` block in `values.yaml` (#1239)
- `volumeMounts: null` / `volumes: null` rendered when empty (#1240)  
- Missing fields in `ingress-gateway` Deployment (#1233, #1235, #1236)

## Proposed change

Add [`chart-testing`](https://github.com/helm/chart-testing) (`ct`) to the CI pipeline to run on every PR that modifies a chart:

```yaml
- name: Lint charts
  run: ct lint --chart-dirs kubernetes/charts --validate-maintainers=false

- name: Template charts  
  run: |
    for chart in kubernetes/charts/*/; do
      helm template test "$chart" | kubeval --strict
    done
```

## Benefits
- Catches schema errors, null values and dead config before merge
- `helm lint --strict` flags `volumeMounts: null` patterns
- `helm template` + `kubeval` validates rendered Kubernetes manifests
- Prevents the class of inconsistencies found in #1233–#1240

title: chore(charts): add helm-docs to CI to auto-generate chart READMEs
body:
## Summary

The chart `values.yaml` files already follow the `helm-docs` comment convention (`# --` prefix on field descriptions), but `helm-docs` is not run in CI. This means the chart READMEs are either missing or manually maintained and can drift from the actual values.

## Proposed change

Add `helm-docs` to the CI pipeline so READMEs for each chart are auto-generated and kept in sync on every PR that touches a chart.

```yaml
- name: Generate chart docs
  run: |
    helm-docs --chart-search-root kubernetes/charts/
```

Since the `# --` annotations are already in place, this would work immediately with no changes to `values.yaml`.

## Benefits
- Chart documentation is always up to date
- New fields added to `values.yaml` are automatically documented
- No manual README maintenance

title: Enhance Credential Vault with scoped placeholder substitutions

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
## Why do you need it?

Credential Vault currently focuses on injecting credentials into HTTP request headers. This covers common bearer, basic, API key, and custom header flows, but some real-world APIs require secrets in other request surfaces:

- OAuth-style token exchanges where `client_secret` is sent in a JSON or form request body.
- Legacy APIs where an API key appears in the query string.
- Path-scoped APIs where a credential-derived account or tenant identifier appears in the URL path.
- WebSocket protocols where a token is sent in the initial client-to-server text message instead of an HTTP header.

One concrete example is an SDK that obtains a short-lived access token by sending:

```json
{
  "appKey": "...",
  "appSecret": "..."
}
```

In this shape, the sandbox process still needs the real secret unless Credential Vault can replace a sandbox-visible placeholder in the request body before forwarding the request. Passing the real secret as an environment variable defeats the main Credential Vault goal: allowing tools and agents to use approved credentials without exposing plaintext credential material inside the sandbox.

## How could it be?

Add a narrow, opt-in placeholder substitution capability under `auth`. The caller would provide a fake placeholder value to the sandbox process, and Credential Proxy would replace that exact placeholder with the real credential only after the outbound request matches the binding.

Keeping substitutions under `auth` makes the binding's credential rendering behavior live in one place. Existing auth types can continue to describe header injection, while `auth.substitutions` becomes an optional supplement for request surfaces that cannot use headers.

Example:

```json
{
  "credentials": [
    {
      "name": "dingtalk-client-secret",
      "source": {
        "type": "inline",
        "value": "real-secret"
      }
    }
  ],
  "bindings": [
    {
      "name": "dingtalk-token-request",
      "match": {
        "schemes": ["https"],
        "hosts": ["api.dingtalk.com"],
        "methods": ["POST"],
        "paths": ["/v1.0/oauth2/accessToken"]
      },
      "auth": {
        "type": "passthrough",
        "substitutions": [
          {
            "credential": "dingtalk-client-secret",
            "placeholder": "__opensandbox_dingtalk_client_secret__",
            "in": ["body"]
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

The sandbox environment would contain only:

```bash
DINGTALK_CLIENT_SECRET="__opensandbox_dingtalk_client_secret__"
```

Credential Proxy would then replace the placeholder in the matched HTTPS request body before forwarding it upstream.

Suggested auth model:

- Keep existing `auth.type` values: `bearer`, `basic`, `apiKey`, and `customHeaders`.
- Add `auth.type: "passthrough"` for bindings that should match, audit, and optionally apply substitutions without injecting any header.
- Add optional `auth.substitutions[]` to every auth type so header injection and placeholder substitution can be composed.
- Avoid modeling text replacement as a mutually exclusive `auth.type`, because that would prevent combinations such as `customHeaders` plus body replacement.

Suggested MVP scope:

- Support literal, case-sensitive string replacement.
- Support explicit surfaces, for example `path`, `query`, `header`, and `body`.
- Default to no substitution unless `auth.substitutions[]` explicitly declares it.
- Require exact credential references and add both placeholder and resolved credential values to the redaction set.
- For `query`, URL-encode the replacement value.
- For `body`, materialize only bounded request bodies, update `Content-Length`, and skip compressed bodies.
- For `application/json`, JSON-string-escape the replacement value.
- For `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, URL-encode the replacement value.
- Skip `multipart/*` bodies in the MVP to avoid corrupting boundaries or binary parts.

Security constraints:

- Require HTTPS for substitutions that inject secret material.
- Continue using the real upstream destination derived from transparent proxy/TLS handling, not a user-controlled `Host` header, as the trust boundary.
- Keep existing egress policy validation: substitution bindings must only activate for hosts explicitly allowed by the sandbox egress policy.
- Treat missing placeholders as an auditable miss, not as a reason to expose the secret to the sandbox.
- Keep substitution surfaces narrow. If a substitution declares `in: ["body"]`, the same placeholder in path, query, or headers must pass through unchanged.

## Other related information

Header injection would remain the default and recommended path for APIs that support it. Placeholder substitution would cover APIs where the credential location is fixed by an existing SDK or protocol and cannot be moved into a header without modifying the client.

## What

Prepare a coordinated release of all five sandbox SDKs by bumping version metadata **and** fixing the default User-Agent version strings that had drifted behind released versions.

### Package versions

| SDK | File | Change |
|---|---|---|
| Go | `sdks/sandbox/go/constants.go` | `Version` 1.0.2 -> 1.0.4 |
| Python | `sdks/sandbox/python/pyproject.toml` | `fallback_version` 0.1.13 -> 0.1.14 |

| C# | `sdks/Directory.Build.props` | `OpenSandboxPackageVersion` 0.1.3 -> 0.1.4 |

### Default User-Agent versions (bug fix)

Each SDK hand-maintains its default User-Agent version string, and every non-Go SDK had drifted behind its released version (JS reported 0.1.8, C# 0.1.2, Python 0.1.13, Kotlin 1.0.15). These are now aligned with the versions being released, and a regression test was added per language asserting the default User-Agent matches the package version so future bumps cannot silently lag again.

Each SDK has real changes since its last release tag (endpoint cache, response extensions, CVE patches, Go sandbox pool). The Go `Version` constant was lagging the already-released `v1.0.3` tag, and the other SDKs' User-Agent strings were similarly stale — the client-reported version was wrong.

title: feat(execd): complete userns uid_mode support (SDK models + mode-aware probe)
body:
Follow-up to #1226, which added the opt-in `uid_mode: "userns"` isolation mode. Two gaps remain for full end-to-end support of userns mode.

## 1. Regenerate SDK models for `uid_mode`

The `uid_mode` field was added to `specs/execd-api.yaml` (`CreateIsolatedSessionRequest`) in #1226, but the generated SDK models across languages still only serialize `uid`, `gid`, and `idle_timeout_seconds`.

Affected SDKs (need regeneration/update of `CreateIsolatedSessionRequest`):
- Go
- TypeScript / JavaScript
- C#
- Kotlin / Java
- Python

Until regenerated, SDK users cannot request `userns` mode without dropping to raw HTTP.

## 2. Mode-aware isolation probe

`probeBwrapSmoke()` currently exercises only the setpriv path (pid/uts/ipc/cgroup namespaces, no user namespace). This has two consequences for userns:

- **False-negative availability**: in environments lacking `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`/`CAP_SETUID` where bwrap is not setuid (the bundled image builds with `-Dsupport_setuid=false`), the *only* mode that can work is `userns`. But the current smoke test fails, `Probe` marks isolation unavailable, and `main.go` never initializes `isolatedRunner` — so a valid userns request can never reach `buildArgv`.
- **No per-mode capability reporting**: `/v1/isolated/capabilities` reports a single global `available` flag; it cannot express "setpriv unavailable but userns available" (or vice versa).

### Proposed approach

- Add a userns smoke probe (`bwrap --unshare-user --unshare-pid ... -- true`) alongside the existing one.
- Track mode-specific availability (e.g. `SetprivAvailable`, `UsernsAvailable`) in `ProbeResult`/`Capabilities`.
- Mark isolation available if *either* mode works; reject a session request only if its specific mode is unsupported.

## Context

- Setuid-bwrap correctness fix (skip `--disable-userns`) already landed in #1226.
- `uid_mode` design and current wiring: `pkg/isolation/bwrap.go`, `pkg/isolation/probe.go`, `pkg/isolation/isolator.go`.

title: feat(chart/opensandbox-server): add standard scheduling fields to server and ingress-gateway Deployments
body:
## Summary

The `opensandbox-server` chart does not support several standard Kubernetes scheduling and security fields for either the server or the ingress-gateway Deployments, making it impossible to configure pod placement, security contexts or scheduling priority without forking the chart.

Notably, the sibling `opensandbox-controller` chart **already supports all these fields** — this PR aligns `opensandbox-server` with it.

Fixes #1241

## Missing fields (added for both server and ingress-gateway)

| Field | Typical use case |
|-------|-----------------|
| `nodeSelector` | Schedule pods on specific nodes or node pools |
| `podSecurityContext` | `runAsNonRoot`, `fsGroup`, `seccompProfile` at pod level |
| `containerSecurityContext` | `allowPrivilegeEscalation`, `capabilities`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem` |
| `podAnnotations` | Prometheus scraping, Vault agent injection, Datadog APM |
| `podLabels` | Extra labels for monitoring or selection |
| `priorityClassName` | Prevent eviction of critical control-plane components |
| `topologySpreadConstraints` | Spread replicas across availability zones for HA |

## Changes

**`values.yaml`** — add under `server` and `server.gateway`:
```yaml
server:
  nodeSelector: {}
  podSecurityContext: {}
  containerSecurityContext: {}
  podAnnotations: {}
  podLabels: {}
  priorityClassName: ""
  topologySpreadConstraints: []
  gateway:
    nodeSelector: {}
    podSecurityContext: {}
    containerSecurityContext: {}
    podAnnotations: {}
    podLabels: {}
    priorityClassName: ""
```

title: feat(chart/opensandbox-server): add standard scheduling fields to server and ingress-gateway Deployments
body:
## Summary

The `opensandbox-server` chart does not support several standard Kubernetes scheduling and security fields for either the server or the ingress-gateway Deployments. This makes it impossible to configure pod placement, security contexts or scheduling priority without forking the chart.

## Missing fields (both server and ingress-gateway)

| Field | Typical use case |
|-------|-----------------|
| `nodeSelector` | Schedule pods on specific nodes (e.g. labeled node pool) |
| `podSecurityContext` | Set `runAsNonRoot`, `fsGroup`, `seccompProfile` at pod level |
| `containerSecurityContext` | Set `allowPrivilegeEscalation`, `capabilities`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem` at container level |
| `podAnnotations` | Prometheus scraping, Vault agent injection, Datadog APM, etc. |
| `podLabels` | Extra labels for monitoring/selection beyond the chart defaults |
| `priorityClassName` | Ensure critical components are not evicted |
| `topologySpreadConstraints` | Spread replicas across zones for HA |

## Proposed fix

Add the fields to `values.yaml` with empty/nil defaults and render them in both `server.yaml` and `ingress-gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
server:
  nodeSelector: {}
  podSecurityContext: {}
  containerSecurityContext: {}
  podAnnotations: {}
  podLabels: {}
  priorityClassName: ""
  topologySpreadConstraints: []
  gateway:
    nodeSelector: {}
    podSecurityContext: {}
    containerSecurityContext: {}
    podAnnotations: {}
    podLabels: {}
    priorityClassName: ""
    topologySpreadConstraints: []
```

## Notes
- All defaults are empty/nil — no breaking change for existing deployments.
- This is the standard set of fields found in charts like `bitnami/*`, `kube-prometheus-stack`, etc.
- `opensandbox-controller` already implements most of these — aligning `opensandbox-server` would make the two charts consistent.

## Summary

The `opensandbox-controller` chart has a `networkPolicy` block in `values.yaml` that has been dead code since it was added. No template ever rendered it, so setting `networkPolicy.enabled: true` had no effect — users who tried to use it were silently ignored.

## Root cause

`values.yaml` declares:
```yaml
networkPolicy:
  enabled: false
  ingress: []
  egress: []
```

But no template in the chart references these values. The `deployment.yaml`, `clusterrole.yaml` and `serviceaccount.yaml` templates make no reference to them.

## Proposed fix

Remove the dead `networkPolicy` block from `values.yaml`.

Adding a NetworkPolicy template is not appropriate for the controller chart because:
1. The controller needs unrestricted access to the Kubernetes API server — a NetworkPolicy would likely cause breakage.
2. No other chart in this project uses NetworkPolicy.

title: feat(sdk/kotlin): publish Kotlin SDK to Maven Central
body:
## Summary

The OpenSandbox Kotlin SDK (`com.alibaba.opensandbox:sandbox`) is not published to Maven Central or any other public Maven repository. This forces users to either build from source or maintain a private mirror, which complicates CI/CD pipelines and onboarding.

## Current situation

The SDK source lives at `sdks/sandbox/kotlin/` and the `build.gradle.kts` already has the Vanniktech Maven Publish plugin configured with `publishToMavenCentral()` — so the infrastructure is in place, but no artifacts have been published yet.

```bash
# Searching Maven Central returns no results:
# https://search.maven.org/search?q=g:com.alibaba.opensandbox
```

## Impact

Without a public Maven artifact, users must:
1. Clone the repository and run `./gradlew publishToMavenLocal` before building their project, or
2. Set up a private Artifactory/Nexus mirror and push the JARs manually, or
3. Use a local file dependency — all of which are fragile in CI/CD environments.

## Proposed solution

Publish the following artifacts to Maven Central under `com.alibaba.opensandbox`:

| Artifact | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| `sandbox` | Main SDK module |
| `sandbox-api` | Generated OpenAPI client |
| `sandbox-bom` | Bill of Materials |

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>com.alibaba.opensandbox</groupId>
  <artifactId>sandbox</artifactId>
  <version>1.0.15</version>
</dependency>
```

The Gradle build already supports this via `publishToMavenCentral()` in `build.gradle.kts`. A GitHub Actions workflow publishing on tag (e.g. `java/sandbox/v*`) would complete the setup.

## Notes

- The publish plugin (`com.vanniktech.maven.publish`) and POM metadata are already configured.
- GPG signing is required for Maven Central — a signing key would need to be added to the repository secrets.
- Alternatively, publishing to GitHub Packages would be a lower-friction first step.
